questions.question_text: When a helium atom loses an electron, it becomes:
questions.explanation_short: Losing one electron leaves helium with a net +1 charge — a positive helium ion (He+), not an alpha particle.
questions.explanation_long: A neutral helium atom has 2 protons and 2 electrons. Removing one electron leaves 2 protons and 1 electron, giving a net charge of +1. This is a positive ion (He+), formed by ionisation, not by any nuclear change.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse ionisation (losing electrons, an atomic/chemical process) with an alpha particle, which is a bare helium nucleus (2p+2n, no electrons) ejected from a much heavier radioactive nucleus.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — an alpha particle is a helium nucleus (He2+) with zero electrons, produced by nuclear decay of a heavy element, not by simple ionisation of helium gas.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a proton is a single particle with no electron shell at all; He+ still has one electron.
explanation_options.c: Correct — removing one of helium's two electrons leaves a singly charged positive ion, He+.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — gaining, not losing, an electron would give a negative ion, and helium does not readily do this.

questions.question_text: Beta ray emitted by a radioactive substance is:
questions.option_a: An electron which was existing outside the nucleus.
questions.option_b: An electron which was existing inside the nucleus.
questions.option_c: An electron emitted by the nucleus as a result of the decay of neutron inside the nucleus.
questions.explanation_short: A beta particle is an electron created in the nucleus when a neutron decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino.
questions.explanation_long: The nucleus contains no electrons. In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. The electron is created at that moment and ejected at high speed as the beta ray, while the proton stays behind, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged. (The printed UHS key marks B, but electrons do not exist inside the nucleus, so C is the correct statement.)
questions.explanation_trick: No electrons live in the nucleus — a beta electron is manufactured there from a neutron.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — orbital electrons are not involved in beta decay; removing them is ionisation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — there are no electrons inside the nucleus to be emitted.
explanation_options.c: Correct — a neutron decays (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄) and the newly created electron leaves as the beta ray.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a pulse of electromagnetic radiation is a gamma ray, not a beta ray.

questions.question_text: An electric charge in uniform motion produces:
questions.explanation_short: A charge moving at constant velocity generates both an electric field (from its charge) and a magnetic field (from its motion/current).
questions.explanation_long: A stationary charge produces only an electric field. Once it moves, it constitutes a current, which by the Biot-Savart/Ampere laws also generates a magnetic field. So a uniformly moving charge is a source of both fields simultaneously.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: charge → electric field always; charge in motion → additionally a magnetic field. Motion never removes the electric field, it only adds the magnetic one.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — incomplete; motion also creates a magnetic field.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — incomplete; the charge itself still creates an electric field regardless of motion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — both fields coexist for a moving charge.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a charge always has at least an electric field.

questions.question_text: What is emitted by a hot metal filament in a cathode ray tube?
questions.explanation_short: A hot filament in a CRT undergoes thermionic emission, releasing electrons that form the cathode ray.
questions.explanation_long: Heating a metal filament gives surface electrons enough thermal energy to overcome the metal's work function and escape — this is thermionic emission. These freed electrons are then accelerated to form the cathode ray beam.
questions.explanation_trick: Cathode rays were historically shown (by J.J. Thomson) to be streams of electrons — the name 'cathode ray tube' is literally built on this fact.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — X-rays are produced when fast electrons are suddenly decelerated hitting a target, not by the heated filament itself.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — protons are far too massive to be thermionically emitted from a metal surface under normal heating.
explanation_options.c: Correct — thermionic emission from the heated filament releases electrons.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — photons may be emitted as heat/light from the hot filament, but the defining 'cathode ray' particle is the electron.

questions.question_text: If the mass of the bob of a pendulum is doubled its time period is:
questions.explanation_short: The period of a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(l/g), does not depend on the bob's mass, so doubling the mass leaves T unchanged.
questions.explanation_long: For small oscillations, a pendulum's period depends only on its length l and gravitational acceleration g via T = 2π√(l/g). Mass cancels out of the equation of motion because both the restoring force (gravity) and inertia scale with mass identically.
questions.explanation_trick: A classic MDCAT trap — any question changing the bob's mass while asking about period should immediately signal 'no change,' since mass doesn't appear in the pendulum period formula.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — would be true only if mass affected T, which it does not.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — same reasoning; mass has no role in T.
explanation_options.c: Correct — T is independent of the bob's mass.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — mass changes don't affect T at all, let alone by a factor of four.

questions.question_text: The centre of Newton rings is dark due to:
questions.explanation_short: The dark centre of Newton's rings results from destructive interference between light reflected at the two nearly touching surfaces.
questions.explanation_long: At the exact point of contact between the lens and glass plate, the path difference between the two reflected rays (plus the extra half-wavelength phase shift from reflection at the denser medium) satisfies the condition for destructive interference, cancelling the reflected light and producing a dark spot.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the phase-shift-on-reflection detail: it's what makes the centre dark (destructive) rather than bright, unlike a naive path-difference-only analysis.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — polarization involves the orientation of light's electric field vector, unrelated to this ring pattern.
explanation_options.b: Correct — destructive interference at near-zero path difference (plus the reflection phase shift) darkens the centre.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — constructive interference would produce a bright, not dark, centre.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — reflection alone doesn't explain darkness; it's the interference between two reflected beams that matters.

questions.question_text: Which one is most stable element on the basis of binding energy?
questions.explanation_short: Iron-56 sits near the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, making it the most stable of the listed nuclei.
questions.explanation_long: Binding energy per nucleon rises from light elements, peaks around iron (Z≈26, A≈56), then slowly falls for heavier elements. Fe has the highest binding energy per nucleon among Sn, Ba, Kr, and Fe, meaning it is the most tightly bound/stable nucleus of the four.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a nuclear stability question lists iron among the options, it's almost always the answer — remember 'iron sits at the peak of the curve.'

explanation_options.a: Wrong — tin (Sn) is heavier than iron and lies past the binding energy peak, so it's less tightly bound per nucleon.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — barium is also past the peak, less stable per nucleon than iron.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — krypton is lighter and to the left of the peak, with lower binding energy per nucleon than iron.
explanation_options.d: Correct — iron is essentially at the maximum of the binding energy curve, the most stable nucleus among common elements.

questions.question_text: Resistance in RC circuit of time constant 2 seconds is 1000 Ohms. What is value of C in the circuit?
questions.explanation_short: Time constant tau = RC, so C = tau/R = 2/1000 = 0.002 F = 2000 uF.
questions.explanation_long: For an RC circuit, the time constant is tau = RC. Given tau = 2 s and R = 1000 Ohm, C = tau/R = 2/1000 = 0.002 F = 2000 uF. The printed UHS key marks C (200 μF), but that gives τ = RC = 0.2 s, not 2 s, so D is kept.
questions.explanation_trick: The time constant formula tau = RC rearranges directly to C = tau/R -- always double-check unit prefixes (uF vs F) when the arithmetic gives a suspiciously round number.

explanation_options.a: Wrong -- 2 uF would require R = 1 MOhm, not 1000 Ohm, for tau = 2 s.
explanation_options.b: Wrong -- 20 uF gives tau = 20e-6*1000 = 0.02 s, far short of 2 s.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- 200 uF gives tau = 200e-6*1000 = 0.2 s, not 2 s.
explanation_options.d: Correct -- by direct calculation C = tau/R = 2/1000 = 2000 uF.

questions.question_text: The Lenz’s law refers to induced __________
questions.explanation_short: Lenz's law describes the direction of the induced current (and hence induced emf) that opposes the change in magnetic flux causing it.
questions.explanation_long: Faraday's law gives the magnitude of induced emf; Lenz's law specifically addresses the direction — the induced current always flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produced it, conserving energy.
questions.explanation_trick: Lenz's law is often stated as being 'about currents' since the minus sign in Faraday's law (which IS Lenz's law in equation form) predicts the direction of induced current, which then drives the induced emf.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — emf's existence/magnitude is Faraday's law; Lenz's law specifically concerns direction of the resulting current.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Lenz's law is not primarily about resistance.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'shear' is unrelated to electromagnetic induction.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Lenz's law gives the direction of induced currents opposing the flux change.

questions.question_text: In which of the following, output is similar to NAND gate if input A=0 and input B=1.
questions.explanation_short: With A=0, B=1: NAND output=1; XOR output=1 (matches); XNOR output=0; NOR output=0 — so XOR (C) matches NAND here.
questions.explanation_long: NAND(0,1) = NOT(0 AND 1) = NOT(0) = 1. XOR(0,1) = 1 (inputs differ). XNOR(0,1) = 0. NOR(0,1) = 0. Only XOR gives the same output (1) as NAND for this specific input combination.
questions.explanation_trick: This only holds for THIS particular input pair — XOR and NAND are different gates overall; always check the truth table for the specific inputs given, not the general gate behavior.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — NOR(0,1) = 0, but NAND(0,1) = 1; they don't match here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — XNOR(0,1) = 0, doesn't match NAND's output of 1.
explanation_options.c: Correct — XOR(0,1) = 1, matching NAND(0,1) = 1 for this input pair.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only XOR matches, not XNOR, so 'both' is incorrect.

questions.question_text: For atomic hydrogen spectrum, which of the following series lies in visible region of electromagnetic spectrum?
questions.explanation_short: The Balmer series, with transitions ending at n=2, produces spectral lines in the visible range for hydrogen.
questions.explanation_long: Hydrogen's spectral series are named by their final energy level: Lyman (n=1, UV), Balmer (n=2, visible), Paschen (n=3, infrared). Only Balmer series wavelengths fall within the visible light range (~400-700 nm).
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize the order: Lyman=UV, Balmer=Visible, Paschen=IR — 'Balmer sees the light' is a handy way to remember it's the visible one.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet region.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Paschen series lies in the infrared region.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Balmer series transitions (to n=2) emit visible wavelengths.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'Bohr series' is not a standard named spectral series.

questions.question_text: __________ are the particles that experience strong nuclear force.
questions.explanation_short: Neutrons, as baryons made of quarks, experience the strong nuclear force, unlike leptons such as electrons, muons, and neutrinos.
questions.explanation_long: The strong nuclear force acts on particles built from quarks (hadrons), which includes protons and neutrons. Electrons, muons, and neutrinos are leptons and do not interact via the strong force at all.
questions.explanation_trick: A quick filter: if a particle is a lepton (electron, muon, neutrino, tau and their neutrinos), it never feels the strong force — only quark-based hadrons like neutrons and protons do.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — electrons are leptons, immune to the strong force.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — muons are also leptons, no strong interaction.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — neutrinos are leptons and barely interact with anything, certainly not via the strong force.
explanation_options.d: Correct — neutrons are hadrons (quark-based) and do experience the strong nuclear force.

questions.question_text: The vertical velocity of ball thrown upward __________ with time.
questions.explanation_short: For a ball thrown upward, gravity decelerates it uniformly, so its vertical velocity decreases linearly with time, reaching zero at the peak.
questions.explanation_long: Under constant gravitational deceleration, v(t) = v0 - gt is a straight-line (linear) relationship between velocity and time. Velocity decreases steadily until it hits zero at maximum height, then becomes negative (falling) -- this is linear decay, not doubling or parabolic decay. The printed UHS key marks C ('Doubles'), which contradicts v = u − gt, so A is kept.
questions.explanation_trick: It's the height-vs-time graph that is parabolic; the velocity-vs-time graph under constant acceleration is always linear.

explanation_options.a: Correct -- by standard kinematics (v = v0 - gt), velocity decreases linearly with time.
explanation_options.b: Wrong -- velocity clearly changes (decreases) due to gravity; it doesn't stay constant.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- velocity does not 'double' during upward motion; it steadily decreases.
explanation_options.d: Wrong -- the velocity-time relationship is linear, not parabolic (height-time is the parabolic one).

questions.question_text: The force required to bend the normally straight path of a particle into a circular path is called __________ force.
questions.explanation_short: The inward force that curves a particle's straight-line path into a circle is the centripetal force.
questions.explanation_long: Centripetal force always points toward the centre of the circular path and is what continuously redirects a moving particle's velocity, bending its otherwise straight trajectory into a circle. Its magnitude is F = mv²/r.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse with 'centrifugal force,' which is a fictitious outward-feeling force in a rotating (non-inertial) reference frame — the real, physical force causing curved motion is centripetal.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not a recognized force term.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — not a standard physics term for this.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — centrifugal force is the apparent outward force felt in a rotating frame, not the real cause of circular motion.
explanation_options.d: Correct — centripetal force is the real inward force causing circular motion.

questions.question_text: A disc at rest without slipping, rolls down a hill of height (3 x 9.8) m. What is its speed in m/sec when it reaches at the bottom?
questions.explanation_short: For a disc rolling without slipping from height h, v = sqrt(4gh/3); with h=29.4 m, v is about 19.6 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: Energy conservation for a rolling disc: mgh = (1/2)mv^2 + (1/2)Iw^2, with I=(1/2)mr^2 and w=v/r, gives mgh = (3/4)mv^2, so v = sqrt(4gh/3). With h = 3x9.8 = 29.4 m and g=9.8: v = sqrt(4x9.8x29.4/3) = sqrt(384.16) ~ 19.6 m/s. The printed UHS key marks A (11.4 m/s), which does not satisfy energy conservation, so B is kept.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the 4/3 factor for a solid disc rolling down a height -- it's less than the frictionless free-fall v=sqrt(2gh) because some energy goes into rotational KE.

explanation_options.a: Wrong -- 11.4 m/s doesn't match the rolling-disc energy equation v=sqrt(4gh/3).
explanation_options.b: Correct -- the rolling-without-slipping energy equation gives v=sqrt(4gh/3) is about 19.6 m/s.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- this would overshoot even simple free-fall from this height.
explanation_options.d: Wrong -- this equals just sqrt(gh)-scale, too small for the actual rolling speed.

questions.question_text: Tuning of the radio is the best example of electrical __________
questions.explanation_short: Tuning a radio to a station means adjusting the receiver's LC circuit to electrically resonate at that station's broadcast frequency.
questions.explanation_long: A radio's tuning circuit contains an inductor and capacitor whose resonant frequency (f = 1/(2π√LC)) is adjusted (usually by varying C) to match the desired station's frequency, sharply amplifying that signal while rejecting others — a textbook case of electrical resonance.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever 'tuning,' 'selecting a specific frequency,' or 'sharp peak response' comes up in physics MCQs, think resonance.

explanation_options.a: Correct — tuning matches the circuit's natural (resonant) frequency to the station's frequency.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — resistance alone doesn't provide frequency selectivity.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — current is just the circuit's response, not the phenomenon being exploited for tuning.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — resonance is the well-established answer.

questions.question_text: A standing wave pattern is formed when the length of string is an integral multiple of __________ wavelength.
questions.explanation_short: Standing waves on a string form when the string length equals an integer number of half-wavelengths.
questions.explanation_long: For a string fixed at both ends, allowed standing wave modes require nodes at both ends, which happens when L = n(λ/2) for integer n. This is why the length must be a multiple of half the wavelength, not the full wavelength.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: string standing waves use half-wavelength segments (nodes at the ends); open-open or closed-closed pipes follow the same half-wavelength rule, while closed-open pipes use quarter-wavelength segments.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not the standard fundamental unit used in this condition.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — using full wavelength would misplace the node/antinode pattern for a string fixed at both ends.
explanation_options.c: Correct — L = n×(λ/2) is the standing wave condition for a string.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — not the standard relation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following lights travels the fastest in optical fibres?
questions.explanation_short: Longer-wavelength invisible infra-red light experiences less dispersion/attenuation and effectively travels fastest through optical fibre compared to visible or UV light.
questions.explanation_long: In optical fibres, the refractive index (and hence signal delay) is wavelength-dependent — chromatic dispersion. Longer wavelengths like infra-red travel with less material dispersion loss, and telecom fibres are specifically designed around infra-red wavelengths (~1310/1550 nm) for minimal signal delay and attenuation.
questions.explanation_trick: Real optical fibre communication systems use infra-red light for this exact reason — a fact worth remembering from applied physics/telecom sections.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — visible light is more prone to dispersion effects in the fibre medium than the chosen infra-red band.
explanation_options.b: Correct — practical/telecom fibre optics rely on infra-red for optimal speed and lowest loss.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — ultraviolet light is even more strongly absorbed/scattered in typical fibre material.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'ordinary light' is not a specific, well-defined wavelength for this comparison.

questions.question_text: The algebraic sum of potential changes in a closed circuit is zero is Kirchhoff’s __________ rule.
questions.explanation_short: Kirchhoff's Second (Voltage) Law states that the algebraic sum of all potential changes around any closed loop equals zero.
questions.explanation_long: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (his second rule) is a statement of energy conservation: summing all EMFs and IR drops around a closed loop always returns to zero, since you return to the same potential where you started.
questions.explanation_trick: Pair the two Kirchhoff rules: First (current) law = conservation of charge at a junction; Second (voltage) law = conservation of energy around a loop.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Kirchhoff's First (current) Law is about current conservation at junctions, not potential changes in a loop.
explanation_options.b: Correct — this is Kirchhoff's Second (Voltage) Law.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — there's no standard 'third' Kirchhoff rule referenced this way.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is a well-established named law (the second rule).

questions.question_text: In LED when an electron combines with a __________ during forward bias conduction, a photon of visible light is emitted.
questions.explanation_short: In an LED under forward bias, an electron recombining with a hole releases its excess energy as a photon of visible light.
questions.explanation_long: Forward biasing an LED's p-n junction drives electrons and holes toward the junction where they recombine. In direct-bandgap semiconductor materials used for LEDs, this recombination energy is released as a photon whose wavelength (colour) depends on the bandgap.
questions.explanation_trick: LED light emission = electron-hole recombination releasing photon energy ≈ bandgap energy; this is the reverse process of what happens in a solar cell (photon absorption creating electron-hole pairs).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — high voltage is not itself a particle the electron combines with.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a photon is the emitted result, not something the electron recombines with.
explanation_options.c: Correct — electron-hole recombination is the mechanism producing the emitted photon.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a positron is antimatter, not the vacancy in the semiconductor's valence band (that's a hole).

questions.question_text: For photons of energy greater than 1.02 MeV the probability of pair production occurrence __________ as the energy increases.
questions.explanation_short: Above the 1.02 MeV threshold, pair production probability rises (increases) as photon energy increases further.
questions.explanation_long: Pair production (photon → electron-positron pair) requires a minimum photon energy of 1.02 MeV (2×electron rest mass energy). Beyond this threshold, as photon energy increases, the cross-section (probability) for pair production generally increases, eventually dominating over Compton scattering and photoelectric absorption at high energies.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the three photon-interaction regimes with energy: photoelectric effect dominates at low energy, Compton scattering at intermediate energy, and pair production (needing ≥1.02 MeV) dominates at high energy — and its likelihood grows with energy above threshold.

explanation_options.a: Correct — pair production probability increases with photon energy above the 1.02 MeV threshold.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — it doesn't vanish; it becomes more likely, not less.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — no such halving occurs; the trend is an increase.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the probability does change (increases) with energy.

questions.question_text: The neutron is assumed to be made of
questions.option_a: One up quark and two down quarks.
questions.option_b: Two up quarks and two down quarks.
questions.option_c: Two up quarks and one down quark.
questions.option_d: One up quark and one down quark.
questions.explanation_short: A neutron is composed of one up quark and two down quarks (udd), giving it zero net charge.
questions.explanation_long: Quark charges: up quark = +2/3e, down quark = -1/3e. A neutron (udd) has charge = 2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0, matching its known neutral charge. A proton, by contrast, is uud with charge +1.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember 'uud=proton (+1), udd=neutron (0)' — swapping the count of up vs down quarks is the classic distractor here.

explanation_options.a: Correct — one up quark + two down quarks (udd) gives zero net charge, matching the neutron.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — two up + two down would be four quarks total, not a valid baryon (baryons have exactly three quarks).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — two up + one down (uud) is a proton's composition (+1 charge), not a neutron.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only two quarks isn't a valid baryon; baryons always have three quarks.

questions.question_text: An __________ missile is called a ballistic missile.
questions.explanation_short: A ballistic missile is unpowered and unguided during most of its flight, following a free-fall/projectile trajectory after initial launch.
questions.explanation_long: A ballistic missile is powered only during a brief initial boost phase; for the majority of its flight (midcourse and re-entry), it follows a ballistic (unpowered, essentially unguided) trajectory determined by gravity and initial launch conditions, unlike a cruise missile which is continuously powered and guided.
questions.explanation_trick: Contrast with 'cruise missile' — powered and guided throughout flight, using continuous thrust and active guidance, the opposite of a ballistic missile's coast-and-fall trajectory.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this describes something like a guided glide bomb, not the classic ballistic missile definition used here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — mismatched: ballistic missiles are essentially unguided during flight, and this option also misdescribes power.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this describes a cruise missile, not a ballistic missile.
explanation_options.d: Correct — after brief initial powered boost, the ballistic missile is essentially unpowered and unguided in flight.

questions.question_text: Two cylinders of equal mass are made from same material. The one with the larger diameter accelerates __________ the other under the action of same torque.
questions.explanation_short: With the same mass and torque, the larger-diameter cylinder has greater moment of inertia (I proportional to r^2), so by alpha=torque/I it accelerates slower, not faster.
questions.explanation_long: For a solid cylinder, I = (1/2)mr^2. Two cylinders of equal mass but different diameters have different r, so the larger-diameter one has a larger I. Under the same applied torque, angular acceleration alpha = torque/I is therefore smaller for the larger cylinder -- it accelerates more slowly than the smaller one. The printed UHS key marks A ('Faster than'), which contradicts α = τ/I, so B is kept.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever comparing angular acceleration under equal torque, remember bigger radius means bigger I means smaller alpha -- inversely proportional, easy to flip by mistake.

explanation_options.a: Wrong -- with a larger I, the bigger cylinder should accelerate slower, not faster.
explanation_options.b: Correct -- by rotational dynamics (I proportional to r^2, alpha=torque/I), the larger cylinder accelerates more slowly.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- different radii under the same torque give different I and hence different alpha, not equal acceleration.
explanation_options.d: Not applicable -- option B is the physically correct outcome.

questions.question_text: The angular frequency of simple pendulum is directly proportional to __________
questions.explanation_short: Angular frequency of a simple pendulum, ω = √(g/l), is proportional to 1/√l (i.e., inversely proportional to the square root of length).
questions.explanation_long: From T = 2π√(l/g), angular frequency ω = 2π/T = √(g/l). This shows ω is proportional to 1/√l — longer pendulums swing with lower angular frequency.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse period (T ∝ √l, increases with length) with angular frequency (ω ∝ 1/√l, decreases with length) — they're inversely related.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ω is not directly proportional to l; it decreases as l increases.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would be proportional to 1/l, not 1/√l.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this represents proportional to √l, the opposite dependence of ω.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ω ∝ 1/√l, i.e., proportional to √(1/l).

questions.question_text: Two waves of slightly different frequencies and traveling in same direction produce ________
questions.explanation_short: Two waves of slightly different frequencies travelling together produce beats — a periodic rise and fall in amplitude.
questions.explanation_long: When two waves of close but unequal frequencies superpose, their phase relationship drifts slowly, causing constructive and destructive interference to alternate at a beat frequency equal to the difference of the two frequencies — heard as a throbbing/pulsing sound.
questions.explanation_trick: Key distinguishing detail: beats require slightly DIFFERENT frequencies; interference/stationary waves typically involve identical frequencies. The word 'slightly different frequencies' is the giveaway for 'beats.'

explanation_options.a: Wrong — general interference doesn't specifically describe the periodic amplitude variation from close-but-different frequencies.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — polarization concerns transverse wave orientation, unrelated to frequency difference effects.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — stationary (standing) waves typically arise from two identical-frequency waves travelling in opposite directions.
explanation_options.d: Correct — beats are the direct result of superposing two close-frequency waves travelling in the same direction.

questions.question_text: A single mode step index fibre has core of about __________ μm diameter
questions.explanation_short: A single-mode step-index optical fibre has a very small core, typically around 5-10 μm in diameter, to support only one propagation mode.
questions.explanation_long: Single-mode fibres need a core diameter comparable to the wavelength of light used (~1 μm range) to restrict propagation to a single mode, typically around 5-10 μm — much smaller than multimode fibres (50-1000 μm core).
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: single-mode = tiny core (~5-10 μm) for one light path; multimode = larger core (50+ μm) allowing multiple light paths/modes, which causes modal dispersion.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — that large range describes multimode fibre cores, not single-mode.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 50 μm is still in the multimode fibre range.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 30 μm is still too large for typical single-mode operation.
explanation_options.d: Correct — roughly 5 μm is representative of a single-mode fibre core diameter.

questions.question_text: A 5 Ohm resistor is indicated by a single __________ color band around its body.
questions.explanation_short: By resistor colour-code convention, a single-band 5 Ω resistor uses green as its distinctive marking in this context.
questions.explanation_long: Standard resistor colour codes assign specific values to colours (black=0,brown=1,red=2,orange=3,yellow=4,green=5,...). A resistor value directly tied to '5' uses green in the relevant digit position, matching the stored answer.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize the resistor colour code mnemonic 'Black Brown Red Orange Yellow Green Blue Violet Grey White' (0-9) — green always maps to 5.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — red corresponds to 2 in the standard code, not 5.
explanation_options.b: Correct — green corresponds to the digit 5 in the standard resistor colour code.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — blue corresponds to 6, not 5.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — brown corresponds to 1, not 5.

questions.question_text: Practically __________ current flows in a reverse biased p-n junction.
questions.explanation_short: In reverse bias the depletion region widens, so practically no current flows (only a tiny leakage current of microamperes).
questions.explanation_long: Reverse biasing a p-n junction pulls majority carriers away from the junction and widens the depletion region, so the junction blocks conduction. Only a very small leakage current carried by minority carriers flows — typically microamperes or less — which is why it is described as practically no current. (The printed UHS key marks D, but 'No current' and 'a few milliamperes' contradict each other and milliamperes is far too large for reverse leakage.)
questions.explanation_trick: Forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks: 'practically no current' is the standard phrase for reverse bias.

explanation_options.a: Correct — apart from a negligible minority-carrier leakage, no current flows.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a very large current flows only in forward bias or at breakdown.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — reverse leakage is of the order of microamperes, not milliamperes.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the two statements contradict each other, so they cannot both be right.

questions.question_text: Cesium coated oxidized silver emits electrons for __________ light.
questions.explanation_short: Cesium-coated oxidized silver has a very low work function, allowing it to emit photoelectrons even from low-energy infrared light.
questions.explanation_long: Photoemissive materials like cesium oxide on silver (Cs2O-Ag, used in older phototubes) have an unusually low work function, letting them respond to photons of even infrared wavelengths, which is why they're used in infrared-sensitive photocells and older night-vision devices.
questions.explanation_trick: This material is specifically famous in photoelectric-effect physics questions for its extremely low work function, well below what's needed for even visible or UV materials — a distinguishing exam fact.

explanation_options.a: Correct — its very low work function allows electron emission even under infrared illumination.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — ultraviolet light has more than enough energy for most materials; this option undersells the special low-work-function property.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — while visible light would also work, the notable/testable property is its response to the lower-energy infrared.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — green is a specific visible wavelength, not the distinguishing feature being tested.

questions.question_text: The cobalt is absorbed by
questions.explanation_short: Cobalt, chemically similar to iron, tends to be absorbed and stored mainly in the liver among body organs.
questions.explanation_long: In terms of biodistribution, cobalt (and radioactive cobalt-60 in medical/industrial contexts) is predominantly taken up and retained by the liver, unlike iodine (thyroid) or strontium/radium (bones).
questions.explanation_trick: Match each element to its characteristic target organ: iodine → thyroid, strontium/calcium/radium → bones, cobalt → liver — a common set of matching questions in radiation biology.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — bones are the target organ for elements like strontium and calcium, not cobalt.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — skin is not the primary site of cobalt accumulation.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the liver is the primary site of cobalt uptake and storage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the thyroid gland specifically concentrates iodine, not cobalt.

questions.question_text: In a step-down transformer the output current __________
questions.explanation_short: A step-down transformer reduces voltage but proportionally increases current at the output (conserving power, ideally).
questions.explanation_long: Ideal transformers conserve power: Vp·Ip = Vs·Is. In a step-down transformer, Vs < Vp, which means Is > Ip — the output current is increased even as the voltage decreases.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the trade-off: step-down transformers trade lower voltage for higher current, and step-up transformers trade higher voltage for lower current — power stays (ideally) the same.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — output current increases, it isn't reduced, in a step-down transformer.
explanation_options.b: Correct — lower output voltage is compensated by higher output current to conserve power.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — current changes because voltage changes and power is conserved; it does not remain the same.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the current does change (increases).

questions.question_text: Force in terms of base units is expressed as
questions.explanation_short: Force = mass × acceleration, with acceleration in m/s², so force's base SI units are kg·m·s⁻².
questions.explanation_long: Newton's second law F=ma gives units of [mass][length][time]⁻² = kg·m·s⁻² (this combination is also named the Newton, N).
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize a handful of derived-unit combinations directly in base units: Force = kg·m·s⁻², Energy/Work = kg·m²·s⁻², Power = kg·m²·s⁻³ — useful shortcuts across multiple questions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — kg·m·s⁻² is the base-unit expression for force (the Newton).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — kg·m²·s⁻² is the unit of energy/work (Joule), not force.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — kg·m²·s⁻³ is the unit of power (Watt), not force.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — option A is correct, so 'none of these' doesn't apply.

aliases: Force in terms of base units is expressed as
kg ms-2.

questions.question_text: 100 joules work has been done by an agency in 10 seconds. What is power of agency?
questions.explanation_short: Power = Work/time = 100 J / 10 s = 10 watts.
questions.explanation_long: Power is defined as the rate of doing work: P = W/t. Substituting the given values, P = 100/10 = 10 W.
questions.explanation_trick: Simple division questions like this are quick points — just remember P=W/t and don't mix up which value is divided by which.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1000 W would result from dividing incorrectly (multiplying instead of dividing).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 100 W ignores the division by time entirely.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 100 J ÷ 10 s = 10 W.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0.10 W is off by two orders of magnitude from the correct calculation.

questions.question_text: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and is directed towards mean position in __________ motion.
questions.explanation_short: Simple harmonic motion is defined by acceleration proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean (equilibrium) position.
questions.explanation_long: SHM's defining equation is a = -ω²x, meaning acceleration is proportional to displacement x, with the negative sign showing it always points back toward the equilibrium (mean) position — the restoring-force condition for SHM.
questions.explanation_trick: This exact phrase ('acceleration proportional to displacement, directed towards mean position') is the textbook definition of SHM — recognize it verbatim in exam questions.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — plain gravitational motion (free fall) has constant acceleration, not one proportional to displacement.
explanation_options.b: Correct — this is precisely the defining condition of simple harmonic motion.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — uniform motion has zero acceleration by definition.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — projectile motion has constant (gravitational) acceleration, not displacement-proportional acceleration.

questions.question_text: In gases, the speed of sound is inversely proportional to __________ of the density when other factors are same.
questions.explanation_short: Speed of sound in a gas, v=sqrt(gamma*P/rho), varies inversely with the square root of density when pressure/other factors are held constant.
questions.explanation_long: From the Newton-Laplace formula for sound speed in gas, v = sqrt(gamma*P/rho), for fixed gamma and P, v is proportional to 1/sqrt(rho) -- speed is inversely proportional to the square root of density.
questions.explanation_trick: The formula v=sqrt(gamma*P/rho) should be memorized directly -- its square-root form makes the exponent for density always 1/2, so watch for options trying to trick you into cube/other powers.

explanation_options.a: Correct -- by v proportional to 1/sqrt(rho), square root is the correct dependence.
explanation_options.b: Wrong -- this would be a stronger dependence than the actual square-root relationship.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- the standard Newton-Laplace relation gives an inverse square-root dependence, not a third-power one.
explanation_options.d: Wrong -- not the standard relationship; the correct dependence uses a square root, not a cube root.

questions.question_text: A watch maker uses __________ to repair the watches.
questions.explanation_short: A watchmaker uses a convex lens (loupe) to magnify tiny watch components for close inspection and repair.
questions.explanation_long: A convex (converging) lens held close to the eye produces a magnified virtual image of small objects, which is exactly what a watchmaker's eyepiece loupe uses to see fine mechanical parts clearly.
questions.explanation_trick: Convex lens = magnifier for near objects (watchmaker's loupe, magnifying glass); concave lens spreads light and is used for correcting myopia, not magnification.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a telescope is for viewing distant objects, not tiny nearby components.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — convex mirrors give reduced, diminished images, not the needed magnification.
explanation_options.c: Correct — a convex lens provides the magnified view needed for fine watch repair work.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a concave lens diverges light and produces a reduced, not magnified, image.

questions.question_text: A 2m long pipe is open at both ends. What is its harmonic frequency?
questions.explanation_short: For a pipe open at both ends the fundamental frequency is f₁ = v/2L = 340/(2 × 2) = 85 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: An open-open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so the fundamental mode fits half a wavelength into the pipe: λ = 2L = 4 m. With the speed of sound v ≈ 340 m/s, f₁ = v/λ = 340/4 = 85 Hz. Higher harmonics are whole-number multiples (170 Hz, 255 Hz, …).
questions.explanation_trick: Open-open pipe: f₁ = v/2L. Closed at one end: f₁ = v/4L.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 42.5 Hz is v/4L, the fundamental of a pipe closed at one end.
explanation_options.b: Correct — f₁ = v/2L = 340/4 = 85 Hz.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 220 Hz is not a harmonic of 85 Hz for this pipe.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 85 Hz is listed, so 'None of these' does not apply.

questions.question_text: A wire has resistance 100 Ohm at 0 °C and 200 Ohm at 100 °C. What is its temperature coefficient in K⁻¹?
questions.explanation_long: The temperature coefficient of resistance is defined by R_T = R₀(1 + αΔT), so α = (R_T − R₀)/(R₀ΔT). Here R₀ = 100 Ω at 0 °C, R_T = 200 Ω at 100 °C, ΔT = 100 K: α = 100/(100 × 100) = 0.01 K⁻¹. The resistance rises, so α is positive. (The printed UHS key marks D, 1/273, which is the expansion coefficient of an ideal gas, not this wire's coefficient.)
questions.explanation_trick: Always divide the change in resistance by the resistance at 0 °C and by the temperature change.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the resistance increases, so α must be positive.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — negative, and 1/273 belongs to gas expansion, not this wire.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 1/273 K⁻¹ is the ideal-gas expansion coefficient; the data give 0.01 K⁻¹.

aliases: A wire has resistance 100 Ohm at 0 oC and 200 Ohm at 100 oC. What is its temperature coefficient in K-1?

questions.question_text: The net magnetic field created by the electrons within an atom is due to the field created by their __________ motion.
questions.explanation_short: An atom's magnetic field is the combined effect of its electrons' orbital motion and their spin.
questions.explanation_long: Each electron behaves as a tiny current loop because it orbits the nucleus (orbital magnetic moment) and also has an intrinsic spin magnetic moment. The net field of the atom is the vector sum of these orbital and spin contributions; when they cancel the substance is diamagnetic, when they do not it is para- or ferromagnetic. (The printed UHS key marks D, 'Orbital × spin', but the contributions add — they are not multiplied.)
questions.explanation_trick: Magnetism of atoms = orbital + spin, added together.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — orbital motion is only one of the two sources.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — spin is only one of the two sources.
explanation_options.c: Correct — both orbital motion and spin produce the atom's net magnetic field.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the two contributions add; a product of them has no physical meaning.

questions.question_text: At high temperature, the proportion of __________ wavelength radiation increase.
questions.explanation_short: As a body gets hotter, the peak of its radiation shifts to shorter wavelengths (Wien's law), so the proportion of short-wavelength radiation increases.
questions.explanation_long: Wien's displacement law, λ_max T = constant, says that raising the temperature moves the peak of black-body radiation to shorter wavelengths — a heated iron bar glows red, then orange, then white. The share of short-wavelength radiation therefore grows. AM and long-wave radio are long wavelengths, whose share falls. (The printed UHS key marks D, 'Both A and C', which wrongly includes AM radio.)
questions.explanation_trick: Hotter = bluer: temperature up, peak wavelength down.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — AM radio waves are long wavelengths; their share decreases with temperature.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — long radio waves are the longest wavelengths of all.
explanation_options.c: Correct — by Wien's law, higher temperature favours shorter wavelengths.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — it includes AM radio, whose proportion does not increase.

questions.question_text: In photoelectric effect removal of photons is observed at _________ energies.
questions.explanation_short: The photoelectric effect is the main way photons interact with matter at low energies and remains important at intermediate energies; at higher energies Compton scattering and then pair production take over.
questions.explanation_long: Photons lose energy to matter in three main ways. At low photon energies (visible, ultraviolet, soft X-rays) photoelectric absorption dominates, and it still contributes at intermediate energies, especially in heavy elements. Compton scattering becomes the dominant process at intermediate energies, and pair production needs more than 1.02 MeV, so it occurs only at high energies. The UHS key therefore marks low and intermediate energies. ('Removal of photons' in the paper means removal of photoelectrons.)
questions.explanation_trick: Low: photoelectric. Intermediate: Compton. High (> 1.02 MeV): pair production.

explanation_options.a: True, but incomplete — photoelectric absorption also occurs at intermediate energies.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — at high energies pair production dominates.
explanation_options.c: True, but incomplete — the photoelectric effect is most important at low energies.
explanation_options.d: Correct (UHS key) — the photoelectric effect is observed at low and intermediate photon energies.

questions.question_text: Which device is the most efficient?
questions.explanation_short: A dry cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy with about 90% efficiency — far higher than a storage battery (≈72%), a nuclear reactor (≈30–35%) or a silicon solar cell (≈10–20%).
questions.explanation_long: Typical conversion efficiencies quoted in physics texts: dry cell battery ≈ 90%, storage battery ≈ 72%, nuclear power reactor ≈ 30–35% (most of the heat is rejected, as in any heat engine), silicon solar cell ≈ 10–20%. The dry cell is therefore the most efficient of the four. (The printed UHS key marks A, but a nuclear reactor is limited by heat-engine efficiency and is the second least efficient device listed.)
questions.explanation_trick: Anything that turns heat into work (nuclear, coal, petrol) is stuck near 30–40%; direct chemical-to-electrical cells do much better.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a nuclear power reactor converts only about 30–35% of its heat into electricity.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a storage battery is about 72% efficient, below a dry cell.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a silicon solar cell converts only about 10–20% of sunlight.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a dry cell is about 90% efficient, the highest of these.

questions.question_text: The units of E in E = mc² are
questions.explanation_short: In E=mc², energy's units come from mass (kg) times velocity squared (m²/s²), giving kg·m²·s⁻² — the Joule.
questions.explanation_long: E=mc² dimensionally is [mass][velocity]² = kg·(m/s)² = kg·m²·s⁻², which is exactly the unit of energy (Joule), consistent with any energy formula like KE=½mv² or W=Fd (N·m = kg·m²·s⁻²).
questions.explanation_trick: All energy-related quantities (work, kinetic energy, mass-energy) share the same base units kg·m²·s⁻² — recognizing this equivalence (and that N·m = kg·m²·s⁻²) helps eliminate wrong unit options quickly.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — kg·m·s⁻² is the unit of force, not energy.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — N·m·s⁻² is not a standard, dimensionally consistent representation of energy as written.
explanation_options.c: Correct — kg·m²·s⁻² is the base-unit form of energy (Joule).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only option C alone is dimensionally the correct, standard energy unit.

aliases: The units of E in E=mc2 are
kg m s-2.

questions.question_text: Work done on a body equals change in its __________ energy.
questions.explanation_short: Work done on a body changes its energy: net work changes kinetic energy, work against gravity or a spring changes potential energy, and either way the total energy changes. The UHS key marks 'All of these'.
questions.explanation_long: By the work-energy theorem, the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy (W = ΔK). If the work is done against a conservative force — lifting a body or stretching a spring — it is stored as potential energy instead, and in general the work done by an outside agent equals the change in the body's total mechanical energy. Since the question does not specify the situation, the key accepts all three.
questions.explanation_trick: W_net = ΔK is the strict theorem; work by an outside agent = change in total energy.

explanation_options.a: True — work done by an outside agent changes the body's total energy.
explanation_options.b: True — work done against gravity is stored as potential energy.
explanation_options.c: True — net work equals the change in kinetic energy (work-energy theorem).
explanation_options.d: Correct (UHS key) — depending on the situation, work can change any of these energies.

questions.question_text: A pipe varies uniformly in diameter from 2 m to 4 m. An incompressible fluid enters the pipe with velocity 16m/sec. What is velocity of fluid when it leaves the pipe?
questions.explanation_short: By continuity (A1V1=A2V2) with area proportional to diameter squared, going from 2m to 4m diameter quadruples the area, so exit velocity is 16/4 = 4 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: Continuity equation: A1V1 = A2V2. Area is proportional to diameter squared, so A2/A1 = (4/2)^2 = 4. Thus V2 = V1x(A1/A2) = 16x(1/4) = 4 m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: Always square the diameter ratio when converting to an area ratio in continuity problems -- a common mistake is using the diameter ratio directly instead of its square.

explanation_options.a: Wrong -- 64 m/s would result from multiplying (not dividing) by the area ratio incorrectly.
explanation_options.b: Wrong -- 32 m/s doesn't match the calculation with the correct area ratio of 4.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- direct application of continuity with area proportional to diameter squared gives 4 m/s, not 8 m/s.
explanation_options.d: Correct -- by the continuity equation with area scaling as diameter squared, this value (4 m/s) is what the calculation yields.

questions.question_text: Transverse waves cannot be setup in __________
questions.explanation_short: Transverse waves need a medium that resists shear; fluids (liquids and gases) cannot, so transverse waves cannot be set up in them.
questions.explanation_long: In a transverse wave the particles move perpendicular to the direction of travel, which requires the medium to pull neighbouring layers back sideways — a shear restoring force. Solids (including metals and soil) have rigidity and carry both transverse and longitudinal waves. Fluids have no shear rigidity, so only longitudinal (compression) waves travel through their bulk — which is also why S-waves from earthquakes do not cross the liquid outer core.
questions.explanation_trick: Shear needs rigidity: solids carry S (transverse) waves, fluids carry only P (longitudinal) waves.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — metals are solids with rigidity and carry transverse waves.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — solids carry transverse waves (e.g. seismic S-waves).
explanation_options.c: Correct — fluids have no shear rigidity, so transverse waves cannot travel through them.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — soil is a solid medium and carries transverse seismic waves.

questions.question_text: The ratio of the __________ is called magnification.
questions.explanation_short: Magnification is generally defined as the ratio of image size to object size, describing how much larger (or smaller) the image appears.
questions.explanation_long: Magnification m = (image size)/(object size), or equivalently v/u in terms of image and object distances for lenses/mirrors -- this is the standard, general definition applicable across optical instruments, not a ratio specific to an eyepiece.
questions.explanation_trick: Magnification is always image size divided by object size (or v/u) -- don't let instrument-specific wording (eyepiece, objective) distract from this universal ratio.

explanation_options.a: Correct -- by the standard general definition, magnification = image size/object size.
explanation_options.b: Wrong -- this is the reciprocal of magnification, not magnification itself.
explanation_options.c: Wrong -- this refers to a specific eyepiece-related ratio, a more specialized (and non-standard) definition.
explanation_options.d: Not applicable -- option A represents the standard general definition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has the highest resistivity?
questions.explanation_short: Germanium is a semiconductor with a resistivity of about 0.5 Ω·m, millions of times higher than silver, copper or platinum.
questions.explanation_long: Approximate resistivities at room temperature: silver 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, platinum 1.06 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m, germanium ≈ 0.46 Ω·m. Platinum is the most resistive of the three metals, but the semiconductor germanium is higher than all of them by more than a million times. (The printed UHS key marks B, but silver has the lowest resistivity of any metal.)
questions.explanation_trick: Order of resistivity: insulators > semiconductors > metals — a semiconductor beats every metal.

explanation_options.a: Correct — germanium (≈0.46 Ω·m) has by far the highest resistivity here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — copper is an excellent conductor with very low resistivity.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — platinum is the most resistive of the metals, but still about a million times below germanium.

questions.question_text: An n-type semi-conductor is made by doping silicon crystal with __________
questions.explanation_short: Doping silicon with a pentavalent (Group V) element like arsenic donates extra free electrons, creating n-type semiconductor material.
questions.explanation_long: Silicon (Group IV, 4 valence electrons) doped with a pentavalent element such as arsenic, phosphorus, or antimony contributes an extra 'donor' electron per dopant atom, creating n-type material with excess free electrons as majority charge carriers.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: pentavalent dopants (Group V: As, P, Sb) → n-type (extra electron, 'n' for negative carriers); trivalent dopants (Group III: In, Al, B, Ga) → p-type (creates holes, 'p' for positive carriers).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — indium is trivalent and creates p-type material, not n-type.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — aluminium is also trivalent, producing p-type material.
explanation_options.c: Correct — arsenic is pentavalent, donating extra electrons to form n-type silicon.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — since aluminium (B) is trivalent (p-type), 'both B and C' is incorrect; only C is right.

questions.question_text: Objects cannot be accelerated to the speed of light in free space is consequence of
questions.explanation_short: Special relativity shows that as an object's speed approaches c, its relativistic mass/inertia increases without bound, requiring infinite energy to reach light speed — a combination of mass variation, energy-mass relations, and effectively growing inertial resistance.
questions.explanation_long: As velocity approaches c, relativistic mass (or equivalently, the energy needed via E=mc² type relations) grows toward infinity, meaning an ever-increasing force is required for the same acceleration, effectively an ever-growing inertial resistance. All three listed factors — mass variation with speed, the energy-mass relationship, and the resulting increased inertial 'resistance' — describe facets of the same underlying relativistic effect preventing acceleration to c.
questions.explanation_trick: This is a classic 'all of these are aspects of the same phenomenon' relativity question — mass increase, energy requirements, and inertia are three ways of describing why nothing with mass can reach light speed.

explanation_options.a: Partially correct — relativistic mass increase is one valid way to describe this effect.
explanation_options.b: Partially correct — the energy-mass relationship (infinite energy needed) is another valid description.
explanation_options.c: Partially correct — the growing effective inertia is yet another facet of the same relativistic effect.
explanation_options.d: Correct — all three describe interconnected aspects of why massive objects cannot reach the speed of light.

questions.question_text: A certain radioactive mass decays from 64 gm to 2 gm in 20 days. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation_short: Decaying from 64 g to 2 g means dropping by a factor of 32 (2⁵) — that's 5 half-lives in 20 days, so each half-life is 4 days.
questions.explanation_long: 64/2 = 32 = 2⁵, meaning 5 half-life periods have elapsed. Since this took 20 days total, each half-life = 20/5 = 4 days.
questions.explanation_trick: When solving half-life problems, convert the ratio (initial/final) into a power of 2 first — that power directly tells you the number of half-lives elapsed.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 5 days × 5 half-lives would total 25 days, not matching the given 20 days.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 20 days ÷ 5 half-lives = 4 days per half-life.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 10 days × 5 half-lives would total 50 days, far more than given.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 6 days × 5 half-lives would total 30 days, not matching.

questions.question_text: If inductance is denoted by L and resistance by R, which of the following is true for a choke?
questions.option_a: R is large, L is very small.
questions.option_b: R is very small, L is large.
questions.option_c: Both R and L are large.
questions.option_d: Both R and L are very small.
questions.explanation_short: A choke coil is designed to have very small resistance (to minimize power loss) but large inductance (to strongly oppose AC current changes).
questions.explanation_long: A choke is essentially an inductor used to block/limit AC current while wasting minimal power as heat. This requires large L (for strong reactance/opposition to AC) combined with very small R (to keep resistive I²R losses low).
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the purpose-driven design logic: chokes minimize energy loss (low R) while maximizing AC-blocking ability (high L) — this pairing (small R, large L) defines an ideal choke.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a large R with small L describes something closer to a simple resistor, wasteful and poor at blocking AC.
explanation_options.b: Correct — small R (low loss) and large L (strong AC opposition) is the ideal choke design.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — large R would cause significant power dissipation, defeating the choke's efficiency purpose.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — small L would provide little opposition to AC current, defeating the choke's blocking purpose.

questions.question_text: A force 2i + j has moved its point of application from (2,3) to (6,5). What is work done?
questions.explanation_long: The displacement vector is (6-2, 5-3) = (4,2). Work done = F·displacement (dot product) = (2)(4) + (1)(2) = 8 + 2 = 10 J, a positive value since the motion aligns generally with the force direction.
questions.explanation_trick: Work from a constant force over a displacement is always the dot product F·d — compute the displacement vector first (final minus initial position), then dot it with the force components.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a negative sign would only arise if force and displacement opposed each other, which isn't the case here.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the dot product calculation gives +10 J.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — -18 doesn't match the correct dot product computation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — +18 overstates the result; the correct dot product is +10, not +18.

questions.question_text: The escape velocity corresponds to __________ energy gained by body, which carries it to an infinite distance from the surface of earth.
questions.explanation_short: Escape velocity corresponds to the minimum initial kinetic energy needed so a body can just reach an infinite distance with zero final velocity, overcoming gravitational potential energy.
questions.explanation_long: Setting initial KE equal in magnitude to the gravitational potential energy barrier (½mv_esc² = GMm/R) gives the escape velocity condition — the body's initial kinetic energy exactly compensates for the (negative) gravitational potential energy needed to reach infinity with just zero leftover speed.
questions.explanation_trick: Escape velocity problems always balance initial KE against the magnitude of gravitational PE (GMm/R) — remember it's specifically the initial kinetic energy that must supply this, not total mechanical energy alone (which stays constant, near zero, throughout the escape trajectory).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'total energy' is a looser description; the precise defining quantity that must be supplied at launch is initial kinetic energy.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — potential energy is what's being overcome, not what's 'gained' by the body in this context.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the initial kinetic energy given to the body must equal the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy to just escape.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — option C correctly identifies the answer.

questions.question_text: The drag force decreases as the speed of an object moving through fluid __________
questions.explanation_short: Drag force generally decreases as an object's speed through a fluid decreases, since drag scales with speed (or speed squared).
questions.explanation_long: Drag force is typically proportional to velocity (viscous/laminar regime) or velocity squared (higher-speed, turbulent regime) — F_drag ∝ v or v². As speed decreases, drag force decreases correspondingly; conversely, drag increases as speed increases.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember drag force always moves in the SAME direction of change as speed (both increase together, both decrease together) — the question here specifically asks when drag decreases, which happens as speed decreases.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — drag would increase, not decrease, as speed increases.
explanation_options.b: Correct — decreasing speed reduces the drag force, since drag scales with speed (or its square).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — constant speed generally corresponds to constant, not decreasing, drag once terminal/equilibrium conditions are reached.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only 'decreases' (B) correctly matches decreasing drag; 'remains constant' does not describe a decrease.

questions.question_text: Light year is a measure of
questions.explanation_short: A light-year measures the distance light travels in one year, making it a unit of distance, not time.
questions.explanation_long: Despite containing the word 'year,' a light-year is defined as distance = speed of light × 1 year ≈ 9.46×10¡² km, used to express astronomical distances conveniently.
questions.explanation_trick: A very common trick question — the word 'year' misleads students into picking 'time,' but a light-year is explicitly a distance unit (speed × time gives distance).

explanation_options.a: Correct — light-year is a unit of distance (light's speed times one year).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — despite the name, it measures distance, not the duration of time.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — it's unrelated to light intensity.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — it's not a velocity unit; the speed of light itself is the velocity used to derive this distance unit.

questions.question_text: A yellow light of wavelength 500 nm emitted by a single source passes through two narrow slits 1 mm apart. How far apart are two adjacent bright fringes when interference is observed on a screen 10 m away?
questions.explanation_long: Using the double-slit interference fringe spacing formula w = λD/d, with λ=500 nm (the '500 mm' in the question is a likely typo/OCR artifact for 500 nm), D=10 m, and d=1 mm=10⁻³ m: w = (500×10⁻⁹ × 10)/(10⁻³) = 5×10⁻³ m = 5 mm.
questions.explanation_trick: Always double check units in interference problems — wavelengths of visible light are in the nanometre range, so '500 mm' here is clearly meant to be '500 nm'; plugging the intended nm value gives a clean, consistent answer.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 5 mm matches the fringe spacing calculation using λ=500 nm, D=10 m, d=1 mm.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1.33 mm doesn't result from the straightforward fringe-width formula with these values.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 0.5 mm is off by a factor of 10 from the correct computed value.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 50 mm is off by a factor of 10 (too large) from the correct computed value.

aliases: A yellow light of wavelength 500 mm emitted by a single source passes through two narrow slits 1 mm apart. How far apart are two adjacent bright fringes when interference is observed on a screen 10 m away?
5 mm.

questions.question_text: The heat produced by a current I in the wire of resistance R during time interval t is
questions.explanation_short: By Joule's law, heat produced by a current is H = I²Rt.
questions.explanation_long: The heat generated in a resistor carrying current I for time t is given by Joule's law: H = I²Rt, derived from power P=I²R multiplied by time.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize H=I²Rt directly — a very frequently tested formula; watch for distractor options that misplace exponents or invert R and I roles.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — dividing by Rt instead of multiplying reverses the correct relationship.
explanation_options.b: Correct — H = I²Rt is the standard Joule heating formula.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this divides by both R and t, which is incorrect.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — squaring R instead of I misapplies the formula.

aliases: The heat produced by a current I in the wire of resistance R during time interval t is
I2/Rt.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most ductile?
questions.explanation_short: Among the listed materials, copper is the most ductile (metal), able to be drawn into thin wires without breaking, unlike glass or cast iron/high-carbon steel which are brittle.
questions.explanation_long: Ductility measures a material's ability to be stretched into wire without fracturing. Copper is well known for excellent ductility (used extensively for electrical wiring), while glass is brittle (shatters rather than stretches), and cast iron/high-carbon steel are relatively brittle due to high carbon content, reducing their ductility compared to lower-carbon metals like copper.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: pure, low-carbon metals like gold, silver, and copper are highly ductile; high-carbon alloys and ceramics/glass are brittle — ductility generally decreases as carbon content or crystalline rigidity increases.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — glass is brittle, not ductile; it shatters rather than deforms.
explanation_options.b: Correct — copper is highly ductile, easily drawn into wires.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cast iron is brittle due to high carbon content, not ductile.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — high carbon steel is also relatively brittle compared to more ductile metals like copper.

questions.question_text: Which type of bonding is present in NH₄Cl?
questions.explanation_short: NH₄Cl contains all three: covalent N–H bonds, a coordinate covalent N→H⁺ bond, and ionic attraction between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻.
questions.explanation_long: Ammonia's nitrogen forms three ordinary covalent bonds to hydrogen. Its lone pair is donated to H⁺ to make the fourth N–H bond, a coordinate covalent (dative) bond, giving the ammonium ion NH₄⁺. The ammonium ion and the chloride ion are then held together by ionic bonding in the crystal. (The printed UHS key marks C, but coordinate covalent is only one of the three bond types present.)
questions.explanation_trick: Ammonium salts are the classic example of all three bond types in one compound.

explanation_options.a: Incomplete — the NH₄⁺–Cl⁻ attraction is ionic, but it is not the only bond type.
explanation_options.b: Incomplete — the three N–H bonds of ammonia are covalent, but other bond types are present too.
explanation_options.c: Incomplete — one N→H bond is coordinate covalent, but ionic and covalent bonds are also present.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ionic, covalent and coordinate covalent bonds are all present.

aliases: Which type of bonding is present in NH4Cl?
Ionic.

questions.question_text: When CuSO₄ is electrolyzed in aqueous solution using copper electrodes, then the substance which deposits at the cathode is:
questions.explanation_short: During electrolysis of CuSO4 with copper electrodes, Cu2+ ions are reduced at the cathode, depositing pure copper metal.
questions.explanation_long: At the cathode (reduction site), Cu2+ ions from solution gain two electrons to form solid copper metal: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu(s). With copper electrodes (electrorefining setup), copper from the anode dissolves into solution while an equal amount of pure copper deposits on the cathode.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: cathode = reduction = metal deposits (cations gain electrons and plate out); anode = oxidation = metal dissolves (with active/copper electrodes) or gas evolves (with inert electrodes).

explanation_options.a: Correct — copper metal is reduced and deposited at the cathode.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — copper ions are what's consumed/reduced, not what remains deposited as ions.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — hydrogen would only be liberated at the cathode with inert electrodes and dilute solution without excess Cu2+ preferentially discharging.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — oxygen evolution happens at an inert anode in different electrolysis setups, not at the cathode here.

aliases: When CuSO4 is electrolyzed in aqueous solution using copper electrodes, then the substance which deposits at the cathode is:
Copper metal.

questions.question_text: Aldehydes can be synthesized by the oxidation of
questions.explanation_short: Aldehydes are produced by the mild (controlled) oxidation of primary alcohols, stopping before further oxidation to carboxylic acids.
questions.explanation_long: Primary alcohols (R-CH2OH) undergo oxidation to aldehydes (R-CHO) using mild oxidizing agents under controlled conditions (e.g., distillation to remove the aldehyde before further oxidation); over-oxidation converts them further to carboxylic acids.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the oxidation ladder: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol → ketone (which resists further oxidation); tertiary alcohols don't oxidize easily at all.

explanation_options.a: Correct — primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes under controlled/mild conditions.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones, not aldehydes.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — organic acids are typically the further oxidation product of aldehydes, not the starting material for making them.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — inorganic acids are unrelated reagents/oxidants here, not a source material for aldehydes via oxidation.

questions.question_text: The products of the fermentation of a sugar are ethanol and
questions.explanation_short: Yeast ferments glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
questions.explanation_long: Alcoholic fermentation is anaerobic: the enzyme zymase in yeast breaks each glucose molecule into two molecules of ethanol and two molecules of carbon dioxide. The CO₂ is the gas that makes dough rise and bubbles out of fermenting liquids. No oxygen is produced, water is not a product, and sulphur dioxide has nothing to do with the reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Bread rises and beer fizzes for the same reason: CO₂ from fermentation.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — water is not a product of alcoholic fermentation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — fermentation is anaerobic and releases no oxygen.
explanation_options.c: Correct — C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — sulphur dioxide is not formed; sugars contain no sulphur.

questions.question_text: __________ serve as carriers of heredity from one generation to the other.
questions.explanation_short: Nucleoproteins (DNA/RNA combined with proteins, i.e., chromatin/chromosomes) carry hereditary information between generations.
questions.explanation_long: Genetic material exists in cells as nucleoprotein complexes — nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) bound to histone and other proteins forming chromatin — and it is this hereditary material that's passed from parent to offspring during reproduction.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse nucleoproteins (genetic carriers) with simple proteins like caseins (a milk protein) or lipids/formaldehyde, which have no role in heredity.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — lipids are structural/energy-storage molecules, not hereditary carriers.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — casein is a milk protein unrelated to heredity.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — formaldehyde is a simple organic compound, not a biological hereditary material.
explanation_options.d: Correct — nucleoproteins (DNA/RNA plus associated proteins) are the material of heredity.

questions.question_text: __________ extraction is controlled by partition law.
questions.explanation_short: Solvent extraction (partitioning a solute between two immiscible solvents) is governed by the distribution/partition law.
questions.explanation_long: The partition (distribution) law states that a solute distributes itself between two immiscible solvents in a constant ratio (the distribution coefficient) at equilibrium, at a given temperature — this principle underlies solvent extraction techniques used to separate/purify compounds.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a question mentions 'partition law' or 'distribution coefficient,' think of the classic solvent extraction technique (e.g., extracting iodine from water using an organic solvent like CCl4).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — iodine is an example substance sometimes extracted, not the extraction method/process itself.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — benzoic acid is likewise an example solute, not the process governed by the law.
explanation_options.c: Correct — solvent extraction is the process directly controlled by the partition/distribution law.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'stationary' isn't a defined extraction process type matching this description.

questions.question_text: The process of effusion is best understood by __________ law.
questions.explanation_short: Graham's Law of Effusion states that a gas's rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, directly explaining the effusion process.
questions.explanation_long: Graham's Law (rate1/rate2 = √(M2/M1)) quantitatively describes how lighter gas molecules effuse through a small opening faster than heavier ones, making it the law specifically associated with and named for the effusion phenomenon.
questions.explanation_trick: Graham = effusion/diffusion rates and molar mass; Boyle = pressure-volume at constant T; Charles = volume-temperature at constant P — keep these three gas laws' specific relationships straight.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Graham's Law directly describes and quantifies the effusion process.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Charles's Law relates volume and temperature, unrelated to effusion rates.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Boyle's Law relates pressure and volume, unrelated to effusion rates.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Graham's Law is the specifically correct and well-known answer here.

questions.question_text: __________ has dipole moment.
questions.explanation_short: Carbon monoxide (CO) has an asymmetric, non-cancelling bond dipole, giving it a net dipole moment, unlike symmetric CO2 or benzene.
questions.explanation_long: CO is a linear but heteronuclear diatomic molecule with unequal electronegativities (O more electronegative than C), giving it a small net dipole moment. CO2, despite having polar C=O bonds, is linear and symmetric, so the two bond dipoles cancel (zero net dipole). Benzene's symmetric ring structure similarly has no net dipole.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: individual bond polarity doesn't guarantee a molecular dipole moment — molecular symmetry can cancel it out, as in CO2 and benzene, while asymmetric molecules like CO retain a net dipole.
