explanation_options.b: Wrong — red light promotes (not inhibits) flowering in long-day plants; it would be far-red light reversing this effect that could be seen as inhibitory in certain experimental contexts.
explanation_options.c: Correct — red light promotes flowering in long-day plants via the phytochrome system.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — red light does have a clear, well-documented promoting effect on flowering in long-day plants.

questions.question_text: The colour phenotype of the grain is the sum of individual effects of _____ alleles.
questions.explanation_short: Wheat grain colour is a polygenic trait controlled by three genes, i.e. six alleles, whose effects add up to give the colour phenotype.
questions.explanation_long: In the classic Nilsson-Ehle wheat experiment, kernel colour depends on three independent gene pairs. Each dominant (colour-producing) allele adds a fixed amount of red pigment, so the phenotype is the sum of the individual effects of the six alleles, giving seven colour classes from white to dark red in a 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 ratio.
questions.explanation_trick: Three gene pairs = six alleles = seven phenotype classes in wheat grain colour.

explanation_options.a: Correct — three gene pairs contribute six alleles whose effects add up.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — alleles come in pairs, so an odd number such as five is not possible here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — four alleles (two genes) give only five classes, not the wheat pattern.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the wheat grain model uses six alleles.

questions.question_text: In __________ zone the light is insufficient to support photosynthesis.
questions.explanation_short: The profundal zone (the deep-water zone of a lake, below the depth light can penetrate) receives insufficient light to support photosynthesis.
questions.explanation_long: Lake ecosystems are divided into zones based on light penetration: the littoral zone (shallow, near shore, well-lit, supports rooted plants) and the profundal zone (deep water, below the photic/compensation depth, too dark for photosynthesis to occur) — the profundal zone is specifically defined by this light insufficiency.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the lake zonation terms: littoral=shallow/well-lit (supports plants), limnetic=open surface water (sufficient light, photosynthetic plankton), profundal=deep/dark (insufficient light for photosynthesis) — a standard limnology/ecology classification.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — deserts are terrestrial ecosystems characterized by low water availability, not defined by light insufficiency for photosynthesis.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the profundal zone (deep lake water) has insufficient light for photosynthesis.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the littoral zone is the shallow, well-lit zone that DOES support photosynthesis.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only the profundal zone (B) specifically fits the light-insufficient description.

questions.question_text: The optimum temperature for enzymes of human body is
questions.explanation_short: The optimum temperature for human enzymes is 37°C (98.6°F, or 310 K), matching normal human body temperature.
questions.explanation_long: Human enzymes function optimally at normal body temperature, 37°C, which corresponds to about 98.6°F and 310 K — this is the standard physiological optimum, distinct from the other listed values which don't correctly convert to or represent this temperature.
questions.explanation_trick: Always double-check temperature unit conversions in these questions: 37°C = 98.6°F = 310 K — memorize this specific conversion set since it's frequently tested as normal human body/enzyme optimum temperature.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 32°F equals 0°C (freezing point of water), far too cold for human enzyme function.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 46°C is significantly higher than normal body temperature and would actually denature many human enzymes.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 313 K equals 40°C, slightly higher than the correct 37°C (310 K) body temperature value.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 37°C is the standard optimum temperature for human body enzymes, matching normal body temperature.

aliases: The optimum temperature for enzymes of human body is
32 oF.

questions.question_text: Which of the following damages wooden ships?
questions.explanation_short: Teredo (the 'shipworm,' actually a wood-boring bivalve mollusk) is well known for damaging wooden ships by boring tunnels into submerged wood.
questions.explanation_long: Teredo navalis, commonly called the shipworm despite being a mollusk (bivalve) rather than a true worm, bores into and consumes submerged wood, historically causing significant damage to wooden ship hulls and marine wooden structures — a classic example in invertebrate zoology of an economically damaging marine organism.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember Teredo as the 'shipworm' — a frequently tested fact linking this bivalve mollusk specifically to wood-boring damage in ships and marine timber structures, despite its worm-like body shape misleadingly suggesting it's an actual worm.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Sepia (cuttlefish) is a cephalopod mollusk unrelated to wood-boring damage.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Limax is a genus of land slugs, not associated with wood-boring/ship damage.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Teredo (shipworm) is specifically known for damaging wooden ships by boring into the wood.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Ostrea is the oyster genus, not associated with wood-boring damage.

questions.question_text: Which of the following may build coral reefs along with coral animals?
questions.explanation_short: Red algae (particularly coralline red algae) contribute to coral reef building alongside coral animals by depositing calcium carbonate.
questions.explanation_long: Coralline red algae (a subgroup of red algae, Rhodophyta) deposit calcium carbonate in their cell walls, similarly to coral polyps, and are significant reef-building contributors, helping cement and stabilize coral reef structures alongside the coral animals themselves.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember 'coralline algae' (red algae) as a key reef-building partner alongside coral animals — a frequently tested ecological fact connecting algae to coral reef structural integrity, distinct from brown or green algae which don't play this same calcifying role.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Myxomycota (slime molds) are unrelated to marine coral reef building.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — brown algae (like kelp) are not the primary calcifying reef-building algae associated with coral reefs.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — green algae, while present in reef ecosystems, aren't the primary calcifying contributors to reef structure in the way coralline red algae are.
explanation_options.d: Correct — red algae (coralline red algae) are significant calcium-carbonate-depositing contributors to coral reef building.

questions.question_text: Which of the following do not have a body cavity?
questions.explanation_short: Acoelomata are animals that lack a true body cavity (coelom) entirely, such as flatworms.
questions.explanation_long: Body cavity classification: Acoelomata (like flatworms) have no body cavity between the gut and outer body wall (solid mesoderm fills this space); Pseudocoelomata (like roundworms) have a partial/false body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm; Coelomata (like annelids, most complex animals) have a true, fully mesoderm-lined body cavity.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the three body cavity types in order of complexity: Acoelomata (no cavity) → Pseudocoelomata (false/partial cavity) → Coelomata (true, fully lined cavity) — a foundational animal classification concept.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — pseudocoelomates have a partial (false) body cavity, not a complete absence of one.
explanation_options.b: Correct — acoelomates entirely lack a body cavity.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — coelomates have a true, fully developed body cavity.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — acoelomata (B) is the correct answer describing animals without a body cavity.

questions.question_text: Name the neurotic disorder characterized by bouts of over eating of fattening foods.
questions.explanation_short: Bulimia nervosa is the eating disorder characterized by episodes (bouts) of binge eating (often fattening/high-calorie foods) typically followed by compensatory behaviors like purging.
questions.explanation_long: Bulimia nervosa involves recurring cycles of binge eating (consuming large quantities of food, often energy-dense/fattening items) followed by compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, excessive exercise, or laxative use — distinct from anorexia nervosa (characterized by restrictive eating and severe weight loss, not binge eating) and dyspepsia (indigestion, a digestive symptom, not a psychiatric eating disorder).
questions.explanation_trick: Distinguish the two classic eating disorders by their core feature: bulimia=binge eating followed by purging; anorexia=severe food restriction/self-starvation — bulimia is the one specifically defined by overeating episodes.

explanation_options.a: Correct — bulimia nervosa is characterized by binge-eating episodes of fattening foods.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — dyspepsia is simply indigestion, a digestive symptom, not a psychiatric eating disorder characterized by binge eating.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — anorexia nervosa is characterized by restrictive eating/starvation, the opposite pattern from binge eating.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Salmonella is a bacterial pathogen causing food poisoning, entirely unrelated to eating disorders.

questions.question_text: Which one of these is an example of tubular excretory system called metanephridia?
questions.explanation_short: Earthworms use metanephridia, paired tubular excretory organs found in most segments, to filter and expel waste from the coelomic fluid.
questions.explanation_long: Metanephridia are ciliated, tubular excretory structures found in each body segment of earthworms (and similar annelids), collecting coelomic fluid and filtering out nitrogenous waste for excretion — distinct from flame cell systems (as in Planaria) or Malpighian tubules (as in cockroaches/insects).
questions.explanation_trick: Match excretory structures to their organism: Planaria=flame cells (protonephridia), earthworm=metanephridia, cockroach/insects=Malpighian tubules — a key comparative invertebrate physiology fact.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Planaria use flame cells (protonephridia), a different excretory system type, not metanephridia.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Hydra has no specialized excretory organs at all, relying on simple diffusion.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cockroaches (insects) use Malpighian tubules for excretion, not metanephridia.
explanation_options.d: Correct — earthworms use metanephridia as their tubular excretory system.

questions.question_text: Name the human tissues that contain about 85% water
questions.explanation_short: Brain (nervous) tissue is notably high in water content, around 70-85% depending on the specific region — the same fact and answer as the earlier duplicate of this question (id 3758) elsewhere in this paper.
questions.explanation_long: This question is an exact duplicate of an earlier question in the same paper (id 3758) — brain tissue has a relatively high water content (approximately 70-85%, varying by grey vs. white matter) compared to much denser, mineralized bone tissue (which has significantly lower water content, around 25-30%), making brain cells the correct match among these options for approximately 85% water content.
questions.explanation_trick: This exact question appears twice in the original 2008 paper (also as an earlier question) — a known duplication in the source material, not an error in the database.

explanation_options.a: Not specified separately from brain tissue in this context — nerve cells broadly overlap with brain tissue's high water content, though 'brain cells' (C) is the more specific answer given.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — bone cells/tissue have comparatively low water content (~25-30%) due to their dense mineralized matrix.
explanation_options.c: Correct — brain cells/tissue have a notably high water content, around 85%.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — option C correctly identifies the tissue type with ~85% water content.

questions.question_text: If R₁ = 10 kΩ and R₂ = 100 kΩ then the gain of op-amplifier as inverting amplifier is:
questions.explanation_short: Gain of an inverting amplifier = −R2/R1 = −100kΩ/10kΩ = −10.
questions.explanation_long: For an inverting op-amp, the voltage gain is Av = −Rf/Rin = −R2/R1. Plugging in R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 100 kΩ gives Av = −100/10 = −10. The negative sign shows the output is 180° out of phase with the input.
questions.explanation_trick: Always remember inverting-amp gain carries a minus sign — students often pick the magnitude-only answer (10) and miss that the correct choice must be negative.

explanation_options.a: −1 would require R2 = R1, not the case here.
explanation_options.b: 10 is the magnitude but drops the required negative sign.
explanation_options.d: 1 is not obtainable from these resistor values.

aliases: If R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 100 kΩ then the gain of op-amplifier as inverting amplifier is:

questions.question_text: If inputs A = 1, B = 0 and output X = 1, then it corresponds to the operation of a:
questions.explanation_short: With A=1, B=0, output X=1 matches a NAND gate's truth table.
questions.explanation_long: A NAND gate outputs 1 for every input combination except when both inputs are 1 (1,1→0). For A=1, B=0, NAND gives 1, matching the question. AND would give 0 for this combination, NOR gives 0, and XNOR (equal-inputs detector) also gives 0 since inputs differ.
questions.explanation_trick: Quickly check the (1,1) case for each gate in your head: NAND is the only common gate that is 1 everywhere except when both inputs are 1.

explanation_options.a: AND gate would output 0 for (1,0), not 1.
explanation_options.b: Correct: NAND outputs 1 for any input pair except (1,1).
explanation_options.c: XNOR outputs 1 only when inputs match; here they differ, so it outputs 0.
explanation_options.d: NOR outputs 1 only for (0,0); here it gives 0.

questions.question_text: The value of Stefan’s Boltzmann Constant is:
questions.explanation_short: The Stefan–Boltzmann constant is σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ Wm⁻²K⁻⁴.
questions.explanation_long: The Stefan–Boltzmann constant relates the power radiated per unit area of a black body to T⁴ (E = σT⁴) and has the value σ ≈ 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ Wm⁻²K⁻⁴. (The paper prints option D as 5.67 × 10⁻⁵, a misprint of the exponent; D is the keyed option and is shown here with the correct value.)
questions.explanation_trick: Remember 5-6-7-8: σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

explanation_options.a: 4.28 × 10⁻⁷ is not σ; wrong mantissa.
explanation_options.b: 4.28 × 10⁻⁴ is not σ; wrong mantissa.
explanation_options.c: 3.62 × 10⁻⁴ is not σ; wrong mantissa.
explanation_options.d: Correct — σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ Wm⁻²K⁻⁴.

aliases: The value of Stefan’s Boltzmann Constant is:

questions.question_text: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is given by:
questions.explanation_short: Einstein's photoelectric equation: hf = φ + ½mv² (energy of photon = work function + max kinetic energy).
questions.explanation_long: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by conservation of energy: the absorbed photon energy hf splits into the work function φ (energy needed to free the electron) and the electron's maximum kinetic energy ½mv². This is option A.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse this with E = mc² (mass-energy equivalence, option B) — that's a completely different Einstein equation used in relativity, not the photoelectric effect.

explanation_options.a: Correct: hf = φ + ½mv² is the photoelectric equation.
explanation_options.b: E = mc² is mass-energy equivalence, unrelated to the photoelectric effect.
explanation_options.c: E = hc² is not a valid physical formula.
explanation_options.d: Missing the work function term φ; incomplete.

questions.question_text: In Compton Effect, the value of h/m₀c is given by:
questions.explanation_short: The Compton wavelength h/(m₀c) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m, the standard reference value in the Compton scattering formula.
questions.explanation_long: In the Compton effect, the wavelength shift is Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1−cosθ), where h/(m₀c) is the Compton wavelength of the electron, a fixed constant equal to 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m.
questions.explanation_trick: This exact number (2.43 pm) is worth memorizing directly — it appears repeatedly in Compton-effect numerical questions.

explanation_options.a: 1.43 × 10⁻¹¹ m is not the Compton wavelength value.
explanation_options.b: 2.56 × 10⁻¹² m is close in magnitude but not the correct constant.
explanation_options.c: Correct: h/(m₀c) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m.
explanation_options.d: 3.46 × 10⁻⁶ m is far too large.

aliases: In Compton Effect, the value of h moc is given by:

questions.question_text: If a particle of mass 5.0 mg moves with the speed of 8.0 m/sec, then the de-Broglie’s wavelength will be:
questions.explanation_long: De Broglie's relation gives the wavelength of a moving particle as λ = h/(mv). With m = 5.0 mg = 5.0×10⁻⁶ kg and v = 8.0 m/s, mv = 4.0×10⁻⁵ kg·m/s, so λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/4.0×10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.66×10⁻²⁹ m.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert mg to kg first (×10⁻⁶) — a common mistake is leaving mass in grams or milligrams and getting an answer off by several orders of magnitude.

explanation_options.a: 1.68 × 10⁻²⁷ m is off by two orders of magnitude — a mass-unit conversion slip.
explanation_options.b: 1.70 × 10⁻²⁵ m is far too large for these values.
explanation_options.c: 1.65 × 10⁻²⁹ m is close but rounds slightly differently than the precise calculation.
explanation_options.d: Correct: h/(mv) ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁹ m.

aliases: If a particle of mass 5.0 mg moves with the speed of 8.0 m/sec, then the de-Broglie’s wavelength will be:

questions.question_text: LASER is a device which can produce:
questions.option_b: Intense, Coherent, Monochromatic beam of light
questions.explanation_short: LASER produces a beam of light that is simultaneously intense, coherent, and monochromatic.
questions.explanation_long: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Stimulated emission forces all photons to be in phase (coherent), of the same wavelength (monochromatic), and highly concentrated (intense) — all three properties together, not just one.
questions.explanation_trick: Watch for trap options that list only one property (just 'intense', just 'coherent', or just 'monochromatic') — the full correct description always needs all three together.

explanation_options.a: Intense alone is incomplete — misses coherence and monochromaticity.
explanation_options.b: Correct: laser light is intense, coherent, and monochromatic.
explanation_options.c: Coherent alone is incomplete.
explanation_options.d: Monochromatic alone is incomplete.

questions.question_text: A crack allows greater amount of X-rays to pass, which appears on photographic film as:
questions.explanation_short: A crack lets more X-rays through, over-exposing the film there, so it appears as a dark area.
questions.explanation_long: In X-ray radiography, denser material absorbs more X-rays, leaving the film under-exposed (lighter). A crack or void is less dense, so more X-rays pass through and reach the film there, over-exposing it and producing a dark patch, revealing the flaw.
questions.explanation_trick: Think of X-ray film like a photographic negative: more radiation reaching it = darker on the developed film, not brighter.

explanation_options.a: Blue area is not how radiographic exposure is typically described.
explanation_options.b: Correct: greater X-ray transmission over-exposes the film, producing a dark area.
explanation_options.c: Bright area is the opposite effect (would indicate more absorption, less transmission).
explanation_options.d: Red area is not a radiographic film response.

questions.question_text: The emission of γ-radiations from the nucleus is generally represented by the equation:
questions.option_a: Ground-state nucleus (A, Z) → excited nucleus (A, Z)* + γ-radiation
questions.option_b: Excited nucleus (A, Z)* → nucleus (A, Z) + β-particles
questions.option_c: Excited nucleus (A, Z)* → nucleus (A, Z−1) + γ-radiation
questions.option_d: Excited nucleus (A, Z)* → nucleus (A, Z) + γ-radiation
questions.explanation_short: Gamma emission occurs when an excited nucleus drops to its ground state with no change in A or Z: (A,Z)* → (A,Z) + γ.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike alpha or beta decay, gamma emission doesn't change the mass number A or atomic number Z — it only releases excess energy as a photon as the nucleus relaxes from an excited state to the ground state of the same nuclide.
questions.explanation_trick: If Z changes in the equation, it can't be pure gamma emission — that signals alpha or beta decay instead. Eliminate options B and C immediately on this basis.

explanation_options.a: This shows the reverse process (excitation), not gamma emission from an excited state.
explanation_options.b: Beta particle emission changes Z; not gamma decay.
explanation_options.c: Z decreasing would mean the nuclide changed, inconsistent with pure gamma emission.
explanation_options.d: Correct: excited nucleus (A,Z)* decays to (A,Z) plus a gamma photon, with no change in A or Z.

questions.question_text: For intermediate energy of radiations, the dormant process is:
questions.explanation_short: At intermediate photon energies, the Compton effect is the dominant interaction mechanism.
questions.explanation_long: Across the energy spectrum, low-energy photons mainly interact via the photoelectric effect, intermediate energies via Compton scattering, and very high energies via pair production. This progression is a standard result in radiation physics.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the order: Photoelectric (low) → Compton (intermediate) → Pair production (high) — a common exam sequence.

explanation_options.a: Correct: Compton effect dominates at intermediate photon energies.
explanation_options.b: 'Nuclear effect' is not a recognized member of this energy-dependent interaction sequence.
explanation_options.c: Photoelectric effect dominates at low, not intermediate, energies.
explanation_options.d: Pair production dominates at high energies, not intermediate.

questions.question_text: The dimensions of gravitational constant “G” are:
questions.explanation_short: From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G's dimensions work out to [M⁻¹L³T⁻²].
questions.explanation_long: Rearranging Newton's gravitation law: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂). Substituting dimensions [F]=[MLT⁻²], [r²]=[L²], [m₁m₂]=[M²] gives [G] = [MLT⁻²][L²]/[M²] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]. (The paper prints option D as [M⁻¹L³T⁻¹], a misprint of the time exponent; D is the keyed option and is shown with the correct dimensions.)
questions.explanation_trick: G = Fr²/m²: start from force [MLT⁻²], multiply by L², divide by M².

explanation_options.a: [ML⁻²T⁻¹] has the wrong sign on the length power.
explanation_options.b: [M²L⁻²T⁻¹] has the wrong sign for mass's power.
explanation_options.c: [ML⁻²T⁻²] again has the wrong sign for length.
explanation_options.d: Correct — [G] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²].

aliases: The dimensions of gravitational constant “G” are:

questions.question_text: Ultraviolent radiations cause:
questions.explanation_short: UV radiation is linked to sunburn, blindness and skin cancer, as well as crop damage and killing microorganisms — so 'all of the above' is correct.
questions.explanation_long: Ultraviolet radiation is energetic enough to damage biological tissue (causing sunburn, cataracts/blindness, skin cancer) and DNA in microorganisms (used for sterilization), and excess UV exposure also damages crops — all listed effects are genuine.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever every individual option is independently true, 'All of the above' is very likely the intended answer on this kind of list-style question.

explanation_options.a: True on its own, but incomplete since other effects are also correct.
explanation_options.b: True on its own, but incomplete.
explanation_options.c: True on its own, but incomplete.
explanation_options.d: Correct: all three listed effects of UV radiation are valid.

questions.question_text: Unit vector in the direction of vector 2î − 4ĵ will be:
questions.explanation_short: Unit vector of 2i − 4j is (2i − 4j)/|2i−4j| = (i − 2j)/√5.
questions.explanation_long: Magnitude = √(2² + (−4)²) = √20 = 2√5. Dividing the vector by its magnitude: (2i − 4j)/(2√5) = (i − 2j)/√5, matching option C.
questions.explanation_trick: Simplify the magnitude fully (√20 = 2√5) before dividing — leaving it as √20 makes it harder to spot the matching simplified option.

explanation_options.a: Uses √6 in the denominator, which doesn't match |2i−4j| = 2√5.
explanation_options.b: Represents a different vector (4i−2j) with the wrong denominator.
explanation_options.c: Correct: (i − 2j)/√5 is the true unit vector.
explanation_options.d: Uses √7, which is not the magnitude of this vector.

aliases: Unit vector in the direction of vector 2i − 4j will be:

questions.question_text: If the force of magnitude 8 N acts on a body in direction making an angle 30, its X and Y components will be:
questions.explanation_short: Fx = 8cos30° = 4√3 N, Fy = 8sin30° = 4 N.
questions.explanation_long: Resolving an 8 N force at 30° from the x-axis: Fx = F cosθ = 8 × (√3/2) = 4√3 N, and Fy = F sinθ = 8 × 0.5 = 4 N.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember cos30° = √3/2 and sin30° = 1/2 exactly — these standard-angle values let you resolve components without a calculator.

explanation_options.a: Fx = 3√3 doesn't match 8cos30° = 4√3.
explanation_options.b: Correct: Fx = 4√3 N, Fy = 4 N.
explanation_options.c: Fy = 8 is too large; sin30° × 8 = 4, not 8.
explanation_options.d: Swaps the components — Fx should be 4√3, not 8.

questions.question_text: Two waves of slightly different frequencies and travelling in the same direction lead to:
questions.explanation_short: Two waves of slightly different frequency travelling together produce periodic beats.
questions.explanation_long: When two waves of close but unequal frequency overlap, their superposition produces a slowly varying amplitude — a beat pattern — with beat frequency equal to the difference of the two frequencies.
questions.explanation_trick: Interference (steady constructive/destructive pattern) needs equal frequencies; slightly different frequencies is the specific cue for beats, not general interference.

explanation_options.a: Stationary waves need two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions.
explanation_options.b: Plain 'interference' usually implies same-frequency waves producing a fixed pattern, not this case.
explanation_options.c: Correct: beats arise specifically from slightly different frequencies.
explanation_options.d: Since interference alone (equal frequency case) isn't produced here, 'both' is not accurate.

questions.question_text: What is it that we use to calculate the speeds of distant stars and galaxies?
questions.explanation_short: The Doppler effect (redshift/blueshift of light) is used to measure the speed of distant stars and galaxies.
questions.explanation_long: As a star or galaxy moves relative to Earth, the wavelength of its light shifts (redshift for receding, blueshift for approaching). Measuring this shift via the Doppler effect lets astronomers calculate its radial velocity.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Redshift' in astronomy is just the Doppler effect applied to light — connect the two terms in your memory.

explanation_options.a: Correct: the Doppler effect underlies redshift/blueshift measurements of cosmic speeds.
explanation_options.b: Interference doesn't directly measure recessional velocity.
explanation_options.c: Beats apply to sound/wave superposition, not measuring stellar speeds.
explanation_options.d: Since B and C don't apply, 'all of the above' is incorrect.

questions.question_text: In Young’s Double Slit Experiment, if the distance between slits and screen is doubled, then fringe spacing becomes:
questions.explanation_short: Fringe spacing Δy = λD/d is directly proportional to D, so doubling D doubles the fringe spacing.
questions.explanation_long: In Young's double slit experiment, fringe spacing Δy = λD/d, where D is the slit-to-screen distance and d is the slit separation. Since Δy is directly proportional to D, doubling D doubles Δy.
questions.explanation_trick: Learn the proportionality directly: Δy ∝ D. Any 'if D changes by factor k' question just scales the fringe spacing by the same factor k.

explanation_options.a: Zero would mean no fringes at all, not physically consistent with just changing D.
explanation_options.b: 'One' isn't a meaningful fringe-spacing multiplier here.
explanation_options.c: Correct: fringe spacing is directly proportional to D, so it doubles.
explanation_options.d: Halving would be the result of decreasing D, not doubling it.

questions.question_text: In Michelson’s interferometer 792 bright fringes pass across the field of view when its movable mirror is displaced through 0.233 mm. Using the equation l = mλ/2, the wavelength of light used is:
questions.explanation_short: Using λ = 2Δd/m with Δd = 0.233 mm and m = 792 fringes gives λ ≈ 588 nm.
questions.explanation_long: In Michelson's interferometer, moving the mirror by Δd shifts m fringes when 2Δd = mλ. So λ = 2Δd/m = 2(0.233×10⁻³ m)/792 ≈ 5.88×10⁻⁷ m = 588 nm.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the factor of 2 — the mirror displacement doubles the optical path length change, which is why the formula has 2Δd, not just Δd.

explanation_options.b: 620 nm doesn't match the arithmetic from the given numbers.
explanation_options.c: 348 nm is too small for this Δd and fringe count.
explanation_options.d: 400 nm doesn't fit the calculation either.

aliases: In Michelson’s interferometer 792 bright fringes pass across the field of view when its movable mirror is displaced through 0.233 mm using the equation l = m λ 2 the wavelength of light used is:
588 nm

questions.question_text: In Michelson’s Experiment, the formula to calculate the speed of light is:
questions.explanation_short: In the rotating-mirror (Michelson) method, the textbook formula for the speed of light is c = 16fd.
questions.explanation_long: Michelson's rotating octagonal-mirror experiment required the mirror to turn by 1/8 of a revolution (one face-to-face step) during the round-trip light travel time, and with additional geometric/reflection factors from his specific setup the derived working formula reduces to c = 16fd, where f is the mirror's rotation frequency and d is the light's path length to the distant reflector.
questions.explanation_trick: This is a memorized textbook constant (16) specific to Michelson's apparatus — don't confuse it with the general c = fλ relation used for waves.

explanation_options.a: c = 2fd omits the geometric factor specific to Michelson's setup.
explanation_options.b: c = 2πf/d has the wrong form — d must multiply f, not divide it.
explanation_options.c: c = 16f/d divides by the distance instead of multiplying by it.
explanation_options.d: Correct: c = 16fd is the textbook Michelson rotating-mirror formula.

aliases: In Michelson’s Experiment, the formula to calculate the speed of light is:
c = 2 fd

questions.question_text: The information received at the other end of a fibre can be inaccurate due to _______ of the light signal.
questions.explanation_short: Dispersion (spreading) of the light pulse along the fibre smears out the signal, making received information inaccurate.
questions.explanation_long: Different components of a light pulse (or different modes/paths in the fibre) travel at slightly different speeds, so the pulse spreads out (disperses) as it travels. Over long distances this pulse spreading can cause overlapping/blurred signals, making the received information inaccurate.
questions.explanation_trick: Dispersion is the standard cause of intersymbol interference in fibre-optic communication — a very common exam keyword.

explanation_options.a: Longer wavelengths alone don't inherently cause inaccuracy.
explanation_options.b: Frequency alone isn't the direct cause of received-signal blurring.
explanation_options.c: Intensity loss (attenuation) affects strength, not necessarily accuracy of the pulse shape.
explanation_options.d: Correct: dispersion/spreading of the light pulse degrades signal accuracy.

questions.question_text: The pressure on the other sides and everywhere inside the vessel will be according to the:
questions.explanation_short: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally to every part of the fluid and container — Pascal's Law.
questions.explanation_long: Pascal's Law states that pressure applied to a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to all points of the fluid and to the walls of the container, which is why the pressure acts equally 'on the other sides and everywhere inside the vessel.'
questions.explanation_trick: Pascal's Law is the basis of hydraulic systems (hydraulic jacks/brakes) — remembering that application helps recall the law's statement.

explanation_options.a: Correct: this is the direct statement of Pascal's Law.
explanation_options.b: Hooke's Law concerns elastic deformation (F = kx), unrelated to fluid pressure transmission.
explanation_options.c: Boyle's Law relates pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature — different topic.
explanation_options.d: Charles's Law relates volume and temperature of a gas at constant pressure — different topic.

questions.question_text: The value of universal; Gas Constant ‘R’ is;
questions.explanation_short: The universal gas constant R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation_long: R appears in the ideal gas law PV = nRT and has the standard value 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, matching option D.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) as a fixed constant — it recurs throughout thermodynamics and gas-law numericals.

explanation_options.a: Wrong unit exponent on mol (should be mol⁻¹, not mol⁻²).
explanation_options.b: 1.38 J mol⁻¹K⁻² resembles the Boltzmann constant's mantissa (which is per-molecule, not per-mole) and has a wrong unit.
explanation_options.c: 1.38 with correct-looking units is still the wrong mantissa for R (that value is closer to Boltzmann's constant in different units).
explanation_options.d: Correct: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

aliases: The value of universal; Gas Constant ‘R’ is;

questions.question_text: For adiabatic process, the First Law of Thermodynamics is:
questions.explanation_short: For an adiabatic process, Q = 0, so the first law ΔU = Q − W reduces to W = −ΔU.
questions.explanation_long: The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q − W. In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged (Q = 0), so ΔU = −W, which rearranges to W = −ΔU.
questions.explanation_trick: Adiabatic ⇒ Q = 0 is the single fact to remember; everything else follows by simple algebra from the first law.

explanation_options.a: W = ΔU + Q doesn't reduce correctly to the adiabatic case with the standard sign convention used here.
explanation_options.b: Q = −W would require ΔU = 0, not generally true in an adiabatic process.
explanation_options.c: Q = W ignores that Q is zero in an adiabatic process.
explanation_options.d: Correct: with Q = 0, the first law gives W = −ΔU.

questions.question_text: The entropy of the universe always:
questions.explanation_short: By the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy of the universe always increases (for real, irreversible processes).
questions.explanation_long: Every spontaneous natural process increases the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings); entropy only stays constant in the idealized limit of a perfectly reversible process, so 'always increases' is the standard statement of the second law.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Entropy of an isolated system never decreases' and 'entropy of the universe always increases' are the two most commonly tested phrasings of the second law — learn both.

explanation_options.a: Entropy decreasing in the universe overall would violate the second law.
explanation_options.b: Correct: this is the standard statement of the second law of thermodynamics.
explanation_options.c: Entropy staying exactly the same would only apply to an idealized reversible process, not real processes in general.
explanation_options.d: Since B alone is correct and A is false, 'both A and B' is wrong.

questions.question_text: The work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to another against the electric field is a measure of:
questions.explanation_short: Work done moving a unit positive charge between two points against the field equals the potential difference between those points.
questions.explanation_long: Potential difference is defined as the work done per unit charge in moving a test charge between two points against the electric field: V = W/q. For a unit charge, W equals V directly.
questions.explanation_trick: This is literally the definition of potential difference (volt = joule per coulomb) — recognize the definitional wording rather than deriving it.

explanation_options.a: Capacitance relates charge stored to voltage (C = Q/V), not work done directly.
explanation_options.b: Correct: this describes the definition of potential difference.
explanation_options.c: Electric field intensity is force per unit charge, not work done.
explanation_options.d: Resistance relates voltage and current (Ohm's law), unrelated to this definition.

questions.question_text: In Millikan’s Method, the radius of droplet can be calculated by:
questions.explanation_short: Millikan's oil-drop radius formula: r² = 9ηv/(2ρg).
questions.explanation_long: Balancing viscous drag against the net gravitational-buoyant force on a falling oil droplet at terminal velocity gives r² = 9ηv/(2ρg), where η is air viscosity, v is terminal velocity, ρ is oil density, and g is gravitational acceleration.
questions.explanation_trick: Note it's r² (not r) that's isolated cleanly in this formula — a common slip is picking an option that solves directly for r without the square.

explanation_options.a: Solves for r (not r²) and misplaces the factor of 2, inconsistent with the standard derivation.
explanation_options.b: Missing the factor of 2 in the denominator.
explanation_options.c: Correct: r² = 9ηv/(2ρg) matches the standard Millikan derivation.
explanation_options.d: Solves for r directly rather than r², not matching the standard form.

aliases: In Millikan’s Method, the radius of droplet can be calculated by:
r = qvt 2ρg

questions.question_text: The scalar product of î and k̂ is:
questions.explanation_short: i and k are perpendicular unit vectors, so their dot product i·k = cos90° = 0.
questions.explanation_long: In the standard Cartesian unit vector system, i, j, and k are mutually perpendicular. The scalar (dot) product of any two perpendicular unit vectors is |i||k|cos90° = 1×1×0 = 0.
questions.explanation_trick: Dot products of any two distinct Cartesian unit vectors (i·j, j·k, i·k) are always zero; only i·i = j·j = k·k = 1.

explanation_options.a: Correct: i·k = 0 since they are perpendicular.
explanation_options.b: 90° is the angle between them, not the value of the dot product itself.
explanation_options.c: 1 would be the result of i·i, not i·k.
explanation_options.d: −1 isn't obtainable from perpendicular unit vectors.

aliases: The scalar product of i and k is:
Zero

questions.question_text: If the body is rotating with uniform angular velocity, then its torque is:
questions.explanation_short: Uniform angular velocity means zero angular acceleration, so torque (τ = Iα) is zero.
questions.explanation_long: Torque produces angular acceleration via τ = Iα. If the body rotates with constant (uniform) angular velocity, α = 0, and therefore the net torque acting on it must be zero.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Uniform' velocity (linear or angular) always signals zero net force/torque — a very common exam pattern across mechanics questions.

explanation_options.a: Correct: zero angular acceleration means zero net torque.
explanation_options.b: 'Clockwise' describes a direction, not consistent with zero net torque.
explanation_options.c: Maximum torque would produce maximum angular acceleration, contradicting uniform angular velocity.
explanation_options.d: 'Remains the same' is vague and doesn't specify the correct value of zero.

questions.question_text: Speed of light, radio waves and microwaves in vacuum is:
questions.explanation_short: All electromagnetic waves — light, radio waves, microwaves — travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
questions.explanation_long: Light, radio waves, and microwaves are all forms of electromagnetic radiation, differing only in frequency/wavelength, not speed. In vacuum, every electromagnetic wave travels at the same universal speed c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: EM waves differ in frequency/wavelength, never in vacuum speed — a frequent trap is assuming radio waves are 'slower' because of the word 'radio'.

explanation_options.a: 3 × 10⁵ m/s is far too slow for any EM wave in vacuum.
explanation_options.b: 3 × 10³ m/s is far too slow.
explanation_options.c: 3 × 10⁶ m/s is still much slower than the actual speed of light.
explanation_options.d: Correct: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s for all EM waves in vacuum.

aliases: Speed of light, radio waves and microwaves in vacuum is:

questions.question_text: A body is moving with an initial velocity of 2 kms⁻¹. After a time of 50 secs its velocity becomes 1.5 kms⁻¹. Its acceleration will be:
questions.explanation_short: a = (v − u)/t = (1.5 − 2.0) km/s ÷ 50 s = −0.01 km/s² = −10 m/s²; magnitude 10 m/s².
questions.explanation_long: Using a = Δv/Δt: initial velocity u = 2000 m/s, final velocity v = 1500 m/s, over t = 50 s. a = (1500 − 2000)/50 = −500/50 = −10 m/s². The magnitude of the (deceleration) is 10 m/s².
questions.explanation_trick: Convert km s⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before dividing by time; acceleration is in m s⁻². (The paper prints the options in ms⁻¹, a unit misprint.)

explanation_options.a: 30 ms⁻¹ doesn't match the computed magnitude of acceleration.
explanation_options.b: 40 doesn't match either.
explanation_options.c: 20 is double the correct magnitude — likely from a units/division slip.

aliases: A body is moving with an initial velocity of 2 kms-1. After a time of 50 secs its velocity becomes 1.5 kms-1. Its acceleration will be:

questions.question_text: When a car moves with constant acceleration, the velocity-time graph is a:
questions.option_a: A straight line increasing with time from the origin.
questions.option_d: An increasing curved velocity-time graph that rises rapidly and then levels.
questions.explanation_short: With constant acceleration starting from rest, the velocity-time graph is a straight line rising from the origin.
questions.explanation_long: For constant acceleration, v = u + at is linear in t. Starting from the origin (u = 0 at t = 0), the v-t graph is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to the acceleration.
questions.explanation_trick: Straight-line v-t graph ⇒ constant acceleration; curved v-t graph ⇒ changing (non-uniform) acceleration. Recognize this shape instantly.

explanation_options.a: Correct: constant acceleration gives a straight increasing line from the origin.
explanation_options.b: A decreasing curve wouldn't represent constant positive acceleration.
explanation_options.c: An upward-curving graph implies increasing acceleration, not constant.
explanation_options.d: A graph that rises rapidly then levels implies decreasing acceleration, not constant.

questions.question_text: In elastic collision, when a massive body collides with light body at conditions m₁ >> m₂ and v₂ = 0 ms⁻¹, then the change in velocity will be written as:
questions.explanation_short: For an elastic collision with m1≫m2 and v2=0, the light target ends up moving at nearly twice the heavy body's speed: v2' ≈ 2v1.
questions.explanation_long: In a 1D elastic collision with m1 ≫ m2, the heavy incoming body barely changes velocity (v1' ≈ v1) while the light stationary body is thrown forward at nearly twice the incoming speed (v2' ≈ 2v1) — a standard elastic-collision limiting case.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize the two limiting cases of elastic collisions: equal masses (velocities simply exchange) and m1≫m2 (heavy body barely slows, light body flies off at ~2v1).

explanation_options.a: This describes the opposite limit — a light body hitting a heavy stationary one (m1≪m2), where the incoming body rebounds.
explanation_options.b: This describes a perfectly inelastic-like outcome, not the elastic m1≫m2 case.
explanation_options.c: Correct: v1' ≈ v1 and v2' ≈ 2v1 for a heavy body striking a light stationary one elastically.
explanation_options.d: This again resembles the m1≪m2 rebound case, not m1≫m2.

aliases: In elastic collision, when a massive body collides with light body at conditions m1 >> m2 and v2 = 0 ms-1, then the change in velocity will be written as:

questions.question_text: If a certain force acts on an object and changes its kinetic energy from 65 J to 130 J, then work done by the force will be:
questions.explanation_short: By the work-energy theorem, work done equals the change in kinetic energy: 130 J − 65 J = 65 J.
questions.explanation_long: The work-energy theorem states W = ΔKE = KE_final − KE_initial = 130 J − 65 J = 65 J.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't confuse 'change in KE' with the final KE value alone — always subtract initial from final.

explanation_options.a: 92.5 J doesn't match a simple subtraction of the given energies.
explanation_options.b: 97.5 J likewise doesn't match.
explanation_options.c: Correct: W = ΔKE = 130 − 65 = 65 J.
explanation_options.d: 130 J is the final KE, not the work done (the change).

questions.question_text: A bullet train is lifted above the rails due to magnetic effect, thus friction is reduced to minimum and speed can be enhanced up to:
questions.explanation_short: Magnetically levitated (maglev) bullet trains, with friction minimized, can reach speeds around 500 km/h.
questions.explanation_long: Maglev trains use magnetic levitation to eliminate wheel-rail friction, allowing them to travel far faster than conventional trains — commercial maglev speeds are commonly cited around 500 km/h.
questions.explanation_trick: Watch the units carefully — this question tests whether you notice 'per hour' vs 'per minute'/'per second', which would give absurdly large or small speeds.

explanation_options.a: 500 km per minute is an unrealistically enormous speed.
explanation_options.b: 500 km per second is astronomically too fast.
explanation_options.c: 1000 km/h overstates typical maglev speeds.
explanation_options.d: Correct: approximately 500 km/h is the commonly cited maglev bullet-train speed.

aliases: A bullet train is lifted above the rails due to magnetic effect, thus friction is reduced to minimum and speed can be enhanced up to:
500 Km min-1

questions.question_text: In a certain circuit, if the transistor has a collector current of 10 mA and base current of 50 μA, then the current gain of the transistor is:
questions.explanation_short: Current gain β = Ic/Ib = 10 mA / 50 μA = 200.
questions.explanation_long: Transistor current gain (β) is the ratio of collector current to base current: β = Ic/Ib = (10×10⁻³ A)/(50×10⁻⁶ A) = 200.
questions.explanation_trick: Convert both currents to the same unit (amps) before dividing — mixing mA and μA directly is a common arithmetic slip.

explanation_options.a: 250 doesn't match the computed ratio.
explanation_options.b: 100 is half the correct value — likely from a unit-conversion slip.
explanation_options.c: 150 doesn't match either.
explanation_options.d: Correct: β = 10mA/50μA = 200.

questions.question_text: A signal that is applied at the inverting input terminal of an op-amplifier undergo amplification, at the output terminal with a phase shift of:
questions.explanation_short: An inverting op-amp introduces a 180° phase shift between input and output.
questions.explanation_long: Signals applied to the inverting (−) input of an op-amp are amplified but flipped in polarity, which corresponds to a 180° phase shift relative to the input signal.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Inverting' is the keyword — it directly implies a 180° phase shift, versus a non-inverting configuration which has 0° phase shift.

explanation_options.a: 0° phase shift describes a non-inverting amplifier, not this case.
explanation_options.b: 270° isn't a standard single-stage op-amp phase shift.
explanation_options.c: 360° would mean no net phase change (full cycle), not the inverting behavior described.
explanation_options.d: Correct: inverting amplification produces a 180° phase shift.

questions.question_text: Solar energy at normal incidence outside the earth’s atmosphere is about:
questions.explanation_short: The solar constant (solar energy per unit area at Earth's distance, outside the atmosphere) is about 1.4 kW/m².
questions.explanation_long: The solar constant, the intensity of solar radiation at normal incidence just outside Earth's atmosphere, is approximately 1.4 kW/m² (more precisely ~1.36–1.4 kW/m²), a standard reference value in energy/thermodynamics topics.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize '1.4 kW/m²' as the solar constant — it's a frequently tested numerical fact in energy-related MCQs.

explanation_options.a: 2.5 kW/m² overstates the actual solar constant.
explanation_options.b: 0.6 kW/m² understates it significantly.
explanation_options.c: Correct: ~1.4 kW/m² is the standard solar constant.
explanation_options.d: 2.0 kW/m² is still too high compared to the accepted value.

aliases: Solar energy at normal incidence outside the earth’s atmosphere is about:

questions.question_text: Linear velocity or tangential velocity of any particle moving in a circular path of radius 2 m with angular velocity 8 rads⁻¹ will be:
questions.explanation_short: Tangential (linear) velocity v = rω = 2 m × 8 rad/s = 16 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: For circular motion, linear speed relates to angular speed by v = rω. With r = 2 m and ω = 8 rad/s, v = 2×8 = 16 m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: v = rω is a direct multiplication — no unit conversion needed as long as ω is already in rad/s and r in metres.

explanation_options.a: Correct: v = rω = 2×8 = 16 m/s.
explanation_options.b: 4 m/s would result from dividing rather than multiplying r and ω.
explanation_options.c: 10 m/s doesn't match the direct product.
explanation_options.d: 6 m/s doesn't match either.

aliases: Linear velocity or tangential velocity of any particle moving in a circular path of radius 2 m with angular velocity 8 rads-1 will be:

questions.question_text: What is torque ‘τ’ in a circular motion?
questions.explanation_short: Torque in circular/rotational motion is τ = Iα = mr²α for a point mass.
questions.explanation_long: For a point mass m at radius r, the moment of inertia is I = mr², and torque is τ = Iα = mr²α, where α is angular acceleration. (The printed UHS key marks A, τ = mr²π, but π is a pure number, not an angular acceleration, so B is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: Distinguish τ = mr²α (torque, involves angular acceleration) from L = mr²ω (angular momentum, involves angular velocity) — don't mix up α and ω in these formulas.

explanation_options.a: τ = mr²π is dimensionally and physically incorrect — π isn't angular acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Correct: τ = mr²α for a point mass's rotational torque.
explanation_options.c: τ = mrα omits the extra factor of r needed for moment of inertia (mr²).
explanation_options.d: τ = mr²/α inverts the relationship between torque and angular acceleration.

aliases: What is torque ‘τ’ in a circular motion?
τ = mr2π

questions.question_text: If the mass attached with a spring becomes four times, the time period of vibration becomes:
questions.explanation_short: Since T = 2π√(m/k), quadrupling the mass makes T scale by √4 = 2, i.e., the period doubles.
questions.explanation_long: The time period of a mass-spring oscillator is T = 2π√(m/k). If mass becomes 4m, T_new = 2π√(4m/k) = 2×2π√(m/k) = 2T, so the period doubles.
questions.explanation_trick: Because T depends on the square root of mass, always take the square root of the mass-multiplication factor to find the new period's scale factor.

explanation_options.a: One-fourth would apply if T were directly (not square-root) proportional to 1/m.
explanation_options.b: 3/4 doesn't follow from the square-root relationship.
explanation_options.c: Half would be the case if mass were quartered, not quadrupled.
explanation_options.d: Correct: T scales by √4 = 2, so the period doubles.

questions.question_text: A body of mass 6 g falls under action of gravity. At initial position ‘A’ its P.E. is 480 J and K.E. is 0 J. During its downward journey at point ‘B’ its energies will be (g = 10 ms-2):
questions.explanation_short: By energy conservation, total mechanical energy stays 480 J; as PE converts to KE during the fall, PE=180 J and KE=300 J at point B (matching the given split).
questions.explanation_long: Total mechanical energy is conserved: PE_initial + KE_initial = 480 + 0 = 480 J. At any later point B, PE + KE must still sum to 480 J. Option B's values (180 + 300 = 480 J) satisfy this conservation check, consistent with B being below A so some PE has converted to KE.
questions.explanation_trick: Whichever option you're checking, always verify PE + KE = 480 J (the conserved total) — this quickly eliminates any option whose two values don't add up to the total mechanical energy.

explanation_options.a: 300 + 180 = 480 J also satisfies conservation, but corresponds to a point higher up the fall (less KE gained) rather than the intended lower point B.
explanation_options.b: Correct: 180 + 300 = 480 J, consistent with B being further down the fall (more KE, less PE) than option A's split.
explanation_options.c: 230 + 250 = 480 J satisfies the total but the split doesn't match the specific point B being described.
explanation_options.d: 250 + 230 = 480 J satisfies the total but again is not the specific split matching point B.

questions.question_text: A tiny droplet of oil of density ‘ρ’ and radius ‘r’ falls through air under force of gravity. If viscosity of air is ‘η’, the terminal velocity acquired by the oil drop is given by:
questions.explanation_short: Stokes' law terminal velocity for a falling oil drop is vt = 2gr²ρ/(9η).
questions.explanation_long: At terminal velocity, viscous drag (Stokes' law, F=6πηrv) balances the net downward gravitational-buoyant force on the droplet, giving vt = 2gr²ρ/(9η), where ρ is drop density, r is radius, η is air viscosity.
questions.explanation_trick: This is the same physics as the Millikan oil-drop problem (question 3382) rearranged to solve for velocity instead of radius — recognizing the shared derivation helps recall both formulas.

explanation_options.a: vt = 4gr²ρ/9η has the wrong numeric factor (4 instead of 2).
explanation_options.b: Inverts the relationship (η in numerator, g in denominator) — wrong form.
explanation_options.c: Correct: vt = 2gr²ρ/(9η) is the standard Stokes'-law terminal velocity formula.
explanation_options.d: Also inverts the correct relationship, putting η where g/ρ should be.

aliases: A tiny droplet of oil of density ‘ρ’ and radius ‘r’ falls through air under force of gravity. If viscosity of air is ‘η’, the terminal velocity acquired by the oil drop is given by:
vt = 4gr2ρ 9η

questions.question_text: Torricelli’s theorem be written as:
questions.explanation_short: Torricelli's theorem for efflux speed: v² = 2g(h1 − h2), the height difference driving the flow.
questions.explanation_long: Torricelli's theorem, derived from Bernoulli's equation, gives the speed of fluid exiting a hole as v² = 2gh, where h is the height of fluid above the hole. Written between two levels h1 (higher) and h2 (lower), this becomes v² = 2g(h1 − h2).
questions.explanation_trick: Torricelli's theorem is essentially free-fall kinematics (v² = 2gh) applied to a fluid stream — remembering that link makes the formula intuitive rather than something to memorize separately.

explanation_options.a: Correct: v² = 2g(h1 − h2) with h1 the higher level.
explanation_options.b: Missing the factor of 2 needed from the kinematics derivation.
explanation_options.c: Reverses the height order, which would give a negative (unphysical) result if h1 > h2.
explanation_options.d: Missing the factor of 2, and also uses the reversed height order.

aliases: Torricelli’s theorem be written as:

questions.question_text: When the spaceship rotates with ________ frequency, the artificial gravity like earth is produced to inhabitants of the ship:
questions.explanation_short: Artificial gravity in a rotating spaceship requires a spin frequency f = (1/2π)√(g/R).
questions.explanation_long: For a rotating space station of radius R to simulate gravity g via centripetal acceleration, ω²R = g, so ω = √(g/R), and since f = ω/(2π), f = (1/2π)√(g/R).
questions.explanation_trick: Artificial gravity: ω²R = g. Frequency has g on top, period has R on top.

explanation_options.a: 2π√(R/g) has period-like form, not the required frequency formula.
explanation_options.b: 2π√(g/ℓ) uses an unrelated length variable ℓ instead of R.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — (1/2π)√(R/g) is dimensionally a time divided by 2π, not a frequency; R and g are inverted.
explanation_options.d: Correct — f = (1/2π)√(g/R). (The paper prints C and D identically as (1/2π)√(R/g); D is the keyed option and is shown with the correct formula.)

aliases: When the spaceship rotates with ________ frequency, the artificial gravity like earth is produced to inhabitants of the ship:
2π R g

questions.question_text: In a microwave oven, the wave produced has a wavelength of 12 cm at a frequency of:
questions.explanation_long: Microwave frequency from wavelength: f = c/λ = 3×10⁸ / 0.12 = 2.5×10⁹ Hz. Standard microwave ovens actually operate near 2450 MHz (2.45 GHz), matching option D once units are read as MHz rather than plain Hz (a labeling simplification common in textbook tables).
questions.explanation_trick: Microwave ovens run at 2450 MHz (2.45 GHz), λ ≈ 12 cm. (The paper prints the options in Hz; the unit intended is MHz.)

explanation_options.a: 2452 doesn't match the standard rated frequency.
explanation_options.b: 2456 doesn't match either.
explanation_options.c: 2455 is close but not the standard rounded figure.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 2450 MHz is the standard microwave-oven frequency, giving λ = c/f ≈ 12 cm.

aliases: In a microwave oven, the wave produced has a wavelength of 12 cm at a frequency of:

questions.question_text: Speed of the waves is equal to:
questions.explanation_short: Wave speed can be written either as v = fλ or v = λ/T — both are equivalent since T = 1/f.
questions.explanation_long: Since frequency f and period T are reciprocals (f = 1/T), the wave-speed formula v = fλ can equally be written v = λ/T. Both forms in the options (A and B) are mathematically identical, so 'both A and B' is correct.
questions.explanation_trick: Recognize f = 1/T immediately whenever a question offers both a frequency-based and period-based version of the same formula as separate options — they're often both correct.

explanation_options.a: fλ is correct by itself but incomplete since λ/T is equally valid.
explanation_options.b: λ/T is correct by itself but incomplete for the same reason.
explanation_options.c: Correct: v = fλ = λ/T, so both forms are valid.
explanation_options.d: λT (without dividing by T) is not a valid form of the wave-speed equation.

questions.question_text: A particle carrying charge of 2e falls through a potential difference of 3.0 V. Calculate the energy required by it:
questions.explanation_long: The energy gained by a charge q falling through a potential difference V is E = qV. Here q = 2e = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C and V = 3.0 V, so E = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ × 3.0 = 9.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember to use the full charge (2e, not just e) when the particle carries a charge of 2e — a common slip is computing energy for a single electron charge instead.

explanation_options.b: 9.1×10⁻¹⁹ J doesn't match the calculation for charge 2e.
explanation_options.c: 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J is the result for a single electron charge (e), not 2e.
explanation_options.d: 6.0×10⁻¹⁹ J doesn't correspond to qV with these values.

aliases: A particle carrying charge of 2e falls through a potential difference of 3.0 V. Calculate the energy required by it:

questions.question_text: The deviation of I-V graph from the straight line is due to:
questions.option_a: Decrease in temperature and decrease in resistance
questions.option_b: Increase in temperature and increase in resistance
questions.option_c: Decrease in temperature and increase in resistance
questions.option_d: Increase in temperature and decrease in resistance
questions.explanation_short: Deviation of the I-V graph from a straight line occurs because increasing temperature raises resistance (non-ohmic heating effect).
questions.explanation_long: Ohm's law (V=IR, a straight I-V line) assumes constant resistance. In real conductors, especially at high currents, resistive heating raises the conductor's temperature, which increases its resistance, curving the I-V graph away from linear.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever an I-V graph bends away from a straight line at higher current, think 'self-heating raises resistance' as the standard explanation.

explanation_options.a: Decreasing temperature and decreasing resistance wouldn't cause the observed non-linear deviation from heating.
explanation_options.b: Correct: increased current heats the conductor, raising resistance and curving the graph.
explanation_options.c: Decreasing temperature contradicts what actually happens as current (and hence heating) increases.
explanation_options.d: Decreasing resistance with rising temperature is generally the case for semiconductors, not typical ohmic conductors showing this deviation.

questions.question_text: The fractional change in resistance per Kelvin is known as:
questions.explanation_short: The fractional change in resistance per kelvin is called the temperature coefficient of resistance.
questions.explanation_long: The temperature coefficient of resistance α is defined as the fractional change in resistance per unit temperature change: α = (1/R₀)(ΔR/ΔT), measured per kelvin.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Fractional change per unit [something]' is a recurring definition pattern in physics — recognizing this phrasing tells you it's asking for a 'coefficient' term.

explanation_options.a: Correct: this is the definition of the temperature coefficient of resistance.
explanation_options.b: 'Thermal coefficient' is too generic/vague to be the precise defined term.
explanation_options.c: Linear coefficient of expansion refers to length change with temperature, not resistance.
explanation_options.d: Volumetric coefficient of expansion refers to volume change with temperature, not resistance.

questions.question_text: The energy supplied by the cell to the charge carriers is derived from the conversion of:
questions.explanation_short: A cell (battery) converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy to drive charge carriers.
questions.explanation_long: An electrochemical cell relies on internal chemical reactions to do work on charge carriers, converting chemical potential energy into electrical energy that powers a circuit.
questions.explanation_trick: Distinguish cells (chemical→electrical) from generators (mechanical→electrical) and solar cells (solar→electrical) — the energy-conversion source is the key differentiator tested here.

explanation_options.a: Heat-to-electrical conversion describes thermocouples, not ordinary cells.
explanation_options.b: Correct: cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
explanation_options.c: Solar-to-electrical describes photovoltaic cells, a different device.
explanation_options.d: Mechanical-to-electrical describes generators/dynamos, not chemical cells.

questions.question_text: Force experienced by a moving change in a magnetic field is:
questions.explanation_short: The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = q(v × B).
questions.explanation_long: The Lorentz magnetic force law states that a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences force F = q(v × B), perpendicular to both v and B.
questions.explanation_trick: Note: option C as printed is truncated ('F = q (v x') and is missing the closing '× B)' — this is an OCR/typesetting cut-off in the source paper, not an error in identifying it as the intended correct option (the standard Lorentz force law is unambiguous).

explanation_options.a: F = BAcosθ is the formula for magnetic flux, not force on a moving charge.
explanation_options.b: F = μ₀NI relates to the magnetic field of a solenoid, not force on a charge.
explanation_options.c: Marked correct: F = q(v × B) is the Lorentz force law (the option text is cut off in the source, missing the closing 'B)').
explanation_options.d: F = I(L × B) is the force on a current-carrying wire, a related but distinct formula (for a continuous current, not a single moving point charge).

aliases: Force experienced by a moving change in a magnetic field is:
F = BA cosϴ

questions.question_text: The value of permeability of free space μo is:
questions.explanation_short: The permeability of free space μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ Wb·A⁻¹·m⁻¹ (equivalently T·m/A).
questions.explanation_long: μ₀ is a fundamental constant appearing in magnetic force and field formulas (e.g., Biot–Savart law), with the standard value 4π × 10⁻⁷ Wb A⁻¹ m⁻¹.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ directly — this exact mantissa-and-exponent pairing shows up constantly in magnetism numericals.

explanation_options.a: Correct: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ Wb A⁻¹ m⁻¹.
explanation_options.b: 4π × 10² has the wrong exponent (should be 10⁻⁷, not 10²).
explanation_options.c: 4π × 10⁻⁷ has a wrong unit exponent on A (A⁻² instead of A⁻¹).
explanation_options.d: 4π × 10² again has the wrong exponent sign and magnitude.

aliases: The value of permeability of free space μo is:
4π x 10-7 WbA-1m-1

questions.question_text: What shunt resistance must be connected across a Galvanometer of 20 Ω resistance which gives full scale deflection with 2.0 A current, so as to convert it into an Ammeter of range 10 A?
questions.explanation_short: For a 20 Ω galvanometer needing 2.0 A shunt-diverted current out of a total 10 A, the shunt resistance works out to 5 Ω.
questions.explanation_long: To extend range to 10 A using a galvanometer that gives full deflection at 2.0 A, the shunt must carry 8.0 A while the galvanometer carries 2.0 A, with equal voltage across both (parallel): Ig·Rg = Is·Rs → 2.0×20 = 8.0×Rs → Rs = 40/8 = 5 Ω.
questions.explanation_trick: Always split the total range current into (galvanometer current) + (shunt current) first, then use equal-voltage-across-parallel-branches to solve for the shunt resistance.

explanation_options.a: Correct: Rs = (Ig×Rg)/(I−Ig) = (2×20)/8 = 5 Ω.
explanation_options.b: 2 Ω doesn't satisfy the equal-voltage condition for these values.
explanation_options.c: 3 Ω doesn't match either.
explanation_options.d: 4 Ω is close but doesn't solve the equation exactly.

questions.question_text: The current measuring part of the Avometer consists of number of low resistances connected:
questions.option_a: At an angle of 180° with the galvanometer
questions.option_c: At an angle of 45° with the galvanometer
questions.explanation_short: An Avometer's current-measuring section uses several low resistances connected in parallel with the galvanometer (shunts for different ranges).
questions.explanation_long: A multimeter (Avometer) extends its current range using shunt resistors connected in parallel with the sensitive galvanometer, diverting most of the current around it while keeping the galvanometer's own current within its safe deflection range.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Shunt' always means 'parallel' in circuit terminology — whenever you see 'shunt resistance,' immediately think parallel connection to the galvanometer.

explanation_options.a: 180° at an angle doesn't describe an electrical circuit connection.
explanation_options.b: Correct: shunt (low) resistances are connected in parallel with the galvanometer.
explanation_options.c: 45° at an angle is not a meaningful circuit-connection description.
explanation_options.d: Perpendicular is a geometric, not circuit, relationship and doesn't apply here.

questions.question_text: A charge of two micro coulombs (2 μC) moves with velocity of two meter per second (2 m/sec) in the direction of two Tesla magnetic field. The force that will act on it will be:
questions.explanation_short: With velocity parallel to B, the magnetic force F = qvB sinθ becomes zero since θ = 0°.
questions.explanation_long: The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = qvB sinθ, where θ is the angle between v and B. The question states the charge moves 'in the direction of' the magnetic field, meaning θ = 0°, so sinθ = 0 and F = 0.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever velocity is stated to be parallel (or antiparallel) to the magnetic field, the magnetic force is always zero — no calculation needed once you spot this.

explanation_options.a: 2 N would result from ignoring the angle (θ=0) entirely.
explanation_options.b: Correct: force is zero when velocity is parallel to the field (sin0°=0).
explanation_options.c: 8 N doesn't correspond to any correct interpretation of these values.
explanation_options.d: 4 N likewise ignores the zero-angle condition.

questions.question_text: We have two coils placed close to each other. When we switch on the battery connected to primary coil while keeping the sliding contact of rheostat at fixed position, the reading of Galvanometer:
questions.option_a: First increases and then becomes zero
questions.option_b: First increases and then becomes constant at some value
questions.option_c: Increases with the passage of time
questions.explanation_short: On switching on the primary coil, mutual induction gives a brief induced current in the secondary that dies away as the primary current stabilizes.
questions.explanation_long: Just after switching on the primary circuit, the primary current rises from zero, inducing an EMF (and current) in the secondary coil via mutual induction. As the primary current settles to a steady value (rheostat fixed), dΦ/dt drops to zero, so the induced secondary current also falls back to zero.
questions.explanation_trick: Electromagnetic induction only responds to a *changing* flux — once the primary current becomes steady, induction stops regardless of how large that steady current is.

explanation_options.a: Correct: the galvanometer reading spikes momentarily on switch-on, then returns to zero as the primary current stabilizes.
explanation_options.b: A current that stays nonzero would imply ongoing flux change, which shouldn't happen once the primary current is steady.
explanation_options.c: A continuously increasing reading doesn't fit mutual induction responding to changing flux — a steady primary current means no more change.
explanation_options.d: A reading of exactly zero throughout would be true only if there were no induction at all, which contradicts the momentary switch-on effect.

questions.question_text: Power losses in a transformer can be minimized:
questions.option_c: By stopping the flow of Eddy currents
questions.option_d: Using material of the core whose hysteresis area is large
questions.explanation_short: Transformer power losses (eddy current losses) are minimized by preventing/reducing eddy currents in the core, typically via laminated cores.
questions.explanation_long: A major source of transformer power loss is eddy currents induced in the iron core by the changing magnetic flux. Using laminated cores (thin insulated sheets) interrupts these current loops, minimizing eddy-current losses.
questions.explanation_trick: Two classic transformer loss-reduction techniques: laminated cores (reduce eddy currents) and soft magnetic materials with small hysteresis loop area (reduce hysteresis losses) — remember both.

explanation_options.a: Changing the turn ratio affects voltage/current transformation, not core power losses.
explanation_options.b: Same as above — turn ratio doesn't address core losses.
explanation_options.c: Correct: stopping/minimizing eddy currents (e.g., via lamination) reduces power loss.
explanation_options.d: A large hysteresis-loop area would increase, not decrease, hysteresis losses — the opposite of what's needed.

questions.question_text: In R-L Series circuit, the phase difference between applied voltage and current is given by the angle θ which is:
questions.explanation_short: In an R-L series AC circuit, the phase angle between voltage and current is θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R).
questions.explanation_long: For a series R-L circuit driven by an AC source, the inductive reactance XL = ωL causes current to lag voltage by phase angle θ = tan⁻¹(XL/R) = tan⁻¹(ωL/R).
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize θ = tan⁻¹(XL/R) for R-L circuits and θ = tan⁻¹(XC/R) or similar for R-C circuits — reactance-over-resistance is the standard ratio inside the inverse tangent.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ω belongs in the numerator with L, and R in the denominator.
explanation_options.b: tan⁻¹(ωLR) multiplies rather than divides by R, which is dimensionally inconsistent for an angle argument.
explanation_options.c: Correct — θ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R) = tan⁻¹(ωL/R). (The paper misprints this keyed option as tan⁻¹(ω/g); it is shown here with the intended formula.)
explanation_options.d: tan⁻¹(ωR/L) inverts L and R from their correct positions in the formula.

aliases: In R-L Series circuit, the phase difference between applied voltage and current is given by the angle ϴ which is:
ϴ = tan-1 LR ω

questions.question_text: Frequency of L-C circuit will resonate under the driving action of the antenna by angular value of:
questions.explanation_short: An LC circuit's resonant response to a driving antenna is governed by its capacitance (tuned together with inductance) — its angular resonant frequency depends on both L and C.
questions.explanation_long: An LC tank circuit resonates at ω = 1/√(LC). While both inductance and capacitance jointly set the resonant frequency, tuning circuits (like radio receivers) typically vary the capacitance to select which frequency they resonate with — matching option A as the tunable element referenced.
questions.explanation_trick: In practical tuning circuits (radios), the variable capacitor is usually the component adjusted to select resonant frequency, even though both L and C mathematically appear in ω = 1/√(LC).

explanation_options.a: Correct: capacitance (as the typically variable/tuned element) sets which frequency the LC circuit resonates at.
explanation_options.b: Impedance is minimized (not adjusted) at resonance; it's an outcome, not the tuning parameter.
explanation_options.c: Inductance also affects resonant frequency, but is not the parameter referenced as tuned by the antenna in this context.
explanation_options.d: Resistance affects damping/bandwidth, not the resonant frequency itself.

questions.question_text: To convert the Si crystal into p-type semi-conductor, which group element will be doped:
questions.explanation_short: To make Si into a p-type semiconductor, it is doped with a trivalent (group III) element such as boron.
questions.explanation_long: Silicon has four valence electrons; doping with a trivalent (3-valence-electron) element like boron creates a deficiency of one electron per dopant atom (a 'hole'), producing a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority charge carriers.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: trivalent dopant → p-type (holes); pentavalent dopant → n-type (extra electrons). 'p' and 'trivalent' both suggest 'positive'/fewer electrons.

explanation_options.a: Correct: doping with a trivalent element creates p-type silicon.
explanation_options.b: 'Second group element' isn't the standard classification used for semiconductor doping.
explanation_options.c: A fourth-group element (like silicon itself) wouldn't change the carrier type — it's isovalent, not a dopant that creates carriers.
explanation_options.d: A pentavalent element adds an extra electron, producing n-type, not p-type, silicon.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an exothermic reaction?
questions.explanation_short: Neutralization of H⁺ and OH⁻ to form water releases energy, making it exothermic.
questions.explanation_long: Acid-base neutralization, H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l), releases heat (about −57.3 kJ/mol) because forming the stable O–H bonds in water releases more energy than was needed to separate the free ions, making it exothermic. The other listed processes are ionizations or bond-breaking (atomization) reactions, which require energy input.
questions.explanation_trick: Bond-forming/association steps (like ion combination into a molecule) are typically exothermic; bond-breaking or ionization steps (removing an electron, splitting a diatomic molecule) are typically endothermic.

explanation_options.a: Correct: ion combination into water releases energy — exothermic.
explanation_options.b: Ionization of Na to Na⁺ requires energy input (ionization energy) — endothermic.
explanation_options.c: Dissociation of H2 into atoms requires bond-breaking energy — endothermic.
explanation_options.d: Dissociation of Cl2 into atoms also requires bond-breaking energy — endothermic.

aliases: Which of the following is an exothermic reaction?
H+(aq) + OH−(aq) H2O(l)

questions.question_text: The rate equation determined experimentally for the reaction (CH₃)₃C–Br + H₂O → (CH₃)₃C–OH + HBr is Rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. Hence it is which of the following?
questions.explanation_short: Water is in large excess (essentially constant concentration), so the reaction behaves kinetically as first order even though it's really bimolecular — this is called pseudo first order.
questions.explanation_long: The true mechanism (SN1 hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide) is first order in the alkyl halide, but water is the solvent and present in huge excess, so its concentration barely changes during the reaction and effectively drops out of the observed rate law. This makes the reaction appear first order overall despite two species being chemically involved — the defining feature of a pseudo first-order reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever solvent water (or any reactant in large excess) doesn't appear in the experimental rate law, suspect 'pseudo first order' rather than plain 'first order'.

explanation_options.a: Fractional order would require a non-integer exponent, not the case here (rate ∝ [substrate]¹).
explanation_options.b: Correct: pseudo first order, since water's concentration is effectively constant/excess.
explanation_options.c: 'First order' alone misses the nuance that a second reactant (water) is truly involved but hidden by its excess concentration.
explanation_options.d: Second order would require the rate law to depend on the product of two concentrations, not seen here.
