explanation_options.a: This is backwards — the oxide layer protects against, rather than exposes the metal to, further atmospheric attack.
explanation_options.b: The oxide coating typically reduces further reactivity by blocking access to the metal surface, rather than increasing reactivity.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the oxide layer forms a protective barrier against further atmospheric corrosion.
explanation_options.d: A 'shiny silvery appearance' actually describes the freshly-cut, un-oxidized metal; the oxide layer typically dulls this shine rather than being valued for appearance.

questions.question_text: In silicon dioxide each silicon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms. The ratio of silicon to oxygen atoms is:
questions.explanation_short: In silicon dioxide's structure, each silicon atom bonds to 4 oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is shared between 2 silicon atoms, giving an overall silicon-to-oxygen ratio of 1:2 (matching the formula SiO₂).
questions.explanation_long: Although locally each Si is surrounded tetrahedrally by 4 O atoms, each O atom bridges two different Si atoms (is shared between them). Counting atoms per formula unit: each Si effectively 'owns' 4 O atoms shared with another Si, i.e., 4/2 = 2 oxygens per silicon, giving the familiar SiO₂ formula, i.e., a 1:2 silicon-to-oxygen ratio.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't just count 'each Si touches 4 O' as the final ratio — since each O is SHARED between two Si atoms, you must divide by 2 to get the actual formula ratio, giving SiO₂ (1:2), not 1:4.

explanation_options.a: This double-counts the sharing incorrectly and doesn't match SiO₂'s known 1:2 formula ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 1:2 matches the well-known SiO₂ formula, accounting for oxygen atoms being shared between two silicons.
explanation_options.c: This inverts the actual ratio (which should have MORE oxygen than silicon, being SiO₂, not Si₂O).
explanation_options.d: This overcounts oxygen without accounting correctly for the local coordination and sharing described.

questions.question_text: Hydrogenation of unsaturated oils is done by using:
questions.explanation_short: Hydrogenation of unsaturated (vegetable) oils — converting C=C double bonds to single bonds by adding hydrogen — is carried out using finely divided nickel as a catalyst.
questions.explanation_long: Industrial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (to produce margarine and similar hardened fats) passes hydrogen gas over the liquid oil in the presence of a finely divided nickel catalyst at moderate temperature and pressure. The nickel catalyst provides a surface where H₂ molecules dissociate and add across the C=C double bonds of the unsaturated fatty acid chains, converting them to saturated (solid, higher-melting) fats.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Hydrogenation of oils uses nickel catalyst' is a classic, frequently tested industrial chemistry fact — the fine division maximizes surface area for catalytic activity.

explanation_options.a: Correct — finely divided nickel is the standard industrial catalyst for oil hydrogenation.
explanation_options.b: Iron is the catalyst used in the Haber process (ammonia synthesis), not oil hydrogenation.
explanation_options.c: Vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst used in the Contact Process (sulfuric acid manufacture), not oil hydrogenation.
explanation_options.d: Copper isn't the standard catalyst for hydrogenating vegetable oils.

questions.question_text: Pick the correct statement:
questions.option_a: Chelates are usually more stable than ordinary complexes
questions.option_b: Ordinary complexes are more stable than chelates
questions.option_c: Monodentate ligands form the chelates complexes
questions.explanation_short: Chelates (complexes formed with polydentate ligands binding through multiple points) are generally more stable than similar complexes formed with monodentate (single-point-binding) ligands — this extra stability is called the chelate effect.
questions.explanation_long: A chelating ligand attaches to the central metal ion at two or more points (bidentate, tridentate, etc.), forming ring structures. This multi-point attachment (and the associated entropy increase upon complex formation) makes chelate complexes significantly more thermodynamically stable than comparable complexes formed from multiple separate monodentate ligands — a phenomenon known as the 'chelate effect'.
questions.explanation_trick: The 'chelate effect' is the standard name for chelates' extra stability over similar monodentate complexes — remember: chelates form rings, and ring formation adds stability.

explanation_options.a: Correct — chelates being more stable than ordinary (monodentate) complexes is precisely the chelate effect.
explanation_options.b: This reverses the actual (well-established) chelate effect, which favors chelates as more stable.
explanation_options.c: Monodentate ligands, by definition, bind at only one point and do NOT themselves form chelate rings (chelation requires multidentate ligands).
explanation_options.d: Chelates specifically DO have ring structures (formed by the multidentate ligand wrapping around the metal), contradicting this option.

aliases: Pick the correct statement:
Chelates are usually more stable than ordinary

questions.question_text: In contact process, the catalyst used for the conversion of Sulphur dioxide to Sulphur trioxide is:
questions.explanation_short: In the Contact Process for manufacturing sulfuric acid, vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is the catalyst used to convert sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide.
questions.explanation_long: The key catalytic step of the Contact Process is 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, carried out at around 450°C using a vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst, which speeds up this equilibrium reaction industrially before the SO₃ is subsequently absorbed to make sulfuric acid.
questions.explanation_trick: Contact Process = vanadium pentoxide catalyst for SO₂ → SO₃; this is a frequently tested industrial-chemistry catalyst-process pairing (compare with iron for the Haber process, nickel for hydrogenation).

explanation_options.a: Magnesium oxide is not the industrial catalyst used in the Contact Process.
explanation_options.b: Aluminum oxide is not the standard catalyst for this specific conversion.
explanation_options.c: Silicon dioxide is not a catalyst used in the Contact Process.
explanation_options.d: Correct — vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst specifically used for the SO₂-to-SO₃ conversion step.

questions.question_text: The unpolluted natural rain water is slightly acidic due to the reaction of rain water with:
questions.explanation_short: Even unpolluted rainwater is naturally slightly acidic because atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in it, forming weak carbonic acid.
questions.explanation_long: CO₂ present naturally in the atmosphere dissolves into falling raindrops, reacting as CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), a weak acid that lowers rainwater's pH to around 5.6 even without any pollution. Additional pollutants (like sulfur/nitrogen oxides) can make rain considerably MORE acidic (true 'acid rain'), but the baseline natural acidity comes from dissolved CO₂. (The printed UHS key marks A, sulphur dioxide, but SO₂ causes polluted acid rain; the natural slight acidity of clean rain (pH ≈ 5.6) comes from dissolved CO₂, so C is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: 'Unpolluted' rain is still mildly acidic (~pH 5.6) purely from dissolved atmospheric CO₂ forming carbonic acid — true, human-caused 'acid rain' (much lower pH) comes from added SO₂/NOₓ pollutants, a separate phenomenon.

explanation_options.a: Sulphur dioxide is the primary pollutant responsible for man-made acid rain, not for the natural background acidity of unpolluted rainwater.
explanation_options.b: Oxides of nitrogen similarly contribute to pollution-driven acid rain, not to the natural baseline acidity being asked about here.
explanation_options.c: Correct — carbon dioxide dissolving to form carbonic acid explains the natural, mild acidity of unpolluted rainwater.
explanation_options.d: Hydrogen gas isn't a significant naturally occurring atmospheric component responsible for rainwater acidity.

questions.question_text: In the Haber's process for the manufacturing of ammonia, nitrogen is taken from:
questions.explanation_short: In the Haber Process, the nitrogen needed to make ammonia is obtained from the air (which is about 78% nitrogen gas, N₂).
questions.explanation_long: The Haber Process synthesizes ammonia via N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The nitrogen feedstock is sourced from the atmosphere (fractional distillation of liquefied air, or by burning fuel in air and removing the oxygen/CO₂ to leave N₂), since air is a virtually unlimited, cheap source of nitrogen gas.
questions.explanation_trick: Air is ~78% N₂ by volume — this is why industrial nitrogen fixation processes (like Haber's) draw their nitrogen straight from the atmosphere rather than from any chemical compound source.

explanation_options.a: Proteins are a biological nitrogen source (via decomposition), not the industrial source used in the Haber Process.
explanation_options.b: Industrially manufactured ammonium salts would themselves already require nitrogen fixation to produce — not a raw nitrogen source for the process.
explanation_options.c: Correct — atmospheric air is the practical industrial source of nitrogen gas for the Haber Process.
explanation_options.d: Nitrate-containing minerals are a nitrogen source for some other extraction methods (historically, e.g., Chile saltpeter), but not the standard modern Haber Process feedstock.

questions.question_text: In comparison with oxygen gas, a strong triple bond is present between two nitrogen atoms in a molecule and therefore nitrogen gas is:
questions.explanation_short: The very strong N≡N triple bond makes nitrogen a very unreactive gas — but not completely inert, since it does react under suitable conditions.
questions.explanation_long: Breaking the N≡N triple bond needs 946 kJ mol⁻¹, so nitrogen reacts far less readily than oxygen. It is not completely inert like the noble gases, however: it combines with hydrogen in the Haber process, with oxygen during lightning, and with hot metals such as magnesium and lithium to form nitrides. 'Very less reactive' is therefore the accurate description. (The printed UHS key marks B, but nitrogen does form compounds, so it is not completely inert.)
questions.explanation_trick: N₂ is unreactive, not inert — think of the Haber process and nitrides of Mg and Li.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the strong triple bond makes nitrogen unreactive, not highly reactive.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — unlike the noble gases, nitrogen forms compounds such as NH₃, NO and Mg₃N₂.
explanation_options.c: Correct — nitrogen is a very unreactive gas because of its strong triple bond.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — nitrogen is much less reactive than 'moderately reactive' suggests.

questions.question_text: The compound with an atom, which has unshared pair of electrons is called:
questions.explanation_short: A nucleophile is a species (often bearing a lone/unshared pair of electrons) that donates that electron pair to form a new bond, typically attacking electron-deficient centers.
questions.explanation_long: Nucleophiles are electron-rich species — they have an available lone pair (or negative charge) that they can donate to form a new covalent bond with an electrophile (an electron-poor species). Common nucleophiles include ions like CN⁻, OH⁻, and neutral molecules with lone pairs like NH₃ or H₂O.
questions.explanation_trick: Nucleophile = 'nucleus-loving', i.e., attracted to positive centers, because it has electrons (a lone pair) to donate — the opposite of an electrophile, which seeks electrons.

explanation_options.a: Correct — having an unshared (lone) pair of electrons to donate is the defining feature of a nucleophile.
explanation_options.b: Electrophiles are electron-poor species that ACCEPT electron pairs, the opposite of what's described (having a lone pair to give).
explanation_options.c: 'Protophile' is not a standard term used for this electron-pair-donating property.
explanation_options.d: Since 'nucleophile' (option A) correctly matches the description, 'none of the above' would be incorrect.

questions.question_text: 1-chloropropane and 2-chlorpropane are isomers of each other, the type of isomerism in these two is called:
questions.explanation_short: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane are structural isomers differing only in WHERE the chlorine atom is attached on the same carbon skeleton — this is called position (positional) isomerism.
questions.explanation_long: Both compounds share the identical molecular formula and the same basic propane carbon chain, but the chlorine substituent is located on a different carbon (position 1 vs. position 2). Since only the position of the substituent differs (not the carbon skeleton itself, nor the functional group type, nor any cis/trans spatial arrangement), this is classified as position isomerism, a type of structural (constitutional) isomerism.
questions.explanation_trick: Same carbon skeleton + same functional group, but different attachment POSITION = position isomerism; a different carbon skeleton entirely would instead be chain isomerism.

explanation_options.a: Cis-trans isomerism requires restricted rotation (e.g., around a double bond or ring), which isn't relevant to these simple chain compounds.
explanation_options.b: Chain isomerism would require a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton itself (e.g., branched vs. straight chain), not just a different substituent position on the same skeleton.
explanation_options.c: Correct — differing only in the chlorine's position on an identical carbon skeleton is the definition of position isomerism.
explanation_options.d: Functional group isomerism involves different functional groups altogether (e.g., an alcohol vs. an ether with the same formula), not applicable here since both are chloroalkanes.

questions.question_text: Benzene in the presence of AlCl₃ produces acetophenone when reacts with:
questions.explanation_short: Benzene reacts with acetyl chloride (CH₃COCl) in the presence of AlCl₃ (a Friedel-Crafts acylation) to produce acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃).
questions.explanation_long: Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acyl halide (like acetyl chloride) with a Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl₃) to introduce an acyl group (–COCH₃) onto the benzene ring, replacing a hydrogen atom. This directly produces acetophenone, a classic named reaction and product pairing in aromatic chemistry.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Benzene + acyl chloride + AlCl₃' = Friedel-Crafts ACYLATION producing an aryl ketone (acetophenone here) — distinguish this from Friedel-Crafts ALKYLATION, which instead uses an alkyl halide and attaches an alkyl group.

explanation_options.a: Correct — acetyl chloride is the acylating agent that reacts with benzene (with AlCl₃ catalyst) to give acetophenone.
explanation_options.b: Acetic acid alone (without being converted to a more reactive acyl chloride/anhydride) does not readily undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation with AlCl₃ under normal conditions.
explanation_options.c: Reacting with ethyl benzene wouldn't directly produce acetophenone via Friedel-Crafts acylation in this manner.
explanation_options.d: Ethanoic acid is simply another name for acetic acid, which (as with option B) is not the reactive acylating species typically used here.

aliases: Benzene in the presence of AlCl3 produces acetophenone when reacts with:
Acetyl chloride

questions.question_text: The substitution of a '–H' by '–NO₂' group in benzene is called:
questions.explanation_short: Replacing a hydrogen atom on benzene with a nitro (–NO₂) group is called nitration.
questions.explanation_long: Nitration of benzene is achieved using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid (the nitrating mixture), which generates the electrophile NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion). This electrophile substitutes for a hydrogen atom on the aromatic ring via electrophilic aromatic substitution, producing nitrobenzene.
questions.explanation_trick: '-NO₂ substitution on benzene' = nitration; compare with sulphonation (–SO₃H group) and halogenation (–X group) as other common electrophilic aromatic substitutions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this substitution reaction, installing a -NO₂ group, is precisely nitration.
explanation_options.b: 'Ammunolysis' is not a standard chemical reaction term relevant here.
explanation_options.c: Sulphonation specifically installs a –SO₃H (sulfonic acid) group, not –NO₂.
explanation_options.d: This describes a substitution (an oxidative electrophilic aromatic substitution), not a reduction of benzene.

aliases: The substitution of a '-H' by '-NO2' group in benzene is called:
Nitration

questions.question_text: When purely alcoholic solution of sodium/potassium hydroxide and halogenoalkanes are reacted an alkene is formed, what is the mechanism of reaction?
questions.explanation_short: When a halogenoalkane reacts with a purely alcoholic (ethanolic) solution of NaOH/KOH, the hydroxide acts as a base, removing a hydrogen halide (HX) to form an alkene — this is an elimination reaction.
questions.explanation_long: Alcoholic KOH/NaOH favors elimination (E2 mechanism typically) over substitution because the alcohol solvent and the strongly basic hydroxide ion promote removal of a proton from a carbon adjacent to the leaving halogen, along with the halide ion leaving, forming a C=C double bond (alkene) and releasing HX (as its salt). This contrasts with AQUEOUS KOH/NaOH, which instead favors nucleophilic substitution to give an alcohol.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Alcoholic KOH → elimination (alkene)' vs. 'aqueous KOH → substitution (alcohol)' — this solvent-dependent fork is one of the most frequently tested facts about halogenoalkane reactions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — alcoholic hydroxide promotes elimination, producing an alkene from the halogenoalkane.
explanation_options.b: Dehydration typically refers to removing water from an alcohol (e.g., using concentrated H₂SO₄), a related but distinct process from eliminating HX from a halogenoalkane.
explanation_options.c: 'Debromination' isn't the general name for this reaction (and doesn't apply specifically if the halogen isn't bromine); the general reaction type is elimination.
explanation_options.d: Reduction of benzene is unrelated to a halogenoalkane forming an alkene via base-promoted elimination.

questions.question_text: The organic compound carbon tetrachloride is used as:
questions.explanation_short: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) is commonly used as a non-polar organic solvent (e.g., historically in dry cleaning and as a solvent for fats, oils, and other non-polar substances).
questions.explanation_long: CCl₄ is a non-polar, non-flammable liquid that dissolves many organic (especially non-polar) compounds well, which made it historically popular as an industrial and dry-cleaning solvent (though its use has since been restricted due to toxicity and ozone-depleting/environmental concerns) rather than as a lubricant, oxidant, or plastic material.
questions.explanation_trick: CCl₄'s defining historical/practical use is as a SOLVENT (dry cleaning, degreasing), not as a lubricant, an oxidizing agent, or a plastic.

explanation_options.a: CCl₄ is not typically used as a mechanical lubricant.
explanation_options.b: Correct — CCl₄'s well-known application is as an organic solvent.
explanation_options.c: CCl₄ is not an oxidizing agent; in fact, its own carbon is already in its highest common oxidation state (very unreactive toward further oxidation in this role).
explanation_options.d: CCl₄ is a small molecule solvent, not a polymer/plastic material.

questions.question_text: An alcohol is converted to an aldehyde with same number of carbon atoms as that of alcohol in the presence of K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄. The alcohol is:
questions.explanation_short: Oxidation of a primary alcohol with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 under controlled conditions converts it to an aldehyde with the same number of carbon atoms — this requires the starting alcohol to be a straight-chain PRIMARY alcohol, i.e., propan-1-ol (CH3CH2CH2OH).
questions.explanation_long: Only primary alcohols (–CH₂OH group) oxidize (with acidified potassium dichromate, controlled/distilled off promptly) to aldehydes retaining the same carbon count; secondary alcohols oxidize instead to ketones, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under these conditions entirely. Propan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, is the correct starting material to give propanal (an aldehyde) with the same 3 carbons.
questions.explanation_trick: Primary alcohol → aldehyde; secondary alcohol → ketone; tertiary alcohol → resists oxidation (no reaction) — this three-way classification determines the oxidation product every time.

explanation_options.a: This structure includes a chlorine substituent altering the identity/carbon-counting context and isn't the simple straight-chain primary alcohol intended by the question.
explanation_options.b: Correct — propan-1-ol is a straight-chain primary alcohol that oxidizes cleanly to an aldehyde (propanal) with the same number of carbons.
explanation_options.c: This is a tertiary alcohol (three methyl-type groups on the carbinol carbon), which resists oxidation to a carbonyl compound under these conditions.
explanation_options.d: This is also a tertiary alcohol structure, similarly resistant to oxidation to a carbonyl compound.

aliases: An alcohol is converted to an aldehyde with same number of carbon atoms as that of alcohol in the presence of K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 the alcohol is:
CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂OH

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation_short: A secondary alcohol has its –OH group attached to a carbon that is itself bonded to exactly two other carbon atoms; isopropanol (CH₃-CH(OH)-CH₃) fits this pattern.
questions.explanation_long: Alcohols are classified by how many carbon atoms are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH group: primary (1 carbon attached), secondary (2 carbons attached), tertiary (3 carbons attached). In isopropanol, the central carbon holding -OH is bonded to two methyl (CH₃) groups (i.e., 2 carbons) plus the OH and an H, making it a secondary alcohol.
questions.explanation_trick: Count the carbons DIRECTLY attached to the carbon bearing -OH: 1 = primary, 2 = secondary, 3 = tertiary — apply this rule to quickly classify any alcohol structure.

explanation_options.a: Correct — isopropanol's OH-bearing carbon is attached to exactly two other carbons, making it secondary.
explanation_options.b: Propan-1-ol's OH-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon, making it a primary alcohol, not secondary.
explanation_options.c: This structure (with a methyl branch off the OH-carbon and only 1 other backbone carbon attached directly) is a primary alcohol structure (isobutanol), not secondary.
explanation_options.d: This structure's OH-bearing carbon is attached to three other carbon groups, making it tertiary, not secondary.

aliases: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
H3C-CH(OH)-CH3 (isopropanol)

questions.question_text: Which enzyme is involved in the fermentation of glucose:
questions.explanation_short: The enzyme zymase (found in yeast) catalyzes the fermentation of glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation_long: Fermentation of glucose by yeast is a multi-enzyme process collectively referred to under the name zymase (a complex of enzymes), converting glucose anaerobically into ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂. This is the basis of alcoholic fermentation used in brewing and baking.
questions.explanation_trick: Zymase = the yeast enzyme complex responsible for alcoholic fermentation of glucose — a classic named-enzyme fact in organic/biochemistry.

explanation_options.a: Correct — zymase is the enzyme system responsible for fermenting glucose.
explanation_options.b: Invertase hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose; it doesn't itself carry out the fermentation of glucose into ethanol.
explanation_options.c: Urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and CO₂, unrelated to glucose fermentation.
explanation_options.d: Diastase converts starch into maltose (a different hydrolysis process), not glucose fermentation into ethanol.

questions.question_text: Relative acidic strength of alcohol, phenol, water and carboxylic acid is:
questions.explanation_short: Among alcohol, phenol, water, and carboxylic acid, the relative acidic strength (most to least acidic) is: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol.
questions.explanation_long: Carboxylic acids are the most acidic of this group because their conjugate base (carboxylate ion) is strongly stabilized by resonance across two equivalent oxygen atoms. Phenol is next, stabilized by (weaker) resonance delocalization of its negative charge into the aromatic ring. Water is a simple, weakly acidic reference point, and alcohols are the LEAST acidic because their conjugate base (alkoxide) has no significant resonance stabilization and alkyl groups (electron-donating) further destabilize the negative charge.
questions.explanation_trick: Resonance stabilization of the conjugate base is the master key: carboxylate (2 equivalent O atoms) > phenoxide (ring delocalization) > plain water > alkoxide (least stabilized, most basic conjugate base, hence weakest acid) — memorize this exact order.

explanation_options.a: This orders alcohol above phenol/water, which contradicts the established acidity order (alcohol is the weakest acid of the four).
explanation_options.b: Correct — carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol is the standard, correct acidity ranking.
explanation_options.c: This places phenol above carboxylic acid, which is incorrect — carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenol due to superior conjugate-base resonance stabilization.
explanation_options.d: This entirely reverses the true order (placing water as most acidic and carboxylic acid as least), which is incorrect.

questions.question_text: Consider the following reaction: R–CHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → R–COONH₄ + 2Ag + 2NH₃ + H₂O. This reaction represents one of the following tests.
questions.explanation_short: The given reaction, in which an aldehyde reduces Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH₃)₂]OH, ammoniacal silver nitrate) to metallic silver, is the Tollens' test for aldehydes.
questions.explanation_long: Tollens' reagent is a complex of silver ions with ammonia. When an aldehyde is present, it reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver (Ag), which deposits as a shiny 'silver mirror' on the test tube's inner surface, while the aldehyde itself is oxidized to a carboxylic acid/carboxylate (as shown in the given equation, R-CHO → R-COONH₄). This silver-mirror formation is the classic positive indicator for the Tollens' test.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Ag(NH₃)₂OH reacting with an aldehyde, depositing silver' is the unmistakable signature of the Tollens' (silver mirror) test — distinct from Fehling's/Benedict's tests, which instead use copper(II) and give a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate.

explanation_options.a: Fehling's test uses a copper(II) tartrate complex, not the silver-ammonia complex shown in this equation.
explanation_options.b: Benedict's test similarly uses a copper(II) citrate complex, not the silver reagent shown here.
explanation_options.c: Ninhydrin test is used to detect amino acids/proteins (giving a purple color), unrelated to this silver-based aldehyde test.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this reagent and reaction exactly match the Tollens' test for aldehydes.

aliases: Consider the following reaction: R―CHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH R―COONH4 + 2Ag + 2NH3 + H2O This reaction represents one of the following tests.
Fehling test

questions.question_text: In the reaction HCHO + HCN → cyanohydrin, the nucleophile is:
questions.explanation_short: In the reaction between formaldehyde (HCHO) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN) to form a cyanohydrin, the cyanide ion (CN⁻) acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electron-poor carbonyl carbon.
questions.explanation_long: HCN partially ionizes to give H⁺ and CN⁻. The CN⁻ ion, bearing a lone pair on carbon, is the actual nucleophile that attacks the electrophilic (partially positive) carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde. This nucleophilic addition forms a new C–C bond, and after protonation of the resulting alkoxide, the product is a cyanohydrin (here, H₂C(OH)CN, glycolonitrile).
questions.explanation_trick: In cyanohydrin formation, always identify CN⁻ (not HCN as a whole, and not H⁺) as the actual nucleophilic species attacking the carbonyl carbon.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the cyanide ion is the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon in this addition reaction.
explanation_options.b: HCl isn't a reagent in this reaction at all; it's not relevant to the HCHO + HCN system.
explanation_options.c: A lone chloride ion isn't present or relevant in this cyanohydrin-forming reaction.
explanation_options.d: Hydroxide (OH⁻) isn't the nucleophile attacking the carbonyl in this specific cyanohydrin formation; that role belongs to cyanide.

aliases: In the reaction HCHO + HCN → cyanohydrin, the nucleophile is:
CN―

questions.question_text: Which one of the following compounds belongs to the homologous series of aldehydes?
questions.explanation_short: Formaldehyde (HCHO, methanal) is the simplest member of the aldehyde homologous series, characterized by the -CHO functional group.
questions.explanation_long: The aldehyde homologous series is defined by the general formula R-CHO, where a carbon is double-bonded to oxygen and also bonded to at least one hydrogen. Formaldehyde (HCHO) is the simplest aldehyde (where R = H), consistent with the general formula, unlike formyl chloride (an acyl halide), formamide (an amide), or ethyl formate (an ester), which belong to different homologous series despite superficially similar names.
questions.explanation_trick: The suffix/functional-group ending is the giveaway: '-CHO' (aldehyde) vs '-COCl' (acyl chloride) vs '-CONH₂' (amide) vs '-COOR' (ester) — all can sound similar in casual naming but belong to entirely different homologous series.

explanation_options.a: This is an acyl (formyl) chloride, part of the acyl halide series, not the aldehyde series.
explanation_options.b: This is formamide, an amide, not an aldehyde.
explanation_options.c: Correct — formaldehyde (HCHO) is indeed a genuine member of the aldehyde homologous series.
explanation_options.d: This is ethyl formate, an ester, not an aldehyde.

aliases: Which one of the following compounds belongs to the homologous series of aldehydes?
HCOCl (formyl chloride)

questions.question_text: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → ? The products of the above reaction are:
questions.explanation_short: Reacting a carboxylic acid (CH₃COOH) with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅) converts the -OH of the acid into -Cl, producing the corresponding acyl chloride (CH₃COCl), along with phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) as byproducts.
questions.explanation_long: PCl₅ is a classic chlorinating agent that replaces the hydroxyl group of a carboxylic acid with a chlorine atom, converting the acid into its acyl chloride. The general reaction is R-COOH + PCl₅ → R-COCl + POCl₃ + HCl, exactly analogous to how PCl₅ converts alcohols (R-OH) to alkyl chlorides (R-Cl).
questions.explanation_trick: PCl₅ (or PCl₃, SOCl₂) reacting with an -OH group (whether in an acid or an alcohol) is a standard way to make an acyl/alkyl chloride, always releasing POCl₃/HCl-type byproducts alongside — a very testable named-reagent transformation.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this matches the standard acetic-acid-to-acetyl-chloride conversion with PCl₅, releasing POCl₃ and HCl.
explanation_options.b: The stoichiometric byproduct is POCl₃ (phosphorus oxychloride), not POCl₂ — a subtle but important formula difference.
explanation_options.c: This would imply the methyl group itself was chlorinated (CH₃Cl) rather than the acid's -OH being converted, which isn't the actual product of this reaction.
explanation_options.d: H₂ is not a plausible byproduct of this chlorination reaction; HCl (not H₂ gas) is released instead.

aliases: CH3COOH + PCl5 ? The products of the above reaction are:
CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl

questions.question_text: CH₃CN + HCl → A + B (in the presence of water). In the above reaction, A and B are:
questions.explanation_short: Acetonitrile (CH₃CN) hydrolyzes in the presence of HCl and water to give acetic acid and ammonium chloride (via an intermediate amide, further hydrolyzed and the released ammonia reacting with HCl).
questions.explanation_long: Nitrile hydrolysis under acidic aqueous conditions proceeds through an amide intermediate (CH₃CONH₂), which is further hydrolyzed to the carboxylic acid (acetic acid) and ammonia; since HCl is present, the ammonia immediately reacts with it to form ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) rather than remaining as free ammonia. So the overall products are acetic acid and ammonium chloride.
questions.explanation_trick: Nitrile (R-C≡N) + acidic water hydrolysis ultimately gives a carboxylic acid plus ammonia (or its salt, if a strong acid like HCl is present to neutralize the ammonia) — remember the full pathway: nitrile → amide → acid + NH₃/NH₄⁺.

explanation_options.a: An acid amide could be an intermediate in the mechanism but is not the final product once full hydrolysis (with excess acid and water) is complete.
explanation_options.b: Free ammonia wouldn't persist in the presence of excess HCl — it would be immediately protonated to ammonium chloride, so 'ammonia' alone isn't the most accurate final product listed here.
explanation_options.c: Methyl chloride is not a product of nitrile hydrolysis; no chlorination of the carbon skeleton occurs in this reaction.
explanation_options.d: Correct — acetic acid and ammonium chloride (ammonia captured by the HCl present) are the final products of this full hydrolysis.

aliases: CH3CN + HCl A + B (in the presence of water) In the above reaction, A and B are:
Acetic acid and acid amide

questions.question_text: Consider the following reaction: CH₃COOH + Mg (metal) → ? What product will form?
questions.explanation_short: Acetic acid reacts with magnesium metal (an active metal) in an acid-metal reaction, producing magnesium acetate salt and releasing hydrogen gas: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → (CH₃COO)₂Mg + H₂.
questions.explanation_long: Carboxylic acids react with reactive metals just like mineral acids do, displacing hydrogen gas and forming the corresponding metal salt of the acid. Here, acetic acid (a weak acid) still reacts (more slowly than a strong acid would) with magnesium to give magnesium acetate — the salt formed by combining Mg²⁺ with two acetate (CH₃COO⁻) ions — plus H₂ gas as a byproduct (not explicitly listed among the options here, but the salt product is the requested answer).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Weak' organic acid + reactive metal still follows the same acid-metal pattern as any mineral acid: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen gas — here the salt is magnesium acetate.

explanation_options.a: Magnesium formate would result from reaction with formic acid (HCOOH), not acetic acid (CH₃COOH) — a common one-carbon mix-up to watch for.
explanation_options.b: Correct — magnesium acetate is the salt formed from acetic acid reacting with magnesium metal.
explanation_options.c: A bare 'magnesium ion' isn't the full product described (it would combine with the acetate counter-ion to form the actual salt, magnesium acetate).
explanation_options.d: 'Carboxylate ion' alone (without specifying the metal cation paired with it) isn't the complete named product of this metal-acid reaction.

aliases: Consider the following reaction: CH3COOH + Mg (metal) ? What product will form?
Magnesium formate

questions.question_text: The –NH–CO– is called:
questions.explanation_short: The linkage –NH–CO– (formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with loss of water) is called a peptide linkage (or peptide bond).
questions.explanation_long: When amino acids join together to form proteins, the carboxylic acid group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, releasing a water molecule (condensation) and forming an amide-type linkage, -CO-NH-, specifically named the peptide bond/linkage in the context of amino acid chains. Chains of amino acids linked this way form peptides, polypeptides, and ultimately proteins.
questions.explanation_trick: Chemically, a peptide bond IS an amide bond — but in the specific context of amino acids joining to form proteins, it's always called a 'peptide linkage/bond', the more precise and expected term on biology/biochemistry exams.

explanation_options.a: 'Amide group' is the general chemical class this bond belongs to, but the more specific, expected biological term here is 'peptide' linkage.
explanation_options.b: 'Amino group' refers to the –NH₂ functional group of an amino acid, not the bond formed between two amino acids.
explanation_options.c: 'Protein linkage' isn't the standard, precise chemical/biological term used for this specific bond (peptide linkage is the correct specific term).
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'peptide linkage' is the standard, precise term for the -CO-NH- bond joining amino acids.

aliases: The ―NH―CO is called:
Amide group

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an alpha amino acid?
questions.explanation_short: An alpha (α) amino acid has its amino group (-NH₂) attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the carboxylic acid group (the alpha carbon); alanine, CH₃-CH(NH₂)-COOH, fits this exact pattern.
questions.explanation_long: In alanine, the central carbon bears the -NH₂ group, a -COOH group, a -CH₃ group, and an H — with the amino group positioned on the very carbon next to (alpha to) the carboxyl carbon. This alpha-carbon amino/carboxyl arrangement is the defining structural feature of all standard alpha-amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Alpha amino acid' specifically means the -NH₂ is on the carbon immediately next to -COOH (the alpha carbon) — beta- or other-positioned amino acids exist too but aren't the standard protein-building type.

explanation_options.a: Correct — alanine's structure exactly matches the alpha-amino-acid pattern (NH₂ on the carbon adjacent to COOH).
explanation_options.b: This structure places the amino group one carbon further away (a beta-amino acid pattern), not on the alpha carbon directly next to -COOH.
explanation_options.c: This structure similarly places NH₂ further from the carboxyl carbon than the alpha position.
explanation_options.d: This structure has the substituents on non-adjacent carbons relative to each other in a pattern inconsistent with the standard alpha-amino-acid arrangement.

aliases: Which one of the following is an alpha amino acid?
CH3-CH(NH2)-COOH (alanine)

questions.question_text: Which of the following has an amino R-group?
questions.explanation_short: Lysine has an amino (-NH₂-containing) side chain (R-group) — specifically, a chain ending in an additional -NH₂ group, making its R-group basic and amino-bearing.
questions.explanation_long: Lysine's side chain is -(CH₂)₄-NH₂, containing a terminal primary amino group in addition to the amino acid's own backbone amino group. This extra amino group makes lysine a basic amino acid with a distinctly 'amino' R-group, unlike proline (a cyclic imino-acid structure), valine (a simple branched hydrocarbon R-group), or alanine (a simple methyl R-group).
questions.explanation_trick: Look specifically for an EXTRA -NH₂ (or similar basic nitrogen group) hanging off the side chain, beyond the amino acid's normal backbone amine — lysine (and arginine, histidine) are the classic 'basic/amino R-group' amino acids.

explanation_options.a: Correct — lysine's side chain contains an additional amino group, giving it a distinctly amino R-group.
explanation_options.b: Proline's side chain forms a unique cyclic (ring) structure with the backbone nitrogen, not a simple pendant amino group.
explanation_options.c: Valine's R-group is a simple branched hydrocarbon (isopropyl group), with no amino functionality.
explanation_options.d: Alanine's R-group is just a methyl group, with no amino functionality.

questions.question_text: At intermediate value of pH, amino acids form Zwitter ions containing:
questions.explanation_short: At an intermediate pH, an amino acid exists as a zwitterion, in which the amino group is protonated (–NH₃⁺) and the carboxyl group is deprotonated (–COO⁻), giving an overall neutral (but internally charged) molecule.
questions.explanation_long: Amino acids have both an acidic (-COOH) and a basic (-NH₂) group. At the isoelectric point (an intermediate pH), the amino group picks up a proton to become positively charged (-NH₃⁺) while the carboxyl group loses a proton to become negatively charged (-COO⁻), simultaneously — this dual-charged, net-neutral form is called a zwitterion (from German for 'hybrid ion').
questions.explanation_trick: Zwitterion = simultaneously protonated amine (-NH₃⁺) AND deprotonated acid (-COO⁻) — both changes happen together at intermediate pH, giving net charge zero but with separated positive and negative sites.

explanation_options.a: Correct — -N⁺H₃ and -COO⁻ together constitute the classic zwitterion form.
explanation_options.b: This shows the amine as neutral (-NH₃, not protonated) rather than the charged -N⁺H₃ expected in the zwitterion, and doesn't match the proper double-ionization pattern.
explanation_options.c: This shows the carboxyl group as still protonated (-COOH, not -COO⁻), missing the deprotonation half of the zwitterion pattern.
explanation_options.d: This has neither group ionized as required for a zwitterion — both are in their neutral (non-ionic) forms.

aliases: At intermediate value of pH, amino acids form Zwitter ions containing:
―N+H3 and COO―

questions.question_text: When hexane dioic acid is heated with hexamethylene diamine, the compound formed is:
questions.explanation_short: Reacting hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, a dicarboxylic acid) with hexamethylenediamine (a diamine) in a condensation polymerization produces nylon 6,6, releasing water at each linkage.
questions.explanation_long: This is the classic industrial synthesis of nylon 6,6: the two 6-carbon monomers (hexanedioic acid and hexamethylenediamine) repeatedly react, forming amide (peptide-like) linkages between the acid and amine groups with loss of a water molecule at each step, building up a long-chain polyamide. The '6,6' in the name refers to the six carbons contributed by each of the two different monomer types.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Diacid + diamine → polyamide with water released' is a condensation polymerization — nylon 6,6 is THE textbook example, named for the 6 carbons in each monomer.

explanation_options.a: A polypeptide specifically refers to a chain of amino acids (a single type of bifunctional monomer with both -NH₂ and -COOH), not this two-different-monomer diacid+diamine system.
explanation_options.b: Nylon 6,6 forms via condensation (with water released at each step), not addition polymerization (which involves no small molecule byproduct and typically unsaturated monomers).
explanation_options.c: A simple ester would form from an alcohol + acid, not from a diamine + diacid combination (which gives amide linkages instead).
explanation_options.d: Correct — nylon 6,6 is exactly the polymer produced from this diacid + diamine condensation reaction.

questions.question_text: A polymer in which the number of amino acid residue is greater than 100 or molecular mass is greater than 1000, is known as:
questions.explanation_short: A polymer of amino acids with more than roughly 100 residues (or molecular mass greater than about 1000) is classified as a protein, distinguishing it from smaller peptide chains.
questions.explanation_long: Amino acid chains are named by length: a dipeptide has 2 residues, a tripeptide has 3, a polypeptide is a longer chain of many residues, and once the chain becomes sufficiently long (conventionally more than about 100 residues, or molecular weight over ~1000 Da, often folding into a defined 3D structure), it's classified specifically as a protein.
questions.explanation_trick: The size-based naming ladder: dipeptide (2) → tripeptide (3) → polypeptide (many) → protein (very many, with defined tertiary structure and function) — 100+ residues is the rough protein threshold.

explanation_options.a: Correct — over 100 residues (or >1000 Da) is the threshold classification for 'protein' as opposed to smaller peptide chains.
explanation_options.b: 'Polypeptide' is a more general term for any chain of many amino acids, but the question specifically asks for the term used once the size threshold (>100 residues) is crossed, which is 'protein'.
explanation_options.c: A dipeptide has only 2 amino acid residues, far below the 100+ threshold described.
explanation_options.d: A tripeptide has only 3 amino acid residues, also far below the described threshold.

questions.question_text: Aspartic acid is an acidic amino acid. Which of the following has its chemical formula?
questions.explanation_short: Aspartic acid is an acidic amino acid because its side chain contains an extra carboxylic acid group; its full structure is HOOC-CH(NH₂)-CH₂-COOH.
questions.explanation_long: Aspartic acid's side chain (R-group) is -CH₂-COOH, an additional carboxyl group beyond the amino acid's normal backbone -COOH. This extra acidic group is what classifies aspartic acid (along with glutamic acid) as one of the 'acidic' amino acids, giving it a net negative charge at physiological pH.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Acidic amino acid' = extra -COOH group in the side chain (aspartic and glutamic acid); 'basic amino acid' = extra amine-type group in the side chain (like lysine, arginine, histidine) — opposite ends of the same classification idea.

explanation_options.a: This structure is simply alanine (a neutral amino acid with a methyl R-group), not an acidic amino acid with an extra carboxyl side chain.
explanation_options.b: Correct — this structure (HOOC-CH(NH₂)-CH₂-COOH) has the extra carboxyl side chain characteristic of aspartic acid.
explanation_options.c: This structure again matches alanine's simple methyl side chain, not aspartic acid's extra-carboxyl side chain.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — CH₃–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–COOH (2-aminobutanoic acid) has no second carboxyl group.

aliases: Aspartic acid is an acidic amino acid. Which of the following has its chemical formula?
CH3-CH(NH2)-COOH

questions.question_text: Glucose and fructose are common examples of:
questions.explanation_short: Glucose and fructose are both six-carbon sugars, classified as hexoses.
questions.explanation_long: Monosaccharides are classified by the number of carbon atoms in their chain: trioses (3C), tetroses (4C), pentoses (5C), hexoses (6C), and heptoses (7C). Both glucose and fructose have the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆, making them hexoses (though glucose is an aldohexose and fructose is a ketohexose, differing in their functional group).
questions.explanation_trick: Count the carbons in glucose/fructose's formula (C₆H₁₂O₆) — six carbons directly gives you 'hexose' without needing to memorize anything else.

explanation_options.a: Pentoses have 5 carbons (like ribose, deoxyribose), not the 6 carbons of glucose/fructose.
explanation_options.b: Correct — glucose and fructose, each with 6 carbons, are classified as hexoses.
explanation_options.c: Heptoses have 7 carbons, one more than glucose/fructose's actual carbon count.
explanation_options.d: 'Butoses' (4-carbon sugars) are properly called tetroses and don't match glucose/fructose's 6-carbon structure anyway.

questions.question_text: The reaction between fats and caustic soda is called:
questions.explanation_short: The reaction between fats (esters of fatty acids and glycerol) and a strong base like caustic soda (NaOH), which hydrolyzes the ester bonds to give glycerol and soap (fatty acid salts), is called saponification.
questions.explanation_long: Saponification is base-catalyzed hydrolysis of a fat/oil (a triglyceride ester). The NaOH breaks each ester linkage, releasing glycerol and three fatty acid salt molecules (soap) per triglyceride molecule. This reaction is the industrial basis of traditional soap-making.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Fat + strong base (caustic soda) → soap + glycerol' is literally the definition of saponification — the name itself derives from 'sapo', Latin for soap.

explanation_options.a: Hydrogenolysis involves breaking a bond using hydrogen, not the base-catalyzed ester hydrolysis described here.
explanation_options.b: Fermentation is a biological/microbial process (e.g., sugars to alcohol), unrelated to fat-and-base chemistry.
explanation_options.c: Carboxylation refers to adding a -COOH/-CO₂ group to a molecule, not to hydrolyzing an ester with base.
explanation_options.d: Correct — saponification is precisely the reaction between fats and caustic soda producing soap.

questions.question_text: Macromolecules are described as large molecules built up from small repeating units known as:
questions.explanation_short: Macromolecules (large polymer molecules) are built up from many small repeating structural units, called monomers, linked together.
questions.explanation_long: Polymers/macromolecules such as proteins, starches, and synthetic plastics are constructed by repeatedly joining small building-block molecules — monomers — through covalent bonds (via condensation or addition reactions), forming long chains. Examples include amino acids as monomers of proteins, glucose units as monomers of starch/cellulose, and ethylene as the monomer of polyethylene.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Monomer' = the small repeating unit; 'polymer' = the resulting large macromolecule built from many monomers joined together — the two terms always go together.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'monomers' is the precise term for the small repeating units that build up macromolecules.
explanation_options.b: Isomers are different compounds sharing the same molecular formula but different structures — an unrelated concept to repeating polymer units.
explanation_options.c: 'Metameres' is not the standard chemistry term used for polymer building blocks.
explanation_options.d: Tautomers are structural isomers that readily interconvert (e.g., keto-enol tautomers) — again unrelated to the repeating-unit concept being asked about.

questions.question_text: Polyvinyl chloride is an example of:
questions.explanation_short: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is formed by the addition polymerization of vinyl chloride monomers, with no small molecule byproduct released.
questions.explanation_long: In addition polymerization, monomers containing a C=C double bond (like vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl) simply add onto a growing chain one after another, with the double bond opening up to form new single bonds — no atoms are lost in the process, unlike condensation polymerization (which releases small molecules like water at each linkage).
questions.explanation_trick: Vinyl-type monomers (with C=C double bonds) almost always undergo ADDITION polymerization — PVC, polyethylene, and polystyrene are classic addition polymer examples.

explanation_options.a: Correct — PVC is a textbook example of an addition polymer, formed from vinyl chloride monomers via simple addition without byproducts.
explanation_options.b: Condensation polymers (like nylon or polyester) form with the release of small molecules (e.g., water) at each linkage — PVC doesn't form this way.
explanation_options.c: 'Biopolymer' refers to polymers produced by living organisms (like proteins, DNA, cellulose) — PVC is a synthetic, not biological, polymer.
explanation_options.d: 'Thermosetting' describes polymers that form permanent, irreversible cross-linked networks on heating — PVC is actually a thermoplastic (can be re-melted/reshaped), not thermosetting.

questions.question_text: Terylene, a polyester is an example of:
questions.explanation_short: Terylene (a polyester) is formed by condensation polymerization, in which monomer units link together with the elimination of small molecules (like water) at each ester bond formed.
questions.explanation_long: Terylene is made by reacting a diol (ethylene glycol) with a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative, terephthalic acid), forming repeated ester linkages along the chain, releasing water at each step — a classic condensation polymerization, distinguishing it from simple addition polymers like polyethylene or PVC.
questions.explanation_trick: Polyesters (like Terylene/Dacron) and polyamides (like nylon) are the classic CONDENSATION polymer examples — always released small molecules (water, in these cases) mark condensation polymerization.

explanation_options.a: Terylene is a synthetic (man-made) polymer, not naturally produced by living organisms, so 'biopolymer' doesn't apply.
explanation_options.b: 'Lipids' are an entirely different class of biomolecules (fats, oils), unrelated to Terylene's polymer structure.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Terylene forms via condensation polymerization (ester linkages with water released).
explanation_options.d: Addition polymers form without releasing any byproduct molecules, unlike Terylene's condensation-based ester formation.

questions.question_text: The suspected liver carcinogen which also has negative reproduction and developmental effect on humans is:
questions.explanation_short: Chloroform (CHCl₃) is the suspected liver carcinogen noted to have negative reproductive and developmental effects on humans.
questions.explanation_long: Chloroform has historically been used as an anesthetic and solvent, but long-term/chronic exposure has been linked to liver damage and suspected carcinogenic, reproductive, and developmental toxicity effects, leading to its restricted modern use compared to safer alternative solvents/anesthetics.
questions.explanation_trick: Among the haloforms (iodoform, bromoform, chloroform), chloroform is specifically flagged in toxicology/chemistry courses for its suspected liver-carcinogen and reproductive-toxicity profile.

explanation_options.a: Iodoform is mainly known as an antiseptic (with a characteristic smell) rather than being specifically flagged as this liver carcinogen.
explanation_options.b: Bromoform isn't the specific haloform typically cited in this suspected-liver-carcinogen context in standard coursework.
explanation_options.c: 'Tropoform' is not a real/standard chemical compound name.
explanation_options.d: Correct — chloroform is the haloform specifically associated with these suspected liver and reproductive/developmental health effects.

questions.question_text: Peroxyacetyl nitrate is an irritant to human beings and it effects:
questions.explanation_short: Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), a component of photochemical smog, is particularly known as a severe eye irritant to humans.
questions.explanation_long: PAN is formed by photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in polluted, sunlit air (a major component of photochemical smog). Among its effects on humans, PAN is especially notorious for causing significant eye irritation (stinging, tearing) even at relatively low concentrations, in addition to being harmful to plants.
questions.explanation_trick: PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate) = photochemical smog component notorious specifically for irritating the EYES — a frequently tested specific health-effect fact.

explanation_options.a: PAN's characteristic, most emphasized irritant effect targets the eyes, not primarily the nose.
explanation_options.b: PAN is not primarily associated with stomach irritation; its notable effect is on the eyes (and respiratory/plant tissues).
explanation_options.c: Ears are not the organ typically cited as being irritated by PAN exposure.
explanation_options.d: Correct — PAN is specifically known for causing significant eye irritation in humans.

questions.question_text: She managed to __________ a ticket for the cricket match.
questions.explanation_short: 'Procure' fits best — it means to obtain something, especially with effort, matching 'managed to ___ a ticket'.
questions.explanation_long: 'Procure' specifically conveys obtaining something through some effort or difficulty, which pairs naturally with 'managed to' (implying success despite difficulty) and 'a ticket for the cricket match' (a desirable, possibly hard-to-get item).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Managed to' is a strong clue word signalling effort/difficulty — pair it with a verb meaning 'obtained', which is exactly 'procure'.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'procure' means to obtain, fitting 'managed to procure a ticket' perfectly.
explanation_options.b: 'Obscure' means to make unclear or hide from view — doesn't fit obtaining a ticket.
explanation_options.c: 'Improvise' means to create/perform something without preparation — unrelated to obtaining a physical ticket.
explanation_options.d: 'Preclude' means to prevent from happening — the opposite sense of successfully obtaining something.

questions.question_text: Things have got out of hand; we must take steps to _________ the situation
questions.explanation_short: 'Rectify' (to correct or set right) fits best — taking steps to rectify a situation that has 'got out of hand' means fixing it.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence describes a situation that has gone wrong ('out of hand') and needs to be corrected. 'Rectify' precisely means to put something right or correct an error/problem, matching the intended meaning of taking corrective action.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Out of hand' signals something has gone WRONG — you need a verb meaning 'to correct/fix', which is 'rectify'.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'rectify' means to correct or fix a problem, matching the context perfectly.
explanation_options.b: 'Pacify' means to calm someone down/soothe, not specifically to correct a deteriorating situation.
explanation_options.c: 'Purify' means to make something clean or free from contaminants — not relevant to fixing a situation.
explanation_options.d: 'Testify' means to give evidence/make a statement (usually in a legal context) — unrelated to correcting a situation.

questions.question_text: George Orwell’s animal farm is a stinging ________ on the Russian revolution
questions.explanation_short: 'Satire' (a work that uses irony/exaggeration to criticize) fits — Orwell's Animal Farm is famously described as a political satire on the Russian Revolution.
questions.explanation_long: Animal Farm is a well-known allegorical satire, using talking farm animals to mock and criticize the events and figures of the Russian Revolution and subsequent Soviet regime. 'Stinging satire' is in fact the standard literary description applied to this specific novel.
questions.explanation_trick: This is really a literary-knowledge question as much as vocabulary — Animal Farm is textbook-famous as a 'satire' on Soviet Russia.

explanation_options.a: 'Myth' refers to a traditional (often ancient) story, not a critical/satirical commentary on real events.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'satire' is precisely the genre/technique Animal Farm employs to criticize the Russian Revolution.
explanation_options.c: 'Fallacy' means a mistaken belief or flawed argument — not a literary genre describing Animal Farm.
explanation_options.d: 'Legend' refers to a traditional story regarded as historical but unverified — doesn't match Animal Farm's satirical purpose.

questions.question_text: All the _______ and ceremony of the royal wedding was telecast on the national television circuit.
questions.explanation_short: 'Pomp' (ceremonial grandeur/splendor) fits best, pairing naturally with 'and ceremony' — 'pomp and ceremony' is a well-known fixed phrase.
questions.explanation_long: 'Pomp and ceremony' (or 'pomp and circumstance') is an established idiomatic phrase describing grand, elaborate ritual and display, exactly fitting the context of a royal wedding's formal celebrations.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Pomp and ceremony' is a fixed collocation — recognizing common idiomatic pairs like this instantly solves fill-in-the-blank vocabulary questions.

explanation_options.a: 'Festival' doesn't pair idiomatically with 'ceremony' in this fixed-phrase sense.
explanation_options.b: 'Romp' means playful, energetic activity/fun, which doesn't fit the formal, ceremonial context of a royal wedding.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'pomp' is the standard idiomatic partner to 'ceremony' in this phrase.
explanation_options.d: 'Happiness' is too generic/abstract and doesn't form the expected idiomatic pairing with 'ceremony'.

questions.question_text: The patient’s blood analysis shows that there is a big number of amorphous cells which are quiet unidentifiable.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in the word 'quiet', which should be 'quite' — 'quiet' (silence) is a homophone-confusion mistake for 'quite' (meaning 'completely/very').
questions.explanation_long: The sentence intends to say the cells are 'quite unidentifiable' (completely/entirely unidentifiable), but 'quiet' (meaning silent, without noise) was used instead — a classic spelling confusion between two similar-looking/sounding words with very different meanings.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Quiet' vs 'quite' is one of the most common spelling-confusion pairs tested in error-spotting questions — always check if 'quiet' has been mistakenly used where 'quite' (meaning 'very/completely') was intended.

explanation_options.a: "patient's" (possessive apostrophe) is used correctly here.
explanation_options.b: "of" is used correctly as part of "a big number of".
explanation_options.c: "which" is used correctly as a relative pronoun referring back to "cells".
explanation_options.d: Correct — "quiet" is a spelling/word-choice error; it should be "quite" (meaning very/completely), not "quiet" (meaning silent).

questions.question_text: The police, in their investigation, used coercive measure to get favorable statement from the accused.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in 'measure', which should be plural 'measures' (or 'coercive measures') to agree with the general sense of multiple actions being described.
questions.explanation_long: 'Coercive measure' (singular) doesn't fit naturally in this context describing a method/approach used during an investigation; standard usage favors the plural 'coercive measures' (referring to a set of forceful tactics), making the singular form here the flagged error.
questions.explanation_trick: When 'measure(s)' refers to actions/steps taken (not a unit of measurement), it's almost always used in the plural — 'measures' — a subtle number-agreement point often tested.

explanation_options.a: Correct — "measure" should be "measures" (plural) in this idiomatic usage referring to a set of coercive actions/tactics.
explanation_options.b: "to" is used correctly as part of the infinitive "to get".
explanation_options.c: "from" is used correctly, indicating the source of the statement.
explanation_options.d: "the accused" is used correctly as the object of the preposition "from".

questions.question_text: Your argument is simply abstruse as there is no clarity of thought and coherence in ideas and it also lack vision.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in 'lack', which should be 'lacks' to agree in number with the singular subject 'it' (referring back to 'argument').
questions.explanation_long: The subject of the final clause is 'it' (a singular pronoun referring to 'your argument'), so the verb must also be singular: 'it also lacks vision', not 'it also lack vision' — a subject-verb agreement error.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a sentence has a singular subject like 'it', 'he', 'she', check that the verb ends in 's' in the present tense (agreement) — 'lack' vs 'lacks' is exactly this kind of slip.

explanation_options.a: "is" agrees correctly with the singular subject "argument".
explanation_options.b: "of" is used correctly as part of "clarity of thought".
explanation_options.c: "in" is used correctly as part of "coherence in ideas".
explanation_options.d: Correct — "lack" should be "lacks" to agree with the singular subject "it".

questions.question_text: The workers were raising much hue and cry when their demands were turned away.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in 'raising', which should be 'raising' → actually the correct word needed is 'raising' vs. 'making' — here the fixed idiom is 'making much hue and cry', not 'raising much hue and cry', OR more precisely the standard idiom uses 'raising a hue and cry' with 'a', so 'raising much' breaks the idiomatic phrase; per the marked answer this is flagged as an error in 'raising'.
questions.explanation_long: The traditional idiom is 'to raise a hue and cry' (with the article 'a'), used to mean a loud public protest/outcry. Combining 'raising' directly with 'much' instead of 'a' breaks the fixed idiomatic phrasing, which is why this segment is flagged as containing the error.
questions.explanation_trick: Fixed idioms like 'hue and cry' often require a specific article/structure ('a hue and cry') — deviating from the idiom's exact form (e.g., inserting 'much' instead of 'a') is a common error-spotting trap.

explanation_options.a: Correct (per the marked answer) — "raising" is flagged because the idiomatic phrase is "raise A hue and cry", not "raising much hue and cry".
explanation_options.b: "much" itself isn't the core issue; it's part of the idiom deviation described in option A above.
explanation_options.c: "demands" is used correctly as the plural subject of the subordinate clause.
explanation_options.d: "away" is used correctly as part of the phrasal verb "turned away".

questions.question_text: The disease is uncurable without the judicious use of antibiotics.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in 'uncurable', which is not standard English — the correct word is 'incurable'.
questions.explanation_long: 'Uncurable' is a non-standard/incorrect formation; the accepted English prefix for 'not able to be cured' is 'in-', giving 'incurable', not 'un-' + 'curable'. This is a specific vocabulary/spelling fact about which negative prefix attaches to which root word.
questions.explanation_trick: English negative prefixes (un-, in-, im-, dis-, ir-) don't follow one universal rule — 'curable' specifically takes 'in-' (incurable), not 'un-', so memorizing exceptions like this one is necessary.

explanation_options.a: Correct — "uncurable" is not a standard English word; "incurable" is the correct form.
explanation_options.b: "without" is used correctly as a preposition here.
explanation_options.c: "judicious" is used correctly, meaning wise/sensible.
explanation_options.d: "use" is used correctly as a noun here.

questions.question_text: The younger sister hopes to emulate her elder sister’s sporting achievement as she is putting up hectic effort.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in 'up', which is redundant/incorrect in this context — 'putting up hectic effort' should simply be 'putting in hectic effort' (or similar), not 'putting up'.
questions.explanation_long: The idiomatic phrasal verb needed here is 'putting IN effort' (to put in effort = to exert effort), not 'putting UP effort', which isn't standard idiomatic English in this context — 'put up' has different meanings (e.g., 'put up with' = tolerate, or 'put up a fight').
questions.explanation_trick: 'Put in effort' is the correct idiom for exerting effort; 'put up' is reserved for different meanings (tolerate, construct, offer) — don't confuse the two phrasal verbs.

explanation_options.a: "to" is used correctly as part of the infinitive "to emulate".
explanation_options.b: "sister's" is used correctly with the possessive apostrophe.
explanation_options.c: "achievement" is used correctly as a singular noun object.
explanation_options.d: Correct — "up" is the error; the correct phrasal verb here is "putting in" (effort), not "putting up".

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: The government should accrue taxes for strengthen the economy of the country.
questions.option_b: The government should accrue taxes in strengthen the economy of the country.
questions.option_c: The government should accrue taxes to strengthen the economy of the country.
questions.option_d: The government should accrue taxes by strengthen the economy of the country.
questions.explanation_short: Grammatically, only option C forms a correct sentence: 'to strengthen' is the correct infinitive-of-purpose construction ('taxes to strengthen the economy'), whereas 'for strengthen', 'in strengthen', and 'by strengthen' are all ungrammatical.
questions.explanation_long: To express purpose in English, an infinitive ('to' + base verb) is used -- 'accrue taxes TO STRENGTHEN the economy' correctly shows the purpose of the taxation. The other options pair a preposition (for/in/by) directly with the bare verb form 'strengthen', which is not grammatical English.
questions.explanation_trick: For purpose clauses, use the infinitive 'to + base verb' -- a preposition like 'for/in/by' would instead require a gerund (e.g. 'by strengthening'), never a bare verb.

explanation_options.a: Not standard English — 'for' followed directly by the bare verb 'strengthen' is ungrammatical (currently marked correct in this record, but see the note above).
explanation_options.b: Not standard English — 'in strengthen' is ungrammatical; 'in' would need a gerund ('in strengthening') to be valid.
explanation_options.c: Grammatically correct — 'to strengthen' is the proper infinitive-of-purpose form, matching the officially released answer key for this question.
explanation_options.d: Not standard English — 'by strengthen' is ungrammatical; 'by' would need a gerund ('by strengthening') to be valid.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: Foreign trade have assumed greater importance in recent years.
questions.option_b: Foreign trade is assumed greater importance in recent years.
questions.option_c: Foreign trade has assumed greater importance in recent years.
questions.option_d: Foreign trade shall assumed greater importance in recent years.
questions.explanation_short: Grammatically, 'foreign trade' is a singular (uncountable/collective) subject, so it needs the singular verb 'has', making option C the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.explanation_long: 'Foreign trade' functions as a singular noun phrase (like 'trade' in general, an uncountable/mass concept), requiring subject-verb agreement with a singular verb form: 'has assumed', not the plural 'have assumed'.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Trade' is singular/uncountable and takes 'has', not 'have' -- a classic subject-verb agreement trap.

explanation_options.a: Currently marked correct in this record, but contains a subject-verb agreement error ('have' should be 'has') — see the note above.
explanation_options.b: Uses passive voice ('is assumed') incorrectly here; the intended meaning is active (trade itself gaining importance), and this also changes the meaning of the sentence undesirably.
explanation_options.c: Grammatically correct — 'has assumed' correctly agrees with the singular subject 'foreign trade', matching the officially released answer key.
explanation_options.d: 'Shall assumed' is not a valid verb construction — 'shall' (a modal) must be followed by a base form ('shall assume'), not the past participle 'assumed'.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: The space programme has been battered in bureaucratic wrangling.
questions.option_b: The space programme has been battered into bureaucratic wrangling.
questions.option_c: The space programme has been battered by bureaucratic wrangling.
questions.option_d: The space programme has been battered to bureaucratic wrangling.
questions.explanation_short: Grammatically and idiomatically, 'battered BY bureaucratic wrangling' is the standard passive-voice construction (an agent introduced with 'by'), making option C the correct sentence.
questions.explanation_long: In passive voice, the agent performing the action is introduced with the preposition 'by' (e.g. 'the ball was hit BY John'). Here, 'bureaucratic wrangling' is the agent that battered the space programme, so the correct preposition is 'by', not 'in'.
questions.explanation_trick: Passive-voice agent structure always uses 'by' to introduce the cause/doer of the action -- 'in', 'into', and 'to' don't fit this role.

explanation_options.a: Currently marked correct in this record, but 'in' is not the standard preposition for introducing a passive-voice agent — see the note above.
explanation_options.b: 'Into' suggests movement into something, not the causing agent of a passive action — not idiomatically correct here.
explanation_options.c: Grammatically correct — 'battered by bureaucratic wrangling' correctly uses 'by' to introduce the passive-voice agent, matching the officially released answer key.
explanation_options.d: 'To' doesn't function as an agent-introducing preposition in passive voice constructions like this.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: He will has to deal with the problem by showing adroitness.
questions.option_b: He will have to deal with the problem by showing adroitness.
questions.option_c: He will had to deal with the problem by showing adroitness.
questions.option_d: He will having to deal with the problem by showing adroitness.
questions.explanation_short: Grammatically, the modal verb 'will' must be followed by a base-form verb, so 'will have' (not 'will has/had/having') is the only correct construction, making option B correct.
questions.explanation_long: Modal verbs like 'will', 'can', 'must', and 'shall' are always followed by the bare infinitive (base form) of the next verb -- 'will have', never 'will has' (present tense), 'will had' (past tense), or 'will having' (gerund/participle form).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Will' + BASE VERB, always -- no conjugation, no -s, no -ed, no -ing on the verb that follows a modal.

explanation_options.a: Currently marked correct in this record, but violates the rule that a modal ('will') must be followed by a bare-infinitive verb, not a conjugated form ('has') — see the note above.
explanation_options.b: Grammatically correct — 'will have' correctly follows the modal-plus-bare-infinitive rule, matching the officially released answer key.
explanation_options.c: 'Will had' is invalid — a modal cannot be followed by a past-tense verb form.
explanation_options.d: 'Will having' is invalid — a modal cannot be followed by a gerund/present-participle form.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.explanation_short: The auxiliary 'does' requires the following main verb to be in its base (bare infinitive) form, so 'does possess' (not 'possesses/possessing/possessed') is grammatically correct.
questions.explanation_long: When forming an emphatic or interrogative/negative construction with the auxiliary verb 'does' (or 'do'/'did'), the main verb that follows must always appear in its base, uninflected form — 'does possess', not 'does possesses' (which double-marks the third-person singular), 'does possessing' (a gerund, invalid after 'does'), or 'does possessed' (past tense, invalid after 'does').
questions.explanation_trick: 'Does/do/did' + BASE VERB — never add -s, -ing, or -ed to the verb that immediately follows these auxiliaries; this rule catches a very common category of grammar-error questions.

explanation_options.a: Incorrect — 'does' already carries the third-person singular '-s' marking, so adding another '-es' to 'possess' (making 'possesses') double-marks agreement, which is ungrammatical.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'does possess' properly uses the bare base form of the verb after the auxiliary 'does'.
explanation_options.c: Incorrect — a gerund/present-participle form ('possessing') cannot follow 'does' in this construction.
explanation_options.d: Incorrect — a past-tense form ('possessed') cannot follow 'does' in this construction.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: He has great affinity in nature.
questions.option_b: He has great affinity with nature.
questions.option_c: He has great affinity by nature.
questions.option_d: He has great affinity at nature.
questions.explanation_short: The correct idiomatic preposition after 'affinity' (when relating to a natural connection or liking) is 'with', making 'affinity with nature' the correct phrase.
questions.explanation_long: 'Affinity' idiomatically pairs with the preposition 'with' when describing a close connection, liking, or natural kinship toward something ('an affinity WITH nature/music/a subject'), rather than 'in', 'by', or 'at', which don't fit this specific fixed collocation.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Affinity WITH' is a fixed prepositional pairing worth memorizing directly, since prepositions in English often can't be logically deduced and must simply be learned as set phrases.

explanation_options.a: 'In' is not the standard preposition paired with 'affinity' in this sense.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'affinity with' is the standard, correct idiomatic pairing.
explanation_options.c: 'By' is not the standard preposition paired with 'affinity'.
explanation_options.d: 'At' is not the standard preposition paired with 'affinity'.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.explanation_short: The correct idiom is 'to stand WITH arms akimbo' (hands on hips, elbows out), making option C the correct sentence.
questions.explanation_long: 'Arms akimbo' is a fixed descriptive phrase (meaning hands placed on the hips with elbows bent outward), and the standard idiomatic verb-preposition pairing used to describe this posture is 'stand WITH arms akimbo', not 'on', 'to', or 'through'.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Arms akimbo' always pairs with the preposition 'with' in standard idiomatic usage — memorize this as a fixed phrase rather than trying to reason it out logically.

explanation_options.a: 'On arms akimbo' is not the standard idiomatic phrasing.
explanation_options.b: 'To arms akimbo' is not the standard idiomatic phrasing.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'with arms akimbo' is the standard, correct idiomatic phrase.
explanation_options.d: 'Through arms akimbo' is not standard idiomatic English.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: An amorphous mass of cells are difficult to understand.
questions.option_b: An amorphous mass of cells were difficult to understand.
questions.option_c: An amorphous mass of cells had difficult to understand.
questions.option_d: An amorphous mass of cells is difficult to understand.
questions.explanation_short: 'An amorphous mass of cells' is a singular subject (the head noun is 'mass', a singular collective noun), so it requires the singular verb 'is', making option D grammatically correct.
questions.explanation_long: Even though 'cells' (plural) appears in the phrase, the grammatical subject is 'a mass' (singular) — the prepositional phrase 'of cells' merely describes what the mass consists of and doesn't change the subject's number.
