questions.question_text: Lactose is a sugar present in milk. It is an example of
questions.explanation_short: Lactose (milk sugar) is a disaccharide.
questions.explanation_long: Lactose is composed of two monosaccharide units — glucose and galactose — joined together, making it a disaccharide.
questions.explanation_trick: Common disaccharides to remember together: Lactose (glucose+galactose, milk sugar), Sucrose (glucose+fructose, table sugar), Maltose (glucose+glucose, malt sugar).

explanation_options.a: Correct — lactose is a disaccharide (two sugar units joined).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — monosaccharides are single sugar units; lactose is made of two.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — polysaccharides are much larger polymers of many sugar units, not just two.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — starch is a plant polysaccharide, an entirely different carbohydrate.

questions.question_text: Macromolecules are described as large molecules built up from small repeating units called:
questions.explanation_short: Macromolecules are built from repeating units called monomers.
questions.explanation_long: A macromolecule (polymer) is a large molecule formed by linking together many smaller repeating units, each called a monomer.
questions.explanation_trick: Monomer (one/single unit) + Polymer (many units linked together) — the basic building-block vocabulary of polymer chemistry.

explanation_options.a: Correct — monomers are the repeating building-block units of macromolecules.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — isomers are molecules with the same formula but different structures, not the repeating units of a polymer.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'metamers' describes a type of structural isomerism, unrelated to polymer building blocks.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — tautomers are rapidly interconverting structural isomers, unrelated to polymer building blocks.

questions.question_text: The increase in concentration of oxidizing agents in smog like H₂O₂, HNO₃, PAN and ozone in the air is called
questions.explanation_short: Increased oxidizing agents (H2O2, HNO3, PAN, ozone) in smog is called photochemical smog.
questions.explanation_long: Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions among vehicle/industrial pollutants, producing secondary oxidizing pollutants like ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), and other reactive oxidizing species.
questions.explanation_trick: Photochemical smog is specifically sunlight-driven and oxidant-rich (ozone, PAN, H2O2) — distinct from the older, more reducing 'London-type' smog dominated by sulfur dioxide and soot.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not a standard named type of smog.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — not a standard named type of smog.
explanation_options.c: Correct — photochemical smog is defined by exactly this oxidizing-agent buildup.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — not a standard named type of smog.

aliases: The increase in concentration of oxidizing agents in smog like H 2O2, HNO3, PAN and ozone in the air is called
Carbonated smog

questions.question_text: Which is the metal, whose elevated concentration is harmful for fish as it clogs the gills thus causing suffocation?
questions.explanation_short: Elevated aluminum harms fish by clogging their gills, causing suffocation.
questions.explanation_long: Aluminum, often released into water bodies by acid rain leaching it from soil, forms precipitates on fish gills at elevated concentrations, physically clogging them and impairing oxygen uptake, leading to suffocation.
questions.explanation_trick: Aluminum toxicity to fish is a specific, frequently cited environmental chemistry consequence of acid rain — distinct from simple heavy-metal poisoning mechanisms of other metals.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — sodium isn't associated with this specific gill-clogging mechanism.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — lead has different toxicity mechanisms (nervous system effects), not primarily gill-clogging.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — zinc has different toxicity mechanisms, not primarily gill-clogging via precipitation.
explanation_options.d: Correct — aluminum is specifically linked to this gill-clogging toxicity in fish.

questions.question_text: An organic compound has empirical formula C₃H₃O, if molar mass of compound is 110.15 g mol⁻¹. The molecular formula of this organic compound is (A, of C=12, H=1.008 and O=16)
questions.explanation_short: Empirical formula mass (55.02) fits into molar mass (110.15) twice, giving molecular formula C6H6O2.
questions.explanation_long: Empirical formula C3H3O has mass = 3(12) + 3(1.008) + 16 = 36 + 3.024 + 16 = 55.024 g/mol. Dividing the given molar mass by this: 110.15/55.024 ≈ 2. Multiplying the empirical formula by 2 gives the molecular formula: C6H6O2.
questions.explanation_trick: Molecular formula = empirical formula × (molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass) — always compute this whole-number multiplier first before scaling up every subscript.

explanation_options.a: Correct — C6H6O2 matches the ×2 scaling.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is just the empirical formula itself, not yet scaled to match the given molar mass.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — would require a ×3 scaling factor, not matching the given molar mass.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — doesn't match the correct stoichiometric doubling of the empirical formula.

aliases: An organic compound has empirical formula C3H3O, if molar mass of compound is 110.15 gmol-1. The molecular formula of this organic compound is (A, of C=12, H=1.008 and O=16)
C6H6O2

questions.question_text: When 8 grams (4 moles) of H₂ react with 2 moles of O₂, how many moles of water will be formed?
questions.explanation_short: 4 moles H2 + 2 moles O2 (exact stoichiometric ratio) produces 4 moles of water.
questions.explanation_long: The balanced equation 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O has a 2:1:2 mole ratio. Given exactly 4 moles H2 and 2 moles O2 (matching the required 2:1 ratio precisely, with neither reactant in excess), the water produced follows the same ratio: 4 moles H2 → 4 moles H2O.
questions.explanation_trick: Check the mole ratio given against the balanced equation's ratio first — here, 4:2 simplifies to exactly 2:1, matching the equation perfectly, so no reactant is in excess and the calculation is a direct proportion.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — exceeds what either reactant can produce given the 2:1 ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — matches the direct 2:2 mole ratio between H2 and H2O.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — exceeds what either reactant can produce.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — underestimates the water produced from the full stoichiometric amounts given.

aliases: When 8 grams (4 moles) of H2 react with 2 moles of O2, how many moles of water will be formed?
Five

questions.question_text: The number of molecules in 22.4 dm³ of H₂ gas at 0 °C and 1 atm are
questions.explanation_short: 22.4 dm³ of any gas at 0 °C and 1 atm is one mole, which contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules (Avogadro's number).
questions.explanation_long: At standard temperature and pressure one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³, and one mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, 6.02 × 10²³. So 22.4 dm³ of hydrogen holds 6.02 × 10²³ H₂ molecules. (The paper prints both B and the keyed option D as 6.02 × 10²²; D is shown here with the correct exponent.)
questions.explanation_trick: 22.4 dm³ at STP ↔ 1 mol ↔ 6.02 × 10²³ particles.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 60.2 × 10²³ is ten times Avogadro's number.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 6.02 × 10²² is only a tenth of a mole.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 6.02 × 10²⁵ is a hundred times too many.
explanation_options.d: Correct — one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules.

aliases: The number of molecules in 22.4 dm3 of H2 gas at 0 °C and 1 atm are

questions.question_text: Correct order of boiling points of the given liquid is
questions.explanation_short: Boiling point order: H2O > HF > NH3 > HCl.
questions.explanation_long: Comparing actual boiling points: H2O (100°C, extensive hydrogen bonding via 2 H's per O) > HF (19.5°C, strong H-bonding but only 1 H per F) > NH3 (-33°C, weaker H-bonding, lower molecular weight) > HCl (-85°C, no hydrogen bonding at all, only weaker dipole-dipole forces).
questions.explanation_trick: H2O has the most extensive hydrogen-bonding network (2 H-bond donors per molecule) giving it the highest boiling point among these hydrides, while HCl (no N/O/F attached, no hydrogen bonding) has the lowest.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — places NH3 last, but NH3 (hydrogen-bonded) boils higher than HCl (non-hydrogen-bonded).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — places HF above H2O, but water's more extensive hydrogen bonding actually gives it the highest boiling point among these four.
explanation_options.c: Correct — matches the actual boiling point order exactly.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same HF/H2O ordering issue as C, plus the NH3/HCl order.

aliases: Correct order of boiling points of the given liquid is
H2O > HF > HCl > NH3

questions.question_text: The relative energies of 4s, 4p and 3d orbitals are in the order
questions.explanation_short: Energy order: 4s < 3d < 4p.
questions.explanation_long: Using the (n+l) rule: 4s has n+l=4 (lowest of the three); 3d has n+l=5, 4p has n+l=5 (tied, so lower n wins — 3d has n=3, lower than 4p's n=4). So the energy order from lowest to highest is 4s < 3d < 4p.
questions.explanation_trick: When two orbitals tie on n+l value, the one with the smaller principal quantum number n has the lower energy — this is exactly what separates 3d from 4p here.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — places 3d below 4p but 4s too high; doesn't match the (n+l) rule calculation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 4s < 3d < 4p matches the (n+l) rule.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — places 4p as lowest, but 4p actually has the highest of the three (tied n+l with 3d, but higher n).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — reverses the order almost entirely.

questions.question_text: With increase in the value of Principal Quantum Number ‘n’, the shape of the s-orbitals remains the same although their sizes
questions.option_d: May or may not remain the same
questions.explanation_short: s-orbital size increases with increasing principal quantum number n (shape stays spherical).
questions.explanation_long: All s-orbitals are spherically symmetric regardless of n, but as n increases, the orbital's size (radial extent, where the electron is most likely found) increases, since higher-energy electrons occupy larger regions of space further from the nucleus.
questions.explanation_trick: Shape stays the same (always spherical for any s-orbital) — only the SIZE grows with increasing n, just like nested spherical shells getting progressively bigger.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — size doesn't decrease with increasing n; it grows.
explanation_options.b: Correct — s-orbital size increases as n increases.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — size does change (increase), not stay the same, as n increases.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is settled physics (size reliably increases with n), not an uncertain 'may or may not' relationship.

questions.question_text: The angle between unhybridized p-orbital and three sp2 hybrid orbitals of each carbon atom in ether is:
questions.explanation_short: An unhybridized p-orbital sits perpendicular (90°) to the plane of the three sp2 hybrid orbitals.
questions.explanation_long:
For an sp2-hybridized carbon (as in ethene/ethylene, forming a pi bond), the three sp2 hybrid orbitals lie in a flat plane at 120° to each other, while the remaining unhybridized p-orbital points perpendicular to that plane — a 90° angle between the p-orbital and the sp2 plane.

**Note:** the question's mention of 'ether' appears to be a wording slip in the source — ordinary ethers (R-O-R) don't involve sp2/p-orbital hybridization at all; this scenario (sp2 carbon with an unhybridized p-orbital forming a pi bond) precisely describes ethene, not ether. The physics answer itself (90°) is correct for the intended sp2-hybridized-carbon scenario regardless of this naming slip.
questions.explanation_trick: sp2 hybrid orbitals lie in a flat plane (120° apart from each other); the leftover unhybridized p-orbital always sits perpendicular (90°) to that plane — this geometry is what allows pi-bond formation above and below the plane.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 120° is the angle between the sp2 orbitals themselves, not between a sp2 orbital and the perpendicular p-orbital.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 90° is the perpendicular angle between the p-orbital and the sp2 plane.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 109.5° is the tetrahedral angle for sp3 hybridization, not relevant to this sp2/p-orbital geometry.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 180° would describe a linear (sp) arrangement, not this sp2/perpendicular-p scenario.

questions.question_text: In ‘H-F’ bond electronegativity difference is ‘1.9’. What is the type of this bond?
questions.explanation_short: An electronegativity difference of 1.9 (H-F) indicates a polar covalent bond.
questions.explanation_long: H-F's electronegativity difference (1.9) is large enough to create a highly polar bond with significant partial ionic character, but not large enough to be classified as a fully ionic bond — it's the textbook example of an extremely polar covalent bond.
questions.explanation_trick: H-F is famous specifically as the MOST polar of the hydrogen halides (H-F, H-Cl, H-Br, H-I) due to fluorine's extreme electronegativity — yet it's still classified as covalent, not ionic.

explanation_options.a: Correct — H-F is the classic example of a highly polar covalent bond.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a 1.9 electronegativity difference is far too large to be a non-polar bond.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a pi bond is a type of bond formed by orbital overlap geometry, not defined by electronegativity difference.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a coordinate covalent bond is defined by both bonding electrons coming from one atom, unrelated to this electronegativity-difference scenario.

questions.question_text: ‘∆H’ will be given a negative sign in
questions.explanation_short: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions.
questions.explanation_long: By convention, a reaction that releases heat to the surroundings (exothermic) has a negative enthalpy change (ΔH < 0), since the system's total enthalpy decreases.
questions.explanation_trick: Exothermic = negative ΔH (heat exits the system, enthalpy content drops); Endothermic = positive ΔH (heat enters, enthalpy content rises) — this sign convention is fixed and worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — exothermic reactions have negative ΔH.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — decomposition reactions are typically endothermic as well, giving positive ΔH.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — dissociation reactions are typically endothermic (bond-breaking absorbs energy), giving positive ΔH.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — endothermic reactions have positive (not negative) ΔH by definition.

questions.question_text: Lattice energy of an ionic crystal is the enthalpy of
questions.explanation_short: Lattice energy is the enthalpy of formation of an ionic crystal from its gaseous ions.
questions.explanation_long: Lattice energy specifically measures the energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of a solid ionic crystal lattice — this is defined as an enthalpy of formation for the crystal.
questions.explanation_trick: Lattice energy = energy released FORMING the crystal from separate gaseous ions (a highly exothermic, energy-releasing process, driven by strong electrostatic attraction) — distinct from enthalpies of dissolution or dissociation which describe breaking the lattice apart.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — combustion enthalpy relates to burning reactions, unrelated to ionic lattice formation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — dissociation enthalpy describes breaking the lattice apart (the reverse process), not forming it.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — dissolution enthalpy describes dissolving the solid in a solvent, a different process from lattice formation.
explanation_options.d: Correct — lattice energy is the enthalpy of formation of the crystal from its gaseous ions.

questions.question_text: As number of solute particles increases, freezing point of the solution:
questions.explanation_short: More solute particles lower the solution's freezing point (freezing point depression).
questions.explanation_long: Freezing point depression is a colligative property: the more solute particles present, the greater the depression of the freezing point below the pure solvent's freezing point.
questions.explanation_trick: More dissolved particles = greater freezing point depression AND greater boiling point elevation — both colligative effects scale directly with the number of solute particles, in opposite directions from the pure solvent's values.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — freezing point does change (decrease) as solute particles increase; it doesn't stay fixed.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — freezing point decreases (not increases) as more solute particles are added.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — there's no increase-then-decrease pattern; it's a steady, direct decrease with more solute.
explanation_options.d: Correct — freezing point steadily decreases as solute particle count increases.

questions.question_text: Boiling point constants help us to determine
questions.explanation_short: Boiling point elevation constants (Kb) are used to determine molar masses.
questions.explanation_long: By measuring how much a solvent's boiling point rises upon dissolving a known mass of solute (ΔTb = Kb × molality), and knowing Kb for that solvent, chemists can back-calculate the solute's molar mass — a classic application of colligative properties.
questions.explanation_trick: Colligative properties (boiling point elevation, freezing point depression) are powerful tools specifically for determining an unknown solute's molar mass experimentally.

explanation_options.a: Correct — boiling point elevation constants are used precisely for molar mass determination.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — volume isn't determined this way either.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — pressure isn't what's being determined via boiling point constants.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — mass alone (without molar mass/moles) isn't the target quantity of this technique.

questions.question_text: In electrolysis of aqueous CuCl₂, the metal deposited at cathode is
questions.explanation_short: Copper metal is deposited at the cathode during electrolysis of aqueous CuCl2.
questions.explanation_long: In aqueous CuCl2 electrolysis, Cu²⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode (gaining electrons) to deposit as copper metal, while chloride ions are oxidized at the anode to form chlorine gas.
questions.explanation_trick: In electrolysis of a metal salt solution, whichever metal cation is actually present in solution gets reduced (deposited) at the cathode — here, that's copper, straightforwardly from CuCl2.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — sodium isn't present in this solution at all (CuCl2, not a sodium salt).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — aluminium isn't present in this solution.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — lead isn't present in this solution.
explanation_options.d: Correct — copper is the metal ion actually present, and it's what deposits at the cathode.

aliases: In electrolysis of aqueous CuCl2, the metal deposited at cathode is
Sodium

questions.question_text: In MgCl₂, the oxidation state of ‘Cl’ is
questions.explanation_short: In MgCl2, chlorine's oxidation state is -1.
questions.explanation_long: Magnesium in MgCl2 has an oxidation state of +2 (typical for Group 2 metals). Since the overall compound is neutral and there are two chlorines, each chlorine must balance +2/2 = -1 per chlorine atom.
questions.explanation_trick: Halogens (Cl, Br, I) in simple metal halide salts are almost always -1 — this is their standard, default oxidation state in the vast majority of compounds.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — chlorine in a compound (not elemental Cl2) isn't zero.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — +2 would be a highly unusual, non-standard oxidation state for chlorine, and doesn't balance charge here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — -2 would require two chlorines to balance a +4 metal, not Mg's +2.
explanation_options.d: Correct — each chlorine is -1, balancing Mg's +2 charge across two chlorines.

aliases: In MgCl2, the oxidation state of ‘Cl’ is
Zero

questions.question_text: Formation of NH3 is reversible and exothermic process, what will happen on cooling?
questions.explanation_short: Cooling an exothermic equilibrium (NH3 formation) shifts it towards more product (more NH3).
questions.explanation_long: Per Le Chatelier's principle, cooling an exothermic equilibrium reaction favours the direction that releases heat — since NH3 formation (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3) is exothermic in the forward direction, cooling shifts the equilibrium towards more NH3 production.
questions.explanation_trick: For an exothermic forward reaction, think of heat as a 'product' — removing heat (cooling) pushes the equilibrium to produce more of that heat, i.e. more forward-direction product.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — cooling favours the exothermic (product-forming) direction, not the reverse.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — same reasoning, cooling doesn't favour the reactant side.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cooling doesn't favour reactant formation for an exothermic forward reaction.
explanation_options.d: Correct — cooling shifts an exothermic equilibrium towards more product.

questions.question_text: A buffer solution is that which resists/minimizes the change in
questions.explanation_short: A buffer solution resists changes in pH.
questions.explanation_long:
A buffer's entire defining function is to minimize pH swings when small amounts of acid or base are added to a solution, by using a weak acid/conjugate base (or weak base/conjugate acid) pair that can absorb the added H+ or OH-.

**Note:** the source data marked 'pKa' as correct — but pKa is a fixed, intrinsic property of a given weak acid (it doesn't 'change' in a way that a buffer would need to resist); the standard, universally taught definition of a buffer's function is resisting changes in pH. The corrected answer reflects this standard definition.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Buffer' literally means something that cushions/absorbs a shock — here, that shock is a change in pH, the property buffers are specifically designed to stabilize.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — pOH is mathematically tied to pH (pH+pOH=14), so resisting pH change also stabilizes pOH, but pH is the standard term used to define a buffer's purpose.
explanation_options.b: Correct — resisting pH change is the fundamental, standard definition of a buffer's function.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — pKa is a fixed constant for a given acid, not something that fluctuates and needs resisting.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — pKb, like pKa, is a fixed constant, not a fluctuating quantity a buffer resists.

questions.question_text: In some reactions, a product formed acts as a catalyst. The phenomenon is called
questions.explanation_short: When a reaction's own product acts as a catalyst for that same reaction, it's called autocatalysis.
questions.explanation_long: Autocatalysis describes a reaction where one of the products formed speeds up the reaction's own rate, often causing the reaction to accelerate as it proceeds (until reactants run low).
questions.explanation_trick: Auto- (self) + catalysis = the reaction catalyzing itself via its own product — a distinctive kinetic pattern (rate increasing before eventually decreasing) that identifies autocatalytic reactions.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — negative catalysis (inhibition) slows a reaction down, the opposite effect.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'activation of catalyst' isn't the standard term for this specific product-as-catalyst phenomenon.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — heterogeneous catalysis refers to the catalyst being in a different physical phase from the reactants, an unrelated classification.
explanation_options.d: Correct — autocatalysis precisely describes a product acting as the reaction's own catalyst.

questions.question_text: The reaction rate in forward direction decreases with the passage of time because
questions.explanation_short: Forward reaction rate decreases over time as reactant concentration decreases.
questions.explanation_long: As a reaction proceeds, reactants are consumed, lowering their concentration — and since reaction rate generally depends on reactant concentration (rate law), the forward rate naturally slows down as the reaction progresses.
questions.explanation_trick: Reaction rate typically depends directly on reactant concentration — as reactants are used up over time, the rate inevitably drops, a simple and intuitive kinetic relationship.

explanation_options.a: Correct — decreasing reactant concentration directly slows the forward rate.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — decreasing product concentration would actually be irrelevant to (or could even increase) the forward rate, not explain its decrease.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the reaction order (a fixed mathematical relationship for a given reaction) doesn't spontaneously change over time.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — temperature isn't assumed to be changing in this scenario; concentration change alone explains the rate decrease.

questions.question_text: Which one remains same along a period?
questions.explanation_short: The number of electron shells stays the same across a period.
questions.explanation_long: By definition, a period groups elements that all have the same number of electron shells (same highest principal quantum number, n) — this stays constant across the period, while other properties like atomic radius, melting point, and conductivity vary considerably.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Period' is literally defined by a fixed shell count — this is the one property guaranteed to stay the same as you move left to right within a single period.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — atomic radius generally decreases across a period, it doesn't stay the same.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — melting points vary considerably (often rising then falling) across a period.
explanation_options.c: Correct — number of shells is fixed within a period by definition.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — electrical conductivity varies significantly (metals to non-metals) across a period.

questions.question_text: More the ionization energy of an element:
questions.explanation_short: Higher ionization energy correlates with LESS metallic character.
questions.explanation_long:
A high ionization energy means an atom holds onto its electrons tightly (hard to remove) — this is characteristic of non-metals, not metals, so higher ionization energy directly correlates with less metallic character.

**Note:** the source data marked 'more reducing power' as correct — but this is backwards: a good reducing agent readily *gives up* electrons (low ionization energy), while high ionization energy means the atom resists losing electrons, making it a POOR reducing agent. The corrected answer, less metallic character, correctly matches high ionization energy.
questions.explanation_trick: High ionization energy = electrons held tightly = non-metal-like behaviour = poor reducing agent = smaller atomic radius. All four of these trend together — memorize them as one connected package.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — higher ionization energy actually correlates with LESS electropositivity (harder to lose electrons and form positive ions).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — high ionization energy means a POOR (not more) reducing agent, since reducing power requires easily losing electrons.
explanation_options.c: Correct — high ionization energy directly correlates with less metallic character.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — higher ionization energy typically correlates with a SMALLER (not bigger) atomic radius, since valence electrons held closer to the nucleus are harder to remove.

questions.question_text: Alkaline earth metal hydroxides decompose on heating. Which of the following reactions is a correct representation of this decomposition?
questions.explanation_short: Alkaline earth metal hydroxides decompose on heating to the metal oxide plus water: M(OH)2 → MO + H2O.
questions.explanation_long: Heating an alkaline earth metal hydroxide drives off water, leaving behind the metal oxide: M(OH)2(s) → MO(s) + H2O(l), a balanced 1:1:1 decomposition.
questions.explanation_trick: M(OH)2 → MO + H2O is a clean, already-balanced equation (2 OH groups on the left provide exactly the O and 2 H's needed for one H2O on the right) — a straightforward decomposition pattern worth recognizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this equation is properly balanced and matches the expected decomposition.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'MOH' represents a Group 1 (not Group 2) hydroxide formula, and the products don't balance correctly either.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — incorrectly produces H2 gas instead of water, and the formula 'MOH2' doesn't correctly represent the hydroxide.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this describes a much more complex decomposition (producing free metal, water, and oxygen) that doesn't match simple thermal decomposition of a Group 2 hydroxide.

aliases: Alkaline earth metal hydroxides decompose on heating. Which of the following reactions is a correct representation of this decomposition?
M(OH)2(s) MO(s) + H2O(l)

questions.question_text: Carbon has the unique ability to form long chains by bonding with other carbon atoms. This property of self-linking in carbon is known as:
questions.explanation_short: Carbon's ability to form chains by bonding with itself is called catenation.
questions.explanation_long: Catenation is the property of an element forming chains (or rings) by bonding repeatedly with atoms of itself. Carbon's exceptional catenation ability (strong, stable C-C bonds) is the foundation of all organic chemistry.
questions.explanation_trick: Catenation = self-chaining (from Latin 'catena', chain) — carbon's catenation ability is unmatched among elements, making possible the vast diversity of organic compounds.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — condensation is a reaction type (losing a small molecule like water), not the property of self-bonding.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — polymerization describes joining monomer units together, a related but distinct concept from the general self-linking property.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cyclization describes forming a ring specifically, a subset of what catenation makes possible, not the general term itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — catenation is the precise term for this self-linking ability.

questions.question_text: Oxidation state of ‘Mn’ in KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄, MnO₂ and MnSO₄ is in the order:
questions.explanation_short: Mn oxidation states: KMnO4 (+7) > K2MnO4 (+6) > MnO2 (+4) > MnSO4 (+2).
questions.explanation_long: Working out each: KMnO4 (K=+1, O4=-8, so Mn=+7); K2MnO4 (2K=+2, O4=-8, so Mn=+6); MnO2 (O2=-4, so Mn=+4); MnSO4 (SO4=-2, so Mn=+2). This gives the order +7, +6, +4, +2.
questions.explanation_trick: Balance the total charge to zero for each neutral compound, using each element's known standard oxidation state (K always +1, O almost always -2, sulfate always -2) to solve for Mn each time.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — swaps the last two values (should be +4 then +2, not +2 then +4).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — swaps the first two values.
explanation_options.c: Correct — +7, +6, +4, +2 matches the charge-balance calculation for each compound in order.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — reverses the entire sequence.

aliases: Oxidation state of ‘Mn’ in KMnO4, K2MnO4, MnO2 and MnSO4 is in the order:

questions.question_text: Which pair of transition elements shows abnormal electronic configuration?
questions.explanation_short: Copper and chromium show abnormal (exception) electronic configurations among transition metals.
questions.explanation_long: Both Cu ([Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, not the 'expected' [Ar]4s²3d⁹) and Cr ([Ar]4s¹3d⁵, not the 'expected' [Ar]4s²3d⁴) deviate from the standard Aufbau-predicted filling order, due to the extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled d-subshells.
questions.explanation_trick: Cu and Cr are THE two classic 'exception' elements in electron configuration questions — always double-check these two specifically whenever a question asks about anomalous transition metal configurations.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Sc and Zn follow the standard, expected electron filling pattern (no anomaly).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Sc follows the standard pattern; only Cu is anomalous in this pair.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Zn follows the standard pattern; only Cu is anomalous in this pair.
explanation_options.d: Correct — both Cu and Cr are the well-known anomalous-configuration pair.

questions.question_text: The acid rain water has pH:
questions.explanation_short: Acid rain typically has a pH below 5.
questions.explanation_long: While natural, unpolluted rainwater is already mildly acidic (~pH 5.6, from dissolved CO2), acid rain — caused by sulfur and nitrogen oxide pollutants forming stronger acids — drops further, typically below pH 5.
questions.explanation_trick: Natural rain ≈ pH 5.6 (from CO2 alone); Acid rain < pH 5 (from added SO2/NOx pollution) — the pollution-driven drop below 5 is what distinguishes 'acid rain' from ordinary rain.

explanation_options.a: Correct — acid rain is characterized by pH below 5.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — pH 7 is neutral, far from acidic.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this range describes natural, unpolluted rainwater, not acid rain specifically.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this range is basic (alkaline), the opposite of acidic.

questions.question_text: In Contact Process for manufacturing sulphuric acid, sulphur trioxide (SO₃) is not absorbed in water because
questions.option_a: The reaction does not go to completion
questions.explanation_short: SO3 isn't directly absorbed in water in the Contact Process because that reaction is highly exothermic (creating uncontrollable acid mist).
questions.explanation_long: Directly dissolving SO3 in water is a highly exothermic reaction that produces a dense, corrosive sulfuric acid mist/fog that's difficult to control and hazardous. Instead, industrially SO3 is absorbed into concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum, which is then safely diluted with water.
questions.explanation_trick: SO3 + H2O directly = uncontrollable acid mist (too exothermic, too fast); SO3 + concentrated H2SO4 = safe, controlled oleum formation instead — this workaround is a standard industrial chemistry safety fact.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the reaction does go to completion; the issue is safety/control, not incompleteness.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the excessive exothermicity (uncontrollable heat/mist) is why direct water absorption is avoided.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the reaction is actually quite fast, not slow; that's part of why it's hard to control.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — SO3 is actually quite soluble in water; solubility isn't the issue here.

aliases: In Contact Process for manufacturing sulphuric acid, Sulphur trioxide (SO 3) is not absorbed in water because
The reaction does not go to completion

questions.question_text: In modern Haber Process Plants, the temperature maintained during the process is
questions.explanation_short: Modern Haber process plants operate at roughly 670-770 K (400-500°C).
questions.explanation_long: The Haber process temperature is a deliberate industrial compromise: higher temperatures would speed up the reaction but favour the (endothermic reverse) decomposition of NH3 per Le Chatelier's principle, reducing yield — so a moderate ~400-500°C range balances reasonable reaction rate against acceptable equilibrium yield.
questions.explanation_trick: Haber process conditions are a classic 'compromise conditions' example in chemistry — moderate temperature (400-500°C) and high pressure (~200 atm) balance rate against yield, rather than optimizing either alone.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 400-500°C (670-770 K) is the standard modern operating range.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — far too low; the reaction would be impractically slow.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — too low a temperature for practical reaction rates in this process.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — close, but not the standard cited range for modern plants.

questions.question_text: In the Haber process for manufacturing of ammonia, Nitrogen is taken from
questions.explanation_short: The Haber process obtains its nitrogen from air.
questions.explanation_long: Air is roughly 78% nitrogen gas (N2), making it an abundant, essentially free source of nitrogen for industrial ammonia synthesis via the Haber process.
questions.explanation_trick: Air is the practical, industrial-scale nitrogen source for Haber process ammonia synthesis — no need to extract nitrogen from more limited biological or mineral sources.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — extracting nitrogen from living-body proteins wouldn't be a practical, large-scale industrial source.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would be an inefficient, circular process (ammonium salts already contain fixed nitrogen).
explanation_options.c: Correct — air is the actual industrial nitrogen source.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — nitrate-containing minerals aren't the standard source used in the Haber process itself.

questions.question_text: Ethene on polymerization, gives the product polyethene. This reaction may be called as
questions.explanation_short: Ethene polymerizing to polyethene is an addition polymerization reaction.
questions.explanation_long: Ethene's monomers (CH2=CH2) link together directly through their double bonds with no small molecule released — this direct joining is the defining feature of addition polymerization.
questions.explanation_trick: Addition polymers form from monomers with a C=C double bond simply linking up (no byproduct lost); condensation polymers lose a small molecule (like water) at each linkage — polyethene is the classic addition-polymer example.

explanation_options.a: Correct — polyethene formation is a textbook example of addition polymerization.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — condensation polymerization loses a small molecule at each step, which doesn't happen when ethene forms polyethene.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — substitution describes replacing one atom/group with another, not monomer linkage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — pyrolysis is thermal decomposition (breaking down), the opposite of building up a polymer.

questions.question_text: In the following, which one is free radical?
questions.explanation_short: A single chlorine atom with an unpaired electron (Cl•) is the free radical among these options.
questions.explanation_long: A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron. Cl⁻ (anion, all electrons paired), Cl2 (stable neutral molecule, all electrons paired), and Cl+ (cation, electrons paired) are not radicals — only a lone Cl atom with a single unpaired electron (Cl•) qualifies as a free radical.
questions.explanation_trick: Free radicals are identified by having an ODD/unpaired electron — ions (with extra or missing electrons still typically paired) and stable neutral molecules (with all electrons paired) generally don't qualify.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Cl⁻ has a complete octet with all electrons paired, not a radical.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Cl+ is a cation, also without an unpaired electron in this context.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Cl2 is a stable diatomic molecule with all electrons paired in bonds/lone pairs.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a lone chlorine atom with one unpaired electron is the free radical.

aliases: In the following, which one is free radical?
Cl―

questions.question_text: The introduction of R–C⁺=O (acyl) group in benzene is called
questions.explanation_short: Introducing an acyl group (R-CO-) into benzene is called acylation.
questions.explanation_long: Friedel-Crafts acylation attaches an acyl group (R-C(=O)-) onto a benzene ring, using an acyl chloride and a Lewis acid catalyst (like AlCl3), producing an aryl ketone.
questions.explanation_trick: Acylation introduces R-CO- (forming a ketone); Alkylation introduces just R- (forming an alkylbenzene) — these are the two related but distinct Friedel-Crafts reactions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — acylation is precisely this acyl-group introduction.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'carbonyl reduction' would describe removing/reducing a carbonyl group, the opposite of introducing one.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — alkylation introduces a plain alkyl group (no carbonyl), a related but different reaction.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — formylation specifically introduces a -CHO group (one carbon, from formyl chloride or similar), a more specific case than the general R-CO- group described here.

aliases: The introduction of R C group in benzene is called
Acylation

questions.question_text: The alkaline hydrolysis of bromoethane, CH₃–CH₂–Br → CH₃–CH₂–OH, gives alcohol as the product. The reagent and the condition used in this reaction are:
questions.explanation_short: Dilute aqueous NaOH, warmed, converts bromoethane to ethanol via substitution.
questions.explanation_long: Hydrolyzing a primary alkyl halide to its corresponding alcohol requires a hydroxide nucleophile in an aqueous (not alcoholic) medium, with mild heating to drive the SN2 substitution — dilute NaOH(aq), warm.
questions.explanation_trick: Aqueous hydroxide favours substitution (giving the alcohol); alcoholic (ethanolic) hydroxide favours elimination (giving an alkene) — the solvent choice is the deciding factor between these two outcomes.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — plain water alone at room temperature is too weak/slow a nucleophile for practical hydrolysis.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — heating in ethanol alone (without a strong nucleophile like hydroxide) wouldn't cleanly give the substitution product.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — KOH in alcohol favours elimination (forming ethene), not substitution to the alcohol.
explanation_options.d: Correct — dilute aqueous NaOH, warmed, is the standard condition for this substitution.

aliases: The alkaline hydrolysis of bromoethane shown below gives alcohol as the product: H3C―CH2―Br H3C―CH2―OH The reagent and the condition used in this reaction may be:
H2O at room temperature

questions.question_text: In the reaction of ethene with bromine the intermediate formed is
questions.option_a: Cyclic bromonium ion (H₂C–CH₂ bridged by Br⁺)
questions.explanation_short: Bromine addition to an alkene proceeds through a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate.
questions.explanation_long: When Br2 adds across a carbon-carbon double bond, the pi electrons attack one bromine atom, displacing the other as Br⁻, and forming a three-membered cyclic bromonium ion bridging both carbons — a positively charged intermediate that the bromide ion then attacks from the opposite face.
questions.explanation_trick: Alkene + Br2 addition is a two-step mechanism: (1) form the cyclic bromonium ion intermediate, (2) Br⁻ attacks from the back side, giving the anti-addition dibromide product — this bromonium-ion step explains the stereochemistry (anti addition) observed.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Br⁺ bridges both carbons, forming the cyclic bromonium ion that Br⁻ then attacks.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a carbanion would need a nucleophile to attack the alkene, but Br₂ acts as an electrophile.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — an open carbocation is not formed; the bromine lone pair bridges the carbons instead.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — vinyl bromide is a substitution product, not an intermediate of addition.

aliases: In the reaction of ethane with bromine the intermediate formed is + H C CH H2 C CH2 2 2 +
Br

questions.question_text: In substitution reactions, dihaloalkane or secondary halogenoalkane give / show:
questions.explanation_short: Secondary halogenoalkanes can undergo both SN1 and SN2 mechanisms.
questions.explanation_long: Secondary alkyl halides sit in a mechanistic middle ground: they're sterically hindered enough to sometimes favour SN1 (carbocation formation) yet still accessible enough for SN2 (direct backside attack), depending on the specific nucleophile, solvent, and conditions — unlike primary substrates (favour SN2 exclusively) or tertiary substrates (favour SN1 exclusively).
questions.explanation_trick: Primary = SN2 only; Tertiary = SN1 only; Secondary = borderline, can go either way (SN1 or SN2) depending on conditions — a frequently tested three-way substrate classification.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — SN1 alone doesn't capture secondary substrates' full mechanistic flexibility.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — SN2 alone doesn't capture secondary substrates' full mechanistic flexibility either.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — E1/E2 describe elimination pathways, a different reaction type from the substitution being asked about here.
explanation_options.d: Correct — secondary substrates can proceed via both SN1 and SN2, depending on conditions.

questions.question_text: The dehydration of ethyl alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 at 140°C gives:
questions.explanation_short: Ethanol + concentrated H2SO4 at 140°C (lower temperature) gives diethyl ether.
questions.explanation_long: At the lower temperature of 140°C, concentrated sulfuric acid promotes intermolecular dehydration between two ethanol molecules, forming diethyl ether. At the higher temperature of 170°C, intramolecular dehydration instead dominates, forming ethene.
questions.explanation_trick: 140°C → ether (intermolecular, two alcohol molecules combine); 170°C → alkene (intramolecular, one alcohol molecule loses water internally) — this specific temperature-outcome pairing is frequently tested.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ethene specifically forms at the higher 170°C, not 140°C as given here.
explanation_options.b: Correct — diethyl ether forms at the lower 140°C dehydration condition.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the starting material is already an alcohol; this option doesn't represent any product/transformation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a carboxylic acid wouldn't form from simple acid-catalyzed dehydration; that would require an oxidizing agent instead.

questions.question_text: Ethanol can be converted in to ethanoic acid by:
questions.explanation_short: Ethanol converts to ethanoic acid via oxidation.
questions.explanation_long: Ethanol (a primary alcohol) is oxidized first to acetaldehyde (ethanal) and then further to acetic acid (ethanoic acid) using oxidizing agents like acidified potassium dichromate — both steps are oxidations.
questions.explanation_trick: Primary alcohol → (oxidation) → aldehyde → (further oxidation) → carboxylic acid — a standard two-step oxidation ladder worth memorizing for any primary alcohol.

explanation_options.a: Correct — oxidation converts ethanol fully to ethanoic acid.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — fermentation is how ethanol is originally produced from sugars, not how it's converted into acetic acid (though bacterial fermentation, not chemical oxidation, is how vinegar forms biologically — the chemistry answer intended here is direct oxidation).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — hydration adds water across a double bond, not applicable to converting an alcohol into an acid.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — hydrogenation adds hydrogen (a reduction), the opposite direction from forming an acid.

questions.question_text: The following structure is of: R₃C–OH (a carbon bearing –OH and three R groups)
questions.explanation_short: A carbon bonded to three R groups plus an OH (R3C-OH) is a tertiary alcohol.
questions.explanation_long: Alcohols are classified by how many carbon-containing groups (R) are attached to the carbinol carbon (the one bearing -OH): one R group = primary, two R groups = secondary, three R groups = tertiary. A structure with three R groups attached to the C-OH carbon is therefore a tertiary alcohol. (The printed UHS key marks A, secondary alcohol, but a carbon carrying three R groups and –OH is a tertiary alcohol, so C is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: Count the R groups (not H's) directly attached to the C-OH carbon: 1 R = primary, 2 R = secondary, 3 R = tertiary — a quick, reliable classification method.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — secondary alcohols have only two R groups on the carbinol carbon, not three.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — primary alcohols have only one R group on the carbinol carbon.
explanation_options.c: Correct — three R groups on the carbinol carbon defines a tertiary alcohol.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this structure has no carbonyl/acid group; it's clearly an alcohol (C-OH), not a carboxylic acid.

aliases: The following structure is of: R R C OH R
Secondary alcohol

questions.question_text: When ethanol is warmed with ethanoic acid in the presence of strong acid catalyst, an ester ethyl ethanoate is formed: CH₃CH₂OH + CH₃CO₂H → CH₃CO₂CH₂CH₃ + H₂O. Which statement is correct?
questions.option_b: O–H bond in ethanoic acid is broken
questions.option_c: O–H bond in ethanol is broken
questions.explanation_short: In Fischer esterification, the alcohol's O-H bond breaks (losing just its H); the acid loses its whole -OH group.
questions.explanation_long: The classic mnemonic for ester formation: 'the acid loses -OH, the alcohol loses only -H' (confirmed by oxygen-18 isotope labeling experiments showing the ester's linking oxygen comes from the alcohol). So during the mechanism, the O-H bond within the ethanol molecule is what breaks, while ethanol's oxygen stays attached to the forming ester.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize: 'Acid loses OH, Alcohol loses H' — this single phrase captures exactly which bond breaks where during Fischer esterification, confirmed by isotope-labeling experiments.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the alcohol isn't reduced in this reaction; no change in oxidation state occurs for either reactant.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — it's the acid's C-OH bond (losing the whole OH group as part of water) that breaks, not specifically framed as its 'O-H bond' being the key cleavage point in the standard mnemonic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the O-H bond in ethanol breaks, with ethanol's oxygen becoming part of the ester linkage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the acid isn't oxidized in this reaction; this is a substitution, not a redox process.

aliases: When ethanol is warmed with ethanoic acid in the presence of strong acid catalyst, an ester ethyl ethanoate is formed. CH3CH2OH + CH3CO2H CH3CO2CH2CH3 During this reaction:
Alcohol is reduced

questions.question_text: Primary alcohols normally give us aldehydes when oxidized in the presence of Na 2Cr3O7, what the product will be, when the secondary alcohols are oxidized in same conditions?
questions.explanation_short: Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones.
questions.explanation_long: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol (with an oxidant like Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4) removes two hydrogens from the carbinol carbon, forming a ketone — unlike primary alcohols, which oxidize first to an aldehyde (and can be oxidized further to a carboxylic acid).
questions.explanation_trick: Primary alcohol → aldehyde → (further oxidation) → carboxylic acid; Secondary alcohol → ketone (stops here, no further oxidation possible without breaking a C-C bond); Tertiary alcohol → resists oxidation entirely.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — forming an alkene would require an elimination (dehydration) reaction, not oxidation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — forming an alkyne would require a very different, more drastic set of reactions, not simple alcohol oxidation.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — alkyl halides form via halogenation reactions, not oxidation of an alcohol.
explanation_options.d: Correct — secondary alcohols oxidize specifically to ketones.

questions.question_text: Formaldehyde reacts with HCN (NaCN + HCl) to give a compound:
questions.explanation_short: Formaldehyde + HCN gives the cyanohydrin addition product: H2C(OH)(CN).
questions.explanation_long: HCN adds across the carbonyl group of formaldehyde (H2C=O) via nucleophilic addition: the cyanide ion attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, and the resulting alkoxide is protonated to give the cyanohydrin product, H2C(OH)(CN) (glycolonitrile).
questions.explanation_trick: Aldehyde/ketone + HCN → cyanohydrin (adds -CN and -OH across the former C=O double bond) — a standard nucleophilic addition reaction for any carbonyl compound.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this cyanohydrin comes from acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO), not formaldehyde.
explanation_options.b: Correct — HCHO + HCN → H₂C(OH)CN, formaldehyde cyanohydrin.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this cyanohydrin comes from acetone.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is an acyl cyanide, not an addition product of HCN.

aliases: Formaldehyde reacts with HCN (NaCN + HCl) to give a compound: H C 3 OH H3 C OH C C CN
H CN

questions.question_text: Iodoform test will not be positive with:
questions.explanation_short: 3-pentanone (diethyl ketone) does NOT give a positive iodoform test — it lacks a methyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon.
questions.explanation_long: The iodoform test requires a CH3-CO- (methyl ketone) or CH3-CH(OH)- pattern. 3-pentanone (CH3CH2-CO-CH2CH3) has ethyl groups on both sides of the carbonyl, with no methyl group directly attached — so it fails the test, unlike methyl ketones, acetaldehyde, or appropriately structured alcohols like ethanol.
questions.explanation_trick: Check specifically for a methyl group DIRECTLY bonded to the carbonyl carbon (or to a carbinol carbon bearing -OH) — 3-pentanone's symmetric ethyl-ethyl structure lacks this pattern entirely, making it the clear exception among ketones/aldehydes here.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 3-pentanone lacks the required methyl-adjacent-to-carbonyl pattern, so it fails the iodoform test.
explanation_options.b: This option (a methyl ketone) DOES give a positive iodoform test, having the required CH3-CO- pattern.
explanation_options.c: This option (representing ethanol) DOES give a positive iodoform test, since ethanol's CH3-CH2-OH structure fits the required CH3-CH(OH)- pattern.
explanation_options.d: This option (acetaldehyde) DOES give a positive iodoform test, having the required CH3-CHO pattern.

aliases: Iodoform test will not be positive with: O
H3C CH2 C CH2 CH3

questions.question_text: When CH₃–CH₂–OH is oxidized in the presence of K₂Cr₂O₇ and H₂SO₄, the product formed is
questions.explanation_short: Ethanol oxidized with excess K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 fully oxidizes to acetic acid (CH3COOH).
questions.explanation_long: Under strong, excess oxidizing conditions (acidified potassium dichromate), a primary alcohol like ethanol is fully oxidized all the way to the carboxylic acid, passing through the aldehyde intermediate along the way — the final, stable product under these vigorous conditions is ethanoic acid.
questions.explanation_trick: Under strong/excess oxidant conditions, primary alcohols oxidize all the way to the carboxylic acid (not stopping at the aldehyde) — the aldehyde is only isolated under milder, controlled distillation conditions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ethanoic acid (acetic acid) is the fully oxidized product under these strong conditions.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this represents formic acid (from methanol), not the two-carbon product expected from ethanol.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this represents a ketone structure, which wouldn't form from oxidizing a primary alcohol like ethanol.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this represents an ester structure, not the direct oxidation product of an alcohol.

aliases: When CH3―CH2―OH is oxidized in the presence of K2Cr2O7 and H2SO4, the product formed is O O
H3C C OH

questions.question_text: He had a heart attack and all attempts to _________ him failed.
questions.explanation_short: Resuscitate means to revive someone, especially after a heart attack.
questions.explanation_long: 'Resuscitate' means to bring someone back to consciousness or life, typically used medically for reviving someone whose heart has stopped or who has stopped breathing.
questions.explanation_trick: Resuscitate is the standard medical term paired with cardiac emergencies (CPR = cardiopulmonary resuscitation) — a direct vocabulary-context match.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'renew' means to make new again, not medically revive a person.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'resuscitate' precisely fits reviving someone after a heart attack.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'revise' means to review/edit, unrelated to reviving a person.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'refurnish' means to furnish again, unrelated to reviving a person.

questions.question_text: The _________ stench of dead animals and plants made Mumtaz ill.
questions.explanation_short: Putrid describes the foul stench of decaying matter.
questions.explanation_long: 'Putrid' means decaying and foul-smelling, exactly describing the stench of dead animals and plants.
questions.explanation_trick: Putrid relates to 'putrefy' (to rot/decay) — the smell of decay is the classic context this word appears in.

explanation_options.a: Correct — putrid precisely describes decay-related foul smell.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'purified' means made clean, the opposite of a foul stench.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'perturbed' means worried/anxious, an emotional state, not a smell.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'purchased' means bought, entirely unrelated to smell.

questions.question_text: While going up the hills, by bus, she felt __________ inside.
questions.explanation_short: Queasy describes the nauseated feeling from motion sickness.
questions.explanation_long: 'Queasy' describes a feeling of nausea or sickness in the stomach, exactly the sensation from motion sickness while riding a bus up winding hills.
questions.explanation_trick: Queasy = stomach discomfort/nausea — the standard word for describing motion sickness or an uneasy stomach.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'fishy' means suspicious or smelling of fish, unrelated to nausea.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'itchy' describes a skin sensation, not stomach discomfort.
explanation_options.c: Correct — queasy precisely describes this nauseated feeling.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'squeezy' isn't a standard word for this sensation.

questions.question_text: The craft statesman manipulated the situation by making false promises and declaring sport festivities as a __________ to fool the public.
questions.explanation_short: 'Red herring' is the correct idiom for a deliberate distraction/misleading clue.
questions.explanation_long: A 'red herring' is something designed to mislead or distract from the real issue — exactly what a politician's false promises and festivities do here, matching the correct spelling and idiom.
questions.explanation_trick: Red herring: an idiom from the old practice of dragging a smoked (reddish) herring across a trail to throw hunting dogs off scent — memorize the exact spelling 'herring' (two r's, two n's).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — misspells 'herring' as 'hearing', an entirely different word.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'red-feather' isn't the correct idiom.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the properly spelled idiom.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — misspells 'herring' as 'haring'.

questions.question_text: SPOT THE ERROR: The theory was discarded as there was no corroborating evidence for its favour.
questions.explanation_short: Error: should be 'evidence IN its favour', not 'evidence FOR its favour'.
questions.explanation_long: The standard idiom is 'evidence in favour of' something — 'for its favour' isn't the correct preposition pairing. The underlined 'for' is the error.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Evidence in favour of X' / 'evidence in X's favour' — memorize 'in' as the fixed preposition here.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'discarded' is used correctly.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'as' (meaning 'because') is used correctly here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'there' is used correctly.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the error; should be 'in its favour'.

discarded

questions.question_text: SPOT THE ERROR: The workers were raising much hue and cry when their demands were turned away.
questions.explanation_short: Error: demands are 'turned down', not 'turned away'.
questions.explanation_long: 'Turn down' is the correct phrasal verb for rejecting a request or demand. 'Turned away' typically means physically refusing someone entry, not rejecting a demand. The underlined 'away' is the error.
questions.explanation_trick: Turn down a request/demand/offer (reject it); Turn away a person (refuse them entry/admission) — these are two different phrasal verbs for two different objects.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'raising' (hue and cry) is used correctly.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'much' is used correctly.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'demands' is used correctly.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the error; should be 'turned down'.

aliases: SPOT THE ERROR: The workers were raising much hue and cry when their demands were turned away. [Diagram/graph/structure required — see original PDF page.]
raising

questions.question_text: SPOT THE ERROR: Aslam was badly cudgeled from his step-brother. He received many bruises and contusions. Thank God! No injury was serious.
questions.explanation_short: Error: should be 'cudgeled BY his step-brother', not 'FROM his step-brother'.
questions.explanation_long: Passive voice requires 'by' to introduce the agent performing the action ('cudgeled by X' = X did the cudgeling). 'From' doesn't work as the agent-marking preposition in passive constructions. The underlined 'from' is the error.
questions.explanation_trick: Passive voice agent marker is always 'by' (X was [verb]ed BY Y) — a fixed grammatical rule regardless of the specific verb.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the error; should be 'by his step-brother'.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'bruises' is used correctly.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'Thank' (God) is used correctly as an exclamation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'was' correctly forms the passive construction.

aliases: SPOT THE ERROR: Aslam was badly cudgeled from his step-brother. He received many bruises and contusions. Thank God! No [Diagram/graph/structure required — see original PDF page.]
from

questions.question_text: SPOT THE ERROR: I extend a cordial invitation for you to visit our farm house. We have grown vegetables without chemical fertilizers over there.
questions.explanation_short: Error: should be 'invitation TO you', not 'invitation FOR you'.
questions.explanation_long: The standard idiom is 'extend an invitation to someone' — 'for you' doesn't fit this specific collocation. The underlined 'for' is the error.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Extend an invitation TO someone' — memorize 'to' as the fixed preposition paired with this specific formal phrase.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the error; should be 'invitation to you'.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'to visit' is a correct infinitive usage.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_b: Why did not Nomana remain true to her husband?

questions.option_d: Why did not Nomana remained true to her husband?
questions.explanation_short: 'Why did not Nomana remain...' — after 'did', the main verb reverts to its base form.
questions.explanation_long: The auxiliary 'did' already carries the past tense, so the main verb that follows must be in its base form: 'remain', not 'remained' or 'remains'.
questions.explanation_trick: Once 'did'/'does'/'do' is used as the question/negation auxiliary, the main verb always drops back to its plain base form — no extra tense marking.

explanation_options.b: Correct — 'did not remain' correctly uses the base form after 'did'.

explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'did not...remained' incorrectly keeps the verb in past tense after 'did'.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_b: All my childhood, I longed desperately to a tricycle.
questions.option_c: All my childhood, I longed desperately for a tricycle.
questions.option_d: All my childhood, I longed desperately at a tricycle.
questions.explanation_short: 'Longed FOR a tricycle' is the correct preposition pairing.
questions.explanation_long: 'Long for something' (to yearn/desire something intensely) is the fixed idiomatic preposition pairing.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Long FOR' — memorize this preposition; 'to', 'at', and 'in for' don't fit this specific verb.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_d: She felt unreal for the voice informed her of the subway accident.
questions.explanation_short: 'She felt unreal AS the voice informed her...' uses 'as' correctly to mean 'while/because'.
questions.explanation_long: 'As' here introduces a clause describing the circumstance/reason for her feeling ('as the voice informed her' = 'because/while the voice informed her') — a standard, grammatical use of 'as' as a conjunction.
questions.explanation_trick: 'As' can mean 'while' or 'because' when introducing a clause — check whether the following words form a complete clause (subject+verb), which 'as', 'that', and 'for' can each introduce differently depending on context and idiom.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'to the voice informed' isn't grammatical; 'to' doesn't correctly connect these clauses.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'as' naturally introduces the causal/simultaneous clause here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'that' would suggest reported content of what was informed, not the reason for feeling unreal.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'for' as a conjunction (meaning 'because') is more formal/archaic and doesn't fit this sentence's natural flow as well as 'as'.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_b: Bill Gates is one of the wealthy person in the world.
questions.option_c: Bill Gates is one of the wealthiest persons in the world.
questions.option_d: Bill Gates is one of the more wealthy person in the world.
questions.explanation_short: 'One of the wealthiest persons' — superlative + plural noun.
questions.explanation_long: The construction 'one of the [superlative] [plural noun]' requires both the superlative form ('wealthiest', not 'wealthy' or 'more wealthy') and a plural noun ('persons', not 'person') since you're picking one out of a group of many wealthy people.
questions.explanation_trick: 'One of the [superlative]est [plural noun]' is a fixed pattern — both the adjective (superlative) and the noun (plural) must match this template together.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — uses the singular 'person' instead of the required plural.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — uses the plain 'wealthy' instead of the superlative 'wealthiest', plus the singular noun issue.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'wealthiest persons' correctly uses both the superlative and plural forms.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'more wealthy' is a comparative, not the needed superlative, plus the singular noun issue.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:
questions.option_a: Her father is a SP in the Punjab Police.
questions.option_b: Her father was a SP in the Punjab Police.
questions.option_c: Her father is an SP in the Punjab Police.
questions.option_d: Her father are a SP in the Punjab Police.
questions.explanation_short: 'An SP' — the article follows the sound, not the spelling.
questions.explanation_long: Even though 'SP' is spelled with a consonant, it's pronounced 'ess-pee', starting with a vowel sound — so the article 'an' is used, following English's sound-based (not spelling-based) article rule.
questions.explanation_trick: Article choice (a/an) depends on the following SOUND, not the first letter's spelling — 'an SP', 'an MBA', 'an FBI agent' all start with consonant letters but vowel sounds when spoken.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'a SP' ignores that 'SP' starts with a vowel sound when spoken aloud.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — while 'was' correctly indicates past tense, it wrongly pairs with 'a SP' instead of 'an SP'.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'an SP' correctly matches the vowel sound of 'ess'.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'are' doesn't agree with the singular subject 'her father', plus the same article issue.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_c: There has musical instruments in the shop.

questions.explanation_long: In an existential 'there' construction, the verb must agree with the noun that actually follows it — here, the plural 'instruments' requires the plural verb 'were', not a singular form.
questions.explanation_trick: 'There + verb + subject' — always check the noun AFTER 'there' to determine whether the verb should be singular or plural, since that noun is the true grammatical subject.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'were' correctly agrees with the plural 'instruments'.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'was' incorrectly treats 'instruments' as singular.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'has' doesn't fit this existential construction pattern at all.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'is' incorrectly treats 'instruments' as singular.

questions.option_b: He died with heart attack in 1982.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence:

questions.option_d: Were you noticed the peach blossoms?

questions.explanation_long: The present perfect tense (have/has + past participle) correctly pairs 'have' with 'noticed' (the past participle form) — 'are', 'will', and 'were' don't correctly combine with 'noticed' in this way.
questions.explanation_trick: Present perfect = have/has + past participle — always double check that the auxiliary matches the verb form that follows it.

questions.question_text: DISSONANCE
questions.explanation_short: DISSONANCE means lack of harmony/agreement — nearest meaning: Inconsistency.
questions.explanation_long: 'Dissonance' describes a lack of harmony or agreement (originally a musical term for a harsh combination of sounds, extended to mean discord or inconsistency in ideas). 'Inconsistency' is the closest match.
questions.explanation_trick: Dissonance (discord) is the opposite of 'consonance' (harmony/agreement) — think of clashing musical notes extended metaphorically to clashing ideas.

explanation_options.a: Correct — inconsistency captures dissonance's sense of disagreement/discord.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'expansion' (growth/enlargement) is unrelated.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'perceptible' (noticeable) is unrelated in meaning.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'warp' (to bend/distort) is unrelated to this meaning of dissonance.

questions.question_text: TRIFLE
questions.explanation_short: TRIFLE (as a minor/slight amount) — nearest meaning: Minor.
questions.explanation_long: As used adjectivally/adverbially ('a trifle'), 'trifle' means something of little importance or a slight amount. 'Minor' is the closest match among the choices.
questions.explanation_trick: Trifle has two senses: a light dessert (noun) and something of little importance/a small amount (the more commonly tested vocabulary sense) — context and available options usually make clear which sense is intended.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'pudding' refers to the dessert sense of trifle, not the vocabulary-test sense of minor importance.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'minor' matches trifle's sense of small/insignificant.

explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'treble' (triple, or a high musical pitch) is unrelated in meaning.

questions.question_text: MURKY
questions.explanation_short: MURKY means dark and difficult to see through — nearest meaning: Unclear.
questions.explanation_long: 'Murky' describes something dark, cloudy, or difficult to see through (literally, like murky water) or figuratively confusing/ambiguous (like a murky situation). 'Unclear' is the closest match.
questions.explanation_trick: Murky applies both literally (dark, cloudy water) and figuratively (a confusing, ambiguous situation) — 'unclear' captures both senses well.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'dusty' (covered in dust) is a related but distinct physical description, not matching murky's core meaning.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'squeamy' (a non-standard variant of squeamish, easily disgusted) is unrelated in meaning.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'clear' is the direct opposite of murky.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'unclear' captures murky's sense of being difficult to see through or understand.

questions.question_text: FAUX
questions.explanation_short: FAUX means fake or false — nearest meaning: False.
questions.explanation_long: 'Faux' (from French) means artificial or fake, imitating something genuine — as in 'faux fur' or 'faux pas' (literally 'false step'). 'False' is the most direct match.
questions.explanation_trick: Faux is a French loanword meaning simply 'false/fake' — commonly seen in English in phrases like 'faux leather' or 'faux pas'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'blunder' (a foolish mistake) is related to the phrase 'faux pas' but isn't the direct meaning of 'faux' itself.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'mistake' is again closer to 'faux pas' as a whole phrase, not 'faux' by itself.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'indiscretion' (a careless mistake in judgment) is similarly related to 'faux pas' contextually, not to 'faux' alone.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'false' is the direct, literal meaning of 'faux'.

questions.question_text: MYRIAD
questions.explanation_short: MYRIAD means countless or innumerable — nearest meaning: Multitude.
questions.explanation_long: 'Myriad' describes an extremely great, often uncountable number of something. 'Multitude' (a great number) is the closest match.
questions.explanation_trick: Myriad literally derives from a Greek word for 'ten thousand', now used generally to mean 'countless' or 'innumerable' — always implies a very large, often uncountable, quantity.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'countable' is nearly the opposite; myriad implies too numerous to easily count.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'multitude' matches myriad's sense of a very great number.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'measured' (precisely quantified) is nearly opposite in spirit to myriad's vastness.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'blurred' (unclear/indistinct) is unrelated to quantity.

questions.question_text: FACILE
questions.explanation_short: FACILE means deceptively simple or superficial — nearest meaning: Superficial.
questions.explanation_long: 'Facile' describes something that appears easy or simple but lacks depth or genuine thought — often used critically (a 'facile argument' is one that oversimplifies a complex issue). 'Superficial' is the closest match.
questions.explanation_trick: Facile isn't a compliment despite sounding like 'easy' — it usually carries a critical edge, implying an answer or argument is too simple/shallow to be taken seriously.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'fallacy' (a flawed argument) is related conceptually but is a noun for the error itself, not the adjective describing something oversimplified.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'depict' (to portray/show) is unrelated, being a different part of speech (a verb) with a different meaning entirely.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'delicate' (fragile, sensitive) is unrelated in meaning.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'superficial' captures facile's sense of deceptive, shallow simplicity.

questions.question_text: MAGNUM
questions.explanation_short: MAGNUM (as in 'magnum opus') means a great work — nearest meaning: Masterpiece.
questions.explanation_long: 'Magnum' comes from Latin meaning 'great' — most familiar in the phrase 'magnum opus' (a great work, an artist's or writer's finest achievement). 'Masterpiece' is the closest match.
questions.explanation_trick: Magnum opus = 'great work' in Latin — a phrase borrowed directly into English to describe someone's crowning achievement.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'masterpiece' matches the 'great work' sense of magnum.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'magnanimity' (generosity of spirit) is a different word sharing only a root, not a synonym.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'modest' (humble, unassuming) is nearly the opposite in tone.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'magnetic' (attracting attention/appeal) shares only superficial spelling similarity, not meaning.

questions.question_text: SIDLE
questions.explanation_short: SIDLE means to move sideways stealthily or timidly — nearest meaning: Sneak.
questions.explanation_long: 'Sidle' describes moving cautiously or shyly, often sideways, as if trying not to be noticed (e.g. 'he sidled up to the group'). 'Sneak' is the closest match among the choices.
questions.explanation_trick: Sidle always implies a cautious, often sideways or timid movement — commonly paired with 'up to' (sidle up to someone/something).

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'sneak' captures sidle's cautious, stealthy movement.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'sift' (to separate/filter, as with flour) is unrelated in meaning.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'siege' (a prolonged military blockade) is an unrelated sound-alike distractor.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'sieve' (a straining tool, or to strain something) is unrelated, another sound-alike distractor.

questions.explanation_long: 'Vertex' (from geometry, the highest point of a shape, or more generally the topmost point of anything) parallels 'zenith' (the highest point, peak, especially of achievement or the sky).
questions.explanation_trick: Vertex (geometric/literal highest point) and zenith (figurative/celestial highest point) are commonly paired as near-synonyms in vocabulary tests.

questions.question_text: The part of neuron fibre which conducts nerve impulses from the cell body is
questions.explanation_short: The axon conducts nerve impulses away from the cell body.
questions.explanation_long: A neuron's axon is the fibre that carries nerve impulses away from the cell body (soma) towards the synapse, while dendrites/dendrons carry impulses towards the cell body.
questions.explanation_trick: Dendrites bring signals IN (towards the cell body); Axon sends signals OUT (away from the cell body) — a fixed directional pairing.

questions.question_text: The number of cranial nerves in human is
questions.explanation_short: Humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
questions.explanation_long: Cranial nerves emerge directly from the brain (rather than the spinal cord), and humans have exactly 12 pairs, each with a specific name and function (e.g. optic, olfactory, vagus).
questions.explanation_trick: 12 pairs of cranial nerves (from the brain) vs. 31 pairs of spinal nerves (from the spinal cord) — two related but distinct numbers worth keeping separate.
