explanation_options.a: Correct — mature mammalian RBCs specifically lack a nucleus.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — RBCs retain their characteristic red color (from hemoglobin), even without a nucleus.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — RBCs do contain fluid (cytoplasm/cytosol) internally.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — hemoglobin is exactly what RBCs retain and rely on for oxygen transport; it isn't absent.

questions.question_text: In a normal person plasma constitutes about ___________ by volume of blood
questions.explanation_short: Plasma constitutes about 55% of blood volume.
questions.explanation_long: Blood is roughly 55% plasma (the liquid component) and 45% formed elements (mostly red blood cells, by hematocrit), a ratio commonly cited in standard physiology references.
questions.explanation_trick: Plasma ≈ 55%, Formed elements (mostly RBCs) ≈ 45% — these two blood-composition percentages are commonly tested together and should add up to 100%.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — doesn't match the standard cited plasma percentage.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — exceeds the standard cited plasma percentage.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 45% is actually closer to the formed-elements percentage, not plasma's share.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 55% is the standard cited plasma percentage of blood volume.

questions.question_text: Which vein has oxygenated blood?
questions.explanation_short: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.
questions.explanation_long: Uniquely among veins, the pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart's left atrium — all other veins carry deoxygenated blood back towards the heart.
questions.explanation_trick: Pulmonary vein = the one exception to 'veins carry deoxygenated blood' (just as the pulmonary artery is the one exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood') — memorize this reversed pulmonary pairing specifically.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the renal vein carries deoxygenated blood from the kidneys, like most other veins.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the subclavian vein carries deoxygenated blood from the arms/shoulders, like most other veins.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the pulmonary vein is the sole oxygenated-blood-carrying vein.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the jugular vein carries deoxygenated blood from the head/neck, like most other veins.

questions.question_text: What is the residual volume of air which always remains inside the lungs of human?
questions.explanation_short: Residual volume of the lungs is approximately 1.5 litres.
questions.explanation_long: Residual volume is the air that always remains in the lungs even after the most forceful exhalation, preventing the lungs from ever fully collapsing — commonly cited as around 1.2-1.5 litres.
questions.explanation_trick: Residual volume ≈ 1.5 L is a specific lung-volume figure worth memorizing directly, distinct from tidal volume (~0.5 L) and total lung capacity (~5-6 L).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — too high compared to the standard cited residual volume figure.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 0.5 L is closer to tidal volume (normal breathing volume), not residual volume.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this figure is closer to total lung capacity, not residual volume specifically.
explanation_options.d: Correct — approximately 1.5 L matches the standard cited residual volume.

questions.question_text: In nephron, most of the reabsorption takes place in the
questions.explanation_short: Most nephron reabsorption occurs at the proximal tubule.
questions.explanation_long: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered water, glucose, amino acids, and ions (roughly 65-70% of the filtrate), making it the primary site of reabsorption along the nephron.
questions.explanation_trick: Proximal tubule = the 'bulk reabsorption' workhorse of the nephron — later segments (loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct) fine-tune the remaining smaller fraction.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the distal tubule performs fine-tuning reabsorption/secretion, but handles a much smaller fraction than the proximal tubule.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the proximal tubule handles the majority of nephron reabsorption.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the ascending limb reabsorbs specific ions (Na+/Cl-) but isn't the site of the bulk of overall reabsorption.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the descending limb is mainly permeable to water (passive reabsorption) but doesn't account for the bulk of total reabsorption compared to the proximal tubule.

questions.question_text: Detection of change and signaling for effector’s response to the control system is a
questions.explanation_short: Detecting a change and signaling for a response defines a feedback mechanism generally.
questions.explanation_long: A feedback mechanism, broadly, is any control system that detects a deviation from a set point and signals for a corrective response — this general description covers both negative feedback (stabilizing) and positive feedback (amplifying) as its two subtypes.
questions.explanation_trick: When a question describes the general detect-and-signal process without specifying whether the response counteracts or amplifies the original change, it's describing the overarching 'feedback mechanism' concept, not one specific subtype.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — negative feedback is one specific subtype (counteracting change), not the general umbrella term being described here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — positive feedback is the other specific subtype (amplifying change), not the general term.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'inter-coordination' isn't the standard term for this detect-and-signal process.
explanation_options.d: Correct — feedback mechanism is the general term encompassing this detect-and-signal process.

questions.question_text: What are three components of mechanism of homeostatic regulations?
questions.option_c: CNS, PNS and diffused nervous system
questions.explanation_short: The three components of homeostatic regulation are receptors, control centre, and effectors.
questions.explanation_long: Homeostatic control systems consist of receptors (detecting changes), a control centre (processing information and determining a response), and effectors (carrying out the corrective response) — a three-part regulatory loop.
questions.explanation_trick: Receptor (detects) → Control centre (decides) → Effector (acts) — this three-step loop structure applies to virtually every homeostatic feedback system in the body.

explanation_options.a: Correct — receptors, control centre, and effectors are precisely the three components.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — sensory/motor/associative neurons describes neuron functional types, a different classification from the homeostatic-loop components.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — CNS/PNS/diffused nervous system describes types of nervous system organization, not this specific three-part homeostatic loop.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — cerebrum/cerebellum/pons are specific brain structures, not the general three-part homeostatic regulation model.

questions.question_text: Blood enters the glomerulus through
questions.explanation_short: Blood enters the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole.
questions.explanation_long: The afferent arteriole carries blood INTO the glomerulus (the capillary tuft where filtration occurs), while the efferent arteriole carries blood OUT of the glomerulus afterward.
questions.explanation_trick: Afferent = arriving/entering (afferent arteriole brings blood IN); Efferent = exiting/leaving (efferent arteriole takes blood OUT) — a consistent 'in vs. out' naming pattern used throughout physiology (also seen with afferent/efferent nerves).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the efferent arteriole carries blood OUT of the glomerulus, the opposite direction.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the afferent arteriole is specifically the vessel bringing blood into the glomerulus.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the renal artery is the larger vessel supplying the whole kidney, not the specific vessel entering the glomerulus itself.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the renal vein carries blood away from the kidney entirely, unrelated to entering the glomerulus.

questions.question_text: Which portion of nephron is under the control of ADH?
questions.explanation_short: ADH controls the distal and collecting ducts of the nephron.
questions.explanation_long: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases the permeability of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to water, promoting water reabsorption and concentrating the urine.
questions.explanation_trick: ADH's specific target segments are the distal tubule and collecting duct — the 'final adjustment' segments of the nephron, where fine-tuned water reabsorption happens based on the body's hydration needs.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Bowman's capsule is the initial filtration site, not under ADH's control.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the ascending arm handles active ion transport but is impermeable to water regardless of ADH.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the distal and collecting ducts are specifically ADH's target segments.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the descending arm is passively permeable to water but isn't specifically regulated by ADH the way the distal/collecting segments are.

questions.question_text: Cause of Parkinson’s disease is death of brain cells that produce
questions.explanation_short: Parkinson's disease is caused by the death of dopamine-producing brain cells.
questions.explanation_long: Parkinson's disease results from the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons (primarily in the substantia nigra), leading to the movement-related symptoms (tremor, rigidity, slowness) characteristic of the disease.
questions.explanation_trick: Parkinson's = dopamine deficiency (from neuron death); L-dopa treatment works by replenishing this specific missing neurotransmitter — a direct cause-and-treatment pairing.

explanation_options.a: Correct — dopamine-producing neuron death is the defining cause of Parkinson's disease.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — acetylcholine deficiency/dysfunction is more associated with conditions like myasthenia gravis or Alzheimer's, not primarily Parkinson's.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — ADH relates to water balance/kidney function, unrelated to Parkinson's disease.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — oxytocin relates to childbirth/bonding, unrelated to Parkinson's disease.
