questions.question_text: The wavelength 'λ' of a wave depends on the speed 'v' of the wave and its frequency 'f'. Decide which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation_short: f = v/λ, since v = fλ.
questions.explanation_long: Wave speed relates to frequency and wavelength by v = fλ. Rearranging for frequency gives f = v/λ.
questions.explanation_trick: Just remember v = fλ ('wave speed = frequency × wavelength') and rearrange algebraically for whichever variable is asked.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this rearranges to v = fλ, i.e. f = v/λ, not f = vλ.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — inverts the relationship.
explanation_options.c: Correct — f = v/λ.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — introduces a λ⁻² that isn't in the wave equation.

aliases: The wavelength 'λ' of a wave depends on the speed 'v' of the wave and its frequency 'f'. Decide which of the following is correct?
f = v λ

questions.question_text: Name the quantity which can be measured by using base unit 'kg m² s⁻³'
questions.explanation_short: kg·m²·s⁻³ is the SI base-unit form of Power (Watt), not Work.
questions.explanation_long:
Work/Energy (Joule) = kg·m²·s⁻². Power (Watt) = Work/time = kg·m²·s⁻³. The given base units have an extra s⁻¹ compared to Joule, which is exactly what dividing by time (to get power) does. So this quantity is Power, not Work.

**Note:** the source data had this marked as Work (option D) — that's a unit-analysis error, since Work's own unit lacks the extra s⁻¹. The dimensionally correct answer is Power (option C), which is what's stored now.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize the two: Joule = kg·m²·s⁻² (work/energy), Watt = kg·m²·s⁻³ (power). One extra time-power in the denominator is the whole difference.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Weight is a force, unit kg·m·s⁻² (Newton).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Pressure is kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² (Pascal).
explanation_options.c: Correct — this is the Watt, the SI unit of power.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Work's unit is kg·m²·s⁻² (Joule), missing one power of s⁻¹.

aliases: Name the quantity which can be measured by using base unit 'kgm2s-3'
Weight

questions.question_text: Ratio of moment of inertia of two objects 'A' and 'B' is 2:3. Which one of the following is the ratio of torques of 'A' and 'B' respectively, if both are being rotated with constant angular acceleration?
questions.explanation_short: τ = Iα; with α fixed, torque ratio equals moment-of-inertia ratio, 2:3.
questions.explanation_long: Torque τ = I·α (moment of inertia × angular acceleration). Since both objects share the same constant angular acceleration α, τ is directly proportional to I. So τ_A : τ_B = I_A : I_B = 2:3.
questions.explanation_trick: When α (or a, for linear motion) is the same for both, the ratio of the 'cause' quantity (torque/force) mirrors the ratio of the inertia term directly — no need to solve for α.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not the given ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — τ ∝ I when α is constant, so 2:3.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is the ratio flipped.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — doesn't match 2:3 in either order.

questions.question_text: Due to some mechanical fault, a lift falls freely from the top of a multistory building. Which of the followings is the apparent weight of a man inside the lift, if mass of man is 80 kg while value of 'g' is 10 m s⁻²?
questions.explanation_short: Free-fall means the lift and the man accelerate at g together, so apparent weight = 0.
questions.explanation_long: Apparent weight is the normal reaction force the floor exerts on the man. In free fall, both the lift and the man accelerate downward at g, so there's no relative pressing between the man and the floor — the normal force (and hence apparent weight) is zero. This is the classic 'weightlessness' scenario.
questions.explanation_trick: Apparent weight = m(g − a), where a is the lift's downward acceleration. Free fall means a = g, so apparent weight = 0 regardless of mass.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this would be less than actual weight (800 N) but not the free-fall case.
explanation_options.b: Correct — free fall gives zero apparent weight.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is the man's actual weight (mg = 80×10), relevant only if the lift weren't falling.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — doesn't correspond to any physical scenario here.

aliases: Due to some mechanical fault, a lift falls freely from the top of a multistory building. Which of the followings is the apparent weight of a man inside the lift, if mass of man is 80 kg while value of 'g' is 10 ms-2?

questions.question_text: Stokes' Law is given as:
questions.explanation_short: Stokes' Law: F = 6πηrv (viscous drag on a sphere).
questions.explanation_long: Stokes' Law gives the viscous drag force on a small sphere moving through a fluid: F = 6πηrv, where η is viscosity, r is the sphere's radius, and v is its speed.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember '6πηrv' as one block — each variable appears to the first power only.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — has r² instead of r.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the standard Stokes' Law expression.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — has v⁻¹, which would make drag decrease with speed (unphysical).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — has extra π and r³, not the Stokes' form.

aliases: Stokes' Law is given as:
F = 6πηr2v

questions.question_text: The product of cross-sectional area of the pipe and the fluid speed at any point along the pipe:
questions.explanation_short: This is the Equation of Continuity: Av = constant.
questions.explanation_long: For an incompressible fluid flowing through a pipe, mass conservation requires that the volume flow rate (Area × velocity) stays the same at every cross-section — this is the equation of continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ = constant.
questions.explanation_trick: Narrower pipe → faster flow, wider pipe → slower flow, but A×v never changes along the pipe.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Av = constant is the continuity equation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — flow wouldn't happen at all if this were zero.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — no exponential relationship exists here.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same reasoning as above.

questions.question_text: A small leak is developed in a large water storage tank. If the height of water above leakage is 10 m, then find the speed of efflux through the leak:
questions.explanation_short: Torricelli's theorem: v = √(2gh) = √(2×9.8×10) ≈ 14 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: Speed of efflux from a small hole at depth h below the surface follows Torricelli's Law: v = √(2gh). With h = 10 m and g = 9.8 m/s², v = √196 = 14 m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: Torricelli's law is just free-fall in disguise — the exit speed of the liquid equals the speed it would reach falling freely through height h.

explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would need g ≈ 5 m/s².
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is just g itself, not the efflux speed.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this would require h = 20.4 m.

questions.question_text: The minimum distance from the eye at which an object can be seen clearly without strain is called:
questions.explanation_short: Near point: closest distance for clear, strain-free vision (~25 cm for a normal eye).
questions.explanation_long: The near point is the minimum distance from the eye at which an object can be viewed distinctly without eye strain. For a normal healthy eye this is conventionally taken as 25 cm.
questions.explanation_trick: Near point = closest clear vision; Far point = farthest clear vision (infinity for a normal eye).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — focal point relates to a lens, not the eye's vision range.
explanation_options.b: Correct — this is the near point.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — yield point is a materials-science term (stress-strain), unrelated to vision.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — far point is the opposite end of the vision range.

questions.question_text: In the diffraction of light around an obstacle, the angle of diffraction is increased then:
questions.option_a: The wavelength of incident light wave is increased
questions.option_b: The wavelength of incident light wave is decreased
questions.option_c: The amplitude of the incident light wave is increased
questions.option_d: The amplitude of the incident light wave is decreased
questions.explanation_short: Diffraction angle increases with wavelength (sinθ ≈ λ/a).
questions.explanation_long: For diffraction around an obstacle or through an aperture of fixed size a, the angular spread of diffraction is approximately θ ≈ λ/a. A larger diffraction angle therefore means the incident wavelength has increased.
questions.explanation_trick: Longer wavelength → more diffraction (bends around obstacles more). This is why radio waves diffract around buildings but visible light barely does.

explanation_options.a: Correct — larger θ needs larger λ, obstacle size fixed.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would shrink the diffraction angle.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — amplitude doesn't affect the diffraction angle, only wavelength (and aperture size) does.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same reasoning as C.

questions.question_text: An object 15 cm from a lens produces a real image 30 cm from the lens. What is the focal length of the lens?
questions.explanation_long: Using the sign convention (real is positive): object distance u = −15 cm, image distance v = +30 cm (real image, same side as light travels). 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/30 − (1/−15) = 1/30 + 1/15 = 1/30 + 2/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so f = +10 cm.
questions.explanation_trick: A real object producing a real image always means a converging (positive-f) lens — you can eliminate any negative-f option immediately.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — doesn't satisfy the lens equation for these distances.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — same.
explanation_options.c: Correct — f = +10 cm from the lens formula.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same.

questions.question_text: What is the formula for critical angle in case of light through two mediums having refractive indexes n₁ and n₂ such that n₁ > n₂?
questions.explanation_short: Critical angle: sinθc = n2/n1 (going from denser n1 to rarer n2).
questions.explanation_long: Total internal reflection's critical angle satisfies Snell's law at 90° refraction: n1 sinθc = n2 sin90° = n2, so sinθc = n2/n1, giving θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1). This requires n1 > n2 (light going from denser to rarer medium), which matches the question.
questions.explanation_trick: Critical angle formula always has the *smaller* refractive index (rarer medium) on top of the ratio inside sin⁻¹.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ratio is inverted (n1/n2 > 1, and sin⁻¹ of something >1 is undefined).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — should be sin⁻¹, not cos⁻¹.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — wrong trig function.
explanation_options.d: Correct — sin⁻¹(n2/n1).

aliases: What is the formula for critical angle in case of light through two mediums having refractive indexes n1 and n2 such that n1 > n2?
sin-1(n1/n2)

questions.question_text: For vibrating mass-spring system, the expression of kinetic energy at any displacement 'x' is given by:
questions.explanation_short: KE at displacement x: ½k(x₀²−x²) = ½kx₀²(1 − x²/x₀²).
questions.explanation_long: In SHM, total energy E = ½kx₀² is constant. Potential energy at displacement x is ½kx². Kinetic energy is the difference: KE = ½kx₀² − ½kx² = ½kx₀²(1 − x²/x₀²). (The printed UHS key marks D, ½mω²x₀, which is not an energy expression at displacement x at all, so A is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: Total energy stays fixed at ½kx₀² throughout the motion — KE and PE just trade off between each other as x changes.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ½kx₀²(1 − x²/x₀²) is exactly the KE expression.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is the *total* energy, constant, not KE at a specific x.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — missing a factor of ω and malformed.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is missing the (1 − x²/x₀²) factor and is really the *total* energy in mω² form, not KE at displacement x.

aliases: For vibrating mass-spring system, the expression of kinetic energy at any displacement 'x' is given by:

questions.question_text: Speed of sound through a gas is measured as 340 m/s at pressure P₁ and temperature T₁. What will be the speed of sound if pressure of gas is doubled but temperature is kept constant?
questions.explanation_short: Speed of sound in a gas depends only on temperature, not pressure, at constant T.
questions.explanation_long:
Speed of sound v = √(γP/ρ). For an ideal gas at constant temperature, density ρ is directly proportional to pressure P (from PV = nRT), so the ratio P/ρ stays constant when T is fixed — doubling pressure alone leaves v unchanged.

**Note:** the source data originally marked this as 342 m/s (implying a slight increase) — that contradicts the standard result that speed of sound is pressure-independent at constant temperature. The corrected answer is 340 m/s (unchanged), which is what's now stored.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Pressure changes, temperature constant' for speed of sound in a gas is a classic trap — the two effects (P and ρ) cancel exactly, so the speed never changes.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — implies pressure alone changes the speed, which it doesn't at constant T.
explanation_options.b: Correct — speed of sound is unaffected by pressure alone at constant temperature.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this would be for room-temperature air's speed, unrelated to this scenario.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same reasoning as A.

aliases: Speed of sound through a gas is measured as 340 m/s at pressure P1 and temperature T1. What will be the speed of sound if pressure of gas is doubled but temperature is kept constant?

questions.question_text: The stress-strain graph, deduced the following limits successively:
questions.option_a: Proportional limit, yield limit, elastic limit
questions.option_b: Yield limit, elastic limit, proportional limit
questions.option_c: Proportional limit, elastic limit, yield limit
questions.option_d: Elastic limit, proportional limit, yield limit
questions.explanation_short: Stress-strain curve order: Proportional limit → Elastic limit → Yield point.
questions.explanation_long: As a material is stretched, it first obeys Hooke's law up to the proportional limit, remains elastic slightly further up to the elastic limit, and then permanently deforms beyond the yield point. The correct successive order is Proportional limit, Elastic limit, Yield limit.
questions.explanation_trick: P before E before Y — 'Proportional, Elastic, Yield' in that exact order as stress increases.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — wrong order (yield before elastic).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — starts from yield, backwards.
explanation_options.c: Correct — proportional, then elastic, then yield.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — starts from elastic limit, out of order.

questions.question_text: Variation of amplitude with respect to time for an oscillation object is shown in figure. Identify the oscillation:
questions.explanation_short: Amplitude stays constant (bounded between +y₀ and −y₀) over time → undamped oscillation.
questions.explanation_long: The graph shows the oscillation's amplitude neither growing nor shrinking with time, staying fixed between +y₀ and −y₀. That's the signature of an undamped (ideal, no energy loss) oscillation. Damped oscillations show a decaying amplitude envelope instead.
questions.explanation_trick: Constant amplitude envelope = undamped. A shrinking envelope = damped/heavily damped, depending on how fast it decays.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — damped motion shows amplitude shrinking over time.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'critical' describes fastest decay without oscillation, not a bounded oscillation.
explanation_options.c: Correct — constant amplitude means undamped.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — heavily damped motion doesn't even complete full oscillations.

aliases: Variation of amplitude with respect to time for an oscillation object is shown in figure. Identify the oscillation: (The amplitude-vs-time graph shows the oscillation staying within fixed limits +Yo and -Yo, i.e. it does NOT decay over time.)
Damped

questions.question_text: A 4.0 m long wire is subjected to stretching force and its length increases by 40 cm. The percent elongation which the wire undergoes is:
questions.explanation_long: Percent elongation is the fractional increase in length expressed as a percentage: ΔL/L × 100. Here ΔL = 40 cm = 0.4 m and L = 4.0 m, giving (0.4/4)×100 = 10%.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert to the same units before dividing — here 40 cm becomes 0.4 m to match the 4.0 m original length.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this would need ΔL = 0.004 m, not 0.4 m.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this treats 40 cm as if the original length were 1 m.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — double the correct value.

questions.question_text: What is the value of universal gas constant?
questions.explanation_short: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation_long: The universal gas constant is R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. 8314 is its value per kilomole, and 83.14 and 831.4 are not values of R in these units. (The paper prints option D with the unit K⁻², a misprint shown corrected here. The printed UHS key marks B, 83.14, which is ten times too large, so D is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.0821 dm³ atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 8314 J is per kilomole, not per mole.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 83.14 is ten times R, and K⁻² is not its unit.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 831.4 is a hundred times R.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

aliases: What is the value of universal gas constant?

questions.question_text: A gas sample contains three molecules each having speed 1 m s⁻¹, 2 m s⁻¹, 3 m s⁻¹. What is the mean square speed?
questions.explanation_short: Mean square speed = (1²+2²+3²)/3 = 14/3.
questions.explanation_long: Mean square speed is the average of the squares of individual speeds: (1² + 2² + 3²)/3 = (1+4+9)/3 = 14/3.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't average the speeds first and then square — square each speed first, then average. That's what 'mean square' means (as opposed to 'root mean square', which then also takes a square root).

explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is just the plain average of the speeds (1+2+3)/3 = 2, doubled.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is the plain (non-squared) average speed.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is the root-mean-square speed, one step further than what's asked.

aliases: A gas sample contains three molecules each having speed 1 ms-1, 2 ms-1, 3 ms-1. What is the mean square speed?

questions.question_text: What is the factor upon which change in internal energy of an ideal gas depends?
questions.option_d: Path followed to change internal energy
questions.explanation_short: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature.
questions.explanation_long: The internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of temperature alone — it depends only on the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which is set by T. Volume or the path taken don't matter for an ideal gas.
questions.explanation_trick: This is a defining property of an *ideal* gas — for real gases, internal energy can also depend on volume (intermolecular forces), but MDCAT physics always assumes ideal-gas behaviour unless stated otherwise.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — volume alone doesn't change internal energy for an ideal gas.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — over-includes volume.
explanation_options.c: Correct — temperature is the sole determinant.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — internal energy is a state function, independent of path.

questions.question_text: What will be the mathematical form of first law of thermodynamics for a system whose variation of volume by pressure is shown?
questions.explanation_short: Isothermal process: ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so the first law gives Q = W.
questions.explanation_long: First law of thermodynamics: Q = ΔU + W. In an isothermal process, temperature doesn't change, and for an ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature — so ΔU = 0. This reduces the first law to Q = W: all heat absorbed goes directly into work done by the gas.
questions.explanation_trick: Isothermal ⇒ ΔU = 0 ⇒ Q = W is one of the most frequently tested thermodynamics facts — memorize this chain directly.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this would imply W = 0, which isn't true for an isothermal expansion/compression.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would need Q = 0 (that's the adiabatic case, not isothermal).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — not a form the first law takes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Q = W for an isothermal process.

aliases: What will be the mathematical form of first law of thermodynamics for a system whose variation of volume by pressure is shown? (The P-V graph shown is labelled 'Isothermal', i.e. temperature is constant, curving from (P1,V1) down to (P2,V2).)
Q = U

questions.question_text: For a heat engine 'A' ratio of Q₁ to Q₂ is 2/3 while that of heat engine 'B', ratio of Q₂ to Q₁ is 1/3. What is the value ηA : ηB?
questions.explanation_short: With consistent Q_rejected:Q_absorbed ratios, ηA:ηB = (1−2/3):(1−1/3) = 1:2.
questions.explanation_long: Efficiency η = 1 − (heat rejected/heat absorbed). Reading each engine's given ratio as rejected:absorbed, engine A has ratio 2/3, giving ηA = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3; engine B has ratio 1/3, giving ηB = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3. So ηA:ηB = (1/3):(2/3) = 1:2.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a heat-engine question gives you a Q1:Q2 ratio, first pin down which one is 'absorbed from the hot reservoir' and which is 'rejected to the cold reservoir' — efficiency is always 1 − (rejected/absorbed).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — doesn't match the computed ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 1:2 from η = 1 − Qrejected/Qabsorbed for each engine.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is closer to a raw ratio of the given fractions rather than the efficiencies.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — inverted from the correct order.

aliases: For a heat engine 'A' ratio of Q1 to Q2 is 2/3 while that of heat engine 'B', ratio of Q2 to Q1 is 1/3. What is the value ηA : ηB?

questions.question_text: What is the charge stored on a 5 μF capacitor charged to potential difference of 12 V?
questions.explanation_short: Q = CV = 5 μF × 12 V = 60 μC.
questions.explanation_long: Charge stored on a capacitor is Q = CV. With C = 5 μF and V = 12 V, Q = 5×12 = 60 μC.
questions.explanation_trick: Keep the μ (micro) prefix attached throughout — 5 μF × 12 V gives an answer in μC directly, no unit conversion needed.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 5 μF × 12 V = 60 μC.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this drops the micro-prefix entirely (would be true only if C were in Farads, not microfarads).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — same magnitude error, wrong prefix placement.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same issue as B.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the proper way to study the sinusoidal wave form of voltage?
questions.option_a: Voltage is connected to 'Y' input and time base is switched on.
questions.option_b: Voltage is connected to 'X' input and time base is switched off.
questions.option_c: Voltage is connected to 'Y' input and time base is switched off.
questions.option_d: Voltage is connected to 'X' input and time base is switched on.
questions.explanation_short: To view a sinusoidal waveform on a CRO: signal to Y-input, time base ON.
questions.explanation_long: On a cathode ray oscilloscope, the vertical (Y) input displays the voltage signal, while the horizontal time base sweeps the beam left-to-right at a steady rate to represent time on the X-axis. With the time base switched on, a sinusoidal voltage traces out its familiar wave shape.
questions.explanation_trick: Y = the signal you're measuring, X (time base) = the clock sweeping it out — time base must always be ON to see a waveform vs. time.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Y-input for voltage, time base on for the X-axis sweep.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — voltage should go to Y, not X, and time base must be on.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — time base off means no horizontal sweep, so no waveform trace.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — voltage on X-input alone doesn't produce a time-based waveform.

questions.question_text: 12-volt battery is applied across 6-ohm resistance to have a steady flow of current. What must be the required potential difference across the same resistance to have a steady current of one ampere?
questions.explanation_short: V = IR = 1 A × 6 Ω = 6 V.
questions.explanation_long: Ohm's law: V = IR. The initial 12 V/6 Ω setup is a distractor — it's not needed. For a steady current of 1 A through the same 6 Ω resistor, the required voltage is 1 × 6 = 6 V.
questions.explanation_trick: Ohm's law problems in MCQs sometimes include an unrelated first scenario purely as a distractor — check what's actually asked before using the earlier numbers.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this is the voltage from the original (unrelated) scenario for 2 A, not 1 A.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 1 A × 6 Ω = 6 V.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — doesn't satisfy V = IR for these values.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same.

questions.question_text: A solenoid is cut into two halves. Magnetic induction due to same current in each half will be:
questions.explanation_short: Field per unit length (n = turns/length) is unchanged when a solenoid is cut in half.
questions.explanation_long: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is B = μ₀nI, where n is turns per unit length — a density, not a total count. Cutting a solenoid into two shorter halves (same winding density, same current) leaves n unchanged for each half, so the field magnitude stays the same as the original.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a question hinges on 'per unit length' quantities, cutting the object physically in half doesn't change that density — only extensive (total) quantities like total turns or total length get halved.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — n (turns/length) doesn't halve just because the solenoid is shorter.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — no physical reason for a doubling.
explanation_options.c: Correct — B = μ₀nI depends on turn density, unchanged after cutting.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — no factor of 4 arises here.

questions.question_text: A long straight current carrying conductor has current directed from bottom to top when held vertically. What will be the direction of magnetic field lines when observed from below the conductor?
questions.explanation_short: Right-hand rule: current flowing away from a viewer below gives a clockwise field (as seen by that viewer).
questions.explanation_long: Current flows vertically upward, i.e. away from an observer positioned below the wire looking up. By the right-hand rule (thumb along current direction, fingers curl in the field's direction), when current flows away from the viewer, the surrounding magnetic field circles clockwise as seen by that viewer.
questions.explanation_trick: Current towards you = counterclockwise field (as you see it); current away from you = clockwise field. Flip your mental picture based on which end you're viewing from.

explanation_options.a: Correct — clockwise, as seen from below (current flowing away from that viewpoint).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the field circles around the wire, it isn't anticlockwise here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — magnetic field lines around a straight wire are always circular, never radially outward.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same reasoning as C.

questions.question_text: What is the output Boolean expression of logic diagram shown in figure below:
questions.explanation_short: Two identical NAND(A,B) outputs OR'd together: (AB)′ + (AB)′.
questions.explanation_long: Each NAND gate computes (A·B)′ from inputs A and B. With both NAND gates fed the same inputs A and B, their outputs are identical: (AB)′. Feeding both into an OR gate gives X = (AB)′ + (AB)′.
questions.explanation_trick: OR'ing two identical signals together just reproduces that same signal — the expression (AB)′+(AB)′ is logically equivalent to (AB)′ alone, but as literally built from the diagram it's written with both terms.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — mixes NOR-style OR-then-invert notation, not what the diagram shows.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — same notation issue, missing the OR between two separate NAND outputs.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — de Morgan's expansion of the NAND output, not the raw circuit expression asked for.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the literal OR of two identical NAND(A,B) outputs.

aliases: What is the output Boolean expression of logic diagram shown in figure below (two NAND gates, each fed by inputs A and B, both feeding into an OR gate whose output is X):

questions.question_text: Three resistors each having value 'R' are connected as shown in figure. What is the equivalence resistance between 'X' and 'Y'?
questions.explanation_short: The three resistors are joined end to end in one path from X to Y, so they are in series: R + R + R = 3R.
questions.explanation_long: Follow the wire from X: it passes through the first R, then a connecting wire leads to the second R, then to the third R and on to Y. There is only one path for the current, so the resistors are in series and their resistances add: R_eq = R + R + R = 3R. R/3 would be three in parallel; R³ is not dimensionally a resistance.
questions.explanation_trick: One path for current = series = add the resistances.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — that is a single resistor.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — R/3 is for three equal resistors in parallel.
explanation_options.c: Correct — three R in series give 3R.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — resistances add; they are never multiplied.

aliases: Three resistors each having value 'R' are connected as shown in figure. What is the equivalence resistance between 'X' and 'Y'?
Structure/arrangement A (see figure)

questions.question_text: The diagram shows a wire, carrying a current 'I', placed between the poles of magnet: In which direction does the force on the wire act?
questions.option_a: Towards the 'N' pole of the magnet
questions.option_d: Towards the 'S' pole of the magnet
questions.explanation_short: F = IL × B: current up the page and field from N to S give a force into the page — 'downwards' when the diagram is viewed from above.
questions.explanation_long: The field between the poles runs from N to S (left to right) and the current flows up the page. By Fleming's left-hand rule (or F = IL × B), the force is perpendicular to both, pointing into the page. The figure is a top view of the magnet, so into the page is downwards. The force is never along the field, so it is not towards either pole.
questions.explanation_trick: Force ⊥ both I and B; a force pointing into the page of a top view is 'downwards'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the force is perpendicular to the field, not along it towards N.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the force points into the page, i.e. downwards.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this is the reverse of the force direction.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the force is perpendicular to the field, not towards S.

questions.question_text: X-rays from a given X-ray tube operating under specified conditions have a minimum wavelength. The value of this minimum wavelength could be reduced by:
questions.option_b: Reducing the temperature of the filament
questions.option_c: Increasing the potential difference between the cathode and the target
questions.option_d: Reducing the pressure in the tube
questions.explanation_short: λmin = hc/eV, so increasing accelerating voltage V decreases λmin.
questions.explanation_long: The minimum X-ray wavelength is set by an electron converting all its kinetic energy into a single photon: eV = hc/λmin, so λmin = hc/(eV). Increasing the accelerating voltage V directly decreases λmin.
questions.explanation_trick: Higher voltage → more energetic electrons → higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) X-ray photons. This inverse relationship is the key fact tested here.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — target temperature doesn't set λmin.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — filament temperature affects X-ray intensity (electron supply), not λmin.
explanation_options.c: Correct — increasing V decreases λmin.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — tube pressure isn't the controlling factor for λmin.

questions.question_text: Helium-neon lasers are used for the:
questions.explanation_short: He-Ne lasers are a standard low-power tool for alignment work, including tunnel-construction surveying.
questions.explanation_long: Helium-neon lasers produce a stable, low-divergence visible beam that's widely used for precision alignment tasks — including surveying and maintaining a straight line during tunnel construction.
questions.explanation_trick: He-Ne lasers = everyday low-power alignment and measurement tool (barcode scanners, surveying, holography) — distinct from high-power lasers used for cutting or medical surgery.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — range-finding is typically done with pulsed higher-power lasers, not standard He-Ne.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — fiber-optic communication uses semiconductor laser diodes, not He-Ne.
explanation_options.c: Correct — tunnel-alignment surveying is a classic He-Ne laser application.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — medical bone welding needs high-power surgical lasers, not a low-power He-Ne.

questions.question_text: What is the type of characteristic X-ray photon whose energy is given by relation 'hf = EM - EK'?
questions.explanation_short: hf = EM − EK is a transition landing on the K-shell from the M-shell: K-beta.
questions.explanation_long: Characteristic X-ray lines are named by which shell an electron falls into and from how far away. Falling into the K-shell (n=1) from the adjacent L-shell gives K-alpha; falling into K from the further M-shell (n=3) gives K-beta. Since this transition is EM → EK, it's K-beta.
questions.explanation_trick: K-alpha = from L→K (adjacent shell, lower energy line); K-beta = from M→K (one shell further, higher energy line).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — K-alpha would be L→K, not M→K.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'M-alpha' isn't the standard notation for this transition.
explanation_options.c: Correct — M→K transition is K-beta.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — not standard notation for this energy difference.

questions.question_text: Kinetic energy of electrons by applying potential difference V₁ across the x-ray tube is KE₁ while V₂ potential difference produce kinetic energy equal to KE₂. What will be the value of KE₁:KE₂ if ratio of potential difference V₁:V₂ = 2:3?
questions.explanation_short: KE = eV, directly proportional to V, so KE1:KE2 = V1:V2 = 2:3.
questions.explanation_long: An electron accelerated through potential difference V gains kinetic energy KE = eV — a direct proportionality. So the ratio of kinetic energies equals the ratio of the accelerating voltages: KE1:KE2 = V1:V2 = 2:3.
questions.explanation_trick: KE ∝ V (linear, not squared) for an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference — don't confuse this with KE ∝ v² for classical kinetic energy in terms of speed.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — inverted ratio.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this would be the ratio if KE ∝ V², which it isn't here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — inverse-square, doesn't apply.
explanation_options.d: Correct — direct proportionality gives 2:3.

aliases: Kinetic energy of electrons by applying potential difference V1 across the x-ray tube is KE1 while V2 potential difference produce kinetic energy equal to KE2. What will be the value of KE1:KE2 if ratio of potential difference V1:V2 = 2:3?

questions.question_text: What will be the relation for the speed of electron accelerated towards the target in X-ray tube by applying potential difference 'V', take mass of electron 'm' and charge on electron 'e'?
questions.explanation_short: eV = ½mv² gives v = √(2eV/m).
questions.explanation_long: An electron of charge e accelerated through potential difference V gains kinetic energy eV, which equals ½mv². Solving for speed: v = √(2eV/m).
questions.explanation_trick: This is the same derivation as the X-ray tube's electron speed — always start from energy conservation (eV = ½mv²) and solve for v.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v = √(2Ve/m).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — variables misplaced under the root.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — V and m/e swapped incorrectly.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — extra factor, not dimensionally matching v.

questions.question_text: For what CAT stands in X-ray technology?
questions.explanation_short: CAT (in X-ray imaging) = Computerized Axial Tomography.
questions.explanation_long: CAT scan stands for Computerized Axial Tomography — a medical imaging technique that combines multiple X-ray images taken from different angles to build cross-sectional images of the body.
questions.explanation_trick: CAT/CT scan is a standard piece of medical-physics general knowledge tested alongside X-ray tube physics in this section.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not a real term for this technology.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Computerized Axial Tomography.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — not a real term for this technology.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — not a real term for this technology.

questions.question_text: During the production of LASER, when the excited state E₂ contains more number of atoms than the ground state E₁, the state is known as:
questions.explanation_short: More atoms in the excited state than the ground state = population inversion.
questions.explanation_long: Normally, more atoms sit in the lower-energy ground state than in excited states (per the Boltzmann distribution). When this is deliberately reversed — more atoms in the excited state E2 than the ground state E1 — it's called population inversion, the essential condition for laser action (stimulated emission to dominate over absorption).
questions.explanation_trick: Population inversion is the prerequisite for any laser to work — without it, absorption would dominate over the stimulated emission needed to amplify light.

explanation_options.a: Correct — population inversion is exactly this reversed distribution.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — ground state is the normal (non-inverted) majority-occupied state.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'excited state' alone doesn't describe the population comparison.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a metastable state is a long-lived excited state, not the population-comparison condition itself.

aliases: During the production of LASER, when the excited state E2 contains more number of atoms than the ground state E1, the state is known as:
Population inversion

questions.question_text: In cloud chamber the path of β-particles is:
questions.explanation_short: Beta particles leave thin, wavy, longer tracks in a cloud chamber (due to scattering and higher penetration).
questions.explanation_long: In a cloud chamber, alpha particles leave thick, straight, short tracks (heavy, low penetration, dense ionization). Beta particles, being much lighter, scatter more (wavy path) and penetrate further (longer track), leaving a thin, wavy, longer trail.
questions.explanation_trick: Track thickness/straightness relates to how easily the particle is deflected: heavy alpha = thick & straight; light beta = thin & wavy. Track length relates to penetration power.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this describes an alpha particle's track.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'shorter' contradicts beta's better penetration than alpha.
explanation_options.c: Correct — thin, wavy, and longer than alpha's track.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — beta tracks are wavy, not straight.

questions.question_text: Among the three types of radioactive radiation, which have strongest penetration power?
questions.explanation_short: Gamma rays have the strongest penetration power among alpha, beta, gamma.
questions.explanation_long: Alpha particles are stopped by paper or skin; beta particles need a few mm of aluminium; gamma rays require thick lead or concrete to be significantly absorbed. This ordering reflects gamma's much higher penetration power.
questions.explanation_trick: Penetration order: Alpha (weakest) < Beta < Gamma (strongest) — the exact reverse of their ionizing power, which goes Alpha (strongest) > Beta > Gamma.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — alpha has the weakest penetration.
explanation_options.b: Correct — gamma penetrates furthest.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — beta is intermediate, not strongest.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the three clearly differ in penetration power.

questions.question_text: Emission of alpha decay from a radioactive substance causes:
questions.option_a: Decreases in 'Z' by 4 and decreases in 'A' by 2
questions.option_b: Decreases in 'A' by 1 and 'Z' remains same
questions.option_c: Decreases in 'Z' by 1 and 'A' remains same
questions.option_d: Decreases in 'A' by 4 and decreases in 'Z' by 2
questions.explanation_short: Alpha decay: mass number A drops by 4, atomic number Z drops by 2.
questions.explanation_long: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons — mass number 4, atomic number 2). Emitting one from a nucleus reduces the parent's mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha decay: A drops by 4, Z drops by 2 — think 'alpha = helium-4, charge +2'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — swaps which quantity drops by 4 vs. 2.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this describes beta-minus decay's effect on A and Z is also wrong (beta leaves A unchanged, increases Z by 1).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this pattern doesn't match alpha decay at all.
explanation_options.d: Correct — A decreases by 4, Z decreases by 2.

questions.question_text: 10 Joule of energy is absorbed by 10-gram mass from a radioactive source. What is the absorbed dose?
questions.explanation_short: Absorbed dose = Energy/mass = 10 J / 0.01 kg = 1000 Gy.
questions.explanation_long: Absorbed dose in gray (Gy) is energy absorbed per unit mass: D = E/m. Converting 10 g to 0.01 kg, D = 10 J / 0.01 kg = 1000 Gy.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert mass to kilograms before dividing — a common trap is leaving mass in grams, which throws the answer off by a factor of 1000.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this would be the answer if mass were left as 10 kg instead of 0.01 kg.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 10 J / 0.01 kg = 1000 Gy.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — off by a factor of 100.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — off by a factor of 10.

questions.question_text: Isotopes are those nuclei of an element that have:
questions.option_a: Same mass number but different atomic number
questions.option_b: Same mass number as well as atomic number
questions.option_c: Different mass number as well as atomic number
questions.option_d: same atomic number but different mass number
questions.explanation_short: Isotopes: same atomic number (Z), different mass number (A).
questions.explanation_long: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons, i.e. same atomic number Z) that differ in their number of neutrons, giving them different mass numbers A.
questions.explanation_trick: Same Z (same element identity) + different A (different neutron count) = isotopes. Same A + different Z would instead be 'isobars'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — describes isobars (same A, different Z), the reverse of isotopes.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — identical nuclei aren't isotopes of each other, they're the same nuclide.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — describes unrelated elements, not isotopes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — same atomic number, different mass number is the definition of isotopes.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following emission takes place in a nuclear reaction? ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + ___
questions.explanation_short: Z rises by 1 and A stays 234: a neutron has turned into a proton, emitting a beta particle.
questions.explanation_long: In ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa the atomic number goes up by one while the mass number is unchanged. This happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron (β-particle) is emitted. Alpha emission would lower Z by 2 and A by 4; gamma rays and photons change neither. (The paper prints the product as ²³²Pa, a misprint — a mass number of 232 cannot be reached by any single one of these emissions; the equation is shown with 234.)
questions.explanation_trick: Z increases by 1, A unchanged → beta-minus emission. Z decreases by 2, A decreases by 4 → alpha emission. Z unchanged, A unchanged, energy released → gamma emission.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — alpha decay would decrease Z by 2, not increase it by 1.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — gamma emission doesn't change Z at all.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Z increasing by 1 is the signature of beta decay.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — photon emission alone (without a nuclear transformation) doesn't change Z.

aliases: Which one of the following emission takes place in a nuclear reaction? 90Th234 -> 91Pa232 + ___
Alpha

questions.question_text: Emission of radiation from radioactive substance is:
questions.option_a: Dependent on both temperature and pressure
questions.option_b: Independent of temperature but dependent on pressure
questions.option_c: Independent of both temperature and Pressure
questions.option_d: Independent of pressure but dependent on temperature
questions.explanation_short: Radioactive decay rate is independent of both temperature and pressure.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike ordinary chemical reaction rates, radioactive decay is a nuclear process governed by the probability of nuclear instability, not by molecular collision rates — so it's unaffected by external temperature or pressure conditions.
questions.explanation_trick: This is a frequently tested contrast: chemical reaction rates depend heavily on temperature/pressure/catalysts; nuclear decay rates depend on none of these, only on the isotope's intrinsic half-life.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — decay rate does NOT depend on either factor.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — decay rate isn't pressure-dependent either.
explanation_options.c: Correct — independent of both temperature and pressure.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — decay rate isn't temperature-dependent.

questions.question_text: In a simple harmonic motion with a radius 'x₀', the velocity of the particle at any point is:
questions.explanation_short: SHM velocity: v = ω√(x₀²−x²), where x₀ is the amplitude.
questions.explanation_long:
In simple harmonic motion, velocity at displacement x is given by v = ω√(x₀² − x²), where x₀ is the amplitude (radius of the corresponding circular motion) and ω is the angular frequency.

**Note:** the source data originally marked the option without a square root (v = ω(x²−x₀²)) as correct — that expression is dimensionally wrong (velocity requires the square root) and would even go negative under the normal case x < x₀. The corrected answer is the properly rooted expression, v = ω√(x₀²−x²).
questions.explanation_trick: SHM velocity is maximum at x=0 (v=ωx₀) and zero at the extremes (x=±x₀) — check any candidate formula against these two limits to catch an error quickly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v = ω√(x₀²−x²), correctly rooted and gives v=ωx₀ at x=0, v=0 at x=x₀.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — missing the square root; also gives a negative value under the root for x<x₀, which is unphysical.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — missing a square term on both x and x₀.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same missing-square issue, and has the sign backwards.

aliases: In a simple harmonic motion with a radius 'xo', the velocity of the particle at any point is:
v = ω√(xo2 - x2)

questions.question_text: Hydrogen burns in chlorine to produce hydrogen chloride. The ratio of masses of reactants in chemical reaction is: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
questions.explanation_short: Mass ratio = molar masses: H2:Cl2 = 2:71 = 1:35.5.
questions.explanation_long: In H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, the reactants combine mole-for-mole (1:1), so the mass ratio equals the molar-mass ratio: H2 (2 g/mol) to Cl2 (71 g/mol) = 2:71, which simplifies to 1:35.5.
questions.explanation_trick: For a 1:1 mole-ratio reaction, the mass ratio of reactants is just their molar-mass ratio directly — no stoichiometric coefficients to juggle.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 2:71 simplifies to 1:35.5.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — doesn't simplify the ratio consistently.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this doubles the chlorine side incorrectly.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — close to the right magnitude but not the exact simplified ratio.

aliases: Hydrogen burns in chlorine to produce hydrogen chloride. The ratio of masses of reactants in chemical reaction is: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl

questions.question_text: A sample of Neon is found to exist as ²⁰Ne, ²¹Ne, ²²Ne. Its mass spectrum shows relative abundances of 90.92% at mass number 20, 0.26% at mass number 21 and 8.82% at mass number 22. What is the relative atomic mass (Ar value) of Neon?
questions.explanation_long:
Relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of isotope masses: 20×0.9092 + 21×0.0026 + 22×0.0882 = 18.184 + 0.0546 + 1.9404 = 20.179 ≈ 20.18 — matching neon's well-known real atomic mass.

**Note:** the source data marked 20.28 (option B) as correct — that doesn't match this calculation. The corrected answer, 20.18 (option A), is confirmed by both the arithmetic and the real, independently known atomic mass of neon.
questions.explanation_trick: Weighted average = Σ(mass number × fractional abundance). Convert percentages to decimals before multiplying.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches both the calculation and neon's real atomic mass (20.18).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — doesn't match the weighted-average calculation.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — too low given ²⁰Ne's dominant 90.92% share only gets you to 18.184 before adding the other isotopes.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — close, but not the precise weighted result.

aliases: A sample of Neon is found to exist as 20Ne, 21Ne, 22Ne. Mass spectrum of 'Ne' is as follow: What is the relative atomic mass (A, value) of Neon? (Mass spectrum: relative abundance 90.92% at mass number 20, 0.26% at mass number 21, 8.82% at mass number 22.)

questions.question_text: The coordination number of Na⁺ in NaCl crystal is:
questions.explanation_short: Na+ coordination number in NaCl is 6 (rock-salt/octahedral structure).
questions.explanation_long: NaCl crystallizes in the rock-salt structure, where each Na+ ion is surrounded by 6 Cl− ions (and vice versa) in an octahedral arrangement.
questions.explanation_trick: NaCl-type (rock salt) structure = coordination number 6 for both ions — a very frequently tested crystal-structure fact.

explanation_options.a: Correct — octahedral coordination, 6 neighbours.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — too low for the rock-salt structure.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 4 is the coordination number for tetrahedral structures like zinc blende (ZnS), not NaCl.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 8 is the coordination number for CsCl-type (body-centered) structures, not NaCl.

aliases: The coordination number of Na+ in NaCl crystal is:

questions.question_text: There are four gases H₂, He, N₂ and CO₂ at 0 °C. Which gas shows greater non-ideal behavior?
questions.explanation_short: CO2 shows the greatest non-ideal behaviour among H2, He, N2, CO2 at 0°C.
questions.explanation_long: Non-ideal (real-gas) behaviour increases with molecular size and intermolecular attractive forces. CO2 is larger and more polarizable than H2, He, or N2, giving it the strongest intermolecular forces and hence the greatest deviation from ideal-gas behaviour, especially near its boiling point.
questions.explanation_trick: Smaller, lighter, weakly-interacting gases (H2, He) behave most ideally; larger, more polarizable, easily liquefiable gases (CO2) deviate most.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — helium is one of the most ideal gases known.
explanation_options.b: Correct — CO2 deviates most from ideal behaviour.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — hydrogen is also very close to ideal.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — nitrogen is fairly close to ideal too, less non-ideal than CO2.

aliases: There are four gases H2, He, N2 and CO2 at 0 °C. Which gas shows greater non-ideal behavior?
He

questions.question_text: Correct order of energy in the given subshells is:
questions.explanation_short: By the (n+l) rule: 3p<4s<3d<5s in energy, so decreasing order is 5s>3d>4s>3p.
questions.explanation_long: Using the Aufbau (n+l) rule: 3p has n+l=4, 4s has n+l=4 (lower n wins tie, so 3p<4s); 3d has n+l=5, 5s has n+l=5 (lower n wins, so 3d<5s). Combining: 3p < 4s < 3d < 5s in energy. Written from highest to lowest: 5s > 3d > 4s > 3p.
questions.explanation_trick: For subshells with the same (n+l) value, the one with the smaller n has lower energy — this is the tie-breaker rule that separates 3p/4s and 3d/5s.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — puts 3p last, but 3p is actually the lowest-energy of the four.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 5s > 3d > 4s > 3p matches the (n+l) rule.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 3p should be lowest, not highest.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same issue, plus 5s/4s order is also swapped.

questions.question_text: Number of electrons in the outermost shell of chloride ion (Cl⁻) is:
questions.explanation_short: Cl⁻ has the [Ar] configuration — 8 electrons in its outermost (3rd) shell.
questions.explanation_long: A chloride ion has gained one electron: 17+1 = 18 electrons total, giving the configuration 2, 8, 8 — an argon-like noble-gas configuration with 8 electrons in the outermost (n=3) shell.
questions.explanation_trick: Cl⁻, like every ion that has 'completed the octet', ends up isoelectronic with the nearest noble gas — here, argon (18 electrons, 8 in the outer shell).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 17 is chlorine's atomic number/total protons, not its outer-shell electron count.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — doesn't match the octet structure of Cl⁻.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — same.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 8 electrons complete the outer shell, matching argon's configuration.

aliases: Number of electrons in the outermost shell of chloride ion (Cl―) is:

questions.question_text: According to valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, the repulsive forces between the electron pair of central atom of molecule are in the order:
questions.option_a: Lone Pair - Lone-Pair > Lone Pair - Bond Pair > Bond Pair - Bond Pair
questions.option_b: Lone Pair - Bond Pair > Lone Pair - Lone Pair > Bond Pair - Bond Pair
questions.option_c: Bond Pair - Bond Pair > Lone Pair - Lone Pair > Lone Pair - Bond Pair
questions.option_d: One Pair - Bond Pair > Bond Pair - Bond Pair > Lone Pair - Lone Pair
questions.explanation_short: VSEPR repulsion strength order: LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP.
questions.explanation_long: In VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy more space and repel more strongly than bonding pairs. The repulsion strength ranks: lone pair–lone pair (strongest) > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair (weakest).
questions.explanation_trick: Lone pairs are 'fatter' (less constrained by a second nucleus), so any repulsion involving a lone pair is stronger than a repulsion between two bond pairs — LP-LP tops the list every time.

explanation_options.a: Correct — LP-LP > LP-BP > BP-BP is the standard VSEPR order.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — puts LP-BP ahead of LP-LP, which is backwards.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — puts BP-BP first, the weakest type of repulsion.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — same issue, BP-BP shouldn't be in the middle either.

questions.question_text: In crystal lattice of ice, each O-atom of water molecule is attached to:
questions.explanation_short: In ice, each O atom is hydrogen-bonded to 4 H atoms (tetrahedral arrangement).
questions.explanation_long: In the ice crystal lattice, each water molecule's oxygen forms 2 covalent O–H bonds within its own molecule and 2 additional hydrogen bonds to neighbouring water molecules' H atoms, giving each O atom a total of 4 H-atom connections arranged tetrahedrally.
questions.explanation_trick: Ice's open, tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded network (each O linked to 4 H) is exactly why ice is less dense than liquid water — a classic paired fact worth remembering together.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 2 covalent + 2 hydrogen bonds = 4 H atoms per O.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — undercounts by one.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — only counts one covalent bond.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — only counts the 2 covalent bonds, ignoring the hydrogen bonds to neighbours.

questions.question_text: Heat of formation (∆Hf°) for CO₂ is:
questions.explanation_short: ΔHf° for CO2(g) is about −394 kJ/mol (commonly cited as −393.5 kJ/mol).
questions.explanation_long: The standard enthalpy of formation of carbon dioxide gas from its elements (C(graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g)) is a well-established thermochemical value, approximately −393.5 kJ/mol, commonly rounded to −394 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation_trick: CO2's formation is exothermic (heat released), so ΔHf° must be negative — that alone eliminates the +394 option immediately.

explanation_options.a: Correct — approximately −394 kJ/mol, the standard textbook value.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — wrong sign; formation of CO2 releases heat, it doesn't absorb it.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — magnitude off from the accepted value.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — close, but not the standard cited value.

aliases: Heat of formation (∆Hf°) for CO2 is:
-394 kJ/mole

questions.question_text: Reactants have high energy than products in:
questions.explanation_short: In exothermic reactions, reactants have higher energy than products (excess energy is released as heat).
questions.explanation_long: An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings because the products end up at a lower energy state than the reactants — the energy difference is given off as heat.
questions.explanation_trick: Exo = 'exit' (energy exits the system) → reactants start higher, products end lower. Endo = energy enters the system → reactants start lower, products end higher.

explanation_options.a: Correct — exothermic reactions have higher-energy reactants than products.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — endothermic reactions have the opposite: products higher than reactants.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — photochemical reactions aren't defined by this energy comparison specifically.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — non-spontaneous reactions aren't defined by this either.

questions.question_text: If 18.0 g of glucose is dissolved in 1 kg of water, boiling point of this solution should be:
questions.explanation_long: Molality of the glucose solution: 18.0 g glucose ÷ 180 g/mol (glucose's molar mass) = 0.1 mol, dissolved in 1 kg water → molality = 0.1 m. Boiling point elevation: ΔTb = Kb·m = 0.52°C/m × 0.1 m = 0.052°C. New boiling point = 100 + 0.052 = 100.052°C.
questions.explanation_trick: Glucose's molar mass (180 g/mol) combined with water's Kb (0.52°C/m) is one of the most commonly recycled colligative-properties setups — memorizing both numbers makes this instant.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this would be the answer for a 1 molal solution, not 0.1 molal.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — ignores the boiling point elevation entirely.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — dissolving a non-volatile solute always raises the boiling point, never lowers it.

questions.question_text: Molal freezing point constant of water is:
questions.explanation_short: Molal freezing point depression constant (Kf) of water is 1.86 °C/m.
questions.explanation_long: Kf, the molal freezing point depression constant for water, is a fixed physical property equal to 1.86 °C per mole of solute per kg of solvent.
questions.explanation_trick: Water's two colligative constants are both worth memorizing together: Kb = 0.52 °C/m (boiling), Kf = 1.86 °C/m (freezing) — freezing point depression is always the larger effect of the two.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 1.86 °C/m is water's Kf.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — not water's Kf value.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — far too large.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0.52 is actually water's Kb (boiling point elevation constant), not Kf.

questions.question_text: In the figure given below, the electron flow in external circuit is from:
questions.explanation_short: In a Zn-Cu galvanic cell, electrons flow externally from zinc (anode) to copper (cathode).
questions.explanation_long: Zinc is the more reactive metal and acts as the anode, where it's oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), releasing electrons into the external circuit. These electrons travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where reduction occurs (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu).
questions.explanation_trick: Electrons always flow externally from anode to cathode (oxidation site to reduction site) in a galvanic cell — memorize 'An Ox, Red Cat' (Anode=Oxidation, Cathode=Reduction) to keep this straight.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — reverses the actual direction; electrons flow away from zinc, not towards it.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — not a meaningful direction without diagram orientation context, and doesn't match the electrochemistry.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the porous partition/salt bridge carries ions internally, not electrons.
explanation_options.d: Correct — zinc (anode, oxidized) to copper (cathode, reduced).

questions.question_text: By considering Arrhenius equation, the graph between '1/T' and 'log K' gives a curve of the type:
questions.option_a: Straight line rising from the origin
questions.option_b: Straight line falling with a negative slope
questions.option_c: Curve rising to a maximum and then falling
questions.explanation_short: Arrhenius equation gives a straight line of log K vs 1/T with a negative slope.
questions.explanation_long: Taking the log of the Arrhenius equation (k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)) gives log k = log A − (Ea/2.303R)(1/T) — a straight line when plotting log k against 1/T, with a negative slope of −Ea/(2.303R). As 1/T increases (temperature decreases), log k decreases.
questions.explanation_trick: This linearized Arrhenius plot is used experimentally to find activation energy Ea directly from the slope — always expect a straight line with negative slope, never a curve.

explanation_options.a: See diagram — doesn't match the expected straight-line, negative-slope shape.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the straight line with negative slope matching the linearized Arrhenius equation.
explanation_options.c: See diagram — doesn't match the expected shape.
explanation_options.d: See diagram — doesn't match the expected shape.

aliases: By considering Arrhenius equation, the graph between '1/T' and 'log K' given a curve of the type:
Graph A

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a redox reaction?
questions.explanation_short: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl is the only complete, balanced redox reaction among the choices.
questions.explanation_long: A redox reaction needs both oxidation and reduction happening together in one balanced equation. 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl shows Na (0 → +1, oxidized) and Cl (0 → −1, reduced) simultaneously. The other options are either a non-redox double displacement (NaCl+AgNO3) or incomplete half-reactions (missing their other half).
questions.explanation_trick: A genuine complete redox reaction must show a species being oxidized AND a species being reduced within the same balanced equation — a lone half-reaction with 'e⁻' floating on one side isn't a complete reaction.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this is a double displacement/precipitation reaction; no oxidation states change.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is only the oxidation half-reaction, incomplete on its own.
explanation_options.c: Correct — shows both oxidation (Na) and reduction (Cl) in one complete equation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this is only the reduction half-reaction, incomplete on its own.

aliases: Which one of the following is a redox reaction?
NaCl + AgNO3 -> NaNO3 + AgCl

questions.question_text: The chemical substance, when dissolved in water, gives "H⁺" is called:
questions.explanation_short: A substance that releases H+ in water is, by definition, an acid.
questions.explanation_long: By the Arrhenius definition, an acid is a substance that dissociates in water to release hydrogen ions (H+).
questions.explanation_trick: Arrhenius acid = releases H+ in water; Arrhenius base = releases OH− in water. This is the most basic acid-base definition and usually the one intended unless a question specifies Bronsted-Lowry or Lewis theory.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the Arrhenius definition of an acid.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — bases release OH−, not H+.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — amphoteric substances can act as both, not defined by releasing only H+.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — neutral substances don't release H+ or OH− in a way that shifts pH from 7.

aliases: The chemical substance, when dissolved in water, gives "H+" is called:
Acid

questions.question_text: The 'pH' of our blood is:
questions.explanation_short: Normal blood pH is tightly maintained around 7.35–7.4 (physiological range ~7.35–7.45).
questions.explanation_long: Human blood pH is buffered (mainly by the bicarbonate buffer system) to stay within a narrow physiological range, typically cited as 7.35–7.45, closely matching the 7.35–7.4 option given here.
questions.explanation_trick: Blood pH is very slightly basic (above 7), not neutral or acidic — even a small deviation outside 7.35–7.45 is medically dangerous (acidosis/alkalosis).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — too wide/high a range for blood pH.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — too high for normal blood.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — slightly too high.
explanation_options.d: Correct — matches the physiological blood pH range.

questions.question_text: In zero order reactions, the rate is independent of:
questions.explanation_short: Zero order reaction: rate is independent of reactant concentration.
questions.explanation_long: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k[A]⁰ = k — a constant, unaffected by changes in reactant concentration.
questions.explanation_trick: Reaction order tells you how sensitive the rate is to concentration: zero order = no dependence at all, first order = directly proportional, second order = proportional to the square.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the definition concerns reactant concentration, not product.
explanation_options.b: Correct — rate is unaffected by reactant concentration in a zero-order reaction.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — rate constant k itself still depends on temperature (via Arrhenius); it's concentration that's independent, not temperature.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — surface area relates to heterogeneous catalysis, not the definition of reaction order.

questions.question_text: What is the trend of melting and boiling point of the elements of short periods as we move from left to right in a periodic table?
questions.option_a: Melting and boiling points first decrease then increase
questions.option_b: Melting and boiling points increase gradually
questions.option_c: Melting and boiling points first increase then decrease
questions.option_d: Melting and boiling points decrease gradually
questions.explanation_short: Across a period, melting/boiling points first rise (to a mid-period peak) then fall sharply.
questions.explanation_long: Moving across a period, melting/boiling points generally rise as metallic/covalent network bonding strengthens (peaking around Group 14, e.g. carbon or silicon), then fall sharply for the molecular non-metals and drop to a minimum for the noble gases.
questions.explanation_trick: Picture Period 3: Na, Mg, Al rise steadily (metallic bonding strengthens); Si peaks (giant covalent network); then P, S, Cl, Ar drop off fast (small, separate molecules with only weak van der Waals forces).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the trend doesn't dip first.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — it doesn't rise the whole way across; it drops sharply after the peak.
explanation_options.c: Correct — rises to a mid-period peak, then decreases.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — doesn't rise first.

questions.question_text: Along a period, atomic radius decreases. This gradual decrease in radius is due to:
questions.option_a: Increase in number of electrons in valence shells
questions.option_b: Increase in number of protons in the nucleus
questions.explanation_short: Atomic radius shrinks across a period due to increasing nuclear charge (more protons), not more shells.
questions.explanation_long:
Across a period, the number of electron shells stays exactly the same — that's the definition of a period. What changes is the number of protons in the nucleus, increasing the effective nuclear charge, which pulls the same-shell electrons in more tightly, shrinking the atomic radius.

**Note:** the source data marked 'increase in number of shells' as correct — this is inconsistent with the very definition of a period, since shell count only increases *down* a group, never across a period. The corrected answer is the increasing nuclear charge (more protons), which is the actual textbook explanation for this trend.
questions.explanation_trick: Shells increase down a group (radius increases); nuclear charge increases across a period (radius decreases). Don't mix up which trend belongs to which direction.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — more valence electrons alone doesn't explain the radius decrease; it's the increased pull from the nucleus that does.
explanation_options.b: Correct — more protons increase nuclear charge, pulling electrons in tighter.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — shell count doesn't decrease across a period at all.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — shell count stays constant across a period; it doesn't increase (that only happens down a group).

questions.question_text: Alkaline earth metal oxides react with water to give hydroxides. The solubility of alkaline earth metal oxides in water increases as we move from top to bottom in a group. Which of the following alkaline earth metal oxides is least soluble in water?
questions.explanation_short: MgO is the least soluble alkaline earth oxide in water (solubility increases down the group).
questions.explanation_long: Solubility of Group 2 (alkaline earth) metal oxides in water increases going down the group (Mg → Ca → Sr → Ba). Being at the top of the group, MgO is the least soluble of the four listed.
questions.explanation_trick: Down a group, ionic lattice energy decreases faster than hydration energy for these oxides, favouring dissolution — so solubility trends increase going down Group 2, the opposite of some other Group 2 property trends.

explanation_options.a: Correct — MgO, at the top of the group, is the least soluble.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — CaO is more soluble than MgO.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — BaO, at the bottom of the group, is the most soluble of the four.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — SrO is more soluble than MgO.

questions.question_text: The electronic structure of carbon monoxide is represented as:
questions.option_a: :C≡O: (one of the three bonds is a coordinate bond from O to C)
questions.option_c: C≡Ö: (one bond a coordinate bond from C to O; no lone pair on C)
questions.explanation_short: Carbon monoxide's structure has a triple bond between C and O, as shown in the diagram.
questions.explanation_long: Carbon monoxide is represented with a triple bond between carbon and oxygen (:C≡O:), giving both atoms a formal octet, with a lone pair on each atom, matching the diagram's structure A.
questions.explanation_trick: CO is isoelectronic with N2, and just like N2's strong triple bond, CO also has a triple bond — one of the strongest bonds known in a diatomic molecule.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches the diagram's triple-bonded structure.
explanation_options.b: See diagram — doesn't match CO's actual bonding.
explanation_options.c: See diagram — doesn't match.
explanation_options.d: See diagram — doesn't match.

aliases: The electronic structure of carbon monoxide is represented as:
Structure A

questions.question_text: Which one pair has the same oxidation state of 'Fe'?
questions.explanation_short: FeSO4 and FeCl2 both have Fe²⁺ (same oxidation state).
questions.explanation_long: Checking each pair: FeSO4 has Fe²⁺ (sulfate is −2), FeCl3 has Fe³⁺ (three chlorides, each −1) — different states. FeCl2 has Fe²⁺ (two chlorides). So FeSO4 and FeCl2 both have Fe²⁺ — matching oxidation states.
questions.explanation_trick: Work out Fe's oxidation state from the known charge of the counter-ion/anion in each compound: sulfate is always −2, chloride is always −1 per ion.
