explanation_options.b: Wrong — sodium chloride (table salt) isn't the characteristic buffering component described here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — sodium hydroxide is a strong, corrosive base, not found in saliva.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — hydrocarbons aren't a component of saliva.

questions.question_text: The total inside capacity of lungs is _____ for man.
questions.explanation_short: Total lung capacity for an average adult is roughly 5-6 litres.
questions.explanation_long: Total lung capacity is the maximum volume of air the lungs can hold, combining vital capacity and residual volume. Commonly cited textbook figures place this around 5-6 litres for an average adult male.
questions.explanation_trick: Total lung capacity is always larger than vital capacity, since it includes the residual air that can never be fully exhaled — don't confuse the two related lung-volume terms.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — higher than the standard cited textbook figure.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — far too low; this undercounts total lung capacity significantly.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — somewhat higher than the standard textbook figure used here.
explanation_options.d: Correct — approximately 5 litres is the standard textbook estimate used for total lung capacity.

questions.question_text: The average life span of red blood cell is about:
questions.explanation_short: Red blood cells live for about four months (120 days) on average.
questions.explanation_long: Mature red blood cells, lacking a nucleus and unable to repair themselves, survive circulating in the blood for approximately 120 days (about four months) before being broken down, primarily in the spleen and liver.
questions.explanation_trick: RBC lifespan = 120 days ≈ 4 months — a specific, frequently tested number worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — approximately 120 days, or four months.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — too short compared to the actual RBC lifespan.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — too long compared to the actual RBC lifespan.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — far too short; this isn't the correct lifespan for RBCs.

questions.question_text: The lymphatic vessels of the body empty the lymph into blood stream at the:
questions.explanation_short: Lymph drains into the bloodstream at the subclavian vein.
questions.explanation_long: The lymphatic system's major vessels (like the thoracic duct) ultimately empty their collected lymph fluid into the bloodstream at the subclavian veins, near the base of the neck.
questions.explanation_trick: Lymph → subclavian vein is the standard endpoint where the lymphatic and circulatory systems reconnect — a direct fact worth memorizing.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — not a standard drainage point for the lymphatic system.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the subclavian vein is where lymph re-enters the bloodstream.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the jugular vein carries blood from the head/neck, but isn't the lymphatic system's primary drainage point.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the bile duct carries bile to the digestive tract, entirely unrelated to the lymphatic system.

questions.question_text: Right atrium is separated from right ventricle by:
questions.explanation_short: The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.
questions.explanation_long: The tricuspid valve (with three flaps/cusps) is located between the right atrium and right ventricle, preventing backflow of blood into the atrium during ventricular contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Tricuspid (3 flaps) = right side of heart; Bicuspid/Mitral (2 flaps) = left side of heart — a straightforward left-right pairing to memorize.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the tricuspid valve is specifically the right atrium-ventricle valve.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the left side of the heart, between the left atrium and ventricle.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — semilunar valves are located at the exits of the ventricles (pulmonary and aortic valves), not between atrium and ventricle.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the septum is the wall dividing the heart's left and right sides, not a valve.

questions.question_text: Site of filtration in nephron is:
questions.explanation_short: Filtration in the nephron occurs at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
questions.explanation_long: Blood filtration begins as blood pressure forces fluid out of the glomerulus's capillaries into the surrounding Bowman's capsule, forming the initial filtrate that will be processed further along the nephron's tubules.
questions.explanation_trick: Filtration happens right at the start of the nephron (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule); everything downstream (proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule) handles reabsorption and secretion, not initial filtration.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together perform filtration.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — proximal and distal tubules handle reabsorption/secretion, not the initial filtration step.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the ascending/descending arms of the loop of Henle handle reabsorption, not filtration.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the loop of Henle's role is establishing the concentration gradient for water reabsorption, not filtration.

questions.question_text: Antidiuretic hormone increases the reabsorption of:
questions.explanation_short: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption.
questions.explanation_long: ADH acts on the kidney's collecting ducts, increasing their permeability to water so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood, concentrating the urine and conserving body water.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Antidiuretic' literally means 'against urination (water loss)' — ADH's whole job is to reduce water loss by promoting its reabsorption.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ADH's specific target is water, not amino acids.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — aldosterone (a different hormone) regulates salt reabsorption, not ADH.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — ammonia handling isn't ADH's function.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ADH's defining role is increasing water reabsorption.

questions.question_text: Active uptake of ______ in the ascending limb or thick loop of Henle is promoted by the action of aldosterone:
questions.explanation_short: Aldosterone promotes active Na+ uptake in the kidney's Na+-handling regions.
questions.explanation_long: Aldosterone is the hormone specifically responsible for promoting active sodium ion reabsorption in the kidney (primarily acting on the distal tubule and collecting duct, with broader Na+ handling also occurring along the ascending loop of Henle), helping regulate blood pressure and electrolyte balance.
questions.explanation_trick: Aldosterone = sodium-retaining hormone (also promotes K+ excretion) — a specific hormone-to-ion pairing worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — aldosterone's defining target ion is sodium, not potassium (though it does promote K+ excretion as a secondary effect).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — chloride follows sodium passively rather than being aldosterone's primary active target.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — calcium regulation is governed by different hormones (like parathyroid hormone), not aldosterone.
explanation_options.d: Correct — aldosterone specifically promotes active sodium reabsorption.

aliases: Active uptake of ______ in the ascending limb or thick loop of Henle is promoted by the action of aldosterone:
K+

questions.question_text: The process through which the body maintains the internal environment from the fluctuations of external environment is called as:
questions.explanation_short: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes.
questions.explanation_long: Homeostasis describes the body's collection of regulatory processes (temperature control, blood glucose regulation, water/salt balance, etc.) that keep the internal environment stable even as external conditions fluctuate.
questions.explanation_trick: Homeo- (similar/same) + -stasis (standing still) = 'staying the same' — the literal word origin describes exactly this stability-maintaining concept.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'behavior of organisms' is too broad and doesn't specifically name this internal-stability concept.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — adaptation refers to evolutionary traits suited to an environment, a different (longer-timescale) concept.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — thermoregulation is just one specific example of homeostasis (temperature control), not the general term itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — homeostasis is the precise general term for this internal-stability maintenance.

questions.question_text: Active pumping out of Na⁺ occurs at which part of nephron:
questions.explanation_short: Active Na+ pumping occurs in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
questions.explanation_long: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle actively transports Na+ (and Cl-) out of the filtrate into the surrounding tissue, while remaining impermeable to water — this active pumping is what establishes the concentration gradient the kidney uses to concentrate urine.
questions.explanation_trick: Descending limb = permeable to water, passive; Ascending limb = impermeable to water, active Na+/Cl- pumping — the two limbs of the loop of Henle have opposite, complementary jobs.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the proximal tubule does reabsorb Na+, but mostly passively/via cotransport tied to nutrient reabsorption, not the specific active pumping process described here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the descending limb is permeable to water, not the site of active Na+ pumping.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the ascending limb specifically performs active Na+ pumping.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — collecting ducts handle final water/urea adjustments under ADH/aldosterone control, not this specific loop-of-Henle Na+ pumping step.

aliases: Active pumping out of Na+ occurs at which part of nephron:
Proximal tubule

questions.question_text: The structures which respond when they are stimulated by impulse coming through motor neuron are:
questions.explanation_short: Effectors respond to motor neuron impulses (muscles or glands).
questions.explanation_long: An effector is any structure (typically a muscle or gland) that produces a response when it receives a signal via a motor neuron, completing the reflex/nervous pathway that begins at a receptor.
questions.explanation_trick: Receptor (detects stimulus) → Motor neuron carries signal → Effector (produces response) — memorize this three-part chain in order.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — receptors detect stimuli at the start of the pathway, not respond to motor signals at the end.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'responders' isn't the standard biological term used here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'transducers' convert one form of energy/signal to another (like at a receptor), not the term for muscle/gland response structures.
explanation_options.d: Correct — effectors are precisely the structures that respond to motor neuron signals.

questions.question_text: Thalamus and cerebrum are the part of:
questions.explanation_short: The thalamus and cerebrum are both structures of the forebrain.
questions.explanation_long: The forebrain includes the cerebrum (responsible for higher cognitive functions) and the thalamus (a relay center for sensory information), among other structures like the hypothalamus.
questions.explanation_trick: Forebrain = cerebrum + thalamus + hypothalamus; Midbrain = smaller relay/reflex center; Hindbrain = cerebellum, pons, medulla — group these structures by their brain region.

explanation_options.a: Correct — both thalamus and cerebrum belong to the forebrain.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the midbrain contains different structures (like the tectum), not the thalamus/cerebrum.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the hindbrain contains the cerebellum, pons, and medulla, not the thalamus/cerebrum.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the spinal cord is a separate structure below the brain entirely.

questions.question_text: There is also EVIDENCE that high levels of ______ may contribute to the onset of Alzheimer's disease:
questions.explanation_short: Elevated aluminum levels have historically been proposed as a possible contributing factor in Alzheimer's disease.
questions.explanation_long: Some earlier research proposed a link between high aluminum exposure/accumulation in the brain and the onset of Alzheimer's disease — a hypothesis commonly cited in textbooks of this era, even though more recent research has found the connection far less clear-cut.
questions.explanation_trick: This is one of several textbook-cited (though scientifically debated) Alzheimer's risk-factor associations — aluminum is the specific metal traditionally paired with this disease in exam contexts.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — magnesium isn't the metal traditionally linked to Alzheimer's in this context.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — molybdenum isn't associated with Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_options.c: Correct — aluminum is the metal traditionally cited in this Alzheimer's-risk association.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — calcium isn't the metal being referenced in this specific association.

questions.question_text: L-dopa or Levodopa is used to get some relief from??
questions.explanation_short: L-dopa (Levodopa) is used to treat Parkinson's disease.
questions.explanation_long: Parkinson's disease results from a shortage of dopamine in certain brain regions. Since dopamine itself can't cross the blood-brain barrier, L-dopa (a dopamine precursor that can cross) is administered instead, where it's converted into dopamine within the brain.
questions.explanation_trick: L-dopa → converted to dopamine in the brain → relieves Parkinson's symptoms (which stem from dopamine deficiency) — a direct drug-to-disease pairing.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — epilepsy is treated with different anticonvulsant medications, not L-dopa.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Alzheimer's treatment targets different neurotransmitter systems (like acetylcholine), not dopamine replacement.
explanation_options.c: Correct — L-dopa is the standard treatment for Parkinson's disease's dopamine deficiency.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — dementia (a broader symptom category) isn't specifically treated with L-dopa the way Parkinson's is.

questions.question_text: Spermatogonia differentiate directly into?
questions.explanation_short: Spermatogonia differentiate directly into primary spermatocytes.
questions.explanation_long: In spermatogenesis, spermatogonia (the stem cells) grow and differentiate into primary spermatocytes, which then undergo meiosis I to become secondary spermatocytes, then meiosis II to form spermatids, which finally mature into spermatozoa.
questions.explanation_trick: The full spermatogenesis sequence: Spermatogonia → Primary spermatocytes → (meiosis I) → Secondary spermatocytes → (meiosis II) → Spermatids → Spermatozoa — memorize this order to answer 'which stage comes directly after which.'

explanation_options.a: Correct — primary spermatocytes are the very next stage after spermatogonia.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — secondary spermatocytes come two steps later, after primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — spermatozoa are the final mature stage, much further down the sequence.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — spermatids come even later, after secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II.

questions.question_text: Treponema palladium causes?
questions.explanation_short: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis.
questions.explanation_long: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, a spirochete (spiral-shaped bacterium).
questions.explanation_trick: Treponema pallidum = syphilis — a direct organism-to-disease pairing frequently tested alongside other STI-causing organisms (Neisseria gonorrhoeae for gonorrhea, HIV for AIDS).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — AIDS is caused by the HIV virus, not a bacterium.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — genital herpes is caused by the herpes simplex virus, not this bacterium.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Treponema pallidum is specifically the causative organism for syphilis.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — gonorrhea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a different bacterium.

questions.question_text: What is the location of interstitial cells in testes?
questions.explanation_short: Interstitial (Leydig) cells are located between the seminiferous tubules in the testes.
questions.explanation_long: Interstitial cells (Leydig cells) sit in the connective tissue spaces between the seminiferous tubules within the testes, distinct from the sperm-producing cells lining the tubules themselves.
questions.explanation_trick: Seminiferous tubules make sperm (inside); Interstitial/Leydig cells make testosterone (in the spaces between tubules) — two different cell populations with two different jobs in the same organ.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the inside of seminiferous tubules contains developing sperm cells, not interstitial cells.
explanation_options.b: Correct — interstitial cells occupy the spaces between the seminiferous tubules.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — germinal epithelial cells line the inside of the tubules, a different location and cell type.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — interstitial cells are located inside the testes (between tubules), not around the outside of the organ.

questions.question_text: A type of cells in human testes which produce testosterone are called?
questions.explanation_short: Interstitial (Leydig) cells produce testosterone.
questions.explanation_long: Leydig (interstitial) cells, located between the seminiferous tubules, are specifically responsible for synthesizing and secreting testosterone in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) stimulation.
questions.explanation_trick: Interstitial/Leydig cells = testosterone; Sertoli cells (inside the tubules) = support developing sperm cells and secrete inhibin — two distinct testicular cell types with distinct jobs.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — germ cells develop into sperm, they don't themselves produce testosterone.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Sertoli cells support sperm development, they don't produce testosterone.
explanation_options.c: Correct — interstitial (Leydig) cells are the testosterone-producing cells.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — spermatocytes are developing sperm cells, not hormone-producing cells.

questions.question_text: The hormone produced from corpus luteum is:
questions.explanation_short: The corpus luteum produces progesterone.
questions.explanation_long: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and some estrogen) to maintain the uterine lining in preparation for a possible pregnancy.
questions.explanation_trick: Corpus luteum = progesterone factory (post-ovulation) — a key hormone-source pairing in the menstrual cycle.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — prolactin is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the corpus luteum.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the corpus luteum.
explanation_options.c: Correct — progesterone is the corpus luteum's characteristic hormone.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — LH (luteinizing hormone) is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the corpus luteum (though LH is what triggers the corpus luteum's formation).

questions.question_text: The length of myofibril from one Z-band to the next is described as:
questions.explanation_short: A sarcomere is the myofibril segment measured from one Z-band to the next.
questions.explanation_long: The sarcomere is the basic repeating contractile unit of a myofibril, bounded on either end by Z-bands (Z-lines), containing the overlapping actin and myosin filaments responsible for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Sarcomere = Z-line to Z-line — the fundamental repeating unit that shortens during contraction, giving skeletal muscle its striped ('striated') appearance.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the sarcolemma is the muscle cell's plasma membrane, not this length measurement.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of a muscle cell, not this length measurement.
explanation_options.c: Correct — sarcomere is precisely this Z-band-to-Z-band unit.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a muscle fiber is the entire muscle cell, containing many sarcomeres in series, not this specific unit.

questions.question_text: The Ca²⁺ ions released during a muscle fiber contraction attach with:
questions.explanation_short: Released Ca++ ions bind to troponin during muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_long: When calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during contraction, they bind to troponin (a regulatory protein on the actin filament), causing tropomyosin to shift and expose the myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling to begin.
questions.explanation_trick: Ca++ binds to Troponin → Troponin moves Tropomyosin → Myosin-binding sites on Actin get exposed — memorize this three-step chain in order.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — myosin is the thick filament that binds actin directly during contraction, not the calcium-binding regulatory protein.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — actin is the thin filament itself, not the specific calcium-binding regulatory protein.
explanation_options.c: Correct — troponin is the direct calcium-binding protein that triggers the contraction cascade.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — tropomyosin moves in response to troponin's calcium-triggered shape change, but doesn't directly bind calcium itself.

aliases: The Ca++ ions released during a muscle fiber contraction attach with:
Myosin

questions.question_text: The joint that allows the movement in several directions is called:
questions.explanation_short: A ball and socket joint allows movement in multiple directions.
questions.explanation_long: Ball and socket joints (like the shoulder and hip) have a rounded 'ball' end of one bone fitting into a cup-shaped 'socket' of another, allowing rotation and movement in essentially all directions.
questions.explanation_trick: Ball and socket = maximum range of motion (shoulder, hip); Hinge joint = one-plane back-and-forth motion only (elbow, knee) — contrast these two joint types by their range of motion.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a hinge joint only allows movement in one plane (like a door hinge), not multiple directions.
explanation_options.b: Correct — ball and socket joints allow movement in multiple directions.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cartilaginous joints (like between vertebrae) allow only limited, slight movement.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — fibrous joints (like skull sutures) allow little to no movement at all.

questions.question_text: Where can we find H zone in the fine structure of skeletal muscle's myofibril?
questions.option_a: In the mid of A band
questions.explanation_short: The H-zone is located in the middle of the A-band.
questions.explanation_long: The A-band (containing thick myosin filaments) has a lighter central region called the H-zone, where only myosin filaments are present without overlapping thin actin filaments — the H-zone narrows as the muscle contracts and the filaments slide closer together.
questions.explanation_trick: A-band = thick (myosin) filaments, includes the H-zone at its center; I-band = thin (actin) filaments only, no myosin — keep these two band regions and their sub-features straight.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the H-zone sits in the middle of the A-band.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the I-band is a separate region containing only thin actin filaments, without an H-zone.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the Z-line is the sarcomere's boundary, not the location of the H-zone.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the H-zone is within the A-band, not along the I-band.

questions.question_text: First vertebra of cervical region of vertebral column is known as:
questions.explanation_short: The Atlas is the first cervical vertebra.
questions.explanation_long: The Atlas (C1) is the topmost cervical vertebra, supporting the skull and allowing nodding movements, named after the Greek mythological figure who held up the sky.
questions.explanation_trick: Atlas (C1, holds up the skull, nodding 'yes') sits directly above the Axis (C2, allows head rotation, shaking 'no') — memorize these two specially named vertebrae together.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the Atlas is the first cervical vertebra.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — sacral vertebrae are located at the base of the spine, near the pelvis, not the neck.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — thoracic vertebrae are in the chest region, below the cervical vertebrae.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the Axis is the second cervical vertebra, not the first.

questions.question_text: Chemically insulin and glucagon are:
questions.explanation_short: Insulin and glucagon are both protein (peptide) hormones.
questions.explanation_long: Both insulin and glucagon, secreted by different cell types within the pancreatic Islets of Langerhans, are peptide hormones — chains of amino acids — rather than steroid (lipid-based) hormones.
questions.explanation_trick: Peptide/protein hormones (insulin, glucagon, growth hormone) act via cell-surface receptors; steroid hormones (like cortisol, estrogen) can cross the cell membrane directly — knowing a hormone's chemical class often tells you its mechanism.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — neither insulin nor glucagon are carbohydrates.
explanation_options.b: Correct — both are peptide/protein hormones.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — steroid hormones (like cortisol) are lipids, but insulin and glucagon are not.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — neither hormone is a nucleic acid.

questions.question_text: Hormones secreted by anterior pituitary and which controls the secretion of hormones of other endocrine glands are known as:
questions.explanation_short: Tropic (trophic) hormones from the anterior pituitary control other endocrine glands' secretions.
questions.explanation_long: Tropic hormones (like TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) are secreted by the anterior pituitary specifically to stimulate and regulate the activity of other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Tropic'/'trophic' hormones don't act directly on most body tissues — their job is specifically to control other endocrine glands, making the pituitary the body's 'master gland.'

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'release factor' more specifically describes hypothalamic hormones that trigger pituitary secretion, not this general category from the anterior pituitary itself.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'inhibitor' describes a hormone that suppresses activity, not this stimulatory category.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'accelerator' isn't a standard endocrine term for this hormone category.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tropic/trophic hormones is the precise term for this category.

questions.question_text: Alpha cells of Islets of Langerhans secrete hormone called:
questions.explanation_short: Alpha cells of the Islets of Langerhans secrete glucagon.
questions.explanation_long: Within the pancreatic Islets of Langerhans, alpha cells secrete glucagon (which raises blood glucose), while beta cells secrete insulin (which lowers blood glucose) — two opposing hormones from two different cell types in the same structure.
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha cells = glucagon (raises blood sugar); Beta cells = insulin (lowers blood sugar) — 'A' before 'B' alphabetically, and glucagon raises sugar before insulin brings it back down, a helpful memory pairing.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — glucocorticoids are produced by the adrenal cortex, not pancreatic alpha cells.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — insulin is secreted by beta cells, not alpha cells.
explanation_options.c: Correct — alpha cells specifically secrete glucagon.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — aldosterone is produced by the adrenal cortex, not the pancreas.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the function of glucagon hormone?
questions.explanation_short: Glucagon converts stored glycogen back into glucose.
questions.explanation_long: Glucagon's primary function is to raise blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis), releasing it into the bloodstream.
questions.explanation_trick: Insulin: glucose → glycogen (storage, lowers blood sugar); Glucagon: glycogen → glucose (release, raises blood sugar) — these two hormones work in exactly opposite directions.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — converting glucose to lipids isn't glucagon's characteristic function.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — converting glucose to proteins isn't glucagon's function.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — converting glucose to glycogen is insulin's job, the opposite direction from glucagon.
explanation_options.d: Correct — glucagon converts glycogen back into glucose, raising blood sugar.

questions.question_text: In passive immunity which of the following components are injected into body?
questions.explanation_short: Passive immunity involves injecting ready-made antibodies (immunoglobulins) directly.
questions.explanation_long: Passive immunity provides immediate but temporary protection by directly supplying pre-formed antibodies (immunoglobulins) — such as through an antivenom injection or maternal antibodies crossing the placenta — rather than stimulating the recipient's own immune system to produce them.
questions.explanation_trick: Active immunity = body makes its own antibodies (via vaccination or natural infection, longer-lasting); Passive immunity = ready-made antibodies given directly (immediate but temporary) — a key immunology distinction.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — injecting antigens is how active immunity (vaccination) works, triggering the body's own antibody production.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'immunogens' is a general term for antigen-like triggering substances, not the specific injected component in passive immunity.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — while antibody-rich serum can be used, 'immunoglobulins' more precisely names the actual protective component being transferred.
explanation_options.d: Correct — passive immunity involves directly supplying pre-made immunoglobulins (antibodies).

questions.question_text: Which part of the antibody recognizes the antigen during immune response?
questions.explanation_short: The variable region of an antibody recognizes and binds the specific antigen.
questions.explanation_long: Each antibody has constant regions (the same across many antibodies) and variable regions (unique to each antibody), with the variable region's specific shape allowing it to recognize and bind one particular antigen.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Variable' region = varies between antibodies = gives each antibody its unique antigen-recognition specificity, just like a unique lock shape matching one specific key.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the heavy chain includes both constant and variable portions; the antigen-binding specificity comes from the variable part specifically, not the heavy chain as a whole.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the variable region/part is what recognizes the specific antigen.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — similarly, the light chain includes both constant and variable portions; the recognition function is tied to the variable part, not the light chain as a whole.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'consonant part' isn't a real antibody structural term (likely a distractor).

questions.question_text: Two identical light chains and two identical heavy chains in antibody molecule are linked by:
questions.explanation_short: Disulfide bridges link the light and heavy chains of an antibody molecule.
questions.explanation_long: An antibody's characteristic Y-shape is held together by disulfide bonds (covalent bonds between sulfur atoms) connecting the two identical heavy chains to each other and to the two identical light chains.
questions.explanation_trick: Disulfide bridges = the 'stitching' that holds an antibody's four-chain structure together — a structural detail worth remembering alongside the antibody's basic Y-shape.

explanation_options.a: Correct — disulfide bridges are precisely what links the chains together.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — peptide bonds link amino acids within each individual chain, not between the separate chains themselves.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — glycerol bonds aren't a relevant concept for protein chain linkage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — ionic bonds aren't the primary linkage holding antibody chains together; that's the disulfide (covalent) bridges.

questions.question_text: Antibodies are produced against invading cells by:
questions.explanation_short: Lymphocytes (specifically B-lymphocytes) produce antibodies against invading cells.
questions.explanation_long: B-lymphocytes, upon activation, differentiate into plasma cells that manufacture and secrete large quantities of antibodies specifically targeted against the invading antigen.
questions.explanation_trick: Lymphocytes = antibody producers (B cells) and cell-mediated attackers (T cells); Neutrophils/Basophils are different white blood cell types with different, non-antibody-producing roles (like general phagocytosis or inflammation).

explanation_options.a: Correct — lymphocytes (B cells specifically) are the antibody-producing white blood cells.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — basophils are involved in allergic/inflammatory responses, not antibody production.
explanation_options.c: Note — this option duplicates option B ('Basophils') as printed in the source data, a data entry quirk rather than a distinct choice.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — neutrophils are phagocytic cells that engulf pathogens directly, not antibody producers.

questions.question_text: In the structure of an antibody molecule, which portion is occupied by variable chains?
questions.explanation_short: Variable chains occupy the upper region (the antigen-binding 'arms') of an antibody's Y-shaped structure.
questions.explanation_long: In the standard depiction of an antibody's Y-shape, the variable regions sit at the tips of the two upper arms — the parts that directly contact and bind the antigen — while the constant regions form the lower 'stem' of the Y.
questions.explanation_trick: Picture the antibody's Y-shape: variable regions (antigen-binding) are at the top of the two arms; constant regions (the 'stalk', interacting with immune cells) are at the bottom.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the lower region is occupied by the constant chains, not the variable ones.
explanation_options.b: Correct — variable chains occupy the upper region, forming the antigen-binding tips.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'middle region' isn't the standard depiction of where variable regions sit.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'in between chains' doesn't describe a specific structural region of the antibody.

questions.question_text: Every molecule of NADH, fed into ETC produces:
questions.explanation_short: Each NADH molecule fed into the electron transport chain yields about 3 ATP.
questions.explanation_long: As electrons from NADH pass through the electron transport chain (through complexes I, III, and IV), enough energy is released to pump protons and generate approximately 3 ATP molecules per NADH, per the classic textbook accounting (FADH2 yields about 2 ATP, entering the chain at a later point).
questions.explanation_trick: NADH → ~3 ATP; FADH2 → ~2 ATP — NADH enters the electron transport chain earlier, passing through more proton-pumping complexes, which is why it yields more ATP than FADH2.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 2 ATP is the yield associated with FADH2, not NADH.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 3 ATP is the standard textbook yield per NADH.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — higher than the standard cited yield.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — higher than the standard cited yield.

questions.question_text: Final acceptor of electrons in respiratory chain is:
questions.explanation_short: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the respiratory (electron transport) chain.
questions.explanation_long: At the end of the electron transport chain, oxygen accepts the electrons (along with protons) to form water — this is why oxygen is essential for aerobic respiration to continue.
questions.explanation_trick: Oxygen = the final electron acceptor, forming water at the chain's end — this is precisely what makes aerobic respiration 'aerobic' (oxygen-dependent).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — cytochrome a is one of the electron carriers within the chain, not the final destination for the electrons.
explanation_options.b: Correct — oxygen is the ultimate final acceptor at the end of the chain.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — cytochrome a3 (part of the same complex as cytochrome a) hands electrons off to oxygen, but oxygen itself is the true final acceptor.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — cytochrome c is an earlier electron carrier in the chain, not the final acceptor.

questions.question_text: The end product of anaerobic respiration in humans and other mammals is:
questions.explanation_short: Anaerobic respiration in humans produces lactic acid.
questions.explanation_long: When oxygen is insufficient (e.g. during intense exercise), human muscle cells switch to anaerobic (lactic acid) fermentation, converting pyruvic acid into lactic acid to regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running.
questions.explanation_trick: Humans/animals: anaerobic respiration → lactic acid; Yeast/plants: anaerobic respiration → ethanol + CO2 — different organisms produce different end products from the same starting glucose.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — pyruvic acid is the intermediate product of glycolysis itself, converted further into lactic acid under anaerobic conditions, not the final end product asked about here.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — ethanol is the end product of anaerobic fermentation in yeast/plants, not humans.
explanation_options.c: Correct — lactic acid is specifically the end product of human anaerobic respiration.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — glucose is the starting material for respiration, not its end product.

questions.question_text: A biochemical process which occurs within a cell to breakdown complex compounds to produce energy is called:
questions.explanation_short: Respiration is the process in a cell that breaks down complex food compounds to release energy.
questions.explanation_long: Cellular respiration is the name of the biochemical process in which glucose and other complex compounds are broken down inside the cell and the energy released is stored as ATP. It proceeds through oxidation-reduction reactions, but 'oxidation reduction' is a type of chemical reaction, not the name of this cellular process. Photosynthesis builds compounds, and photophosphorylation is ATP synthesis driven by light. (The printed UHS key marks C, but the process defined here is respiration, so A is used.)
questions.explanation_trick: Breakdown for energy = respiration; build-up using light = photosynthesis.

explanation_options.a: Correct — respiration breaks down complex compounds to release energy.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — photosynthesis makes complex compounds and stores energy.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — redox reactions occur in respiration, but that is a reaction type, not the name of the process.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — photophosphorylation is ATP formation in the light reactions of photosynthesis.

questions.question_text: Which part of chlorophyll molecule absorbs light?
questions.explanation_short: The porphyrin ring (the 'head' of the chlorophyll molecule) absorbs light.
questions.explanation_long: Chlorophyll's structure has a light-absorbing porphyrin ring (a flat, ring-shaped structure with a central magnesium ion) attached to a long hydrocarbon phytol tail that anchors the molecule within the thylakoid membrane. The actual light absorption happens in the porphyrin ring.
questions.explanation_trick: Porphyrin ring = light-absorbing 'head'; Phytol tail = membrane-anchoring 'tail' — chlorophyll's two functional parts serve two different jobs.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the phytol tail anchors the molecule in the membrane; it doesn't absorb light.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the porphyrin ring is the light-absorbing part of chlorophyll.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — pyrrole rings are the four smaller sub-units that together make up the larger porphyrin ring structure, not a separate distinct answer.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the thylakoid membrane houses the chlorophyll molecules, but isn't itself the light-absorbing part of the molecule.

questions.question_text: The DNA molecule formed from messenger-RNA by reverse transcriptase is called??
questions.explanation_short: DNA made from mRNA via reverse transcriptase is called complementary DNA (cDNA).
questions.explanation_long: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is synthesized in the lab using reverse transcriptase to copy an mRNA template into DNA — useful because cDNA lacks introns, representing only the coding (expressed) sequence.
questions.explanation_trick: cDNA = 'copy DNA' made from mRNA (no introns); genomic DNA = the original DNA (with introns) — cDNA is specifically the reverse-transcribed, intron-free version.

explanation_options.a: Correct — complementary DNA (cDNA) is precisely this reverse-transcribed product.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — recombinant DNA refers to DNA combined from different sources (e.g. inserted into a plasmid), a different concept.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'chimeric DNA' is another term sometimes used loosely for recombinant DNA, not specifically this mRNA-derived DNA.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — plasmid DNA refers to the small circular DNA molecules used as vectors, not DNA made from mRNA.

questions.question_text: The agent which separates the two strands of DNA in PCR is??
questions.explanation_short: Heat is used to separate (denature) the two DNA strands during PCR.
questions.explanation_long:
PCR's first step (denaturation) heats the reaction to around 94-98°C, breaking the hydrogen bonds holding the DNA double helix together and separating it into single strands — a purely thermal process, unlike DNA replication inside a living cell.

**Note:** the source data marked 'DNA ligase' as correct — but DNA ligase's actual job is joining DNA fragments together (sealing nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone), not separating strands. The corrected answer is heat, PCR's actual denaturation mechanism — a defining feature that distinguishes PCR (in vitro, heat-driven) from natural DNA replication (in vivo, enzyme-driven via helicase).
questions.explanation_trick: PCR's three steps: Denaturation (heat separates strands) → Annealing (primers bind) → Extension (DNA polymerase builds new strands) — heat, not any enzyme, does the strand separation in PCR specifically.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together; it doesn't separate strands.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — primers bind to the single-stranded template during annealing, after separation has already happened.
explanation_options.c: Correct — heat is what physically separates the two DNA strands during PCR's denaturation step.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — helicase separates DNA strands during natural cellular replication, but PCR (performed in a test tube) uses heat instead of this enzyme.

questions.question_text: Cystic fibrosis patient lack a gene that codes for trans-membrane carrier of??
questions.explanation_short: Cystic fibrosis patients lack a functional gene for the chloride ion (Cl-) transmembrane carrier.
questions.explanation_long: Cystic fibrosis results from a defective CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane conductance Regulator) gene, which normally codes for a channel that transports chloride ions across cell membranes — its malfunction leads to thick, sticky mucus buildup.
questions.explanation_trick: CFTR = Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane conductance Regulator — the name of the defective gene literally tells you it's a transmembrane transport protein, specifically for chloride ions.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — sodium transport isn't the primary defect in cystic fibrosis (though it's indirectly affected).
explanation_options.b: Correct — chloride ion transport is the specific defect in cystic fibrosis.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — calcium transport isn't the defect associated with cystic fibrosis.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — potassium transport isn't the defect associated with cystic fibrosis.

aliases: Cystic fibrosis patient lack a gene that codes for trans-membrane carrier of??
Na+ ions

questions.question_text: The phage commonly used as a vector in genetic engineering is?
questions.explanation_short: Lambda phage is a commonly used vector in genetic engineering.
questions.explanation_long: Bacteriophage lambda is widely used in genetic engineering as a cloning vector, capable of carrying larger DNA inserts than plasmids and efficiently infecting bacterial cells to deliver the recombinant DNA.
questions.explanation_trick: Lambda phage = a go-to cloning vector alongside plasmids, especially useful for larger DNA fragments — a specific named vector worth remembering directly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — lambda phage is the standard phage vector used in genetic engineering.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'gamma phage' isn't a standard named cloning vector.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — T2 phage is a well-studied virulent phage (used historically in the Hershey-Chase experiment), not the standard cloning vector.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — T4 phage is another well-studied virulent phage, not the standard genetic engineering vector.

questions.question_text: Restriction endonucleases are naturally occurring enzymes of:
questions.explanation_short: Restriction endonucleases naturally occur in bacteria.
questions.explanation_long: Bacteria naturally produce restriction endonucleases as part of a defense system against invading viral (phage) DNA — cutting foreign DNA at specific recognition sequences while protecting their own DNA through methylation.
questions.explanation_trick: Restriction enzymes = bacterial 'immune defense' against phages — this natural bacterial origin is exactly why these enzymes became such a powerful tool for genetic engineering (cutting DNA at precise sequences).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — viruses are what these enzymes defend against, not where they naturally originate.
explanation_options.b: Correct — bacteria are the natural source of restriction endonucleases.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — fungi aren't the natural source of these particular enzymes.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — plants aren't the natural source of restriction endonucleases.

questions.question_text: In an ecosystem mycorrhizae are an example of:
questions.explanation_short: Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association of a fungus with plant roots; the UHS key marks symbiosis.
questions.explanation_long: A mycorrhiza is a close, long-term association between a fungus and the roots of a plant: the fungus takes up water and minerals for the plant, and the plant supplies sugars to the fungus. In the textbook it is given as an example of symbiosis. Because both partners benefit, the association is also correctly described as mutualism, which is one kind of symbiosis, so option C is also scientifically sound. The UHS key marks B.
questions.explanation_trick: Symbiosis is the umbrella term; mutualism (both benefit), commensalism and parasitism are its kinds.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — in predation one organism kills and eats the other.
explanation_options.b: Correct (UHS key) — mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association.
explanation_options.c: Also accurate — it is a mutualistic kind of symbiosis, but the key marks B.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — in parasitism one partner is harmed.

questions.question_text: As a result of destruction of ozone layer there is significant increase in:
questions.explanation_short: Ozone layer destruction increases the amount of harmful ultraviolet radiation reaching Earth's surface.
questions.explanation_long: The ozone layer normally absorbs most incoming ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. When ozone is depleted, more UV radiation penetrates to Earth's surface, increasing risks like skin cancer and ecological damage.
questions.explanation_trick: Ozone layer's main job = blocking UV radiation — its depletion directly and specifically increases UV exposure, distinct from greenhouse gases (which trap heat, a separate climate issue).

explanation_options.a: Correct — ozone depletion directly increases UV radiation reaching the surface.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — greenhouse gases relate to global warming/the greenhouse effect, a separate environmental issue from ozone depletion.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — nitrogen oxides are pollutants that can contribute to ozone depletion, not a direct result of it.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — sulfur oxides are separate pollutants (contributing to acid rain), not a direct result of ozone depletion.

questions.question_text: Higher rate of a biological activity in a nutrient rich pond water is called:
questions.explanation_short: Eutrophication is excessive biological activity/growth in nutrient-enriched water.
questions.explanation_long: Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients (like nitrogen and phosphorus, often from agricultural runoff) enter a water body, causing explosive growth of algae and other organisms, which can deplete oxygen and harm aquatic life.
questions.explanation_trick: Eutrophication = 'well-nourished' water leading to overgrowth (often algal blooms) — a specific ecological term for this nutrient-driven biological explosion.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'water pollution' is too generic a term for this specific nutrient-driven phenomenon.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — air pollution is unrelated to water nutrient enrichment.
explanation_options.c: Correct — eutrophication is the precise term for this nutrient-driven biological activity increase.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'industrial effects' is too vague/generic a term.

questions.question_text: Living part of ecosystem is:
questions.explanation_short: The community is the living (biotic) part of an ecosystem.
questions.explanation_long:
An ecosystem consists of a community (all the living organisms interacting in an area) plus the abiotic (non-living) environment they inhabit. The community specifically represents the biotic component.

**Note:** the source data marked 'biosphere' as correct — but the biosphere is a much larger-scale concept, referring to the entire global zone of life across all of Earth's ecosystems combined, not 'the living part of' a single ecosystem specifically. The corrected answer, community, is the standard textbook term for an ecosystem's biotic component.
questions.explanation_trick: Ecosystem = Community (biotic, living organisms) + Abiotic environment (non-living factors); Biosphere = the sum of ALL ecosystems on Earth — don't confuse the scale of 'one ecosystem's living part' with 'the whole planet's life zone'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the lithosphere is the solid, non-living rock/soil part of Earth.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the hydrosphere is the non-living water component of Earth.
explanation_options.c: Correct — community is the standard term for an ecosystem's living, biotic component.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — biosphere refers to the entire global life-supporting zone across all ecosystems, not the living part of a single ecosystem specifically.

questions.question_text: A living association between two living organisms of different species which is beneficial to both the partners is called:
questions.explanation_short: Mutualism is a relationship between two species that benefits both partners.
questions.explanation_long: Mutualism describes a close, ongoing biological relationship where both participating species gain a benefit from the interaction (e.g. bees and flowering plants, or mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots).
questions.explanation_trick: Mutualism = both benefit; Commensalism = one benefits, other unaffected; Parasitism = one benefits, other harmed — memorize this three-way comparison of symbiotic relationship types.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — commensalism benefits only one partner while leaving the other unaffected, not both benefiting.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — parasitism benefits one partner at the other's expense, not both.
explanation_options.c: Correct — mutualism is specifically the both-benefit relationship type.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — predation involves one organism consuming another, not a mutual benefit.

questions.question_text: The structures which are reduced during the course of evolution and have no apparent function are called:
questions.explanation_short: Reduced, functionless evolutionary remnants are called vestigial organs.
questions.explanation_long: Vestigial organs are structures that have become reduced in size and lost their original function over evolutionary time, remaining as remnants of a structure that was functional in an ancestral species (e.g. the human appendix, or whale pelvic bones).
questions.explanation_trick: Vestigial organs are classic evidence for evolution — structures that make sense only as leftover traces of an ancestor's functional anatomy, not as something with a current purpose.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'regenerated organs' describes a different concept (regrowth after damage), unrelated to evolutionary reduction.
explanation_options.b: Correct — vestigial organs is the precise term for these functionless evolutionary remnants.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'saltatory organs' isn't a standard biological term matching this description.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — while colloquially 'useless' fits, 'vestigial' is the precise scientific/technical term expected here.

questions.question_text: When a gene suppresses the effect of another gene at another locus the phenomenon is termed as:
questions.explanation_short: Epistasis is when a gene at one locus suppresses/masks the effect of a gene at a different locus.
questions.explanation_long: Epistasis occurs when the expression of one gene (at one location on a chromosome) masks or modifies the phenotypic expression of a different gene located elsewhere — a form of gene interaction between genes at separate loci.
questions.explanation_trick: Epistasis = between DIFFERENT loci (one gene masking another elsewhere); Dominance = between alleles at the SAME locus — this locus distinction is the key difference between these two masking concepts.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — over-dominance describes a heterozygote phenotype exceeding both homozygotes, a different phenomenon.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — pleiotropy describes one gene affecting multiple traits, not one gene masking another gene's effect.
explanation_options.c: Correct — epistasis specifically describes this cross-locus gene-masking effect.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — co-dominance describes both alleles at the same locus being expressed simultaneously, a different phenomenon.

questions.question_text: Phenylketonuria is an example of:
questions.explanation_short: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by a point mutation.
questions.explanation_long: PKU results from a mutation in the gene coding for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase — typically a point mutation (a change at a single DNA base position) that disrupts the enzyme's function, preventing proper breakdown of phenylalanine.
questions.explanation_trick: Single-gene enzyme-deficiency disorders like PKU typically trace back to point mutations — a small, specific change disrupting one protein's function, rather than a larger-scale chromosomal change.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — polyploidy involves having extra complete sets of chromosomes, an entirely different, much larger-scale genetic change.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'transmutation' isn't the standard genetics term used for this type of mutation.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — inversion involves a segment of a chromosome being reversed, a structural chromosomal change, not this single-gene point mutation.
explanation_options.d: Correct — PKU is the classic textbook example of a point mutation.

questions.question_text: A situation in which one gene affects two or more unrelated characters is called:
questions.explanation_short: Pleiotropy is when one gene affects multiple, seemingly unrelated characteristics.
questions.explanation_long: Pleiotropy describes a single gene influencing several distinct phenotypic traits at once, often because the gene's product plays a role in multiple different biological pathways (e.g. the gene for sickle cell anemia also affects malaria resistance).
questions.explanation_trick: Pleiotropy = ONE gene, MANY effects; Polygenic inheritance = MANY genes, ONE effect (like height) — these two concepts are the mirror image of each other, easy to mix up by name alone.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — epistasis describes one gene masking a different gene's effect, not one gene causing multiple effects.
explanation_options.b: Correct — pleiotropy is precisely this one-gene, multiple-effects phenomenon.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'dominance relation' describes how alleles interact at a single locus, unrelated to this multi-trait concept.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — polygenes describes many genes contributing to a single trait, the reverse relationship from pleiotropy.

questions.question_text: The mutation which causes change in the sequence of DNA is called:
questions.explanation_short: A mutation altering the DNA base sequence itself is called a point mutation.
questions.explanation_long: A point mutation is a change at a single specific position in the DNA sequence (a substitution, insertion, or deletion of one or a few bases), directly altering the genetic code — distinct from chromosomal mutations, which change the structure or number of whole chromosomes.
questions.explanation_trick: Point mutation = changes the DNA sequence itself (gene-level); Chromosomal mutation (including deletion/inversion) = changes chromosome structure/number (much larger scale) — match the scale of change to the correct mutation category.

explanation_options.a: Correct — point mutation is specifically a DNA sequence-level change.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — chromosomal mutations involve larger structural/numerical changes to entire chromosomes, not the sequence itself at a single point.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — deletion is one specific type of chromosomal (or point) mutation, not the general term for sequence changes being asked about here.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — inversion is a chromosomal structural mutation (a segment reversed), not this sequence-level change.
