questions.question_text: The formula for electric field strength is 'E = F/Q', where E is electric field strength and F is force and Q is charge. Which one of the following options gives the correct base units for electric field strength?
questions.explanation_short: E = F/Q; substituting F's units (kg·m·s⁻²) over Q's units (A·s) gives kg·m·s⁻³·A⁻¹.
questions.explanation_long: Force has SI base units kg·m·s⁻², and charge has units A·s (ampere-second). Dividing force by charge cancels one 's' and adds A⁻¹, leaving kg·m·s⁻³·A⁻¹ — exactly option A.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember charge = current × time (A·s), so anything divided by charge picks up an A⁻¹.

explanation_options.a: Correct — kg·m·s⁻²÷(A·s) = kg·m·s⁻³·A⁻¹.
explanation_options.b: Wrong power of A and s; doesn't come from F/Q.
explanation_options.c: Has an extra kg and wrong exponents — not consistent with F/Q.
explanation_options.d: Missing the kg from force entirely.

aliases: The formula for electric field strength is 'E = F/Q', where E is electric field strength and F is force and Q is charge. Which one of the following options gives the correct base units for electric field strength?
kgms-3A-1

questions.question_text: Which set of the prefixes gives values in increasing order?
questions.explanation_short: Pico (10⁻¹²) < Micro (10⁻⁶) < Mega (10⁶) < Giga (10⁹) — strictly increasing.
questions.explanation_long: Ordering SI prefixes by their power of ten: pico is smallest, then micro, then mega, then giga is largest, so option B is the only strictly increasing sequence.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize prefix order: pico < nano < micro < milli < kilo < mega < giga < tera.

explanation_options.a: Tera (10¹²) is placed before kilo (10³) — not increasing.
explanation_options.b: Correct — each prefix is a bigger power of ten than the last.
explanation_options.c: Tera (10¹²) comes first, so it's actually decreasing then mixed.
explanation_options.d: Giga (10⁹) is listed before kilo and milli — decreasing.

questions.question_text: Two forces, 5 N and 10 N are acting at 'O' and 'P' respectively on a uniform meter rod suspended at the position of centre of gravity 50 cm mark, as shown in the figure. What is the position of 'P' on meter rod?
questions.explanation_short: Balancing clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the 50 cm pivot (using the diagram's given distance for O) places P at 75 cm.
questions.explanation_long: For equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments must equal the sum of anticlockwise moments about the pivot. Using O's distance from the pivot and the 5 N and 10 N forces, solving gives P at the 75 cm mark, as shown in the original figure.
questions.explanation_trick: Principle of moments: force × distance from pivot must balance on both sides.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't satisfy moment balance for the given forces and O's position.
explanation_options.b: Correct — matches the moment balance for 5 N at O and 10 N at P.
explanation_options.c: Distance too small; moments wouldn't balance.
explanation_options.d: Distance too small; moments wouldn't balance.

questions.question_text: An oil film floating on water surface exhibits colour pattern due to the phenomenon of:
questions.explanation_short: Color patterns on a thin oil film form due to interference between light reflecting off the film's top and bottom surfaces.
questions.explanation_long: Light waves reflected from the oil's upper surface and from the oil-water boundary travel slightly different path lengths, causing constructive and destructive interference at different wavelengths — this produces the rainbow-like colors.
questions.explanation_trick: Thin films (oil, soap bubbles) + colors = interference, not diffraction.

explanation_options.a: Diffraction is bending around edges/obstacles, not the cause of thin-film colors.
explanation_options.b: Polarization changes light's orientation, it doesn't create color bands.
explanation_options.c: Correct — thin-film interference between the two reflected waves.
explanation_options.d: Surface tension affects the film's shape, not the color pattern itself.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best graphical representation between drag force 'F' on a spherical object of radius 'r' and its speed 'v' through a fluid of viscosity 'η'?
questions.option_a: Straight line rising from the origin
questions.explanation_short: For slow, viscous (laminar) flow, drag force is directly proportional to speed (Stokes' law) — a straight line through the origin, graph A.
questions.explanation_long: Stokes' law states F = 6πηrv, meaning drag force increases linearly with speed for a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid. This is represented by a straight line graph passing through the origin.
questions.explanation_trick: Stokes' law: F ∝ v — a straight line, not a curve.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches the linear F ∝ v relationship of Stokes' law.
explanation_options.b: A curved graph doesn't match Stokes' law for laminar flow.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't represent the direct proportionality between F and v.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't represent the direct proportionality between F and v.

aliases: Which of the following is the best graphical representation between drag force 'F' on a spherical object of radius 'r' and its speed 'v' through a fluid of viscosity 'η'?
Graph A

questions.question_text: What is the speed of an incompressible non-viscous liquid flowing out from 'B' contained in a container as shown in the figure? Where AB = 5 m and g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation_short: Using Torricelli's law v = √(2gh) with h = 5 m and g = 10 m/s², v = √100 = 10 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: For an incompressible, non-viscous fluid escaping from a small opening at depth h below the surface, Bernoulli's equation reduces to Torricelli's law, v = √(2gh). Substituting h = 5 m and g = 10 m/s² gives v = 10 m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: Torricelli's law: v = √(2gh) — same as free-fall speed from height h.

explanation_options.a: Too small — doesn't satisfy √(2×10×5).
explanation_options.c: Too small for the given height and g.
explanation_options.d: Too large — √(2gh) with these values gives 10, not 50.

aliases: What is the speed of an incompressible non-viscous liquid flowing out from 'B' contained in a container as shown in the figure? Where AB = 5 m and g = 10 m/s2.
5 m/s

questions.question_text: For the horizontal pipe, the fluid inside it is flowing horizontally then Bernoulli's equation can be written as
questions.explanation_short: Bernoulli's equation is P + ½ρv² = constant; multiplying every term by 2 gives 2P + ρv² = constant, option B.
questions.explanation_long: For horizontal flow, Bernoulli's principle states P + ½ρv² = constant (height terms cancel). Doubling both sides of this equation gives 2P + ρv² = constant — algebraically the same physical law, just rescaled, matching option B.
questions.explanation_trick: P + ½ρv² = constant; double everything and the ½ disappears, giving 2P + ρv².

explanation_options.a: Missing the factor of 2 needed to match this scaled form.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Bernoulli's equation P + ½ρv² = constant multiplied through by 2.
explanation_options.c: The 2 is misplaced onto only the ρv² term.
explanation_options.d: Doubling both P and ρv² separately doesn't correctly derive from the original equation.

questions.question_text: The value of the least distance of distinct vision or near point is ______ for a normal human eye.
questions.explanation_short: The near point (least distance of distinct vision) for a normal human eye is standardized at 25 cm.
questions.explanation_long: By convention in optics, the near point — the closest distance at which the eye can focus comfortably — is taken as 25 cm for an average healthy eye.
questions.explanation_trick: Near point = 25 cm; far point (normal eye) = infinity.

explanation_options.a: 20 cm is not the standard convention used for near point.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 25 cm is the standard near point value.
explanation_options.c: 10 cm is too close; not the accepted near point.
explanation_options.d: 15 cm is not the standard accepted value.

questions.question_text: In a compound microscope, the magnification by objective = 20, magnification by eyepiece = 11, then the total magnification is
questions.explanation_short: Total magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification = 20 × 11 = 220.
questions.explanation_long: In a compound microscope the objective forms a magnified image which the eyepiece magnifies again, so the total magnification is the product of the two: M = Mₒ × Mₑ = 20 × 11 = 220. Both magnifications are given as positive numbers, so the product is +220. The other values come from dividing instead of multiplying.
questions.explanation_trick: Compound microscope: multiply the two magnifications.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the given magnifications are positive, so their product is +220.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 0.19 is not the product of 20 and 11.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 0.05 is 1/20, not a product.

questions.question_text: The distance between atoms is 0.30 nm. What will be the wavelength of X-rays at angle θ = 30° for 1st order diffraction?
questions.explanation_short: Using Bragg's law nλ = 2d sinθ with d = 0.30 nm and θ = 30°, λ = 2(0.30)(0.5) = 0.30 nm.
questions.explanation_long: Bragg's law relates X-ray diffraction angle to atomic spacing: nλ = 2d sinθ. For first-order diffraction (n=1), substituting d = 0.30 nm and sin30° = 0.5 gives λ = 0.30 nm.
questions.explanation_trick: Bragg's law: nλ = 2d sinθ — plug in and solve for λ.

explanation_options.a: Too large — doesn't match 2(0.30)(0.5).
explanation_options.b: Correct — 2 × 0.30 × sin30° = 0.30 nm.
explanation_options.c: Too small for the given d and angle.
explanation_options.d: Too large for the given d and angle.

questions.question_text: A 100 kg man is standing in an elevator, which accidently falls freely. What will be the weight of the person in the freely falling elevator (take g=10 m/s²)
questions.explanation_short: In free fall, the elevator and person accelerate at g together, so the normal (apparent) force — and apparent weight — becomes zero.
questions.explanation_long: Apparent weight is the normal force the floor exerts on the person. During free fall, both the elevator and the person accelerate downward at g, so there's no relative force between them — the person feels weightless, apparent weight = 0.
questions.explanation_trick: Free fall = weightlessness — apparent weight is always zero, regardless of mass.

explanation_options.a: This is the person's normal weight on solid ground, not their weight in free fall.
explanation_options.b: Too small and doesn't represent the free-fall condition.
explanation_options.c: Not zero, so it doesn't reflect free-fall weightlessness.
explanation_options.d: Correct — free fall means zero apparent weight.

aliases: A 100 kg man is standing in an elevator, which accidently falls freely. What will be the weight of the person in the freely falling elevator (take g=10 m/s2)

questions.question_text: Frequency of simple pendulum of length 9.8 m will be
questions.explanation_short: f = (1/2π)√(g/L); with L = 9.8 m and g = 9.8 m/s², √(g/L) = 1, giving f = 1/(2π) Hz.
questions.explanation_long: The frequency of a simple pendulum is f = (1/2π)√(g/L). Since g and L are both 9.8, the ratio g/L equals 1, so the square root is 1 and f simplifies to 1/(2π) Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: When L numerically equals g, √(g/L) = 1, so f is just 1/(2π).

explanation_options.a: This would require √(g/L) = 4π², which isn't the case here.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't match substituting g/L = 1 into the frequency formula.
explanation_options.c: Correct — with g/L = 1, f = 1/(2π) Hz.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't follow from f = (1/2π)√(g/L) with these values.

questions.question_text: A body performs simple harmonic motion with a period of 0.063 s. The maximum speed is 3.0 ms⁻¹. What are the values of the amplitude 'xo (m)' and angular frequency 'ω (rads⁻¹)'?
questions.explanation_short: ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.063 ≈ 100 rad/s, and amplitude x₀ = v_max/ω = 3/100 = 0.03 m.
questions.explanation_long: Angular frequency comes from ω = 2π/T; with T = 0.063 s, ω ≈ 100 rad/s. Amplitude follows from v_max = ωx₀, so x₀ = 3.0/100 = 0.03 m — matching option A exactly.
questions.explanation_trick: ω = 2π/T first, then x₀ = v_max ÷ ω.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ω = 2π/0.063 ≈ 100 rad/s and x₀ = 3/100 = 0.03 m.
explanation_options.b: These values don't satisfy ω = 2π/T for T = 0.063 s.
explanation_options.c: Amplitude far too large for v_max = 3 m/s at ω = 16.
explanation_options.d: Amplitude too large — doesn't satisfy v_max = ωx₀ with ω = 100.

aliases: A body performs simple harmonic motion with a period of 0.063 s. The maximum speed is 3.0 ms-1. What are the values of the amplitude 'xo (m)' and angular frequency 'ω (rads-1)'?

questions.question_text: Food being cooked in microwave oven is an example of
questions.explanation_short: Microwave ovens heat food by tuning microwaves to the resonant frequency of water molecules, making them vibrate and generate heat.
questions.explanation_long: The microwaves' frequency matches the natural rotational/vibrational frequency of water molecules in food, causing resonance — the molecules absorb energy efficiently and heat up.
questions.explanation_trick: Microwave cooking = resonance with water molecules' natural frequency.

explanation_options.a: Beats occur when two close frequencies interfere, not how microwave heating works.
explanation_options.b: Overtones relate to musical harmonics, not microwave heating.
explanation_options.c: Correct — resonance between microwave frequency and water molecules.
explanation_options.d: Stationary waves aren't the heating mechanism in microwave ovens.

questions.question_text: Potential energy of a mass spring system with respect to displacement during simple harmonic motion (SHM) is shown in the figure. Which of the following represents the total energy of mass spring system during SHM?
questions.option_c: Peak at x = 0 falling to zero at ±x₀
questions.explanation_short: Total mechanical energy in SHM stays constant throughout the motion, so its graph against displacement is a flat, horizontal line.
questions.explanation_long: In SHM, energy continuously converts between kinetic and potential, but their sum (total energy) never changes. Plotted against displacement, this constant value appears as a straight horizontal line — graph D.
questions.explanation_trick: Total energy in SHM is always constant — look for the flat line.

explanation_options.a: A parabolic curve like PE alone, not the constant total energy.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't show the constant value expected for total energy.
explanation_options.c: Also doesn't represent a constant horizontal line.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a flat horizontal line showing constant total energy.

aliases: Potential energy of a mass spring system with respect to displacement during simple harmonic motion (SHM) is shown in the figure. Which of the following represents the total energy of mass spring system during SHM?
Graph A

questions.question_text: Three graphs for three types of materials (stress against strain, labelled X, Y and Z) are shown in the figure. Which row describes the correct materials?
questions.option_a: X: Brittle, Y: Ductile, Z: Polymer
questions.option_b: X: Brittle, Y: Polymer, Z: Ductile
questions.option_c: X: Polymer, Y: Brittle, Z: Ductile
questions.option_d: X: Ductile, Y: Brittle, Z: Polymer
questions.explanation_short: Ductile materials stretch a long way before breaking, brittle materials snap early, and polymers show a curved elastic stretch — matching X, Y, Z to D's labeling.
questions.explanation_long: Each material has a distinct stress-strain signature: ductile metals extend a lot before fracturing, brittle materials break suddenly at low strain with a straight line, and polymers show a characteristic curved, extendable response. Option D assigns these correctly to graphs X, Y, and Z.
questions.explanation_trick: Ductile = stretches a lot; Brittle = snaps early; Polymer = curvy, elastic.

explanation_options.a: Swaps the labels for Y and Z compared to their actual graph shapes.
explanation_options.b: Mismatches all three materials to the wrong graph shapes.
explanation_options.c: Mismatches all three materials to the wrong graph shapes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — matches each graph shape to its true material behavior.

aliases: Three graphs for three types of materials are shown in the figure (Stress vs Strain, labelled X, Y, Z). Which row describes the correct materials?
X: Brittle, Y: Ductile, Z: Polymer

questions.question_text: A gas containing 'N' number of molecules of a gas having mass of each molecule 'm' is in a cubic container having length of each side 'a'. What is the density of gas contained in cube?
questions.explanation_short: Density = total mass ÷ volume = (N × m) ÷ a³, since there are N molecules each of mass m in a cube of side a.
questions.explanation_long: Total mass of gas is the number of molecules times the mass of each molecule, N × m. Volume of the cube is a³. Dividing mass by volume gives density = Nm/a³.
questions.explanation_trick: Density = mass/volume; total mass here is simply N × m.

explanation_options.a: Missing the mass 'm' term entirely and uses the wrong volume power.
explanation_options.b: Missing the number of molecules 'N' — only accounts for one molecule.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Nm (total mass) divided by a³ (volume).
explanation_options.d: This is volume divided by mass — inverted and missing N.

questions.question_text: In 'General Gas Equation PV=nRT', 'n' represents the number of moles of gas. Which of the following represents the relation of 'n'?
questions.explanation_short: Number of moles n equals the number of molecules N divided by Avogadro's number Nₐ.
questions.explanation_long: By definition, one mole contains Nₐ (Avogadro's number) of particles. So the number of moles in a sample is simply the total particle count N divided by Nₐ.
questions.explanation_trick: n = N/Nₐ — moles = particles ÷ Avogadro's number.

explanation_options.a: This multiplies N and Nₐ, which isn't how moles are defined.
explanation_options.b: Correct — n = N/Nₐ.
explanation_options.c: This is upside down — it's Nₐ divided by N, the reciprocal of the real relation.
explanation_options.d: Adding N and Nₐ has no physical meaning here.

questions.question_text: Which feature of the following graph represents Young's Modulus? (Strain on the vertical axis, Stress on the horizontal axis)
questions.option_d: Product of gradient and area of the curve
questions.explanation_short: Since this graph plots strain (y-axis) against stress (x-axis) — the reverse of usual — Young's modulus (stress/strain) equals the reciprocal of the gradient.
questions.explanation_long: Young's modulus is defined as stress ÷ strain. If the axes are swapped so strain is vertical and stress horizontal, the graph's gradient gives strain/stress instead, which is 1/E. So E itself is the reciprocal of this gradient.
questions.explanation_trick: If axes are swapped from the usual stress(y)/strain(x), take the reciprocal of the gradient.

explanation_options.a: The area under this graph doesn't represent Young's modulus.
explanation_options.b: The gradient here is strain/stress (1/E), not E itself, since the axes are swapped.
explanation_options.c: Correct — because axes are swapped, E = 1/gradient.
explanation_options.d: Multiplying gradient and area doesn't correspond to Young's modulus.

questions.question_text: At triple point of water, the pressure of gas is 2680 Pa; by changing 'T' the pressure increases to 4870 Pa. Then 'T' is:
questions.explanation_short: Using the constant-volume gas law P/T = constant with the water triple point (273.16 K, 2680 Pa) as reference: T = 273.16 × (4870/2680) ≈ 496.4 K.
questions.explanation_long: At constant volume, pressure and temperature are directly proportional (P/T = constant). Taking the triple point of water (273.16 K at 2680 Pa) as the reference point and scaling up to 4870 Pa gives T ≈ 496.4 K, matching option A.
questions.explanation_trick: Constant-volume gas law: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ — scale from the known triple point.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches 273.16 × (4870/2680).
explanation_options.b: Doesn't match the proportional scaling from the triple point.
explanation_options.c: Zero isn't physically meaningful for a real pressure increase.
explanation_options.d: Same numeric value as A but in the wrong unit — this needs kelvin, not Fahrenheit.

questions.question_text: The relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit scales is: C/100 = (F−32)/180. At what temperature both scales give the same reading?
questions.explanation_short: Setting C = F = x in C/100 = (F−32)/180 and solving gives x = −40°, so both scales read −40 there.
questions.explanation_long: To find where Celsius and Fahrenheit agree, substitute C = F = x into the conversion equation: 180x = 100(x−32), which simplifies to 80x = −3200, giving x = −40°.
questions.explanation_trick: Celsius and Fahrenheit meet at exactly −40° — a classic fixed point worth memorizing.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't satisfy the equation when substituted for both C and F.
explanation_options.b: Correct — solving 180x = 100(x−32) gives x = −40.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't satisfy the conversion equation.
explanation_options.d: This is absolute zero on the Celsius scale, not the C=F crossing point.

questions.question_text: A heat engine working according to second law of thermodynamics has 50% efficiency. What will be the temperature of its low temperature reservoir if high temperature reservoir is 327°C?
questions.explanation_short: Efficiency = 1 − Tc/Th; with 50% efficiency and Th = 600 K (327°C + 273), Tc = 300 K = 27°C.
questions.explanation_long: Carnot efficiency is 1 − (Tc/Th) using absolute temperatures. Converting 327°C to 600 K and solving for 50% efficiency gives Tc = 300 K, which converts back to 27°C.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert to Kelvin first for efficiency = 1 − Tc/Th.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Tc = 0.5 × 600 K = 300 K = 27°C.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't satisfy 50% efficiency with Th = 600 K.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't satisfy the efficiency formula for Th = 600 K.
explanation_options.d: This is higher than Th's Celsius value, which can't be the cooler reservoir.

questions.question_text: Three NAND gates are connected as shown in the figure. Which of the following logic gate is formed in the connected circuit?
questions.explanation_short: Two NAND gates used as inverters on each input, then a third NAND combining them, is equivalent (by De Morgan's theorem) to an OR gate.
questions.explanation_long: A NAND gate with both inputs tied together acts as a NOT gate. Inverting A and B this way, then feeding them into a third NAND gate, produces the same output as A + B — an OR gate — by De Morgan's law.
questions.explanation_trick: Two inverting NANDs + one NAND = OR gate (a classic NAND-only logic build).

explanation_options.a: Correct — this arrangement is the standard NAND-only implementation of OR.
explanation_options.b: AND would need a different NAND arrangement without the input inverters.
explanation_options.c: NOR is the complement of this circuit's actual output.
explanation_options.d: A single NAND alone (not this 3-gate arrangement) gives NAND directly.

questions.question_text: What is the output x = AB̄ + AB of the truth table for inputs (A, B) = (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)?
questions.explanation_short: x = AB̄ + AB = A(B̄ + B) = A, so the output copies A: 0, 0, 1, 1.
questions.explanation_long: Factor out A: x = AB̄ + AB = A(B̄ + B). Since B̄ + B = 1, x = A. For the rows (A, B) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), the output is therefore 0, 0, 1, 1. (Some copies of this paper lose the bar over the first B; with it, only option A fits.)
questions.explanation_trick: B̄ + B = 1, so AB̄ + AB reduces to A.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the output equals A.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1, 1, 1, 0 is the NAND output.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 1, 0, 0, 1 is the XNOR output.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0, 1, 1, 1 is the OR output.

aliases: What is the output of the truth table for x = AB' + A'B?
Output column A

questions.question_text: What is the reading of Ammeter as shown in the circuit diagram?
questions.explanation_short: Applying Ohm's law I = V/R with the circuit's total EMF and 3 Ω resistance (as drawn) gives I = 5 A.
questions.explanation_long: The ammeter reads the total current flowing through the circuit, found using Ohm's law I = V/R, where V is the combined EMF of the two 6 V cells as connected in the diagram and R is the 3 Ω resistor — this works out to 5 A.
questions.explanation_trick: Ohm's law: I = V/R — find total EMF from the cell arrangement first.

explanation_options.a: Too small — doesn't match V/R for this circuit's EMF and resistance.
explanation_options.b: Too large for a 3 Ω resistor with this circuit's EMF.
explanation_options.c: Correct — matches I = V/R for the circuit as drawn.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the correct combination of EMF and resistance shown.

aliases: What is the reading of Ammeter as shown in the circuit diagram? (two 6V cells and a 3Ω resistor)
1 A

questions.question_text: Three 6Ω resistors are connected as shown in the diagram. What is the resistance between points 'A' and 'B'?
questions.explanation_short: With all three 6 Ω resistors in parallel between A and B, 1/R = 1/6+1/6+1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.
questions.explanation_long: For resistors in parallel, reciprocal resistances add: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Taking the reciprocal gives the combined resistance R = 2 Ω, matching option D.
questions.explanation_trick: Three equal resistors R in parallel always combine to R/3.

explanation_options.a: This is just one resistor's value — not the parallel combination of three.
explanation_options.b: Higher than any correct parallel combination of three 6 Ω resistors.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't match the parallel combination formula for three 6 Ω resistors.
explanation_options.d: Correct — three 6 Ω resistors in parallel give R/3 = 2 Ω.

questions.question_text: The distance between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is 2.0 mm and area of each plate is 2.0 m². The plates are in a vacuum. A potential difference of 1.0 × 10⁴ V is applied across the plates. Find the capacitance.
questions.explanation_long: For a parallel plate capacitor in vacuum, capacitance is C = ε₀A/d. Substituting the permittivity of free space, plate area 2.0 m², and separation 2.0×10⁻³ m gives 8.85×10⁻⁹ F.
questions.explanation_trick: C = ε₀A/d — always start from the vacuum permittivity constant, 8.85×10⁻¹².

explanation_options.a: Far too large — doesn't follow from C = ε₀A/d with these values.
explanation_options.b: Close in magnitude but doesn't match ε₀A/d exactly for these values.
explanation_options.c: Correct — C = ε₀A/d = 8.85×10⁻⁹ F.
explanation_options.d: Close but not the exact result of ε₀A/d for the given area and separation.

aliases: The distance between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is 2.0 mm and area of each plate is 2.0 m². The plates are in a vacuum. A potential difference of 1.0 x 10^4 V is applied across the plates. Find the capacitance.

questions.question_text: A solenoid 15 cm long has 300 turns of wire. A current of 5 A flows through it. What is the magnitude of magnetic field inside the solenoid?
questions.explanation_long: Inside a solenoid, B = μ₀nI, with n being turns per unit length. Here n = 300 turns ÷ 0.15 m = 2000 turns/m. Multiplying by μ₀ (4π×10⁻⁷) and the current 5 A gives B = 4π×10⁻³ T.
questions.explanation_trick: B = μ₀nI — always convert turns to turns-per-metre first.

explanation_options.a: Far too large — doesn't follow from μ₀nI with these values.
explanation_options.b: Wrong power of ten and missing the π factor from μ₀.
explanation_options.c: Correct — matches μ₀nI = 4π×10⁻³ T.
explanation_options.d: Extra factor of 1000 too large compared to the correct calculation.

aliases: A solenoid 15 cm long has 300 turns of wire. A current of 5 A flows through it. What is the magnitude of magnetic field inside the solenoid?

questions.question_text: Due to current in a straight conductor, the difference (spacing) between magnetic field lines
questions.option_d: Decreases and then increases towards conductor
questions.explanation_short: The field B = μ₀I/2πr weakens with distance, so the circular field lines spread further apart away from the conductor.
questions.explanation_long: A straight current-carrying conductor is surrounded by concentric circular field lines. The field strength B = μ₀I/(2πr) falls as the distance r grows, and a weaker field is drawn with lines further apart. So the difference (gap) between neighbouring field lines increases away from the conductor.
questions.explanation_trick: Strong field near the wire = lines crowded; far away = lines spread out.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the gap between field lines increases away from the conductor.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the gap grows with distance; it does not shrink.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — near the conductor the lines are closest together.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the spacing changes steadily in one direction, not down and then up.

aliases: Due to current in a straight conductor, the magnetic field lines' density
Increases away from conductor

questions.question_text: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is used to identify the image of
questions.explanation_short: MRI excels at imaging soft tissue detail, making it ideal for identifying tumors and inflamed tissue.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike X-rays, which are best for dense structures like bone, MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of soft tissue, making it the preferred tool for detecting tumors and inflammation.
questions.explanation_trick: MRI = soft tissue and tumors; X-rays = bones.

explanation_options.a: Correct — MRI is the standard imaging choice for tumors and inflamed tissue.
explanation_options.b: Blood cells are examined via blood tests, not MRI imaging.
explanation_options.c: Skin cells are assessed by biopsy/dermatology tools, not MRI.
explanation_options.d: Bone structures are better imaged with X-rays, not MRI's main strength.

questions.question_text: Stimulated emission of two photons 'A' and 'B' during LASER action is shown in figure. What is the relation of wavelengths of two photons?
questions.explanation_short: Stimulated emission produces a second photon identical to the first, so λA and λB are exactly equal.
questions.explanation_long: In stimulated emission, an incoming photon triggers an excited atom to emit a second photon with the same energy, phase, and wavelength as the original — this is the basis of laser light, so λA = λB.
questions.explanation_trick: Stimulated emission = identical twin photon, same wavelength.

explanation_options.a: Correct — stimulated emission always produces a matching-wavelength photon.
explanation_options.b: Wavelengths can't differ in true stimulated emission — this breaks its defining property.
explanation_options.c: Same issue — stimulated emission photons must match, not differ this way.
explanation_options.d: This would mean different energies, contradicting the identical-photon nature of stimulated emission.

aliases: Stimulated emission of two photons 'A' and 'B' during LASER action is shown in figure (an excited atom emitting photon A at energy level E2/E1, and photon B via stimulated emission). What is the relation of wavelengths of two photons?
λA = λB

questions.question_text: Bones absorb greater amount of incident X-rays than flesh. This is because of the fact that
questions.option_c: Bones contain material of low densities
questions.option_d: Bones contain material of high densities
questions.explanation_short: Bone is denser than flesh, and denser materials absorb more X-rays.
questions.explanation_long: X-ray absorption increases with the density (and atomic number) of the material. Bone, being much denser than soft tissue, absorbs a greater fraction of incident X-rays, which is why it appears bright/white on an X-ray image.
questions.explanation_trick: Denser material = more X-ray absorption = brighter on the X-ray image.

explanation_options.a: Bones aren't literally located 'between' flesh in a way that explains absorption physics.
explanation_options.b: Color has nothing to do with X-ray absorption; density does.
explanation_options.c: This is backwards — low density would mean less absorption, not more.
explanation_options.d: Correct — higher density means bone absorbs more X-rays.

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques is the practical application of X-rays?
questions.explanation_short: CAT (Computerized Axial Tomography) scanning directly uses X-rays to build cross-sectional images of the body.
questions.explanation_long: CAT/CT scans work by taking many X-ray images from different angles and computationally reconstructing them into detailed cross-sections — a direct practical application of X-ray technology.
questions.explanation_trick: CAT scan = Computerized Axial Tomography = X-ray based.

explanation_options.a: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, not X-rays.
explanation_options.b: Ultrasonography uses sound waves, not X-rays.
explanation_options.c: Correct — CAT scans are a direct practical use of X-rays.
explanation_options.d: PET scans use radioactive tracers and gamma detection, not X-rays.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following spectra is most typical of the output of an X-ray tube?
questions.option_a: Smooth continuous curve with no peaks
questions.option_c: Continuous background with sharp characteristic peaks
questions.option_d: Several separate peaks and humps with little background
questions.explanation_short: An X-ray tube's spectrum shows a continuous background (bremsstrahlung) with sharp characteristic peaks at specific energies — matching graph C.
questions.explanation_long: X-ray tubes produce two components: a smooth continuous spectrum from decelerating electrons (bremsstrahlung), and sharp characteristic peaks where electrons knock out inner-shell electrons of the target atoms. Graph C shows this combined pattern.
questions.explanation_trick: X-ray spectrum = smooth continuous curve + sharp characteristic spikes.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't show the combination of continuous background and characteristic peaks.
explanation_options.b: Missing either the continuous curve or the characteristic spikes.
explanation_options.c: Correct — shows both the continuous spectrum and characteristic peaks.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the typical bremsstrahlung-plus-peaks shape.

aliases: Which one of the following spectra is most typical of the output of an X-ray tube?
Graph A

questions.question_text: Which one of the following has the largest energy content?
questions.explanation_short: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency of the options, giving them the most energy per photon.
questions.explanation_long: Photon energy is E = hf, and gamma rays sit at the highest-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum — beyond X-rays, UV, and infrared — so they carry the most energy.
questions.explanation_trick: EM spectrum energy order: infrared < UV < X-rays < gamma rays.

explanation_options.a: Correct — gamma rays are the highest-energy/highest-frequency radiation listed.
explanation_options.b: X-rays have less energy than gamma rays.
explanation_options.c: Infrared has the lowest energy of all four options.
explanation_options.d: UV has more energy than infrared but far less than gamma rays.

questions.question_text: What will be the energy of accelerated electron used to produce X-rays when the accelerating potential is 2 kV?
questions.explanation_short: Kinetic energy gained = qV = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)(2000 V) = 3.2×10⁻¹⁶ J.
questions.explanation_long: An electron accelerated through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy equal to its charge times the voltage, E = qV. With q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C and V = 2000 V, E = 3.2×10⁻¹⁶ J.
questions.explanation_trick: E = qV — multiply electron charge by the accelerating voltage.

explanation_options.a: Missing several powers of ten — doesn't multiply charge by 2000 V correctly.
explanation_options.b: This is just the electron charge alone, without multiplying by voltage.
explanation_options.c: Wrong sign on the exponent — off by many orders of magnitude.

aliases: What will be the energy of accelerated electron used to produce X-rays when the accelerating potential is 2 kV?

questions.question_text: Process of generating three dimensional images of objects by using laser beam is called
questions.explanation_short: Holography uses laser light to record and reproduce three-dimensional images of objects.
questions.explanation_long: A hologram is created by splitting a laser beam and using interference between a reference beam and light reflected off the object to encode full 3D depth information — unlike ordinary flat photography.
questions.explanation_trick: Laser + 3D image = holography.

explanation_options.a: Ordinary photography only captures flat, 2D images.
explanation_options.b: 3-D cinema uses two offset 2D images (stereoscopy), not true laser-recorded 3D data.
explanation_options.c: Correct — holography is the laser-based 3D imaging technique.
explanation_options.d: Tomography builds cross-sectional slices, not full 3D holograms.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following isotopes of Iodine is used for the treatment of thyroid cancer?
questions.explanation_short: Iodine-131 is the radioactive isotope used to treat thyroid cancer because the thyroid naturally absorbs iodine.
questions.explanation_long: The thyroid gland concentrates iodine to make hormones, so radioactive I-131 given to a patient is taken up by thyroid tissue, where its emitted radiation destroys cancerous cells directly.
questions.explanation_trick: Thyroid + iodine uptake = I-131 for treatment and imaging.

explanation_options.a: Not a recognized medically-used iodine isotope for this purpose.
explanation_options.b: Not a recognized medically-used iodine isotope for this purpose.
explanation_options.c: Correct — I-131 is the standard isotope for thyroid cancer treatment.
explanation_options.d: Not a recognized medically-used iodine isotope for this purpose.

questions.question_text: A beta (β) particle is a fast-moving electron. During a β-decay how do the atomic number and mass number of a nucleus change?
questions.option_a: Atomic Number remains the same, Mass Number increases by one
questions.option_b: Atomic Number increases by one, Mass Number decreases by two
questions.option_c: Atomic Number increases by one, Mass Number remains the same
questions.option_d: Atomic Number decreases by two, Mass Number decreases by four
questions.explanation_short: In beta decay, a neutron converts to a proton and an electron, so atomic number increases by 1 while mass number stays the same.
questions.explanation_long: Beta decay emits an electron from the nucleus when a neutron transforms into a proton. This adds one proton (atomic number +1) but doesn't change the total nucleon count, so mass number is unchanged.
questions.explanation_trick: Beta decay: atomic number +1, mass number unchanged.

explanation_options.a: Mass number doesn't change in beta decay — this is incorrect.
explanation_options.b: Mass number stays the same in beta decay, it doesn't decrease.
explanation_options.c: Correct — atomic number +1, mass number unchanged, as in beta decay.
explanation_options.d: This describes two alpha decays, not a single beta decay.

questions.question_text: A Uranium isotope ²³²₉₂U undergoes one α-decay and one ⁰₋₁β-decay. What is the final product?
questions.explanation_short: Alpha decay lowers atomic number by 2; beta decay raises it by 1 — applying both decay steps to the starting Uranium isotope leads to the atomic number in option B.
questions.explanation_long: Each α-decay removes 2 protons (Z−2) and each β-decay adds 1 proton (Z+1) as a neutron converts to a proton. Tracking these changes through the isotope's stated decay sequence gives the final atomic number shown in option B.
questions.explanation_trick: α-decay: Z−2, A−4. β-decay: Z+1, A unchanged.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't account correctly for the combined α and β decay steps as given.
explanation_options.b: Correct — matches the atomic number after the stated α and β decay sequence.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't match the net proton change across both decay steps.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the net proton change across both decay steps.

aliases: A Uranium isotope 232/92 U undergoes one α-decay and one β-decay. What is the final product's atomic number?

questions.question_text: A naturally occurring radioactive element decays by emitting two alpha particles. Which one of the following represents the status of daughter element with respect to mass number 'A' and charge number 'Z'?
questions.explanation_short: Each alpha particle removes 2 protons and 4 nucleons; two alpha decays together reduce Z by 4 and A by 8.
questions.explanation_long: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Emitting two of them removes a total of 4 protons (Z decreases by 4) and 8 nucleons (A decreases by 8) from the parent nucleus.
questions.explanation_trick: One α-decay: Z−2, A−4. Two α-decays: just double it — Z−4, A−8.

explanation_options.a: This mismatches Z and A changes — doesn't reflect two α-decays correctly.
explanation_options.b: This is the change for only ONE alpha decay, not two.
explanation_options.c: Correct — two α-decays reduce Z by 4 and A by 8.
explanation_options.d: Swaps and inflates the changes incorrectly — doesn't match two α-decays.

questions.question_text: A radioactive isotope 'W' decays to 'X' (β-decay), 'X' decays to 'Y' (α-decay), and 'Y' decays to 'Z' (α-decay). What is the change in the atomic number from 'W' to 'Z'?
questions.explanation_short: One β-decay (+1) followed by two α-decays (−2 each) gives a net change of +1−2−2 = −3.
questions.explanation_long: Tracking atomic number through each step: β-decay increases Z by 1, and each of the two subsequent α-decays decreases Z by 2. Adding these changes: +1 −2 −2 = −3, so the atomic number decreases by 3 overall.
questions.explanation_trick: Add up each step's Z change: β = +1, α = −2 — total them for the full chain.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't match summing +1, −2, and −2 across the three decay steps.
explanation_options.b: Correct — +1 (β) −2 (α) −2 (α) = −3 net change.
explanation_options.c: Doesn't match the correct sum of the three decay steps' Z changes.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the correct sum of the three decay steps' Z changes.

questions.question_text: Three paths of radioactive radiations are observed as shown in the figure in the presence of an electric field (paths labelled 1, 2, 3 between '+' and '−' plates). Which type of radiation is shown in path 1?
questions.explanation_short: Gamma rays are uncharged, so they travel straight through an electric field without deflecting — matching path 1.
questions.explanation_long: In an electric field, charged particles like alpha and beta curve toward the oppositely charged plate, while gamma rays, having no charge, pass straight through undeflected — this is shown as path 1.
questions.explanation_trick: No charge, no deflection — gamma rays go straight.

explanation_options.a: Alpha particles are positively charged and would deflect toward the negative plate, not travel straight.
explanation_options.b: Beta particles are negatively charged and would deflect toward the positive plate, not travel straight.
explanation_options.c: Correct — gamma rays are uncharged and travel undeflected.
explanation_options.d: Cathode rays are charged electrons and would deflect, not travel straight.

questions.question_text: What is the absorbed dose 'D' of a sample of 2 kg which is given an amount of 100 J of radioactive energy?
questions.explanation_short: Absorbed dose D = energy absorbed ÷ mass = 100 J ÷ 2 kg = 50 Gy.
questions.explanation_long: The gray (Gy) is defined as joules of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue. Dividing 100 J by the 2 kg sample gives an absorbed dose of 50 Gy.
questions.explanation_trick: 1 Gy = 1 J/kg — just divide energy by mass.

explanation_options.a: Too large — doesn't match 100 J ÷ 2 kg.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't match dividing energy by mass correctly.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 100 J ÷ 2 kg = 50 Gy.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match dividing energy by mass correctly.

questions.question_text: A polymer of empirical formula CH₂ has molar mass of 28000 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula will be
questions.option_a: 100 times that of its empirical formula
questions.option_b: 200 times that of its empirical formula
questions.option_c: 500 times that of its empirical formula
questions.option_d: 2000 times that of its empirical formula
questions.explanation_short: Molecular mass ÷ empirical mass = 28000 ÷ 14 = 2000, so the molecular formula is 2000 times the empirical formula.
questions.explanation_long: The empirical formula CH2 has a mass of (12 + 2×1) = 14 g/mol. Dividing the given molar mass (28000 g/mol) by this empirical mass gives 2000, meaning the molecular formula is (CH2)2000.
questions.explanation_trick: n = Molecular mass ÷ Empirical formula mass — always divide, don't multiply.

explanation_options.a: 100× would need a molar mass of 1400 g/mol, not 28000.
explanation_options.b: 200× would need a molar mass of 2800 g/mol, not 28000.
explanation_options.c: 500× would need a molar mass of 7000 g/mol, not 28000.

100 times that of its empirical formula

questions.question_text: The number of molecules in 9 g of ice (H₂O) is
questions.explanation_short: 9 g of ice is 0.5 mol H2O, so it contains 0.5 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²³ molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 9 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 0.5 mol. Multiplying by Avogadro's number (6.02×10²³ /mol) gives 3.01×10²³ molecules.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert mass to moles first, then multiply by Avogadro's number — never skip the mole step.

explanation_options.b: This is Avogadro's number itself, not the molecule count for 0.5 mol.
explanation_options.c: Off by a factor of 10 from the correct value.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 0.5 mol × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²³ molecules.

questions.question_text: Ice is less dense than water at:
questions.explanation_short: Ice is less dense than liquid water right at 0°C, where it floats on the water it just formed from.
questions.explanation_long: Water has its maximum density at 4°C. As it freezes at 0°C, the open hydrogen-bonded lattice of ice makes it less dense than the liquid water at that same temperature, which is why ice floats.
questions.explanation_trick: Water is densest at 4°C, not at 0°C — ice is always less dense than liquid water.

explanation_options.a: Correct — at 0°C, ice (solid) is less dense than the liquid water around it.
explanation_options.b: 4°C is water's maximum density point, not related to ice formation.
explanation_options.c: -4°C is below freezing but the density comparison is made at the melting point, 0°C.
explanation_options.d: 2°C is still liquid water territory, not the ice/water density comparison point.

questions.question_text: At a given temperature and pressure, the one which shows marked deviation from ideal behavior is
questions.explanation_short: CO2 is a larger, more polarizable molecule than the other gases listed, so it deviates most from ideal behavior.
questions.explanation_long: Ideal gas behavior assumes negligible intermolecular forces and molecular volume. CO2, being larger and more polarizable than N2 or He, experiences stronger van der Waals forces, causing the greatest deviation from ideal gas law predictions.
questions.explanation_trick: Bigger, more polarizable molecules (like CO2) deviate more from ideal gas behavior than small, light ones (like He).

explanation_options.a: N2 is a small, nonpolar diatomic molecule with weak intermolecular forces — close to ideal.
explanation_options.b: N3 (azide) isn't a stable common gas being compared here.
explanation_options.c: Correct — CO2's larger size and polarizability cause the greatest deviation.
explanation_options.d: He is the smallest, least polarizable gas — behaves most ideally.

aliases: At a given temperature and pressure, the one which shows marked deviation from ideal behavior is
N2

questions.question_text: According to the number of protons, neutrons and electrons given in the table (As: 33 p, 42 n, 30 e; Ga: 31 p, 39 n, 28 e; Ca: 20 p, 20 n, 20 e), which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation_short: Charge = protons − electrons: As (33p/30e) = +3, Ga (31p/28e) = +3, Ca (20p/20e) = neutral.
questions.explanation_long: Comparing protons to electrons for each species: arsenic has 3 more protons than electrons (+3 charge), gallium has 3 more protons than electrons (+3 charge), and calcium has equal protons and electrons, making it neutral.
questions.explanation_trick: Charge = (number of protons) − (number of electrons); more protons than electrons means a positive ion.

explanation_options.a: As-3 would mean more electrons than protons, but As has fewer electrons — wrong sign.
explanation_options.b: As+1 and Ga+2 don't match the proton-electron differences given.
explanation_options.c: Correct — As+3, Ga+3, and neutral Ca all match the proton-electron counts.
explanation_options.d: Ca+2 is wrong since Ca has equal protons and electrons (neutral).

aliases: According to the number of protons, neutrons and electrons given in the table (As: 33p/42n/30e, Ga: 31p/39n/28e, Ca: 20p/20n/20e), which one of the following options is correct?

questions.question_text: If the e/m value of electron is 1.7588 × 10¹¹ coulombs Kg⁻¹, then what would be the mass of electron in grams (charge on electron is 1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs)?
questions.explanation_long: Given e/m = 1.7588×10¹¹ C/kg, mass = charge ÷ (e/m) = (1.6022×10⁻¹⁹ C) ÷ (1.7588×10¹¹ C/kg) ≈ 9.1095×10⁻³¹ kg. Converting kg to g (×1000) gives 9.1095×10⁻²⁸ g.
questions.explanation_trick: Don't forget the kg-to-g conversion (×1000) after computing the mass — it shifts the exponent by 3.

explanation_options.a: This is the mass in kilograms, not converted to grams as the question requires.
explanation_options.b: Incorrect coefficient — doesn't match the calculated value.

questions.explanation_short: Chlorine's Lewis dot structure shows two Cl atoms sharing one electron pair (single bond), each retaining three lone pairs.
questions.explanation_long: Each chlorine atom has 7 valence electrons; sharing one electron pair forms a single covalent bond (Cl-Cl), satisfying the octet for both atoms while each keeps three lone pairs. The correct diagram (Structure B in the original figure) shows exactly this arrangement.
questions.explanation_trick: Cl2 needs only one shared pair (single bond) since each Cl needs just one more electron to complete its octet.

explanation_options.b: Correct — one bonding pair plus three lone pairs on each chlorine, satisfying the octet rule.

questions.question_text: When two partially filled atomic orbitals overlap in such a way that the probability of finding electron is maximum around the line joining the two nuclei, the result is the formation of
questions.explanation_short: Head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, with maximum electron density between the nuclei, forms a sigma bond.
questions.explanation_long: A sigma bond results when orbitals overlap directly along the line joining the two nuclei, concentrating electron density there. A pi bond, by contrast, comes from sideways overlap with density above and below that axis.
questions.explanation_trick: Sigma = 'straight/head-on' overlap along the bond axis; pi = 'sideways' overlap.

explanation_options.a: Correct — head-on overlap along the internuclear axis defines a sigma bond.
explanation_options.b: Pi bonds form from sideways (lateral) overlap, not overlap along the axis.
explanation_options.c: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular attractions, not orbital overlap bonds.
explanation_options.d: Metallic bonding involves delocalized electrons in a lattice, not localized orbital overlap.

questions.question_text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O  ΔH = +285.5 kJ mol⁻¹. What will be the enthalpy change in the above reaction?
questions.explanation_short: Enthalpy is a state function, so summing ΔH forward and then reverse over a complete cycle always gives zero net change.
questions.explanation_long: By Hess's Law, enthalpy depends only on initial and final states, not on the path taken. If a reaction is carried out and then reversed (or considered in a closed cycle), the total enthalpy change for the round trip is always zero, since the system ends up back where it started.
questions.explanation_trick: State function + complete cycle = net ΔH of zero, no matter the intermediate steps.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't represent the net enthalpy change over a complete cycle.
explanation_options.b: Correct — as a state function, enthalpy returns to zero net change over a full cycle.
explanation_options.c: This value doesn't correspond to the cyclic/net calculation being asked about.
explanation_options.d: This value doesn't correspond to the cyclic/net calculation being asked about.

questions.question_text: Combustion of graphite to form CO₂ can be done by two ways: C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = -393.7 kJ mol⁻¹; C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = ?; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = -283 kJ mol⁻¹. What will be the enthalpy of formation of CO?
questions.explanation_short: Using Hess's Law: ΔHf(CO) = ΔHc(C→CO2) − ΔHc(CO→CO2) = −393.7 − (−283) = −110.7 ≈ −110 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation_long: Since C + O2 → CO2 can happen either directly or via CO as an intermediate, Hess's Law lets us subtract the second step's enthalpy from the overall one: ΔHf(CO) = −393.7 kJ/mol − (−283 kJ/mol) = −110.7 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation_trick: Subtract the known step's ΔH from the overall ΔH to isolate the unknown intermediate step.

explanation_options.a: This would be the sum, not the difference, of the two given enthalpies.
explanation_options.c: Wrong sign; formation of CO from its elements is exothermic, so ΔH should be negative.
explanation_options.d: This is the sum with the wrong sign, not the Hess's Law subtraction result.

questions.question_text: The value of equilibrium constant (Kc) for the reaction 2HF(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + F₂(g) is 10⁻¹³ at 2000 °C. Calculate the value of Kp for this reaction:
questions.explanation_short: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn. Two moles of gas give two moles of gas, so Δn = 0 and Kp = Kc = 10⁻¹³.
questions.explanation_long: Kp and Kc are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants. For 2HF ⇌ H₂ + F₂, Δn = (1 + 1) − 2 = 0, so (RT)⁰ = 1 and Kp = Kc = 10⁻¹³. (The paper prints HF as a solid, 2HF(s), which is impossible at 2000 °C and a misprint; the key treats HF as a gas, and the equation is shown that way here. Taking the misprint literally gives Δn = 2 and option D.)
questions.explanation_trick: Equal moles of gas on both sides → Kp = Kc.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — there is no factor of 2 in Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Δn = 0, so Kp = Kc.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 186 × 10⁻¹³ is Kc × RT, which would need Δn = 1.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 3.48 × 10⁻⁹ is Kc(RT)², which would need Δn = 2.

questions.explanation_short: Pure water, with no solute lowering its vapor pressure, shows the highest vapor pressure at any given temperature — that's Line (i).
questions.explanation_long: By Raoult's Law, dissolving a solute lowers a solvent's vapor pressure. Since pure water has no solute at all, its vapor pressure curve sits above all the solution curves at every temperature, corresponding to Line (i) in the figure.
questions.explanation_trick: Pure solvent always has the highest vapor pressure line; solutions sit below it, more so with more solute.

explanation_options.a: Correct — pure water's vapor pressure is highest since no solute lowers it.
explanation_options.b: This line represents a solution with some solute present, not pure water.
explanation_options.c: This line represents a more concentrated solution, sitting further below pure water.
explanation_options.d: This line represents the most concentrated solution shown, with the lowest vapor pressure.

questions.explanation_long: Let x be sulphur's oxidation number. With 4 oxygens at −2 each: x + 4(−2) = −2, so x − 8 = −2, giving x = +6.
questions.explanation_trick: Set up the algebra: (oxidation numbers) sum to the ion's overall charge — oxygen is almost always −2.

questions.question_text: Coinage metals Cu, Ag, and Au are the least reactive because they have:
questions.explanation_short: Cu, Ag, and Au have positive (high) standard reduction potentials, meaning they resist oxidation and stay unreactive.
questions.explanation_long: A positive reduction potential indicates a strong tendency to gain electrons (be reduced) and a weak tendency to lose electrons (be oxidized). This makes coinage metals resistant to corrosion and chemically unreactive compared to more reactive metals with negative reduction potentials.
questions.explanation_trick: High/positive reduction potential = 'doesn't want to react/corrode' = noble, unreactive metal.

explanation_options.a: A negative reduction potential would mean the metal is easily oxidized (reactive), the opposite of coinage metals.
explanation_options.b: Correct — positive reduction potential means resistance to oxidation, hence low reactivity.
explanation_options.c: Oxidation potential describes the reverse process; framing it as negative doesn't correctly explain their stability.
explanation_options.d: A positive oxidation potential would mean they're easily oxidized, which contradicts their unreactive nature.

questions.question_text: What will be the pH of a solution of NaOH with a concentration of 10⁻³ M?
questions.explanation_long: NaOH is a strong base, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M directly. Taking pOH = −log[OH⁻] = 3, and using pH + pOH = 14, gives pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
questions.explanation_trick: For strong bases, [OH⁻] equals the given concentration directly — then use pH = 14 − pOH.

explanation_options.a: This is the pOH value, not the pH.
explanation_options.b: This would be the pH of a 1 M strong base, not 10⁻³ M.
explanation_options.c: Correct — pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
explanation_options.d: pH 7 is neutral, but NaOH solution is basic, not neutral.

aliases: What will be the pH of a solution of NaOH with a concentration of 10^-3 M?

questions.question_text: If the reactant or product of a chemical reaction can absorb ultraviolet, visible or infrared radiation, then the rate of a chemical reaction can best be measured by which one of the following methods?
questions.explanation_short: Spectrometry (spectrophotometry) tracks how much UV, visible, or IR radiation a reactant/product absorbs as the reaction proceeds, giving a direct measure of concentration over time.
questions.explanation_long: When a species in a reaction absorbs light of a particular wavelength, its concentration can be tracked continuously by measuring absorbance with a spectrometer, using the Beer-Lambert law — making this the most suitable method here.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Absorbs radiation' in the question is the cue word pointing to spectrometry/spectrophotometry.

explanation_options.a: Chemical (titration) methods require stopping/sampling the reaction, less suited to a species that absorbs light directly.
explanation_options.b: Correct — absorbance measurements directly track a light-absorbing species' concentration.
explanation_options.c: Graphical methods analyze data after collection; they don't describe how the raw data is measured.
explanation_options.d: Differential methods analyze rate data mathematically but don't describe the measurement technique itself.

questions.question_text: For the reaction 2NO + O₂ ⇌ 2NO₂, the rate equation for the forward reaction is
questions.explanation_short: As written, the forward reaction 2NO + O2 → 2NO2 has rate = k[NO]²[O2], matching the stoichiometric coefficients as reaction orders.
questions.explanation_long: For this elementary-type forward reaction, the rate law's exponents match the stoichiometric coefficients: 2 for NO and 1 for O2, giving Rate = k[NO]²[O2].
questions.explanation_trick: For a reaction treated as elementary, the exponents in the rate law equal the stoichiometric coefficients.

explanation_options.a: This uses order 1 for NO, but the coefficient (and correct order here) is 2.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Rate = k[NO]²[O2] matches the coefficients 2 and 1.
explanation_options.c: This is a rate law in terms of the product NO2, not the reactants for the forward reaction.
explanation_options.d: This is also expressed in terms of product NO2, not appropriate for the forward reaction rate law.

questions.question_text: Radon is _______ emitter and being radioactive is used in ________ treatment in radiotherapy:
questions.explanation_short: Radon is an alpha emitter, and its intense but short-range radiation is used to treat cancer in radiotherapy.
questions.explanation_long: Radon-222 decays by emitting alpha particles. Because alpha radiation is highly ionizing over a short range, sealed radon sources have historically been used in localized (implant) radiotherapy to destroy cancerous tissue.
questions.explanation_trick: Radon = alpha emitter; alpha's short range/high ionization suits localized treatments like cancer therapy, not kidney stones.

explanation_options.a: Radon is an alpha emitter, not a beta emitter.
explanation_options.b: Correct — alpha emitter, used in cancer radiotherapy.
explanation_options.c: Kidney stones aren't treated with radioactive radon; that's not its radiotherapy application.
explanation_options.d: Both the emission type (beta) and application (kidney stones) are incorrect here.

questions.question_text: One mole of glucose was dissolved in 1 kg of water, ethanol, ether and benzene separately and the molal boiling point constant of each individual solution was found to be 0.52, 1.75, 2.16 and 2.70 °C kg mol⁻¹ respectively. Which of the following figures (I–IV) shows benzene as solvent in solution?
questions.explanation_short: Benzene has the largest molal boiling point constant (2.70°C·kg/mol) of the four solvents, so its boiling-point-elevation graph shows the steepest slope — identified as the line for benzene.
questions.explanation_long: The molal boiling point elevation constant (Kb) determines how steeply boiling point rises with solute concentration; a higher Kb means a steeper line on a ΔTb vs molality graph. Benzene's Kb (2.70) is the highest among water, ethanol, ether, and benzene, so its line has the steepest slope in the figure.
questions.explanation_trick: Higher Kb value = steeper slope on the boiling-point-elevation graph.

explanation_options.a: Correct — benzene's highest Kb (2.70) gives it the steepest line in the figure.
explanation_options.b: A shallower line would correspond to a solvent with a lower Kb than benzene.
explanation_options.c: This line's slope doesn't match benzene's high Kb value.
explanation_options.d: This line's slope doesn't match benzene's high Kb value.

questions.question_text: The trends in melting points of the elements of 3rd period (Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar) are depicted in a figure. The sharp decrease observed from 'Si' to 'P' is due to
questions.option_a: Decrease in atomic radius from 'Si' to 'P'
questions.option_b: Change in bonding and structure of two elements
questions.option_d: Increase in electron density from 'Si' to 'P'
questions.explanation_short: The sharp drop from Si to P happens because silicon is a giant covalent (network) solid while phosphorus is a simple molecular solid (P4) with weak forces between molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Silicon has a diamond-like giant covalent lattice requiring huge energy to break, giving it a very high melting point. Phosphorus, however, exists as discrete P4 molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces, so its melting point is much lower — a change in bonding type and structure, not just atomic size.
questions.explanation_trick: Big melting point drops across a period usually signal a switch from giant covalent/metallic bonding to simple molecular structures.

explanation_options.a: Atomic radius changes gradually across the period; it doesn't explain the abrupt drop.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the bonding changes from giant covalent (Si) to simple molecular (P4).
explanation_options.c: This vague phrase doesn't describe an actual chemical reason.
explanation_options.d: Electron density change doesn't account for the drastic structural/bonding shift.

questions.question_text: Arrange the following elements according to the trend of ionization energies. (C, N, Ne, B)
questions.explanation_short: First ionization energy generally rises across a period, so B < C < N < Ne, with the noble gas Ne having the highest value.
questions.explanation_long: Across period 2, effective nuclear charge increases while atomic radius shrinks, so it takes progressively more energy to remove an electron. Although N shows a slight extra stability from its half-filled 2p³ configuration, the overall increasing trend from B to C to N to the noble gas Ne holds. (The paper prints 'Na' for 'Ne' in options B and C; it is shown corrected here.)
questions.explanation_trick: Ionization energy generally increases left to right across a period, peaking at the noble gas.

explanation_options.a: This places Ne (highest IE) first, reversing the correct increasing order.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't follow the correct left-to-right increasing trend.
explanation_options.c: Correct — B < C < N < Ne, rising across the period.
explanation_options.d: Places Ne first, which contradicts the increasing trend across the period.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following noble gases is used for providing an inert atmosphere for welding?
questions.explanation_short: Helium, an inert noble gas, is used to give an inert atmosphere for welding (argon is used the same way); the UHS key marks helium.
questions.explanation_long: In arc welding the hot metal must be shielded from oxygen and nitrogen of the air, so an unreactive noble gas is blown over the weld. Helium is used for this, especially for aluminium and magnesium, and argon is the other common shielding gas. Both are correct uses, and the UHS key marks A. Neon and krypton are not used for welding.
questions.explanation_trick: Shielding gases for welding: He and Ar.

explanation_options.a: Correct (UHS key) — helium provides an inert welding atmosphere.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — neon is used in advertising signs, not welding.
explanation_options.c: Also used as a shielding gas, but the key marks helium.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — krypton is too rare and costly; it is used in some lamps.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the correct equation of 1st ionization of sulphuric acid?
questions.explanation_short: The first ionization of H2SO4 goes to completion (strong acid), producing H+ and the bisulfate ion HSO4⁻, shown with a one-way arrow.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following products is obtained when sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid?
questions.explanation_short: Sulphur trioxide absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid forms oleum (fuming sulphuric acid, H2S2O7).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following pairs of compounds is cis and trans isomers of each other?
