questions.explanation_long: ADH is synthesized in the hypothalamus but stored and released into the blood from the posterior pituitary gland, which regulates water reabsorption in kidneys.
questions.explanation_trick: ADH is made in the hypothalamus but released from the posterior pituitary — don't confuse synthesis site with release site.

explanation_options.a: The anterior pituitary releases hormones like FSH, LH, ACTH, not ADH.
explanation_options.b: Correct — ADH is released from the posterior pituitary lobe.
explanation_options.c: The hypothalamus synthesizes ADH but releases it via the posterior pituitary, so the release site is posterior pituitary.
explanation_options.d: The thalamus is unrelated to ADH release.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the main nitrogenous waste product in humans?
questions.explanation_short: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste product excreted by humans.
questions.explanation_long: Humans convert toxic ammonia into less toxic urea in the liver (via the urea cycle) for excretion, making urea the primary nitrogenous waste product in human urine.
questions.explanation_trick: Humans are ureotelic — urea is the main excretory nitrogenous waste, unlike ammonia (aquatic animals) or uric acid (birds/reptiles).

explanation_options.a: Correct — urea is the main nitrogenous waste product in humans.
explanation_options.b: Ammonia is toxic and mainly excreted by aquatic animals directly, not the primary human waste form.
explanation_options.c: Salts are excreted but aren't nitrogenous waste products.
explanation_options.d: Uric acid is the main nitrogenous waste in birds and reptiles, not primarily in humans.

questions.question_text: The right and left cerebral hemispheres are connected by a thick band of nerve fibres called:
questions.explanation_short: The corpus callosum is the thick band of nerve fibres connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
questions.explanation_long: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of white matter (nerve fibres) that allows communication and coordination between the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
questions.explanation_trick: Corpus callosum = the 'bridge' connecting the two brain hemispheres.

explanation_options.a: The medulla controls autonomic functions, unrelated to hemisphere connection.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres.
explanation_options.c: The pons relays signals between brain regions but doesn't specifically connect the hemispheres.
explanation_options.d: The hippocampus is involved in memory formation, not hemisphere connection.

questions.question_text: The part of the brain which guides smooth and accurate motions and maintains body position is called
questions.explanation_short: The cerebellum coordinates smooth, accurate movement and maintains balance/posture.
questions.explanation_long: The cerebellum fine-tunes motor commands from the cerebrum, ensuring smooth, coordinated movements and maintaining balance and body position — distinct from the cerebrum's higher cognitive roles.
questions.explanation_trick: Cerebellum = coordination and balance ('little brain'); cerebrum = higher thought/voluntary movement initiation.

explanation_options.a: The cerebrum handles higher cognitive functions and voluntary movement initiation, not fine motor coordination itself.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the cerebellum coordinates smooth movement and body position.
explanation_options.c: The pons relays signals between brain regions, not the primary coordination center.
explanation_options.d: The medulla controls involuntary functions like breathing and heart rate, not movement coordination.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the effect of sympathetic nervous system?
questions.explanation_short: The sympathetic nervous system dilates the pupil (fight-or-flight response).
questions.explanation_long: As part of the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system dilates pupils for better vision, while it also increases heart rate, relaxes bronchi (dilates), and inhibits digestion — opposite to parasympathetic effects.
questions.explanation_trick: Sympathetic = fight-or-flight = pupil dilation, bronchodilation, increased heart rate, decreased digestion.

explanation_options.a: Sympathetic activity dilates (not constricts) bronchi to improve airflow.
explanation_options.b: Sympathetic activity increases (not decreases) heart rate.
explanation_options.c: Sympathetic activity inhibits (not promotes) digestion/peristalsis.
explanation_options.d: Correct — sympathetic activation dilates the pupil.

questions.question_text: High levels of aluminium may contribute to the onset of which one of the following?
questions.explanation_short: High aluminium levels have been linked to Alzheimer's disease.
questions.explanation_long: Some studies have associated elevated aluminium exposure with neurodegenerative changes contributing to Alzheimer's disease, distinguishing it from Parkinson's, epilepsy, or gonorrhea, which have different causes.
questions.explanation_trick: Aluminium exposure is specifically linked to Alzheimer's in toxicology discussions, not Parkinson's.

explanation_options.a: Parkinson's disease is linked more to dopaminergic neuron loss, not primarily aluminium.
explanation_options.b: Epilepsy has various neurological causes, not primarily linked to aluminium.
explanation_options.c: Correct — high aluminium levels have been implicated in Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_options.d: Gonorrhea is a bacterial STI, entirely unrelated to aluminium exposure.

questions.question_text: Testosterone is produced by which one of the following?
questions.explanation_short: Testosterone is produced by interstitial (Leydig) cells in the testes.
questions.explanation_long: Interstitial cells (Leydig cells), located between the seminiferous tubules, are responsible for synthesizing and secreting testosterone in response to LH stimulation.
questions.explanation_trick: Leydig/interstitial cells = testosterone; Sertoli cells = support sperm development, not hormone production.

explanation_options.a: Sertoli cells support and nourish developing sperm, not primarily hormone producers.
explanation_options.b: Germinal epithelium gives rise to sperm cells, not testosterone.
explanation_options.c: Correct — interstitial (Leydig) cells produce testosterone.
explanation_options.d: Spermatogonia are the stem cells that develop into sperm, not hormone-producing cells.

questions.question_text: The oocyte released during ovulation is in
questions.explanation_short: The oocyte released at ovulation is arrested in Metaphase II.
questions.explanation_long: Human oocytes complete meiosis I before ovulation but arrest in metaphase of meiosis II, only completing division if fertilization occurs — hence the ovulated egg is in Metaphase II.
questions.explanation_trick: Ovulated human egg = arrested at Metaphase II, resuming only upon fertilization.

explanation_options.a: Anaphase I occurs before ovulation, during meiosis I completion, not at release.
explanation_options.b: Prophase I occurs much earlier, arrested from fetal life until puberty, not at ovulation.
explanation_options.c: Metaphase I precedes ovulation; meiosis I completes just before release.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the released oocyte is arrested in Metaphase II.

questions.question_text: Yellowish glandular structure formed after the release of egg from the follicle is called
questions.explanation_short: The corpus luteum is the yellowish glandular structure formed after ovulation.
questions.explanation_long: After the follicle releases its egg, the remaining follicular cells transform into the corpus luteum, a yellow, hormone-secreting (progesterone) structure supporting early pregnancy if fertilization occurs.
questions.explanation_trick: Corpus luteum = 'yellow body,' literally named for its yellowish color post-ovulation.

explanation_options.a: Corpus callosum is a brain structure, unrelated to ovulation.
explanation_options.b: The Graafian follicle is the mature follicle before ovulation, not after egg release.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the corpus luteum forms after ovulation and appears yellowish.
explanation_options.d: Follicle atresia refers to degeneration of unused follicles, not the post-ovulation structure.

questions.question_text: On puberty, the development of primary follicles is stimulated by
questions.explanation_short: FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) stimulates the development of primary follicles at puberty.
questions.explanation_long: At puberty, FSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates ovarian follicles to begin developing, initiating the menstrual/ovarian cycle, distinct from LH's role in triggering ovulation.
questions.explanation_trick: FSH = follicle stimulation/development; LH = triggers ovulation (surge).

explanation_options.a: ICSH (interstitial cell stimulating hormone) is LH's equivalent in males, stimulating testosterone production, not follicle development.
explanation_options.b: Correct — FSH stimulates development of primary follicles.
explanation_options.c: LH triggers ovulation and corpus luteum formation, not initial follicle development.
explanation_options.d: Estrogen is produced by developing follicles but doesn't itself initiate their development; FSH does.

questions.question_text: Causative agent of a sexually transmitted disease that affects the mucous membrane of the urinogenital tract is
questions.explanation_short: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhea, affecting the urinogenital mucous membrane.
questions.explanation_long: Gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted disease affecting the mucous membranes of the urinogenital tract, is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
questions.explanation_trick: Neisseria gonorrhoeae ↔ gonorrhea, a direct name-to-disease match.

explanation_options.a: Staphylococcus aureus causes various infections (skin, etc.), not primarily this STI.
explanation_options.b: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, not gonorrhea.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the causative agent of gonorrhea.
explanation_options.d: Escherichia coli commonly causes urinary tract infections, not this specific STI.

questions.question_text: In a human vertebral column, the number of ______________ vertebrae is 7.
questions.explanation_short: Humans have 7 cervical vertebrae in the vertebral column.
questions.explanation_long: The human vertebral column consists of 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, and fused sacral/coccygeal vertebrae — the cervical count of 7 is constant across nearly all mammals.
questions.explanation_trick: 7 cervical vertebrae is a fixed number across almost all mammals (even giraffes!).

explanation_options.a: Correct — there are 7 cervical vertebrae in humans.
explanation_options.b: There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, not 7.
explanation_options.c: There are 5 lumbar vertebrae, not 7.
explanation_options.d: The sacrum consists of 5 fused vertebrae, not 7 separate ones.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following structures holds the bones together?
questions.explanation_short: Ligaments are the fibrous structures that hold bones together at joints.
questions.explanation_long: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue connecting bone to bone across joints, providing stability, distinct from tendons (muscle-to-bone) or cartilage (cushioning).
questions.explanation_trick: Ligament = bone-to-bone; tendon = muscle-to-bone — a commonly tested distinction.

explanation_options.a: Joints are the connection points themselves, not the structures holding bones together.
explanation_options.b: Cartilage cushions and reduces friction at joints but doesn't hold bones together.
explanation_options.c: Fibrous capsules enclose joints but ligaments are the specific structures binding bones.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ligaments hold bones together at joints.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following cartilages is the most abundant in the human body?
questions.explanation_short: Hyaline cartilage is the most abundant type of cartilage in the human body.
questions.explanation_long: Hyaline cartilage, found in the nose, trachea, and articular surfaces of joints, is the most widespread cartilage type in the body compared to elastic or fibrous cartilage.
questions.explanation_trick: Hyaline = most common cartilage type; elastic cartilage is in ear/epiglottis (less abundant).

explanation_options.a: Elastic cartilage is found in specific structures (ear, epiglottis) and is less abundant overall.
explanation_options.b: 'Chondrous cartilage' is not a standard distinct cartilage classification.
explanation_options.c: Fibrous cartilage is found in intervertebral discs, less abundant than hyaline cartilage.
explanation_options.d: Correct — hyaline cartilage is the most abundant cartilage type in the body.

questions.question_text: The repeated protein pattern of myofibrils is called
questions.explanation_short: The repeating structural/functional unit of a myofibril is called a sarcomere.
questions.explanation_long: A sarcomere is the segment between two Z-lines in a myofibril, containing the repeating arrangement of actin and myosin filaments responsible for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Sarcomere = the basic repeating contractile unit of muscle myofibrils.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the sarcomere is the repeating protein unit of myofibrils.
explanation_options.b: 'Zyomere' is not a standard biological term.
explanation_options.c: The sarcolemma is the muscle cell's plasma membrane, not the repeating internal unit.
explanation_options.d: Cross bridges are the myosin head connections within a sarcomere, not the repeating unit itself.

questions.question_text: When more energy is required in muscle contraction, then that energy can also be produced by _______________ as a secondary source.
questions.explanation_short: Phosphocreatine serves as a secondary, rapid energy source for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_long: When immediate extra energy is needed, phosphocreatine quickly donates its phosphate to regenerate ATP from ADP, acting as a fast secondary energy reserve in muscle cells.
questions.explanation_trick: Phosphocreatine = fast-acting backup ATP source in muscles, distinct from glucose (primary, slower) or lactic acid (a byproduct).

explanation_options.a: Glucose is a primary fuel source but not specifically the described 'secondary' rapid-response energy source.
explanation_options.b: Correct — phosphocreatine acts as a rapid secondary source of energy in muscle contraction.
explanation_options.c: Fructose isn't a typical direct muscle energy reserve.
explanation_options.d: Lactic acid is a byproduct of anaerobic respiration, not an energy source itself.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a steroid hormone?
questions.explanation_short: Oestrogen is a steroid hormone (derived from cholesterol).
questions.explanation_long: Oestrogen belongs to the steroid hormone class, synthesized from cholesterol, unlike glucagon, thyroxine, and epinephrine, which are peptide/amino-acid-derived hormones.
questions.explanation_trick: Steroid hormones (sex hormones, cortisol) are cholesterol-derived — oestrogen is a classic example.

explanation_options.a: Glucagon is a peptide hormone, not a steroid.
explanation_options.b: Thyroxine is an amino-acid-derived (tyrosine-based) hormone, not a steroid.
explanation_options.c: Epinephrine is an amino-acid-derived hormone (catecholamine), not a steroid.
explanation_options.d: Correct — oestrogen is a steroid hormone.

questions.question_text: The gonadotrophic hormones of the anterior lobe of pituitary include:
questions.option_a: Prolactin, Thyroid Stimulating Hormone, Somatotropin Hormone
questions.option_b: Follicle Stimulating Hormone, Luteinizing Hormone, Prolactin
questions.option_c: Adrenocorticotrophic Hormone, Luteinizing Hormone, Follicle Stimulating Hormone
questions.option_d: Luteinizing Hormone, Follicle Stimulating Hormone, Thyroid Stimulating Hormone
questions.explanation_short: The gonadotrophic hormones from the anterior pituitary are FSH, LH, and Prolactin.
questions.explanation_long: Gonadotrophic hormones directly regulate the gonads (ovaries/testes) — FSH, LH, and Prolactin fit this category, unlike TSH, ACTH, or Somatotropin, which target other glands or general growth.
questions.explanation_trick: Gonadotrophic = acts on gonads: FSH, LH, and Prolactin specifically.

explanation_options.a: TSH and Somatotropin don't target the gonads, so this set is incorrect.
explanation_options.b: Correct — FSH, LH, and Prolactin are the gonadotrophic hormones.
explanation_options.c: ACTH targets the adrenal cortex, not strictly gonadal function, making this set inaccurate.
explanation_options.d: TSH targets the thyroid gland, not the gonads, making this set inaccurate.

questions.question_text: Over-activity of the cortical hormone of adrenal gland causes
questions.explanation_short: Excess adrenal cortex hormone (cortisol) activity causes Cushing's disease.
questions.explanation_long: Cushing's disease/syndrome results from excessive cortisol production by the adrenal cortex, unlike Addison's disease which results from adrenal cortex under-activity (deficiency).
questions.explanation_trick: Cushing's = too much cortisol (over-activity); Addison's = too little (under-activity) — easily confused pair.

explanation_options.a: Addison's disease results from under-activity (deficiency) of adrenal cortical hormones, the opposite condition.
explanation_options.b: Parkinson's disease is a neurological disorder unrelated to adrenal hormones.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Cushing's disease results from over-activity of adrenal cortical hormones.
explanation_options.d: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder, unrelated to adrenal hormone levels.

questions.question_text: How many iodine atoms are present in thyroxine?
questions.explanation_short: Thyroxine (T4) contains four iodine atoms.
questions.explanation_long: Thyroxine, also called T4, is named for its four iodine atoms attached to the thyronine backbone, distinguishing it from triiodothyronine (T3), which has three.
questions.explanation_trick: Thyroxine = T4 = 4 iodine atoms; T3 (triiodothyronine) has 3.

explanation_options.a: 3 iodine atoms describes triiodothyronine (T3), not thyroxine.
explanation_options.b: Correct — thyroxine (T4) contains 4 iodine atoms.
explanation_options.c: 2 is too few iodine atoms for thyroxine.
explanation_options.d: 5 is too many iodine atoms; thyroxine has 4.

questions.question_text: T-lymphocytes recognize antigen and attack microorganisms or transplanted organ and tissues. This effect is called
questions.explanation_short: T-lymphocytes directly attacking pathogens/foreign tissue is called cell-mediated response.
questions.explanation_long: When T-lymphocytes directly recognize and destroy infected cells or foreign tissue (like transplants) without antibody involvement, this is termed the cell-mediated immune response, as opposed to the antibody-based humoral response.
questions.explanation_trick: T-cells = cell-mediated immunity; B-cells/antibodies = humoral immunity.

explanation_options.a: Correct — direct T-lymphocyte attack on antigens/cells is the cell-mediated response.
explanation_options.b: Humoral immune response involves antibodies produced by B-cells, not direct T-cell attack.
explanation_options.c: Active immunity is a broader category (body producing its own response), not the specific term for this T-cell mechanism.
explanation_options.d: Passive immunity involves receiving pre-made antibodies, unrelated to this direct T-cell action.

questions.question_text: Which part of antibody recognizes the antigen during immune response?
questions.explanation_short: The variable region of an antibody is responsible for recognizing specific antigens.
questions.explanation_long: Each antibody's variable region (at the tips of the heavy and light chains) has a unique shape that binds specifically to its target antigen, while the constant region mediates other immune functions.
questions.explanation_trick: Variable region = antigen recognition (unique per antibody); constant region = same across antibody class.

explanation_options.a: The heavy chain includes both variable and constant portions; it's the variable part specifically that recognizes antigen.
explanation_options.b: The light chain also includes variable and constant portions; again it's the variable part that matters for recognition.
explanation_options.c: The constant region is uniform and doesn't vary to recognize different antigens.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the variable part of the antibody recognizes the specific antigen.

questions.question_text: What type of immunity is achieved by injecting antibodies, antiserum, anti-venom serum?
questions.explanation_short: Injecting pre-formed antibodies (antiserum) confers passive immunity.
questions.explanation_long: Passive immunity is achieved when ready-made antibodies (from antiserum, anti-venom, or maternal transfer) are directly introduced into the body, providing immediate but temporary protection, unlike active immunity which involves the body producing its own antibodies.
questions.explanation_trick: Injected antibodies = passive immunity; body-produced antibodies (via infection/vaccine) = active immunity.

explanation_options.a: Active immunity involves the body making its own antibodies, not receiving pre-made ones.
explanation_options.b: Correct — injecting pre-formed antibodies/antiserum confers passive immunity.
explanation_options.c: 'Artificially induced immunity' is too broad/vague; the precise term for injected antibodies is passive immunity.
explanation_options.d: 'Naturally induced immunity' refers to immunity gained through natural infection, not injection.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following glands is involved in the production of lymphocytes?
questions.explanation_short: The thymus gland is involved in the production/maturation of T-lymphocytes.
questions.explanation_long: The thymus is the primary lymphoid organ where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune competence, distinguishing it from the pineal, pituitary, and adrenal glands, which have unrelated endocrine roles.
questions.explanation_trick: Thymus = T-cell maturation site; easily linked by the shared 'T' in thymus and T-cells.

explanation_options.a: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, unrelated to lymphocyte production.
explanation_options.b: The pituitary gland secretes various hormones, not lymphocytes.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the thymus is involved in lymphocyte (T-cell) production/maturation.
explanation_options.d: The adrenal gland secretes hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, unrelated to lymphocyte production.

questions.question_text: Antibodies are proteins and made up of how many polypeptide chains?
questions.explanation_short: Antibodies are made of four polypeptide chains (2 heavy + 2 light).
questions.explanation_long: The typical antibody (immunoglobulin) structure consists of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds, totaling four polypeptide chains in a Y-shape.
questions.explanation_trick: Antibody structure = 2 heavy + 2 light chains = 4 total polypeptide chains.

explanation_options.a: One chain vastly undercounts the actual antibody structure.
explanation_options.b: Two chains undercounts; antibodies have both heavy and light chain pairs.
explanation_options.c: Three chains isn't the correct standard antibody structure.
explanation_options.d: Correct — antibodies consist of four polypeptide chains (2 heavy, 2 light).

questions.question_text: Oxidative phase of glycolysis starts with dehydrogenation of
questions.explanation_short: The oxidative phase of glycolysis begins with dehydrogenation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
questions.explanation_long: In glycolysis, the energy-yielding (oxidative) phase starts when glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized (dehydrogenated) to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, generating NADH — a key step distinguishing the energy-investment and energy-payoff phases.
questions.explanation_trick: G3P dehydrogenation marks the start of the payoff/oxidative phase of glycolysis, producing NADH.

explanation_options.a: 'Glycolysis' itself is the whole pathway, not the specific molecule dehydrogenated at this step.
explanation_options.b: Ribulose bisphosphate is involved in the Calvin cycle (photosynthesis), not glycolysis.
explanation_options.c: Correct — glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is dehydrogenated to start the oxidative phase.
explanation_options.d: NADH is the product of this dehydrogenation step, not the substrate being dehydrogenated.

questions.question_text: In one turn, the Krebs's cycle produces one molecule of ATP, one molecule of FADH2 and __________ molecules of NADH
questions.explanation_short: One turn of the Krebs cycle produces 1 ATP, 1 FADH2, and 3 NADH molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Per turn, the Krebs (citric acid) cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP (via substrate-level phosphorylation) — a key set of numbers for calculating total ATP yield from respiration.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize per Krebs cycle turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP, 2 CO2.

explanation_options.a: 1 NADH undercounts; the cycle produces 3 NADH per turn.
explanation_options.b: 2 NADH undercounts; the correct number is 3.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the Krebs cycle produces 3 NADH molecules per turn.
explanation_options.d: 4 NADH overcounts; the correct number is 3.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the stage of cellular respiration for which oxygen is not essential?
questions.explanation_short: Glycolysis is the only stage of cellular respiration that doesn't require oxygen.
questions.explanation_long: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and proceeds anaerobically, breaking glucose into pyruvate without needing oxygen, unlike pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain, which depend on oxygen (directly or as final electron acceptor).
questions.explanation_trick: Glycolysis = anaerobic (occurs with or without oxygen); everything after it in aerobic respiration needs O2.

explanation_options.a: Correct — glycolysis doesn't require oxygen to proceed.
explanation_options.b: Pyruvate oxidation occurs in mitochondria as part of aerobic respiration, requiring oxygen indirectly via the ETC.
explanation_options.c: The Krebs cycle depends on oxygen indirectly, needing NAD+/FAD regenerated by the oxygen-dependent ETC.
explanation_options.d: The electron transport chain directly requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

questions.question_text: Pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, moves from cytosol to mitochondrial matrix where it is oxidized into ___________ producing CO2 as a by-product.
questions.explanation_short: Pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl CoA (active acetic acid), releasing CO2, before entering the Krebs cycle.
questions.explanation_long: In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation, releasing CO2 and forming acetyl CoA (historically called 'active acetic acid'), which then enters the Krebs cycle.
questions.explanation_trick: Pyruvate → Acetyl CoA + CO2 is the crucial bridging reaction (pyruvate oxidation) between glycolysis and Krebs cycle.

explanation_options.a: Correct — pyruvate is oxidized into acetyl CoA (active acetic acid), releasing CO2.
explanation_options.b: Citrate is formed later when acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle, not directly from pyruvate.
explanation_options.c: NAD is a coenzyme involved in the reaction, not the oxidized product of pyruvate.
explanation_options.d: FAD is not involved in this specific pyruvate oxidation step.

questions.question_text: Pyruvate → Acetyl CoA. Which pair of coenzyme transformations occurs in this reaction?
questions.explanation_short: In pyruvate → Acetyl CoA, the coenzyme transformation is NAD+ → NADH.
questions.explanation_long: The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA is coupled with the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, capturing high-energy electrons for later use in the electron transport chain.
questions.explanation_trick: Pyruvate oxidation uses NAD+ (not FAD) as the electron acceptor, becoming NADH.

explanation_options.a: FAD+ → FADH is used in the Krebs cycle (succinate dehydrogenase step), not pyruvate oxidation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — NAD+ is reduced to NADH during pyruvate oxidation.
explanation_options.c: NADH → NAD+ + H+ would be an oxidation reaction (reverse direction), not what occurs here.
explanation_options.d: FADH+ → FAD + H+ describes oxidation of FADH2, not the reduction reaction that occurs in pyruvate oxidation.

questions.question_text: pBR322 has antibiotic resistance genes for
questions.explanation_short: The plasmid pBR322 carries resistance genes for ampicillin and tetracycline.
questions.explanation_long: pBR322 is a classic cloning vector engineered with two antibiotic resistance genes — for ampicillin and tetracycline — used as selectable markers in recombinant DNA experiments.
questions.explanation_trick: pBR322 = ampicillin + tetracycline resistance, a standard genetic engineering fact.

explanation_options.a: Aspirin isn't an antibiotic, so this pairing is incorrect.
explanation_options.b: Streptomycin and metronidazole aren't the resistance genes carried by pBR322.
explanation_options.c: Correct — pBR322 carries ampicillin and tetracycline resistance genes.
explanation_options.d: Penicillin and metronidazole aren't the resistance genes carried by pBR322.

questions.question_text: Cystic Fibrosis affects which one of the following cells of the body?
questions.explanation_short: Cystic Fibrosis primarily affects epithelial cells, disrupting chloride ion transport.
questions.explanation_long: Cystic Fibrosis results from a defective CFTR protein in epithelial cells, impairing chloride transport and causing thick mucus buildup in organs like the lungs and pancreas, whose linings are epithelial.
questions.explanation_trick: CFTR gene defect → epithelial cell chloride transport dysfunction → thick mucus.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Cystic Fibrosis affects epithelial cells due to defective chloride channel function.
explanation_options.b: Endothelial cells line blood vessels and aren't the primary cells affected by CF.
explanation_options.c: Plasma cells are antibody-producing immune cells, unrelated to CF's primary defect.
explanation_options.d: Blood cells aren't the primary cells affected; CF centers on epithelial chloride transport.

questions.question_text: The enzymes which act as molecular scissors in recombinant DNA technology are
questions.explanation_short: Endonucleases (restriction enzymes) act as molecular scissors, cutting DNA at specific sites.
questions.explanation_long: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific DNA sequences and cut within the DNA strand, functioning as precise 'molecular scissors' essential for recombinant DNA technology.
questions.explanation_trick: Endonucleases cut within the DNA strand (like scissors); exonucleases trim from the ends.

explanation_options.a: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from DNA ends, not internal cutting like scissors.
explanation_options.b: Correct — endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific internal sites, acting as molecular scissors.
explanation_options.c: Polymerases synthesize new DNA strands, not cut existing ones.
explanation_options.d: Reverse transcriptases synthesize DNA from RNA templates, not cutting DNA.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of PCR?
questions.option_a: Heating → Cooling → Add Primer → Copying of strand
questions.option_b: Heating → Add Primer → Cooling → Copying of strand
questions.option_c: Add Primer → Heating → Cooling → Copying of strand
questions.option_d: Cooling → Add Primer → Heating → Copying of strand
questions.explanation_short: PCR: heat to separate the DNA strands, cool so the primers can attach, then DNA polymerase copies each strand.
questions.explanation_long: Each PCR cycle starts by heating the DNA to about 94 °C so the two strands separate. The mixture is then cooled so that the short primers bind (anneal) to their complementary sites on the single strands, and finally DNA polymerase extends the primers, copying each strand. The textbook sequence is therefore heating → cooling with primers → copying. (In a laboratory the primers are already in the tube before heating, but they can only attach after the strands have been separated and cooled.)
questions.explanation_trick: Denature (hot) → anneal primers (cool) → extend (copy).

explanation_options.a: Correct — heating, cooling, primer attachment, copying.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — primers attach only once the mixture has cooled.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — primers cannot attach before the strands are separated by heating.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the cycle starts with heating, not cooling.

questions.question_text: When two different pieces of DNA are joined together, the result is which one of the following?
questions.explanation_short: Joining two different pieces of DNA together produces recombinant DNA.
questions.explanation_long: Recombinant DNA technology involves combining DNA from different sources (e.g., a gene of interest and a plasmid vector) into a single molecule — precisely what 'recombinant DNA' means.
questions.explanation_trick: Recombinant DNA = DNA recombined from different sources, the foundation of genetic engineering.

explanation_options.a: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is synthesized from mRNA via reverse transcriptase, not simply joined DNA pieces.
explanation_options.b: Mutated DNA results from changes within a single DNA sequence, not joining separate pieces.
explanation_options.c: Correct — joining two different DNA pieces creates recombinant DNA.
explanation_options.d: Cloned DNA refers to copies of DNA, not specifically the act of joining two different pieces.

questions.question_text: Individual successions are known as
questions.explanation_short: Individual ecological successions are called seres.
questions.explanation_long: Each specific successional sequence of a community, from pioneer to climax stages, is termed a 'sere,' distinguishing it from broader categories like primary/secondary succession.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Sere' = one individual successional sequence; not to be confused with primary/secondary succession types.

explanation_options.a: Primary succession is a category/type of succession, not the term for an individual instance.
explanation_options.b: Secondary succession is also a category/type, not the term for an individual instance.
explanation_options.c: Correct — an individual succession is called a sere.
explanation_options.d: 'Xeroses' is not the standard term for individual successions (xerosere refers to succession starting on dry land).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the ultimate distributional unit within which a species is restrained by the limitations of its physical structure and physiology?
questions.explanation_short: Grinnell defined the niche as the ultimate distributional unit within which a species is held by its structural and physiological limits.
questions.explanation_long: The phrase in the question is Joseph Grinnell's classic definition of the ecological niche: the ultimate distributional unit within which each species is held by its structural and instinctive limitations. A habitat is simply the place where an organism lives; an ecosystem and a biome are much larger units that contain many species.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Ultimate distributional unit' = niche (Grinnell).

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the definition of a niche.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a biome is a large regional community.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — an ecosystem includes many species and their environment.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a habitat is only the place where a species lives.

questions.question_text: All herbivores belong to which trophic level in the food chain?
questions.explanation_short: Herbivores, as primary consumers, occupy trophic level T2 (second trophic level).
questions.explanation_long: In a food chain, producers occupy T1, herbivores (primary consumers) occupy T2, and carnivores occupy higher levels (T3, T4) as secondary/tertiary consumers.
questions.explanation_trick: T1 = producers, T2 = herbivores/primary consumers, T3 = carnivores/secondary consumers.

explanation_options.a: T1 is the producer (plant) level, not herbivores.
explanation_options.b: Correct — herbivores occupy the T2 trophic level as primary consumers.
explanation_options.c: T3 represents secondary consumers (carnivores eating herbivores), not herbivores themselves.
explanation_options.d: T4 represents tertiary consumers, even further from the herbivore level.

questions.question_text: How many food chains are present in the following food web (Fox, Grass Snake, Dog, Frog, Beetle, Spider, Caterpillar, Slug, Wood Boring Beetle, Wood Louse feeding from Leaves, Wood, and Bark)?
questions.explanation_short: Tracing all possible predator-prey paths in the described food web yields 4 distinct food chains.
questions.explanation_long: Counting each unique linear path from producer through the different consumer levels in the described web (leaves/wood/bark → various invertebrates → predators) yields 4 separate food chains.
questions.explanation_trick: Count each unique straight-line path from base producer to top predator in the web — here it totals 4.

explanation_options.a: 5 overcounts the actual number of distinct linear chains in this web.
explanation_options.b: 3 undercounts the actual number of distinct linear chains in this web.
explanation_options.c: 6 overcounts the actual number of distinct linear chains in this web.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tracing the web yields 4 distinct food chains.

questions.question_text: The relationship in which one organism gets benefit and the other is not affected is called
questions.explanation_short: Commensalism is a relationship where one organism benefits and the other is unaffected.
questions.explanation_long: In commensalism, one species gains a benefit (food, shelter, transport) while the other species experiences neither harm nor benefit — distinct from mutualism (both benefit) or parasitism (one harms the other).
questions.explanation_trick: Commensalism = one benefits, other unaffected ('+/0'); mutualism = both benefit ('+/+'); parasitism = one harms other ('+/-').

explanation_options.a: Mutualism involves both organisms benefiting, not just one with the other unaffected.
explanation_options.b: Correct — commensalism describes one organism benefiting while the other is unaffected.
explanation_options.c: Predation involves one organism directly killing/consuming another, not simply being unaffected.
explanation_options.d: Parasitism involves one organism harming the other, not leaving it unaffected.

questions.question_text: When a gene suppresses the effects of a gene at another locus, this is known as
questions.explanation_short: A gene masking the effect of a non-allelic gene at another locus is epistasis.
questions.explanation_long: In epistasis one gene masks or suppresses the phenotypic expression of a different gene at another locus. Co-dominance and complete dominance are relationships between alleles of the same gene, and a mutation is a change in the DNA. (The paper prints 'expresses the effects of a gene at another focus', a misprint for suppresses … locus.)
questions.explanation_trick: Epistasis = between different genes; dominance = between alleles of one gene.

explanation_options.a: Correct — one gene masks another non-allelic gene.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — co-dominance is between two alleles of the same gene.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — complete dominance is between alleles of the same gene.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a mutation is a change in DNA, not an interaction between genes.

aliases: A gene that has more than one phenotypic effect is called
Pleiotropic

questions.question_text: A gene which affects two or more unrelated characteristics is called
questions.explanation_short: A single gene affecting two or more unrelated characters is pleiotropic.
questions.explanation_long: Pleiotropy is when one gene influences several apparently unrelated traits; for example, the sickle-cell allele affects red cell shape, resistance to malaria and damage to many organs. An epistatic gene masks another gene; dominant describes an allele that hides its partner; a mutant gene is simply altered.
questions.explanation_trick: Pleio = many: one gene, many effects.

explanation_options.a: Correct — one gene, several unrelated effects.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — an epistatic gene masks the effect of another gene.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — dominance is about one allele hiding another.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — mutant only means the gene is altered.

aliases: A gene which masks the expression of another non-allelic gene is called
Pleiotropic

questions.question_text: Position of a gene within a DNA molecule is
questions.explanation_short: The specific position of a gene on a DNA molecule/chromosome is called its locus.
questions.explanation_long: A gene's locus is its fixed physical location on a chromosome or DNA molecule, a fundamental concept in genetics distinguishing gene mapping from other unrelated terms.
questions.explanation_trick: Locus = the gene's 'address' on the chromosome.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the locus is the specific position of a gene on DNA.
explanation_options.b: Origin typically refers to the starting point of DNA replication, not a gene's position.
explanation_options.c: Amplicon refers to a DNA segment produced by amplification (e.g., PCR product), not gene position.
explanation_options.d: Filial refers to generational offspring in genetics crosses, unrelated to gene position.

questions.question_text: Sickle cell anemia is a type of
questions.explanation_short: Sickle cell anemia results from a base substitution mutation in the hemoglobin gene.
questions.explanation_long: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a single point mutation (base substitution) changing one amino acid (glutamic acid to valine) in the beta-globin chain, not an insertion, deletion, or transposition.
questions.explanation_trick: Sickle cell anemia = classic example of a point mutation (base substitution), not a frameshift mutation.

explanation_options.a: Insertion would add extra bases, causing a frameshift, not the single-base change seen in sickle cell anemia.
explanation_options.b: Transposition involves DNA segments moving position, not the mechanism behind sickle cell anemia.
explanation_options.c: Deletion would remove bases, causing a frameshift, unlike the specific single substitution in sickle cell anemia.
explanation_options.d: Correct — sickle cell anemia arises from a single base substitution mutation.

questions.question_text: In male the sex determining gene is
questions.explanation_short: The SRY gene on the Y chromosome is the male sex-determining gene.
questions.explanation_long: The SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene, located on the Y chromosome, triggers development of male characteristics (testes) in the embryo, making it the key sex-determining gene in males.
questions.explanation_trick: SRY = Sex-determining Region Y — the specific gene, not just the XY chromosome pair itself.

explanation_options.a: XY refers to the chromosome pair itself, not the specific gene responsible for triggering male development.
explanation_options.b: Correct — SRY is the specific gene on the Y chromosome that determines maleness.
explanation_options.c: 'SYX' is not a recognized gene name.
explanation_options.d: 'SXX' is not a recognized gene name.

papers.name: MDCAT 2015
papers.notes:
Full pass (Aug 2026) against learnospot.com/uhs-mdcat-past-paper-5 (independent full-paper transcription) plus direct chemistry/physics/biology verification and viewing the 6 already-attached source images. Went from 192 to 217 active+verified.

7 answer-key corrections (see prior note) + reconstructed/decoded 5 more from genuinely garbled OCR text where the underlying content was still recoverable (1865 dipeptide stem rewritten from decoded atoms + cross-confirmed against learnospot; 1893 IUPAC name decoded from structure fragments; 1896 SN2 mechanism decoded, textbook inversion confirms answer; 2035 'inhibits'->'stimulates' corrected, independently verified secretin stimulates pancreatic secretion; 1868 zwitterion reconstructed as the standard 4 protonation states of an amino acid, the canonical option set for this question type — correct option confirmed by a surviving text fragment).

3 remain inactive, and unlike the above, these are NOT being reconstructed because the missing information is positional/relational, not just badly formatted — there is no single well-defined 'standard' way to fill the gap without guessing:
- Q1902 (alpha-carbon): needs to know which drawn carbon was numbered '1' vs '2' vs '3' vs '4' in the original diagram — arbitrary per-diagram, not recoverable from text.
- Q1967 (food-web trophic level): needs the actual arrows/who-eats-whom relationships; a jumbled species list carries no relational information to reconstruct from.
- Q1900 (DNPH product): the correct chemical product IS knowable (acetaldehyde's 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone), but the 3 wrong options have no canonical standard form the way 1868's did — could have been a wrong reagent, wrong carbonyl, wrong stoichiometry, etc. — too open-ended to responsibly reconstruct.
papers.student_note: This paper has 217 of the original 220 questions. The remaining 3 (one Biology food-web question, two Chemistry structure questions) each need information from the original diagram that we could not recover from any available source, so they're left out rather than guessed at.

questions.question_text: One method of creating an inverted population is known as _________ and consist of illuminating the laser material with light.
questions.explanation_short: Population inversion is created by optical pumping, illuminating the laser material with light so more atoms sit in the excited state than the ground state.
questions.explanation_long: Optical pumping means shining light of the right energy onto the laser medium so atoms absorb photons and jump to a higher energy level. Done fast enough, more atoms end up excited than in the ground state — a population inversion, the condition needed for laser action.
questions.explanation_trick: "Pump" = push atoms up with light. Optical pumping = light does the pushing.

explanation_options.a: Correct — optical pumping is exactly the process of illuminating the laser material with light to create population inversion.
explanation_options.b: Excitation is the general result (an atom moving to a higher state), not the specific illumination technique used to achieve it.
explanation_options.c: Bremsstrahlung is X-ray radiation emitted when fast electrons decelerate near a nucleus — unrelated to laser pumping.
explanation_options.d: Holography is a 3D imaging technique using laser light, not a method of creating population inversion.

questions.question_text: In population inversion (Ruby Laser) atoms can reside in the excited state for:
questions.explanation_short: In a ruby laser the chromium ions sit in a metastable excited state for about 10⁻³ s, long enough for population inversion to build up.
questions.explanation_long: Ordinary excited states decay in about 10⁻⁸ s, far too quickly for many atoms to accumulate there. A ruby laser works because its upper lasing level is metastable: atoms stay in it for roughly 10⁻³ s, which lets more atoms collect in the excited state than in the ground state (population inversion). Note: the printed key for this paper marks 10⁻⁸ s, the lifetime of an ordinary excited state; the metastable lifetime that makes population inversion possible is 10⁻³ s.
questions.explanation_trick: Normal excited state ≈ 10⁻⁸ s; metastable (laser) state ≈ 10⁻³ s.

explanation_options.a: 10⁻¹¹ s is far shorter than any excited-state lifetime relevant to a laser.
explanation_options.b: About 10⁻⁸ s is the lifetime of an ordinary excited state — too short for population inversion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the metastable state of ruby holds atoms for about 10⁻³ s, allowing population inversion.
explanation_options.d: 10³ s (over 16 minutes) is vastly longer than any atomic excited-state lifetime.

aliases: In population inversion (Ruby Laser) atoms can reside in the excited state for:

questions.question_text: If electrons of charge ‘e’ moving with velocity ‘v’ are accelerated through a potential difference ‘V’ and strike a metal target, then velocity of electrons is:
questions.explanation_short: The electron gains kinetic energy eV, so ½mv² = eV and v = √(2Ve/m).
questions.explanation_long: Work done on charge e by a potential difference V is eV, and it all becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = eV. Rearranging gives v² = 2eV/m, so v = √(2Ve/m).
questions.explanation_trick: Charge through a p.d.: eV = ½mv² → v = √(2eV/m).

explanation_options.a: Ve/m has the units of v², not v — the square root and the factor 2 are both missing.
explanation_options.b: Missing the factor 2 that comes from ½mv².
explanation_options.c: The factor 2 belongs in the numerator, not the denominator.
explanation_options.d: Correct — from eV = ½mv², v = √(2Ve/m).

aliases: If electrons of charge ‘e’ moving with velocity ‘v’ are accelerated through a potential difference ‘V’ and strike a metal target, then velocity of electrons is: Ve Ve

questions.question_text: In X-ray tube, electrons after being accelerated through velocity ‘v’ strike the target, then the wavelength of emitted X-rays is:
questions.explanation_short: An electron can give at most its whole energy eV to one photon, so the X-ray wavelength is never less than λmin = hc/eV.
questions.explanation_long: The most energetic photon is produced when an electron loses all its kinetic energy eV in a single collision: hc/λmin = eV, so λmin = hc/eV. Every other photon carries less energy and therefore has a longer wavelength, so the emitted wavelengths are not less than hc/eV. Note: the printed key for this paper marks "equal to hc/eV", which is only the cut-off value; the continuous spectrum as a whole satisfies λ ≥ hc/eV.
questions.explanation_trick: Cut-off wavelength: λmin = hc/eV — everything else is longer.

explanation_options.a: Reverses the inequality — hc/eV is a lower limit on wavelength, not an upper one.
explanation_options.b: Correct — no photon can carry more than eV, so λ is never less than hc/eV.
explanation_options.c: h/mV is not the X-ray cut-off relation (it resembles a de Broglie wavelength with V in place of velocity).
explanation_options.d: hc/eV is only the shortest (cut-off) wavelength; most emitted X-rays are longer than this.

aliases: In X-ray tube, electrons after being accelerated through velocity ‘v’ strike the target, then the wavelength of emitted X-rays is: hc h
Not greater than

questions.question_text: In the reaction ²³⁴₉₂Th → ²³⁴₉₁Y + ⁰₋₁e, the electron ⁰₋₁e is emitted from the:
questions.explanation_short: In β-decay the electron is created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton; it does not come from an orbit.
questions.explanation_long: β-decay is a nuclear process: a neutron in the nucleus converts into a proton, an electron (the β-particle) and an antineutrino. The atomic number rises by one while the mass number stays the same. The emitted electron was never one of the orbital electrons.
questions.explanation_trick: β-particle = n → p + e⁻ inside the nucleus.

explanation_options.a: 1st-orbit electrons are ordinary atomic electrons, not β-particles.
explanation_options.b: 2nd-orbit electrons are ordinary atomic electrons, not β-particles.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the β electron is created in the nucleus as a neutron becomes a proton.
explanation_options.d: Valence electrons take part in chemistry, not in radioactive decay.

aliases: In the reaction, 234 92Th → 234 91Y + -10e the electron -10e emits from the
1st Orbit

questions.question_text: According to the equation X → Y + 3α particles, where X has atomic number Z and mass number A, what are the atomic and mass numbers of ‘Y’?
questions.explanation_short: Emitting 3 alpha particles removes 6 protons and 12 nucleons total, so Y has atomic number Z−6 and mass number A−12.
questions.explanation_long: Each alpha particle carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons (mass number 4, atomic number 2). Losing 3 alpha particles removes 3×2=6 protons and 3×4=12 nucleons total, so the daughter nuclide Y has atomic number Z−6 and mass number A−12.
questions.explanation_trick: Each alpha = −2 (atomic number), −4 (mass number). Three alphas = −6 and −12.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 3 alpha particles reduce Z by 6 and A by 12.
explanation_options.b: This matches the effect of only one alpha particle, not three.
explanation_options.c: An increase in Z or unchanged A is inconsistent with alpha emission, which always decreases both.
explanation_options.d: An increase in Z is inconsistent with alpha decay, which only removes protons, never adds them.

aliases: According to the equation ZX A → Y + 3α particles, what are the atomic and mass numbers of ‘Y’?

questions.question_text: A certain radioactive nuclide of mass number ‘x’ decays by β-emission and α-emission to a second nuclide of mass number ‘t’. Which of following correctly relates ‘x’ and ‘t’?
questions.explanation_short: Alpha decay reduces mass number by 4 while beta decay leaves mass number unchanged, so after one of each, x = t + 4.
questions.explanation_long: An alpha particle removes 4 nucleons (mass number drops by 4), while a beta particle is just an electron ejected from the nucleus and doesn't change the mass number at all. So going from mass number x to t via one alpha and one beta emission, only the alpha step matters for mass number: x − 4 = t, i.e. x = t + 4.
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha changes mass number by 4; beta changes it by 0.

explanation_options.a: Correct — only the alpha emission affects mass number, giving x = t + 4.
explanation_options.b: This has the sign backwards — mass number decreases with alpha emission, not increases.
explanation_options.c: A drop of only 3 doesn't match any combination of alpha (−4) and beta (0) mass-number changes.
explanation_options.d: A drop of only 1 doesn't match the −4 change caused by a single alpha particle.

questions.question_text: During the decay of radioactive isotope ²³²₉₀X to a stable isotope, six α-particles and four β-particles are emitted. What is the atomic number ‘Z’ and mass number ‘A’ of the stable isotope?
questions.explanation_short: Six alpha particles reduce Z by 12 and A by 24; four beta particles then increase Z by 4 with no further change to A, giving Z = 90−12+4 = 82 and A = 232−24 = 208.
questions.explanation_long: Starting nuclide has Z=90 (implied by ₉₀X). Each alpha removes 2 protons and 4 mass units: 6 alphas remove 12 protons and 24 mass units. Each beta emission converts a neutron to a proton, raising Z by 1 without changing A: 4 betas add 4 to Z. Net: Z = 90 − 12 + 4 = 82, and A = 232 − 24 = 208 (using the natural parent mass number 232, consistent with a thorium-232 decay series).
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha: Z−2, A−4. Beta: Z+1, A unchanged. Tally them separately.

explanation_options.a: Z=70 doesn't match 90−12+4=82; this option miscounts the proton changes.
explanation_options.b: Z=78 undercounts the +4 contribution from the four beta emissions.
explanation_options.c: A=212 doesn't match the mass-number arithmetic (232−24=208) for six alpha emissions.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Z = 82 and A = 208 follow from six alpha (−12, −24) and four beta (+4, 0) emissions starting from A=232, Z=90.

aliases: During the decay of radioactive isotopes 90X to a stable isotope, six α-particles and four β- particles are emitted, what is the atomic number ‘Z’ and mass number ‘A’ of the stable isotopes.

questions.question_text: Cobalt 60 is used in medicine and is an intense source of:
questions.explanation_short: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy as an intense source of γ-rays.
questions.explanation_long: Co-60 undergoes β-decay to an excited nickel-60 nucleus, which then emits two high-energy γ-ray photons (1.17 and 1.33 MeV). Those penetrating γ-rays are what medicine uses — for cancer radiotherapy and for sterilising equipment. The β-particles are low-energy and absorbed almost immediately.
questions.explanation_trick: Cobalt-60 = cancer therapy = gamma.

explanation_options.a: Co-60 does not emit α-particles.
explanation_options.b: Co-60 does emit weak β-particles, but they are not what makes it a useful medical source.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Co-60 is the classic intense γ-ray source for radiotherapy.
explanation_options.d: Co-60 decay does not release neutrons.

questions.question_text: In fluid flow, for the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. If velocity of the fluid at one end is doubled, then what will be the cross-sectional area at this end?
questions.explanation_short: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ means area is inversely proportional to velocity, so doubling v halves the area.
questions.explanation_long: For an incompressible fluid the volume flow rate Av is constant along the pipe. If v doubles at one end, A must become half so that the product stays the same.
questions.explanation_trick: Av = constant → A ∝ 1/v.

explanation_options.a: Doubling the area would double the flow rate, breaking continuity.
explanation_options.b: Correct — A ∝ 1/v, so doubling velocity halves the area.
explanation_options.c: (½)² = ¼ would apply only if A ∝ 1/v², which continuity does not say.
explanation_options.d: Area must decrease, not increase, when velocity increases.

aliases: In fluid flow, for the equation of continuity A 1v1 = A2v2. If velocity of the fluid at one end is doubled, then what will be the cross-sectional area at this end?
Double

questions.question_text: The value of least distance vision for normal eye is
questions.explanation_short: The least distance of distinct vision (near point) of a normal eye is 25 cm.
questions.explanation_long: A normal adult eye can focus sharply on objects no closer than about 25 cm. This near-point distance is the standard value used in formulas for the magnifying power of magnifiers and microscopes.
questions.explanation_trick: Near point d = 25 cm (M = 1 + d/f).

explanation_options.a: 20 cm is closer than a normal eye can comfortably focus.
explanation_options.b: 30 cm is not the standard near-point value.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the standard near point of a normal eye is 25 cm.
explanation_options.d: 40 cm is more typical of an ageing (presbyopic) eye.

questions.question_text: The distance between two dark adjacent fringes is mathematically written as:

questions.question_text: In normal adjustment of compound microscope, the eye piece is positioned so that the final image is formed at:
questions.explanation_short: In normal adjustment of a compound microscope, the eyepiece is positioned so the final image forms at the near point (least distance of distinct vision) for maximum magnification with least eye strain.

For a microscope, this final image is formed at the near point (about 25 cm), the closest point of clear vision, giving maximum usable magnification without straining the eye.

questions.question_text: Mathematical formula of maximum velocity (v₀) for a body executing simple harmonic motion is:
questions.explanation_short: In SHM the maximum speed, at the mean position, is v₀ = ωx₀.
questions.explanation_long: Velocity in SHM is v = ω√(x₀² − x²), where x₀ is the amplitude. At the mean position x = 0, so the speed is greatest: v₀ = ωx₀.
questions.explanation_trick: Max speed = ω × amplitude.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v₀ = ωx₀ at the mean position.
explanation_options.b: k/m equals ω², not ω, so this is dimensionally wrong.
explanation_options.c: This is a rearranged speed at a general displacement x, not the maximum.
explanation_options.d: Multiplying by mass m gives the wrong units for velocity.

questions.question_text: A body is having weight 20 N, when the elevator is descended with a = 0.1 ms⁻², then the value of tension ‘T’ is:
questions.explanation_short: Descending with acceleration a, T = m(g − a) = (20/9.8)(9.8 − 0.1) ≈ 19.8 N.
questions.explanation_long: The mass is m = W/g = 20/9.8 ≈ 2.04 kg. For downward acceleration, mg − T = ma, so T = m(g − a) = 2.04 × 9.7 ≈ 19.8 N — slightly less than the weight. Note: this paper's printed key marks 1.98 N, which is off by a factor of ten; 19.8 N is the physically correct tension.
questions.explanation_trick: Accelerating down → tension a little below weight.

explanation_options.b: Correct — T = m(g − a) ≈ 19.8 N.

questions.question_text: Sodium 24 has half-life of 15 hour and it is used in medicine to estimate:
questions.explanation_short: Radioactive sodium-24 is used as a tracer to measure plasma (blood) volume.
questions.explanation_long: Na-24 has a short 15-hour half-life and mixes evenly through the plasma. Injecting a known activity and measuring how diluted it becomes gives the plasma volume. Iron-59 is the isotope used for iron studies and iodine-131 for the thyroid.

explanation_options.c: Iron metabolism is traced with Fe-59, not Na-24.
explanation_options.d: The thyroid is studied with iodine-131.

questions.question_text: The unit of temperature in base unit is:
questions.explanation_short: The SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin.
questions.explanation_long: The seven SI base units include the kelvin (K) for thermodynamic temperature. Celsius and Fahrenheit are derived or non-SI scales, and "degree" is not a unit on its own.
questions.explanation_trick: SI base temperature unit: K, written without a degree sign.

explanation_options.a: Celsius is a derived scale, not the SI base unit.
explanation_options.b: "Degree" alone is not a defined unit.

explanation_options.d: Fahrenheit is a non-SI scale.

questions.question_text: The dimensions of pressure is:
questions.explanation_short: Pressure = force/area = (mass×acceleration)/area, giving dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻²].
questions.explanation_long: Force has dimensions [MLT⁻²]. Dividing by area [L²] gives pressure's dimensions: [MLT⁻²]/[L²] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²].
questions.explanation_trick: Pressure dimensions: take force [MLT⁻²] and divide by area [L²].

explanation_options.a: This dimensional combination doesn't reduce from force/area.
explanation_options.b: This is missing the correct negative time exponent needed for pressure.
explanation_options.c: This dimensional combination doesn't reduce from force/area.
explanation_options.d: Correct — [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is the standard dimensional formula for pressure.

questions.question_text: In Wilson Cloud Chamber which of the following tracks represented β-particles?
questions.explanation_short: In a Wilson cloud chamber, beta particles leave long, thin, wavy or curling tracks because they're light and easily scattered.
questions.explanation_long: Alpha particles are heavy and leave short, thick, straight tracks due to strong, consistent ionization. Beta particles, being much lighter electrons, are easily deflected by collisions, producing long, thin, wavy or curling tracks as they scatter through the chamber.
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha = short & thick & straight. Beta = long & thin & wavy.

explanation_options.a: This describes alpha-particle tracks (short, thick, straight), not beta.
explanation_options.b: Many short, thin tracks better fits scattered low-energy particles broadly but not the classic beta description.
explanation_options.c: Correct — beta particles produce long, thin, wavy/curling tracks due to their light mass and easy scattering.
explanation_options.d: Many short, dense, tangled tracks doesn't match the characteristically long, wavy beta track.

questions.question_text: Mass flow per second of the fluid is given by:
questions.explanation_short: Mass flow rate of a fluid equals density times cross-sectional area times velocity: ρAv.
questions.explanation_long: The mass passing a point per second equals the volume flow rate (Av) multiplied by the fluid's density (ρ), giving mass flow rate = ρAv — a direct consequence of the continuity equation applied to mass rather than volume.
questions.explanation_trick: Mass flow rate = density × area × velocity (ρAv).

explanation_options.a: Correct — ρAv is the standard formula for mass flow rate.
explanation_options.b: Av alone gives volume flow rate, not mass flow rate — it's missing the density factor.
explanation_options.c: This rearrangement doesn't correctly represent ρAv as a product of the three physical quantities.
explanation_options.d: ρ alone is just density, not a flow rate at all.

questions.question_text: The dimension of coefficient of viscosity is:
questions.explanation_short: Viscosity's dimensional formula is [ML⁻¹T⁻¹], derived from its definition as shear stress divided by velocity gradient.
questions.explanation_long: Viscosity η relates shear stress (force/area, [ML⁻¹T⁻²]) to velocity gradient (velocity/length, [T⁻¹]). Dividing gives [ML⁻¹T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹].
questions.explanation_trick: Viscosity dimensions: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹] — one power each of mass, inverse length, inverse time.

explanation_options.a: This combination has an extra inverse length power not present in viscosity's actual dimensions.
explanation_options.b: This combination has the wrong sign on the length exponent.
explanation_options.c: This combination has the wrong sign on the length exponent.
explanation_options.d: Correct — [ML⁻¹T⁻¹] is the standard dimensional formula for coefficient of viscosity.

aliases: The dimension of coefficient of viscosity is:

questions.question_text: What should be the length of simple pendulum whose period is 6.28 second at a place where g = 10 ms⁻².
questions.explanation_short: Using T = 2π√(L/g) with T = 6.28 s and g = 10 m/s², solving for L gives L = g(T/2π)² = 10×1² = 10 m.
questions.explanation_long: The pendulum period formula T = 2π√(L/g) rearranges to L = gT²/(4π²). Plugging in T = 6.28 s (which makes T/2π exactly 1 second) and g = 10 m/s² gives L = 10 × 1² = 10 m.
questions.explanation_trick: T = 6.28 s is a giveaway — since 2π ≈ 6.28, T/2π = 1, making the arithmetic simple: L = g × 1² = g.

explanation_options.a: 0.28 m is far too small for the given period and g value.
explanation_options.b: 10.8 m is close but doesn't match the exact calculation of L = g(T/2π)².
explanation_options.c: 6.28 m confuses the period value itself with the computed length.
explanation_options.d: Correct — L = g(T/2π)² = 10×1 = 10 m.

aliases: What should be the length of simple pendulum whose period is 6.28 second at a place where g = 10 ms-2.

questions.question_text: What should be the ratio of kinetic energy to total energy for simple harmonic oscillator?
questions.explanation_short: KE/E = ½k(x₀² − x²) ÷ ½kx₀² = 1 − x²/x₀².
questions.explanation_long: Total energy in SHM is E = ½kx₀². At displacement x the kinetic energy is ½k(x₀² − x²). Dividing gives KE/E = 1 − x²/x₀²: equal to 1 at the mean position and 0 at the extremes.
questions.explanation_trick: KE fraction = 1 − (x/x₀)².

explanation_options.a: Correct — KE/E = 1 − x²/x₀².
explanation_options.b: The ratio equals 1 only at x = 0, not in general.
explanation_options.c: Proportional to kinetic energy but not divided by total energy — not a ratio.
explanation_options.d: ½x² is not a dimensionless energy ratio.

aliases: What should be the ration of kinetic energy to total energy for simple harmonic oscillator? x2

questions.question_text: An observer moves with velocity ‘v₀’ toward a stationary source, then the number of waves received in one second is:
questions.explanation_short: An observer moving toward a stationary source meets waves faster: f′ = f(v + v₀)/v.
questions.explanation_long: Moving toward the source, the observer's speed relative to the waves is v + v₀ while the wavelength is unchanged, so the number of waves received per second rises to f′ = f(v + v₀)/v.
questions.explanation_trick: Observer moving: change the numerator; source moving: change the denominator.

explanation_options.a: v/(v + v₀) is the form for a source moving away, which lowers the frequency.
explanation_options.b: v/(v − v₀) is the form for a source moving toward the observer.
explanation_options.c: Correct — f′ = f(v + v₀)/v for an observer approaching a stationary source.
explanation_options.d: (v − v₀)/v is for an observer moving away from the source.

aliases: An observer moves with velocity ‘vo’ toward a stationary source, then the number of waves received in one second is: v v + vo

questions.question_text: Strain energy in a deformed energy is stored in the form of:
questions.explanation_short: Strain energy is stored in a deformed body as (elastic) potential energy.
questions.explanation_long: Work done in deforming a body is stored because of the change in its shape or configuration — that is potential energy, released when the body springs back.
questions.explanation_trick: Energy stored by position or shape = potential energy.

explanation_options.a: "Elastic energy" describes the source, but the energy form asked for is potential energy.
explanation_options.b: Correct — strain energy is elastic potential energy.
explanation_options.c: Plastic deformation dissipates energy rather than storing it.
explanation_options.d: A statically deformed body is not moving, so it has no kinetic energy.

questions.question_text: A wire of area of cross section ‘A’ and original length ‘l’ is subjected to a load ‘L’. A second wire of same material with an area is ‘2A’ and length ‘2l’ is subjected to the same load ‘L’. If the extension in first wire is ‘X’ and second wire is ‘Y’, find the ratio ‘X/Y’.
questions.explanation_short: Extension = Fl/(AY). The second wire has 2l/2A = l/A, so its extension is the same: X/Y = 1/1.
questions.explanation_long: From Young's modulus, extension ΔL = FL/(AY). Both wires carry the same load and are the same material. For the second wire, length and area both double, so L/A is unchanged and the extension is identical. Hence X/Y = 1.
questions.explanation_trick: ΔL ∝ L/A — double both, nothing changes.

explanation_options.a: 1/4 would need the second wire's L/A to be four times larger.
explanation_options.b: 1/2 would need only the length to double.
explanation_options.c: Correct — L/A is unchanged, so the extensions are equal.
explanation_options.d: 2/1 would need only the area to double.

questions.question_text: Two sample of gases ‘1’ and ‘2’ are taken at same temperature and pressure but the ratio of number of their volume is V₁:V₂ = 2:3. What is the ration of number of moles of the gas sample?
questions.explanation_short: At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes contain equal numbers of moles (Avogadro's law), so the mole ratio equals the volume ratio, 2:3.
questions.explanation_long: Avogadro's law states that at fixed temperature and pressure, volume is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas. Since V1:V2 = 2:3, the mole ratio n1:n2 must also be 2:3.
questions.explanation_trick: Same T and P → moles ratio = volume ratio directly (Avogadro's law).

explanation_options.c: Squaring the ratio isn't justified by Avogadro's law, which is a direct proportionality.
explanation_options.d: Correct — by Avogadro's law, the mole ratio directly equals the given volume ratio, 2:3.

questions.explanation_long: Kinetic theory gives the pressure of a gas as P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩. Solving for the root-mean-square speed gives vrms = √(3P/ρ).

questions.question_text: When the rate of gas changes without change in temperature, the gas is said to undergo:
questions.explanation_short: A process where pressure changes at constant temperature (with volume adjusting accordingly) is called an isothermal process.
questions.explanation_long: "Isothermal" specifically means constant temperature. When a gas's pressure (and correspondingly its volume, via Boyle's law) changes while temperature is held fixed, that's an isothermal process — distinct from adiabatic (no heat exchange), isochoric (constant volume), or isobaric (constant pressure) processes.
questions.explanation_trick: Iso-thermal = same temperature throughout the process.

explanation_options.a: Correct — isothermal specifically describes a process at constant temperature.
explanation_options.b: Adiabatic refers to no heat transfer, not constant temperature.
explanation_options.c: Isochoric refers to constant volume, not constant temperature.
explanation_options.d: Isobaric refers to constant pressure, not constant temperature.

questions.question_text: What is the 273 k on the Celsius scale of temperature?
questions.explanation_long: Absolute zero is −273.15 °C, so converting kelvin to Celsius means subtracting 273.15. 273 K is therefore 0.15 degrees below the freezing point of water: −0.15 °C.
questions.explanation_trick: Subtract 273.15 — careful with the extra 0.15.

questions.question_text: If heat ‘Q₁’ is absorbed at temperature ‘T’ and heat ‘Q₂’ is absorbed at temperature of triple point of water, then unknown temperature of system (in K) is:
questions.explanation_short: By the thermodynamic definition of the Kelvin scale using the triple point of water as reference, the unknown temperature is T = 273.16 × (Q1/Q2).
questions.explanation_long: The thermodynamic (Kelvin) temperature scale is defined by comparing heat exchanged at an unknown temperature to heat exchanged at the fixed triple point of water (273.16 K): T/273.16 = Q1/Q2, giving T = 273.16 × Q1/Q2.

questions.question_text: Which combinations of seven identical resistors each of 2 Ω gives rise to the resultant of 10/11 Ω?
questions.explanation_short: Two 2 Ω in parallel give 1 Ω; five in series give 10 Ω; these two groups in parallel give (1 × 10)/(1 + 10) = 10/11 Ω.
questions.explanation_long: Split the seven resistors into a group of 2 in parallel (2/2 = 1 Ω) and a group of 5 in series (5 × 2 = 10 Ω). Connecting the two groups in parallel gives R = (1 × 10)/(1 + 10) = 10/11 Ω.

explanation_options.b: 4 in parallel (0.5 Ω) with 3 in series (6 Ω) gives 3/6.5 ≈ 0.46 Ω.
explanation_options.c: 3 in parallel (⅔ Ω) with 4 in series (8 Ω) gives about 0.62 Ω.
explanation_options.d: Correct — (2 ∥) = 1 Ω and (5 in series) = 10 Ω; 1 ∥ 10 = 10/11 Ω.

questions.explanation_short: Each third of the wire is R/3; three equal R/3 resistors in parallel give (R/3)/3 = R/9.

questions.question_text: The resistance of a piece of wire is 12 Ω. It is bent to form an equilateral triangle. What is the equivalent resistance between any two corners of the triangles?
questions.explanation_short: Each side is 4 Ω. Between two corners, one side (4 Ω) is in parallel with the other two in series (8 Ω): 32/12 ≈ 2.7 Ω.
questions.explanation_long: The 12 Ω wire makes three 4 Ω sides. Between any two corners, one side (4 Ω) is in parallel with the path through the other two sides (8 Ω), so R = (4 × 8)/(4 + 8) = 2.67 Ω ≈ 2.7 Ω. Note: this paper's printed key marks 2.0 Ω, but the circuit gives 2.7 Ω.

explanation_options.c: 4.0 Ω is a single side, ignoring the parallel path.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 4 Ω ∥ 8 Ω = 2.67 Ω ≈ 2.7 Ω.

questions.question_text: Magnetic field strength is measure in:
questions.explanation_short: Magnetic field strength (flux density) B is flux per unit area: Wb m⁻², which is the tesla.
