questions.explanation_long: Pyrogens (e.g. released during infection) act on the hypothalamus to raise its temperature set point, which is why the body then generates and conserves heat (shivering, vasoconstriction) until it reaches this new, higher 'target' temperature — producing a fever.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Pyro-' = fire/heat — pyrogens are literally the fever-causing agents.

explanation_options.a: Pepsin is a digestive enzyme in the stomach, unrelated to the hypothalamic set point.
explanation_options.b: Correct — pyrogens raise the hypothalamus's temperature set point, producing fever.
explanation_options.c: Prions are misfolded infectious proteins (e.g. in CJD), not set-point regulators.
explanation_options.d: Androgens are sex hormones, not set-point regulators.

questions.question_text: During inspiration the space inside the chest cavity is increased due to:
questions.option_b: The relaxation of the muscles of the diaphragm
questions.option_c: Relaxation of the external intercostal muscles
questions.option_d: The contraction of the muscles of the diaphragm
questions.explanation_short: Diaphragm contraction flattens it downward, enlarging the chest cavity during inspiration.
questions.explanation_long: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract to lift the ribs up and out. Both actions increase the volume of the chest cavity, dropping pressure inside it below atmospheric pressure so air flows in.
questions.explanation_trick: Contraction of the diaphragm enlarges the chest — relaxation of the diaphragm is what happens on expiration, the opposite of what this question describes.

explanation_options.a: Pressure decreases (not increases) inside the chest as its volume increases — that's what draws air in.
explanation_options.b: Relaxation of the diaphragm is what happens during expiration, which shrinks the cavity, not expands it.
explanation_options.c: It's contraction, not relaxation, of the external intercostal muscles that raises the rib cage during inspiration.
explanation_options.d: Correct — diaphragm contraction flattens it downward, increasing chest cavity volume during inspiration.

questions.question_text: Which of the following hormone stimulates the ovulation from the follicle into oviduct?
questions.explanation_short: The LH surge triggers ovulation, releasing the egg from the follicle into the oviduct.
questions.explanation_long: A mid-cycle surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) triggers the final maturation and rupture of the dominant follicle, releasing the secondary oocyte into the oviduct — this is ovulation.
questions.explanation_trick: LH surge = ovulation trigger; FSH drives earlier follicle growth, not the release itself.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the LH surge triggers ovulation, the release of the oocyte from the follicle.
explanation_options.b: FSH stimulates follicle growth earlier in the cycle but is not the trigger for ovulation itself.
explanation_options.c: Estrogen regulates the cycle (and triggers the LH surge) but doesn't directly cause ovulation.
explanation_options.d: Progesterone maintains the uterine lining after ovulation; it doesn't trigger the release of the egg.

questions.question_text: The covalent bond or bridge between two monosaccharides to form a disaccharide is called a:
questions.explanation_short: The bond linking two monosaccharides into a disaccharide is a glycosidic bond.
questions.explanation_long: When two monosaccharides join via a condensation reaction (losing a water molecule), the covalent bond formed between them is called a glycosidic bond — e.g. the bond linking glucose and fructose in sucrose.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Glyco-' signals sugar — glycosidic bond = the sugar-linking bond formed in condensation reactions.

explanation_options.a: A carboxyl bond isn't a recognized sugar-linking bond type.
explanation_options.b: A hydroxyl bond isn't a bond category — hydroxyl (-OH) groups are what react to form the glycosidic bond.
explanation_options.c: Hydrogen bonds are weak intermolecular attractions, not the covalent bond joining monosaccharides.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the glycosidic bond is the covalent bond joining two monosaccharides into a disaccharide.

questions.question_text: Site of protein synthesis is:
questions.explanation_short: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis (translation).
questions.explanation_long: Ribosomes — free in the cytoplasm or bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum — translate mRNA into polypeptide chains, making them the cell's protein synthesis machinery.
questions.explanation_trick: Ribosomes = 'protein factories'; don't confuse with lysosomes (digestion) which sound similar.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins.
explanation_options.b: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break substances down; they don't synthesize protein.
explanation_options.c: The Golgi body modifies, sorts, and packages proteins after synthesis — it doesn't make them.
explanation_options.d: Cisternae are membrane sacs (e.g. within the ER/Golgi) used for transport and storage, not protein synthesis.

questions.question_text: Water and Minerals move down their concentration gradient through plasmodesmata, to cells of cortex, endodermis, pericycle and then to sap in the xylem cells. This is also known as the
questions.explanation_short: Movement of water/minerals through the continuous cytoplasm of connected cells (via plasmodesmata) is the symplastic pathway.
questions.explanation_long: In the symplastic pathway, water and dissolved minerals move through the living cytoplasm of connected plant cells, passing cell to cell via plasmodesmata, eventually reaching the xylem sap — distinct from the apoplastic pathway, which moves through cell walls and intercellular spaces outside the cell membrane.
questions.explanation_trick: Sym- = 'together' — symplastic pathway travels through the shared, connected cytoplasm (via plasmodesmata).

explanation_options.a: Correct — movement through the connected cytoplasm via plasmodesmata is the symplastic pathway.
explanation_options.b: 'Mineral absorption pathway' isn't one of the two recognized water/mineral transport routes (symplastic vs apoplastic).
explanation_options.c: The vacuolar pathway is a variant that also passes through cell vacuoles, but the question describes movement via plasmodesmata connecting cytoplasm, which is specifically symplastic.
explanation_options.d: The apoplastic pathway moves through cell walls and intercellular spaces, not through plasmodesmata connecting living cytoplasm.

questions.question_text: Given below is the diagram of nephron without vascular supply. What is name of Part C?
questions.explanation_short: Part C in the nephron diagram (the coiled tubule directly after the loop of Henle, before the collecting duct) is the distal convoluted tubule.
questions.explanation_long: Following the nephron's tubule from the glomerulus: A (proximal convoluted tubule) → loop of Henle (descending/ascending, labeled B/D) → C (distal convoluted tubule) → collecting duct. C sits in the position of the distal tubule, closest to where it joins the collecting duct.
questions.explanation_trick: Trace the nephron in order: proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct — match each labeled part to its position in that sequence.

explanation_options.a: The collecting duct is the final straight tube after the distal tubule, not the coiled part labeled C.
explanation_options.b: The proximal tubule (usually labeled A, right after the glomerulus) is a different, earlier part of the nephron.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Part C, positioned after the loop of Henle and before the collecting duct, is the distal convoluted tubule.
explanation_options.d: The loop of Henle is the long hairpin section connecting the proximal and distal tubules, a different structure from C.

questions.question_text: Xerophytes have small thick leaves to:
questions.option_b: Help them survive in salty environment
questions.option_c: Limit water loss by reducing the surface area
questions.option_d: Limit water loss by increasing the surface area
questions.explanation_short: Xerophytes have small, thick leaves to reduce surface area and limit water loss by transpiration.
questions.explanation_long: Small, thick leaves reduce the surface area exposed to air, cutting down the rate of transpiration — a key adaptation that helps xerophytes conserve water in dry habitats.
questions.explanation_trick: Smaller surface area = less water lost to transpiration — the core xerophyte strategy.

explanation_options.a: Floating on water is a hydrophyte adaptation, not relevant to dry-adapted xerophytes.
explanation_options.b: Surviving salty environments describes halophytes, a different adaptation from general water conservation.
explanation_options.c: Correct — reducing surface area with small, thick leaves limits water loss by transpiration.
explanation_options.d: Increasing surface area would increase, not limit, water loss — the opposite of what xerophyte leaves do.

questions.question_text: Among followings which cellular organelle contains circular DNA similar to those found in bacteria?
questions.explanation_short: Chloroplasts (like mitochondria) contain their own small circular DNA, a legacy of their bacterial ancestry.
questions.explanation_long: Both chloroplasts and mitochondria have their own circular DNA, similar to bacterial chromosomes, supporting the endosymbiotic theory that these organelles descended from once free-living prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
questions.explanation_trick: Circular DNA in an organelle is the tell-tale sign of the endosymbiotic theory — think chloroplasts and mitochondria together.

explanation_options.a: Ribosomes are protein-synthesis structures, not DNA-containing organelles.
explanation_options.b: Lysosomes are digestive vesicles; they don't contain their own DNA.
explanation_options.c: Correct — chloroplasts contain circular DNA, similar to bacterial DNA, supporting their bacterial origin.
explanation_options.d: The nucleus contains linear, not circular, chromosomal DNA.

questions.question_text: A person was married to his cousin and both are heterozygous for sickle cell anemia. Among their four kids, what will be the proportion of affected homozygotes?
questions.explanation_short: Two carrier (Aa × Aa) parents have a 1/4 (25%) chance per child of an affected homozygote (aa).
questions.explanation_long: Both parents are heterozygous carriers (Aa) for sickle cell trait. Crossing Aa × Aa gives offspring in a 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa ratio, so the proportion of affected homozygotes (aa) among the children is 25%.
questions.explanation_trick: Aa × Aa is the classic monohybrid cross — always gives a 1:2:1 genotype ratio, so 25% homozygous recessive.

explanation_options.a: 50% is the proportion of heterozygous carriers (Aa), not the homozygous affected (aa) group.
explanation_options.b: Correct — a standard Aa × Aa cross gives 25% aa (affected homozygotes).
explanation_options.c: 75% would be the proportion showing the dominant phenotype (unaffected carriers + normal), not the affected homozygote proportion specifically.
explanation_options.d: 100% would only occur if both parents were themselves homozygous affected (aa × aa), not carriers.

questions.question_text: The route of urine excretion from kidney to outside of body is:
questions.explanation_short: Urine flows kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → outside the body.
questions.explanation_long: Urine is formed in the kidneys, drains through the ureters to the urinary bladder for storage, and finally leaves the body through the urethra during urination.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the order alphabetically-ish: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra — each tube named for where it carries urine next.

explanation_options.a: Correct — kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra is the correct order of urine excretion.
explanation_options.b: This reverses the order entirely; urine starts at the kidney, it doesn't end there.
explanation_options.c: This skips the bladder before the urethra, which is incorrect — urine is stored in the bladder before passing through the urethra.
explanation_options.d: This has urethra and bladder swapped — urine passes through the urethra last, after leaving the bladder.

questions.question_text: The phase of mitosis in which sister chromatids move towards opposite poles:
questions.explanation_short: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during anaphase.
questions.explanation_long: In anaphase, the centromeres split and spindle fibers pull the now-separate sister chromatids to opposite poles of the cell, setting up two identical sets of chromosomes for the two daughter cells.
questions.explanation_trick: An-'apart'-phase — anaphase is when the chromatids move apart.

explanation_options.a: Prophase is when chromosomes condense and the spindle begins to form, before any separation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — anaphase is the stage where sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
explanation_options.c: Telophase is after separation, when chromosomes decondense and nuclear envelopes reform.
explanation_options.d: Metaphase is when chromosomes align at the cell's equator, just before they separate.

questions.question_text: The Plasmid pBR322 has antibiotic resistance genes for:
questions.explanation_short: Plasmid pBR322 carries resistance genes for ampicillin and tetracycline, a classic selectable-marker plasmid.
questions.explanation_long: pBR322 is a widely used cloning vector carrying two antibiotic-resistance genes — ampicillin resistance (ampR) and tetracycline resistance (tetR) — which let researchers select for bacteria that have taken up the plasmid.
questions.explanation_trick: pBR322 is the textbook example: remember it by its two markers, Amp and Tet resistance.

explanation_options.a: Doxycycline resistance isn't one of pBR322's two classic markers (it's tetracycline, a related but distinct drug).
explanation_options.b: Streptomycin resistance is not one of pBR322's markers.
explanation_options.c: pBR322 carries ampicillin (not doxycycline) resistance alongside tetracycline resistance.
explanation_options.d: Correct — pBR322 famously carries genes for resistance to ampicillin and tetracycline.

questions.question_text: The nitrogen containing bases in nucleotide are of two types; Purines and Pyrimidines; the purines bases are:
questions.explanation_short: The purine bases are adenine and guanine (the double-ring nitrogenous bases).
questions.explanation_long: Nitrogenous bases split into purines (double-ring: adenine and guanine) and pyrimidines (single-ring: cytosine, thymine, uracil). So the purine bases are specifically adenine and guanine.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember 'PURe As Gold' — PURines = Adenine and Guanine.

explanation_options.a: Cytosine is a pyrimidine, not a purine, so this pairing is wrong.
explanation_options.b: Cytosine (a pyrimidine) is incorrectly grouped here with the purines.
explanation_options.c: Correct — adenine and guanine are the two purine bases.
explanation_options.d: Thymine is a pyrimidine, not a purine, so this pairing is wrong.

questions.question_text: The following flowchart depicts the steps of the Calvin Cycle. Which option according to you fits in as the correct answer of the missing step?
questions.explanation_short: The missing step regenerating the CO2 acceptor in the Calvin cycle is ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP).
questions.explanation_long: The Calvin cycle's final stage regenerates ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) from G3P, using the remaining ATP — RuBP is what Rubisco then combines with a new CO2 molecule to restart the cycle. This regeneration step is the missing box in the diagram, feeding back into Rubisco.
questions.explanation_trick: The cycle only keeps turning because RuBP is regenerated each round — that's the missing link back to Rubisco.

explanation_options.a: Hydrogenase isn't part of the Calvin cycle.
explanation_options.b: Oxaloacetate belongs to the Krebs cycle (or C4 photosynthesis), not the standard Calvin cycle.
explanation_options.c: Correct — ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) is regenerated to complete the cycle and combine with CO2 again.
explanation_options.d: Pyruvate is a glycolysis product, unrelated to the Calvin cycle.

questions.question_text: DNA polymerase enzyme for PCR is isolated from bacteria Thermus aquaticus because:
questions.option_a: It can withstand high denaturation temperature.
questions.option_b: It can withstand low denaturation temperature.
questions.option_c: It can work at high speed
questions.option_d: It can be used again and again.
questions.explanation_short: Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus) is used in PCR because it withstands the high denaturation temperatures (~95°C) of each cycle.
questions.explanation_long: PCR repeatedly heats DNA to ~95°C to denature (separate) the strands. An ordinary DNA polymerase would be destroyed at this temperature, but Taq polymerase — from the heat-loving bacterium Thermus aquaticus — is heat-stable and survives repeated denaturation cycles, so it doesn't need to be replenished each round.
questions.explanation_trick: Thermus aquaticus lives in hot springs — its polymerase is built to survive heat, exactly what repeated PCR denaturation demands.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Taq polymerase's heat tolerance lets it survive PCR's high denaturation temperature each cycle.
explanation_options.b: PCR's denaturation step uses high, not low, temperatures — Taq's usefulness is its high-temperature stability.
explanation_options.c: Speed isn't the key reason Taq is chosen; its defining advantage is heat stability across repeated cycles.
explanation_options.d: Reusability follows from its heat stability — but the underlying reason is that it withstands the high denaturation temperature, not reusability itself as a separate property.

questions.question_text: The type of energy reduced by the enzymes for biological reactions to occur is called the:
questions.explanation_short: The energy barrier enzymes lower for a reaction to occur is called the activation energy.
questions.explanation_long: Activation energy is the minimum energy input needed to get reactants over the energy barrier to form products. Enzymes work by lowering this activation energy, making reactions proceed faster at body temperature.
questions.explanation_trick: Enzymes are catalysts — catalysts always work by lowering activation energy, never by changing the reaction's overall energy release.

explanation_options.a: Light energy is a specific energy source (e.g., in photosynthesis), not the general term for the energy barrier of a reaction.
explanation_options.b: Correct — activation energy is the energy barrier that enzymes lower to speed up reactions.
explanation_options.c: 'Active energy' isn't a standard biochemical term.
explanation_options.d: Heat energy is a form of energy, not the specific term for the barrier enzymes reduce.

questions.question_text: The function of calcium ions in muscle contraction is to:
questions.option_a: Bind to troponin molecule and cause them to move
questions.option_b: Aid in the transmission of nerve impulse
questions.option_d: Bind to tropomyosin molecule and cause them to form cross bridges
questions.explanation_short: Calcium ions bind to troponin, shifting tropomyosin and exposing the actin-binding sites needed for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_long: When calcium is released into the sarcoplasm, it binds to troponin on the actin filament. This causes a conformational change that moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing myosin heads to bind and form cross-bridges, driving contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Ca2+ binds troponin (not tropomyosin directly) — troponin's shape change is what then moves tropomyosin out of the way.

explanation_options.a: Correct — calcium binds troponin, triggering the shift that exposes actin's myosin-binding sites.
explanation_options.b: Nerve impulse transmission at the neuromuscular junction relies on acetylcholine, not calcium acting on troponin.
explanation_options.c: Calcium doesn't polarize light; that's unrelated to muscle contraction physiology.
explanation_options.d: Calcium binds troponin, not tropomyosin directly — tropomyosin only moves as a secondary effect.

questions.question_text: What is common in both Competitive and Non-Competitive Inhibition?
questions.explanation_short: Both competitive and non-competitive inhibition are reversible types of enzyme inhibition.
questions.explanation_long: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly at the active site (blocked by raising substrate concentration), while non-competitive inhibitors bind reversibly elsewhere on the enzyme (not overcome by more substrate). Both are reversible — the inhibitor can detach and normal activity can resume — unlike irreversible inhibition.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Competitive vs non-competitive' describes where they bind; 'reversible vs irreversible' describes whether they detach — these two are both reversible types.

explanation_options.a: Irreversible inhibition permanently disables the enzyme — the opposite of what both of these types do.
explanation_options.b: Feedback inhibition is a specific regulatory mechanism (end-product inhibits an earlier enzyme), not a shared property of these two.
explanation_options.c: Correct — both competitive and non-competitive inhibition are reversible forms of inhibition.
explanation_options.d: 'Non-reversible' contradicts the actual shared property — both these inhibition types are reversible, not irreversible.

questions.question_text: Inside ovary, primary oocyte divides through first meiotic division forming two haploid cells, secondary oocyte and:
questions.explanation_short: Meiosis I of the primary oocyte produces a secondary oocyte and a polar body (the smaller, non-functional cell).
questions.explanation_long: The primary oocyte's first meiotic division is unequal: most of the cytoplasm goes to the large secondary oocyte, while the rest of the genetic material is discarded into a small, non-functional first polar body.
questions.explanation_trick: Oogenesis divisions are unequal on purpose — the polar body is the 'genetic trash' cell that lets the egg keep most of the cytoplasm/nutrients.

explanation_options.a: Correct — meiosis I of the primary oocyte produces a secondary oocyte and a (first) polar body.
explanation_options.b: An oogonium is the earlier, undifferentiated diploid stem cell that gives rise to primary oocytes, not a product of meiosis I.
explanation_options.c: A follicle cell is a supporting somatic cell surrounding the oocyte, not a product of its meiotic division.
explanation_options.d: An ovum (mature egg) only forms after meiosis II is completed, typically after fertilization triggers it — not directly from meiosis I.

questions.question_text: Homozygous means:
questions.option_a: having two identical alleles of a gene.
questions.option_d: two different alleles of a gene.
questions.explanation_short: Homozygous means having two identical alleles of the same gene.
questions.explanation_long: An organism is homozygous for a gene when both alleles at that locus (one from each parent) are identical — e.g. AA or aa. Heterozygous, by contrast, means the two alleles differ (e.g. Aa).
questions.explanation_trick: Homo- = same; homozygous = same alleles at a locus, not just 'same genes' in general.

explanation_options.a: Correct — homozygous means two identical alleles of the same gene.
explanation_options.b: 'Two identical genes' is imprecise — homozygosity is about identical alleles at one specific gene locus, not generic gene copies.
explanation_options.c: 'Alleles in an organism' is too vague — it doesn't capture the requirement that the two alleles be identical.
explanation_options.d: Two different alleles of a gene describes heterozygous, the opposite condition.

questions.question_text: Which hormonal pair would maintain the endometrium and make it receptive for implantation of embryo?
questions.option_c: Luteinising Hormone and Follicle Stimulating Hormone
questions.explanation_short: Estrogen and progesterone together maintain the endometrium and prepare it for embryo implantation.
questions.explanation_long: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes both estrogen and progesterone, which thicken and vascularize the endometrium, making it receptive to a fertilized embryo.
questions.explanation_trick: LH and FSH trigger the cycle's events, but it's the ovarian hormones — estrogen and progesterone — that actually build up and maintain the uterine lining.

explanation_options.a: LH is a pituitary trigger hormone, not one of the two hormones that directly maintain the endometrium.
explanation_options.b: FSH stimulates follicle development, not endometrial maintenance.
explanation_options.c: LH and FSH are pituitary hormones that regulate the ovary, not the pair that directly maintains the endometrium.
explanation_options.d: Correct — estrogen and progesterone together maintain and prepare the endometrium for implantation.

questions.question_text: Starch is present in tubers, fruits and grains but absent in animal cells, instead animals have a substance stored in liver and muscles known as:
questions.explanation_short: Animals store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles, the animal equivalent of plant starch.
questions.explanation_long: Plants store excess glucose as starch, while animals store it as glycogen, a similarly branched glucose polymer, mainly stockpiled in liver and muscle cells for quick energy mobilization.
questions.explanation_trick: Starch is to plants what glycogen is to animals — both are storage polysaccharides of glucose.

explanation_options.a: Glucose is the simple sugar itself, not the storage form animals keep it in.
explanation_options.b: Correct — glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, kept mainly in liver and muscle.
explanation_options.c: Galactose is a different monosaccharide, not a storage polysaccharide.
explanation_options.d: Glucagon is a hormone that triggers glycogen breakdown, not the stored substance itself.

questions.question_text: Now-a-days every new born gets regular shots of vaccine for polio. It contains _______________ for polio to make a child immune against this disease.
questions.explanation_short: Vaccines contain antigens that stimulate the immune system to build immunity without causing the disease.
questions.explanation_long: A vaccine introduces antigens (from a weakened, inactivated, or partial pathogen) that the immune system recognizes and responds to by producing antibodies and memory cells, providing immunity without the child developing the actual disease.
questions.explanation_trick: Vaccines put in antigens; the body then makes its own antibodies in response — don't confuse the two.

explanation_options.a: Antisera contain ready-made antibodies given for immediate, passive protection, not what a vaccine typically supplies.
explanation_options.b: Antibodies are what the body produces in response to a vaccine, not what a standard vaccine directly contains.
explanation_options.c: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections; they have nothing to do with triggering immunity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — vaccines contain antigens that trigger the immune system to build active immunity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following blood vessels contain semilunar valves?
questions.explanation_short: Veins contain pocket-shaped semilunar valves along their length that stop blood flowing backwards.
questions.explanation_long: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so veins (especially in the limbs) have semilunar, pocket-like valves that open toward the heart and close against backflow. Arteries carry high-pressure blood and have no valves in their walls; the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves sit at the exits of the ventricles, where these arteries leave the heart. The UHS key and the FSc textbook give veins.
questions.explanation_trick: Low-pressure vessels need valves → veins.

explanation_options.a: Arteries have no valves along their walls; the aortic and pulmonary valves belong to the heart's outlets.
explanation_options.b: Correct — veins have semilunar valves that prevent backflow.
explanation_options.c: Arterioles have no valves.
explanation_options.d: Capillaries are one cell thick and have no valves.

questions.question_text: The main neurotransmitter for synapses is _________ which lie outside the central nervous system.
questions.explanation_short: Acetylcholine is the main neurotransmitter used at synapses in the peripheral nervous system, outside the CNS.
questions.explanation_long: Acetylcholine (ACh) is released at many peripheral synapses — including the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia — making it the principal neurotransmitter operating outside the central nervous system.
questions.explanation_trick: ACh = the classic peripheral neurotransmitter; noradrenaline is the other major one, but ACh is specifically highlighted at junctions like the neuromuscular junction.

explanation_options.a: Choline is a precursor/breakdown product involved in acetylcholine's synthesis and recycling, not the neurotransmitter itself.
explanation_options.b: Correct — acetylcholine is the main neurotransmitter operating at synapses outside the CNS.
explanation_options.c: Acetaldehyde is a metabolic intermediate (e.g. in alcohol metabolism), unrelated to synaptic transmission.
explanation_options.d: Phosphatidylcholine is a membrane phospholipid, not a neurotransmitter.

questions.question_text: The thick filaments in a myofibril of muscles are made of ___________.
questions.explanation_short: Thick filaments in a myofibril are made of the protein myosin.
questions.explanation_long: A sarcomere's thick filaments are composed of myosin molecules, whose globular heads form cross-bridges with the thin (actin) filaments to generate the sliding motion of muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Thick = myosin, thin = actin — a simple pairing worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells, unrelated to myofibril structure.
explanation_options.b: Myoglobin stores oxygen within muscle cells; it's not a structural filament protein.
explanation_options.c: Actin makes up the thin filaments, not the thick ones.
explanation_options.d: Correct — myosin is the protein making up the thick filaments of a myofibril.

questions.question_text: The prokaryotes possess small ribosome of size:
questions.explanation_short: Prokaryotic ribosomes are the smaller 70S type (versus 80S in eukaryotes).
questions.explanation_long: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (made of 30S and 50S subunits), smaller than the 80S ribosomes found in the eukaryotic cytoplasm — a difference exploited by many antibiotics that selectively target 70S ribosomes.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember '70S prokaryotes, 80S eukaryotes' as a fixed pair.

explanation_options.a: 40S is one subunit of the eukaryotic 80S ribosome, not the whole prokaryotic ribosome.
explanation_options.b: Correct — prokaryotic ribosomes are the smaller 70S type.
explanation_options.c: 65S is not a standard ribosome size used in biology.
explanation_options.d: 60S is the other subunit of the eukaryotic 80S ribosome, not the prokaryotic ribosome itself.

questions.question_text: The structure present in a eukaryotic cell but absent in prokaryotic cells is
questions.explanation_short: A true, membrane-bound nucleus is present in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotic cells.
questions.explanation_long: Eukaryotic cells house their DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus, while prokaryotic cells have their DNA free in the cytoplasm (in a nucleoid region) without a surrounding nuclear envelope — the defining structural difference between the two cell types.
questions.explanation_trick: Eu-karyotic = 'true nucleus'; pro-karyotic = 'before nucleus' — the nucleus itself is the giveaway feature.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a membrane-bound nucleus is present in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotic cells.
explanation_options.b: Both cell types contain DNA; it's the membrane-bound nucleus housing it that differs, not DNA's presence.
explanation_options.c: Both cell types have ribosomes (70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes) — ribosomes themselves aren't the exclusive feature.
explanation_options.d: Both cell types have a cell surface (plasma) membrane.

questions.question_text: The process in which a complementary copy of the code from a gene is produced by RNA Polymerase in the nucleus:
questions.explanation_short: RNA polymerase producing a complementary mRNA copy of a gene in the nucleus is called transcription.
questions.explanation_long: Transcription is the process by which RNA polymerase reads a gene's DNA template and synthesizes a complementary mRNA strand, which then carries the genetic code out of the nucleus for translation.
questions.explanation_trick: Trans-'script'-ion = copying DNA's script into RNA — the direct DNA-to-RNA copying step.

explanation_options.a: Proof reading refers to error-checking during DNA replication, not RNA synthesis.
explanation_options.b: DNA replication copies DNA into DNA, using DNA polymerase, not RNA polymerase making RNA.
explanation_options.c: Correct — transcription is RNA polymerase producing a complementary RNA copy of a gene.
explanation_options.d: Translation is the later step of building a protein from mRNA at the ribosome, not the RNA-synthesis step itself.

questions.question_text: Sara is a chemistry student who is carrying out an experiment between an alcohol and acetic acid in the laboratory. The product formed at the end of the experiment will be:
questions.explanation_short: An alcohol reacting with acetic acid (esterification) produces an ester and water.
questions.explanation_long: When an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid like acetic acid, they undergo esterification, forming an ester and releasing a water molecule as a byproduct — a classic condensation reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water — memorize this reaction pairing directly (esterification).

explanation_options.a: Glucose and oxygen would be photosynthesis products, unrelated to an alcohol-acid reaction.
explanation_options.b: Glycogen is a storage polysaccharide, not a product of alcohol reacting with acetic acid.
explanation_options.c: Correct — an alcohol reacting with acetic acid (esterification) yields an ester and water.
explanation_options.d: Glycerol and sulfuric acid aren't the products of a simple alcohol + acetic acid reaction.

questions.question_text: In genetics, the term locus refers to the _________ of the gene on the chromosome.
questions.explanation_short: A gene's locus is its specific position on the chromosome.
questions.explanation_long: 'Locus' (Latin for 'place') refers to the fixed physical position a particular gene occupies along a chromosome — each gene has its own characteristic locus.
questions.explanation_trick: Locus = location — the term literally means 'place' in Latin.

explanation_options.a: Frequency (e.g. allele frequency) is a population-genetics concept, unrelated to a gene's physical location.
explanation_options.b: 'Copy' isn't what locus refers to; it's about location, not duplication.
explanation_options.c: Correct — locus refers to the specific position of a gene on the chromosome.
explanation_options.d: Inversion is a type of chromosomal mutation, not the term for a gene's normal position.

questions.question_text: If 15 µm size object is observed under light microscope using 5X eyepieces and 10X objective, its magnified image size will be:
questions.explanation_short: Magnification = eyepiece × objective = 5×10 = 50; magnified size = 15µm × 50 = 750µm.
questions.explanation_long: Total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective power: 5 × 10 = 50×. Magnified image size = actual size × magnification = 15 µm × 50 = 750 µm.
questions.explanation_trick: Always multiply eyepiece and objective powers together first to get total magnification, then multiply by the actual object size.

explanation_options.a: 250µm would result from a magnification of about 16.7×, not the actual 50× (5×10) combined power here.
explanation_options.b: 50µm is smaller than the original 15µm object, which can't be right for a magnified image.
explanation_options.d: 500µm corresponds to a magnification of about 33×, not the correct 5×10=50× combined power.

questions.question_text: Which enzyme is administered to the patients of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease (SCID)?
questions.explanation_short: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme replacement is given to SCID patients, since ADA deficiency is a known cause of this immunodeficiency.
questions.explanation_long: One well-known cause of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a deficiency of adenosine deaminase (ADA), which lets toxic metabolites build up and kill developing lymphocytes. Treatment includes ADA enzyme replacement therapy (or gene therapy targeting ADA).
questions.explanation_trick: ADA-SCID is a famous, specifically named subtype of SCID — treated by giving the missing enzyme, ADA, itself.

explanation_options.a: Pancreatic enzymes are for digestion, unrelated to treating immunodeficiency.
explanation_options.b: Correct — adenosine deaminase (ADA) is administered to patients with ADA-deficiency-related SCID.
explanation_options.c: β-galactosidase is a lactose-digesting enzyme, unrelated to SCID treatment.
explanation_options.d: β-lactamase is a bacterial enzyme that breaks down antibiotics, unrelated to SCID treatment.

questions.question_text: Change in frequency of alleles that occurs by chance is called as:
questions.explanation_short: Random, chance-driven change in allele frequency is called genetic drift.
questions.explanation_long: Genetic drift is the random fluctuation of allele frequencies in a population from generation to generation, especially pronounced in small populations, driven purely by chance rather than selective advantage.
questions.explanation_trick: Drift = random 'drifting' of allele frequencies by chance, as opposed to natural selection's non-random, fitness-based change.

explanation_options.a: Natural selection changes allele frequency based on differential fitness, not pure chance.
explanation_options.b: Migration (gene flow) changes allele frequency by individuals moving between populations, not by chance within one population.
explanation_options.c: Mutation introduces new alleles; it's a source of variation, not the chance-based shift in existing allele frequencies.
explanation_options.d: Correct — genetic drift is the random, chance-based change in allele frequency.

questions.question_text: The finger like infoldings which are formed by inner membrane of mitochondria are called:
questions.explanation_short: The finger-like folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane are called cristae.
questions.explanation_long: The mitochondrial inner membrane folds inward to form cristae, finger-like projections that greatly increase the surface area available for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, boosting ATP production.
questions.explanation_trick: Cristae = 'crests/folds' — picture the inner membrane crumpled inward to add surface area.

explanation_options.a: The matrix is the fluid-filled interior space of the mitochondrion, not the folded membrane itself.
explanation_options.b: Porins are channel proteins in the outer mitochondrial membrane, not the folded structure itself.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cristae are the finger-like infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
explanation_options.d: Ribosomes are separate protein-synthesis particles found within the matrix, not membrane folds.

questions.question_text: The main nitrogenous excretory product of humans is:
questions.explanation_short: Urea is the main nitrogenous excretory product in humans.
questions.explanation_long: Humans convert toxic ammonia (from amino acid breakdown) into less toxic urea in the liver via the urea cycle, and this urea is then excreted by the kidneys as the primary nitrogenous waste product.
questions.explanation_trick: Humans are 'ureotelic' — they excrete nitrogen mainly as urea, unlike birds/reptiles (uric acid) or aquatic animals (ammonia).

explanation_options.a: Uric acid is the main nitrogenous waste in birds, insects, and reptiles, not humans.
explanation_options.b: Ammonia is toxic and is what's converted into urea in humans before excretion — it's not the main excreted form.
explanation_options.c: Correct — urea is the main nitrogenous excretory product in humans.
explanation_options.d: Ammonium is a related ion but not the primary excreted nitrogenous waste form in humans.

questions.question_text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is responsible for the metabolism of:
questions.explanation_short: Smooth ER handles lipid metabolism, including lipid and steroid synthesis.
questions.explanation_long: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and specializes in lipid synthesis and metabolism (including steroid hormones), as well as detoxification — distinct from the rough ER, which handles protein synthesis (via its attached ribosomes).
questions.explanation_trick: Smooth ER (no ribosomes) = lipids; rough ER (has ribosomes) = proteins.

explanation_options.a: Carbohydrate metabolism isn't the smooth ER's defining role.
explanation_options.b: Protein synthesis and processing is the rough ER's job (via its attached ribosomes), not the smooth ER's.
explanation_options.c: Nucleic acid metabolism isn't a defining smooth ER function.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the smooth ER is responsible for lipid metabolism and synthesis.

questions.question_text: Acetylecholine and Noradrenaline are two types of _____________ used in our nervous system.
questions.option_b: Channel and carrier proteins in the cell membrane of a Neurone.
questions.explanation_short: Acetylcholine and noradrenaline are both neurotransmitters used in the nervous system.
questions.explanation_long: Both acetylcholine (used at many peripheral synapses) and noradrenaline (used mainly in the sympathetic nervous system) are chemical messengers released by neurons to transmit signals across synapses — classifying them together as neurotransmitters.
questions.explanation_trick: Both chemicals carry a nerve impulse across a synaptic gap — that shared job is exactly what defines a neurotransmitter.

explanation_options.a: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted into the blood by glands, not neurotransmitters released at synapses.
explanation_options.b: Channel and carrier proteins are membrane transport structures, not the chemical messengers themselves.
explanation_options.c: They are chemical signaling molecules, not catalytic enzymes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — acetylcholine and noradrenaline are both neurotransmitters used in the nervous system.

questions.question_text: The reflex action is the phenomena which only involves:
questions.explanation_short: A reflex action involves only receptors, effectors, and the spinal cord — bypassing the brain for speed.
questions.explanation_long: A reflex arc is a rapid, involuntary response: a receptor detects a stimulus, a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord, which processes it directly and sends a motor signal to an effector (muscle/gland) — all without needing to involve the brain.
questions.explanation_trick: Reflexes are fast precisely because they skip the brain — only receptors, spinal cord, and effectors are involved.

explanation_options.a: Reflexes specifically bypass the brain for speed; including 'brain' here is incorrect.
explanation_options.b: Correct — a reflex arc involves only receptors, effectors, and the spinal cord, bypassing the brain.
explanation_options.c: This list omits effectors (needed to actually produce the response) and wrongly includes the brain.
explanation_options.d: This omits the spinal cord and neurons, which are essential links connecting receptor to effector in a reflex arc.

questions.question_text: In which situation, Genes are not assorted independently during Meiosis in a chromosome?
questions.option_a: When genes are not linked and their loci are far apart.
questions.option_b: When there are too many Genes on a chromosome.
questions.option_c: When some genes have mutated on the chromosome.
questions.option_d: When genes are linked and their loci are close to each other.
questions.explanation_short: Genes fail to assort independently (they're linked) when their loci lie close together on the same chromosome.
questions.explanation_long: Genes on the same chromosome that are located close together tend to be inherited together (linked) because crossing over rarely separates them — violating Mendel's law of independent assortment, which strictly applies only to genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one.
questions.explanation_trick: Close together on the same chromosome = linked = don't assort independently; far apart or on different chromosomes = assort independently.

explanation_options.a: Genes that are not linked and far apart do assort independently — this describes the opposite of the situation asked about.
explanation_options.b: The number of genes on a chromosome isn't what determines linkage — physical closeness (proximity of loci) is.
explanation_options.c: Mutation of individual genes doesn't determine whether genes assort independently.
explanation_options.d: Correct — genes that are linked with loci close together tend not to assort independently.

questions.question_text: A person got an infection, he became ill but then he survived. What do you think which type of immunity he would have developed?
questions.explanation_short: Surviving a natural infection produces naturally induced active immunity, since the body made its own antibodies.
questions.explanation_long: When a person is infected and their own immune system responds by producing antibodies and memory cells, this is naturally induced active immunity — 'natural' because it arose from a real infection (not a vaccine), and 'active' because the person's own immune system did the work.
questions.explanation_trick: Active = body makes its own antibodies; natural = triggered by real infection (not a vaccine) — combine both to get the precise term.

explanation_options.a: Correct — surviving a natural infection produces naturally induced active immunity.
explanation_options.b: 'Artificially induced' would apply to a vaccine, not a natural infection.
explanation_options.c: 'Active immunity' alone is correct but incomplete — the more precise, specific answer names it as naturally induced.
explanation_options.d: Passive immunity involves receiving ready-made antibodies (e.g. from mother or antiserum), not producing your own after infection.

questions.question_text: During spermatogenesis, the __________, which are haploid cells eventually mature into spermatozoa/mature sperms:
questions.explanation_short: Spermatids are the haploid cells produced by meiosis that mature into spermatozoa.
questions.explanation_long: Spermatogenesis proceeds: spermatogonia → primary spermatocytes (meiosis I) → secondary spermatocytes (meiosis II) → spermatids (haploid) → mature spermatozoa (after a maturation process called spermiogenesis).
questions.explanation_trick: Spermatids are the last haploid cell stage before final maturation into sperm — 'spermatid' sounds like 'nearly a sperm,' which is exactly what it is.

explanation_options.a: Secondary spermatocytes still need to complete meiosis II to become spermatids; they mature further before becoming spermatids.
explanation_options.b: Primary spermatocytes are diploid, before meiosis I even begins.
explanation_options.c: Spermatogonia are the diploid stem cells at the very start of the process, not the haploid stage that matures into sperm.
explanation_options.d: Correct — spermatids are the haploid cells that mature into spermatozoa.

questions.question_text: Transgenic mice have been used to produce:
questions.explanation_short: Transgenic mice have been engineered to produce a growth hormone.
questions.explanation_long: Genetically modified ('transgenic') mice carrying an inserted growth hormone gene have famously been used to demonstrate enhanced growth, producing extra growth hormone as a proof-of-concept for gene transfer technology.
questions.explanation_trick: The classic 'giant mouse' experiment used an inserted growth hormone gene — a landmark transgenic biology example.

explanation_options.a: Protein-rich milk is a goal pursued in transgenic livestock (e.g. goats/cows), not the classic transgenic mouse example.
explanation_options.b: Correct — transgenic mice carrying a growth hormone gene have been used to produce extra growth hormone.
explanation_options.c: Protein-rich meat isn't the classic transgenic mouse application.
explanation_options.d: Extra hair isn't a recognized transgenic mouse application.

questions.question_text: According to the theory of natural selection, organisms produce:
questions.option_c: Offspring according to the resources available
questions.explanation_short: Natural selection theory holds that organisms produce more offspring than their environment can support, driving competition.
questions.explanation_long: Darwin observed that populations have the reproductive potential to produce far more offspring than available resources can sustain, creating a 'struggle for existence' — the competitive pressure that natural selection acts upon.
questions.explanation_trick: Overproduction of offspring is the starting premise of natural selection — it's what creates the resource competition selection then acts on.

explanation_options.a: Correct — organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, driving competition and selection.
explanation_options.b: Producing fewer offspring than resources support wouldn't create the competitive pressure natural selection relies on.
explanation_options.c: Matching offspring number exactly to available resources would remove the struggle for existence Darwin's theory depends on.
explanation_options.d: Organisms don't produce offspring 'to create resources' — that reverses cause and effect.

questions.question_text: The photosynthetic pigments of plants are arranged as clusters in thylakoid membranes. The reaction centers of these clusters consist of ________ molecules.
questions.explanation_short: The reaction centers of the photosynthetic pigment clusters consist of chlorophyll molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Photosynthetic pigments are organized into photosystems (clusters) within the thylakoid membrane; the special pair of chlorophyll a molecules at the core of each cluster forms the reaction center, where light energy is converted into a flow of excited electrons.
questions.explanation_trick: Every photosystem's reaction center is built from chlorophyll a specifically — the pigment that actually loses an electron when excited by light.

explanation_options.a: ATP is a product generated downstream of the light reactions, not a pigment forming the reaction center.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the reaction centers of the photosynthetic pigment clusters are made of chlorophyll molecules.
explanation_options.c: Glucose is a downstream product of the Calvin cycle, unrelated to the pigment reaction center.
explanation_options.d: Carotenoids are accessory pigments that pass captured light energy to the chlorophyll reaction center, but aren't the reaction center itself.

questions.question_text: Meselson and Stahl transferred few bacteria grown in N15 medium to N14 medium for replicating their DNA. What would be the result after two rounds of replication?
questions.explanation_short: After two rounds of semi-conservative replication starting from N15 DNA in N14 medium, the result is 50% hybrid and 50% light duplex DNA.
questions.explanation_long: Meselson-Stahl showed DNA replication is semi-conservative. Starting with fully heavy (N15) DNA and replicating in light (N14) medium: after round 1, all DNA is hybrid (N15/N14). After round 2, each hybrid strand separates and pairs with a new light strand, giving 50% hybrid and 50% fully light duplex DNA — no heavy duplex remains.
questions.explanation_trick: Each replication round halves the fraction of heavy strands present in any one duplex; after round 2, exactly half the molecules are hybrid and half are fully light, with zero fully heavy duplexes left.

explanation_options.a: Correct — after two rounds, the DNA population is 50% hybrid duplex and 50% light duplex.
explanation_options.b: No heavy duplex DNA remains after round 2 in a semi-conservative model — all original heavy strands are diluted into hybrids by then.
explanation_options.c: 100% heavy duplex would only be true generation zero, before any replication in light medium occurred.
explanation_options.d: 100% hybrid duplex was true after round 1, not round 2 — by round 2, half the duplexes have become fully light.

questions.question_text: In an action potential, the permeability of sodium ions in the neurons increases due to:
questions.option_c: The action of the acetylcholinesterase enzyme
questions.option_d: Sodium ions forming an ionic bonding
questions.explanation_short: The opening of voltage-gated sodium channels/gates increases sodium ion permeability during an action potential's depolarization phase.
questions.explanation_long: When a neuron reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, sharply increasing the membrane's permeability to Na+, which rushes in and depolarizes the cell — the rising phase of the action potential.
questions.explanation_trick: Depolarization = sodium channels open; repolarization = sodium channels close and potassium channels open — keep the two phases and their channels straight.

explanation_options.a: Repolarization is driven by sodium channels closing and potassium channels opening — the opposite phase from what's described here.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sodium permeability increases because voltage-gated sodium channels/gates open.
explanation_options.c: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine at synapses; it doesn't control axonal sodium channels.
explanation_options.d: Sodium ions moving through channels is a physical flow, not the formation of an 'ionic bond' — this option misuses the chemistry term.

questions.question_text: During the G₂ phase:
questions.option_a: Specific enzymes are synthesized and DNA base units are accumulated
questions.option_b: The chromosomes are left with only one chromatid
questions.option_d: Energy is stored for Chromosome movement and mitotic specific proteins(Tubulin) are produced
questions.explanation_short: In G2, the cell stores energy and produces mitosis-specific proteins (like tubulin) needed for chromosome movement.
questions.explanation_long: G2 is the final preparatory phase before mitosis: the cell continues growing, checks that DNA replication was completed correctly, and synthesizes mitosis-specific proteins (such as tubulin for spindle fibers) while stockpiling energy needed for chromosome movement during division.
questions.explanation_trick: G2 = final gear-up phase — energy storage and mitosis-specific protein (tubulin) synthesis, right before M phase begins.

explanation_options.a: Enzyme synthesis and DNA base accumulation in preparation for replication describes G1, not G2.
explanation_options.b: Chromosomes still have two sister chromatids at this point (until anaphase separates them) — this doesn't describe G2.
explanation_options.c: Chromosome number/DNA content is duplicated during S phase, which comes before G2, not during it.
explanation_options.d: Correct — G2 stores energy for chromosome movement and produces mitosis-specific proteins like tubulin.

aliases: During the G2 phase:
Specific enzymes are synthesized and DNA base units are accumulated

questions.question_text: Thin filaments of muscles contain _______ chains of actin molecules.
questions.explanation_short: Thin filaments contain two intertwined chains of actin molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Each thin filament in a myofibril is built from two strands of globular actin (F-actin), twisted together in a double helix, along with regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin.
questions.explanation_trick: Actin's double helix = two chains twisted together — a structural detail worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: Four chains overstates the actual structure of the thin filament.
explanation_options.b: One chain would just be a single strand of G-actin monomers, not the actual double-helical thin filament.
explanation_options.c: Three chains isn't the correct count for thin filament structure.
explanation_options.d: Correct — thin filaments contain two intertwined chains of actin molecules.

questions.question_text: Which cell organelle is responsible for cell secretion?
questions.explanation_short: The Golgi body packages and secretes cell products, making it responsible for cell secretion.
questions.explanation_long: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids (received from the ER) into vesicles that are then secreted from the cell, making it the organelle responsible for cellular secretion.
questions.explanation_trick: Golgi = the cell's packaging and shipping department — secretion is its signature job.

explanation_options.a: The mitochondrion generates ATP through respiration, not secretion.
explanation_options.b: The chloroplast carries out photosynthesis, not secretion.
explanation_options.c: The ribosome synthesizes proteins, but doesn't package/secrete them.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the Golgi body packages and secretes cellular products.

questions.question_text: Most proteins are made up of:
questions.explanation_short: Most proteins are built from 20 standard types of amino acids.
questions.explanation_long: Although hundreds of amino acids exist in nature, proteins in living organisms are built almost exclusively from a standard set of 20 amino acids, encoded by the genetic code.
questions.explanation_trick: 20 standard amino acids is a foundational biology number worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: 16 undercounts the standard set used to build proteins.
explanation_options.b: 10 significantly undercounts the standard 20 amino acids.
explanation_options.c: 170 vastly overstates the number of amino acid types actually used to build proteins.
explanation_options.d: Correct — proteins are made up of 20 standard types of amino acids.

questions.question_text: A disease caused by gradual breakdown of the thin walls of alveoli is _____.
questions.explanation_short: Gradual breakdown of the thin alveolar walls is called emphysema.
questions.explanation_long: Emphysema is a chronic lung disease in which the delicate walls of the alveoli are gradually destroyed, merging small air sacs into larger, less efficient ones and drastically reducing the surface area for gas exchange.
questions.explanation_trick: Emphysema = destroyed alveolar walls = reduced surface area for gas exchange — the defining structural damage.

explanation_options.a: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection of the lungs, not primarily alveolar wall breakdown.
explanation_options.b: Asthma involves airway inflammation and constriction (bronchi/bronchioles), not alveolar wall destruction.
explanation_options.c: Correct — emphysema is caused by gradual breakdown of the thin alveolar walls.
explanation_options.d: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes, not the alveoli themselves.

questions.question_text: If sequence in DNA is CCCTAGAG, then what would be the sequence in messenger RNA after transcription?
questions.explanation_short: DNA CCCTAGAG transcribes to mRNA GGGAUCUC (complementary bases, T→A becomes U).
questions.explanation_long: Transcription pairs each DNA base with its RNA complement (A↔U, T↔A, C↔G, G↔C). Template CCCTAGAG becomes: C→G, C→G, C→G, T→A, A→U, G→C, A→U, G→C, giving mRNA sequence GGGAUCUC.
questions.explanation_trick: In RNA, adenine pairs with uracil (not thymine) — this catches out anyone who forgets to swap T for U on the template's A bases.

explanation_options.a: Correct — base-by-base complementary pairing of CCCTAGAG gives GGGAUCUC.
explanation_options.b: This uses T instead of U in the RNA sequence, but RNA never contains thymine — it should be U.
explanation_options.c: This doesn't correctly complement every base in the original sequence.
explanation_options.d: This doesn't correctly complement every base in the original sequence.

questions.question_text: Taxonomy includes the arrangement of organisms into different taxa. Which of the following represents the correct hierarchy of various taxa of classification?
questions.option_a: Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum
questions.option_c: Species, genus, order, family, class, phylum
questions.option_d: Species, genus, family, class, order, phylum
questions.explanation_short: The standard taxonomic hierarchy, largest to smallest, is species, genus, family, order, class, phylum.
questions.explanation_long: Taxonomic classification narrows down from broad to specific... but written from most-specific to broadest as this question lists it: species, genus, family, order, class, phylum (continuing up to kingdom and domain).
questions.explanation_trick: Remember the classic mnemonic (Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species) and simply read it in reverse for this question's order.

explanation_options.a: Correct — species, genus, family, order, class, phylum is the correct sequence of this hierarchy.
explanation_options.b: This list skips several ranks (genus, species, order/family overlap) and starts at the wrong level.
explanation_options.c: This swaps order and family out of their correct sequence.
explanation_options.d: This swaps class and order out of their correct sequence.

questions.question_text: Complementary DNA molecule is
questions.option_d: a small segment of chromosomal DNA
questions.explanation_short: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is DNA synthesized from an mRNA template using reverse transcriptase.
questions.explanation_long: cDNA is made by reverse-transcribing mRNA back into DNA, producing an artificial DNA copy of the mRNA (and therefore lacking introns) — widely used in cloning and gene expression studies.
questions.explanation_trick: cDNA = 'copy DNA' made from mRNA — the 'complementary' refers to it being the DNA complement of an existing mRNA strand.

explanation_options.a: 'An artificial DNA' is too vague and doesn't capture that it's specifically synthesized from mRNA.
explanation_options.b: cDNA is double-stranded once synthesized, not single-stranded like the original mRNA template.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cDNA is DNA synthesized from (i.e., made using) an mRNA template.
explanation_options.d: cDNA is not a segment cut from chromosomal DNA — it's newly synthesized from mRNA, and importantly lacks introns present in genomic DNA.

questions.question_text: Capsid, the protective coat of a virus is made up of _______________ subunits known as capsomeres.
questions.explanation_short: A virus's capsid is made of protein subunits called capsomeres.
questions.explanation_long: The capsid, the protective outer shell of a virus, is built from repeating protein subunits called capsomeres, which self-assemble into the characteristic shapes (helical, icosahedral, etc.) of different viruses.
questions.explanation_trick: Capsid = protein coat; capsomeres = the protein subunits building it — both terms are protein-based, not nucleic-acid-based.

explanation_options.a: Lipid makes up the viral envelope in enveloped viruses, not the protein capsid itself.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the capsid is built from protein subunits called capsomeres.
explanation_options.c: RNA can be the viral genome inside the capsid, but it's not the capsid's structural material.
explanation_options.d: DNA can be the viral genome inside the capsid, but it's not the capsid's structural material.

questions.question_text: In plants, which sugar is transported from source to sink through sieve tubes?
questions.explanation_short: Sucrose is the sugar transported from source to sink through phloem sieve tubes.
questions.explanation_long: Plants translocate sugars in phloem sieve tubes mainly as sucrose (a non-reducing disaccharide), moved from 'source' tissues (like leaves) to 'sink' tissues (like roots or fruits) via active loading and pressure flow.
questions.explanation_trick: Phloem transport = sucrose specifically, not glucose — sucrose's non-reducing nature makes it a stable transport sugar.

explanation_options.a: Fructose is a monosaccharide, not the disaccharide form typically transported in phloem.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sucrose is the main sugar transported through phloem sieve tubes.
explanation_options.c: Glucose is a monosaccharide, not the typical transported form in phloem sap.
explanation_options.d: Starch is an insoluble storage polysaccharide, not something that can be transported through sieve tubes.

questions.question_text: If a carrier haemophilic female (X^H X^h) is married to a haemophilic male (X^h Y). What will be the ratio of presence of haemophilia in the children. Select best answer from given condition.
questions.option_a: 100% all females and males will be haempohilic
questions.option_b: carrier female 25%, haemophilic female 25%, 25% normal male and 25% haemophilic male.
questions.option_c: females and males both have 50% chances of getting haemophilia
questions.option_d: females have 50% chances of getting haemophilia and males will be 100% haemophilic
questions.explanation_short: XHXh × XhY gives 1/4 carrier female : 1/4 haemophilic female : 1/4 normal male : 1/4 haemophilic male.
questions.explanation_long: Crossing a carrier female (XHXh) with a haemophilic male (XhY) produces four equally likely offspring genotypes: XHXh (carrier female), XhXh (haemophilic female), XHY (normal male), and XhY (haemophilic male) — each at 25%.
questions.explanation_trick: Set up the full 2×2 Punnett square with the mother's two X alleles against the father's X and Y — don't just eyeball fractions, since both daughters and sons can independently be affected here.

explanation_options.a: This overstates the outcome — not all offspring turn out haemophilic; a quarter are unaffected in each sex.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the cross gives 25% each of carrier female, haemophilic female, normal male, and haemophilic male.
explanation_options.c: This doesn't reflect the actual outcome; daughters and sons don't each have a flat 50% haemophilia risk here — some daughters are only carriers (unaffected) and some sons are entirely normal.
explanation_options.d: Not all males are haemophilic in this cross — half the sons (XHY) are completely normal.

questions.question_text: As a result of replication, parental DNA would become completely dispersed and that each strand of all the daughter molecules would be a mixture of old and new DNA. This is called as:
questions.explanation_short: The 'each strand of daughter DNA is a mixture of old and new' model described is the dispersive idea, later disproven by Meselson-Stahl.
questions.explanation_long: The dispersive model of replication proposed that parental DNA is broken and dispersed, so each daughter strand ends up as a patchwork of old and new DNA. This was one of the three original hypotheses (conservative, semi-conservative, dispersive) tested — and disproven — by the Meselson-Stahl experiment, which confirmed semi-conservative replication instead.
questions.explanation_trick: Three original models: conservative (originals stay together), semi-conservative (each daughter gets one old + one new strand), dispersive (both strands are patchworks of old and new) — this question's wording matches dispersive specifically.

explanation_options.a: The conservative idea proposed the original double helix stays fully intact, with an entirely new copy made separately — not a mixed patchwork.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the dispersive idea proposed that daughter DNA strands would be scattered mixtures of old and new DNA.
explanation_options.c: 'Disruptive idea' isn't one of the three classic replication models.
explanation_options.d: Semi-conservative replication (the actual, confirmed mechanism) keeps one whole old strand and one whole new strand per duplex — not a scattered mixture within each strand.

questions.question_text: A student of chemical engineering mistakenly engulfed the toxic compound "A" which was a potent inhibitor of certain enzyme. He was immediately brought to hospital where Dr. injected intravenously substrate "B" to minimize the toxic effect of compound A. His life was saved from serious damages. The treatment method shows that compound A was a __________ inhibitor.
questions.explanation_short: Since a substrate (not more enzyme) reversed the toxic effect, compound A was a competitive reversible inhibitor.
questions.explanation_long: Giving extra substrate B out-competed the toxic inhibitor A for the enzyme's active site, restoring normal enzyme function and saving the patient. This out-competing effect — reversed by adding more substrate — is the hallmark of competitive, reversible inhibition.
questions.explanation_trick: If more substrate can reverse an inhibitor's effect, the inhibitor must be binding the same (active) site competitively and reversibly — that's the diagnostic clue in this scenario.

explanation_options.a: 'Temperature sensitive' isn't a recognized inhibitor classification relevant to this substrate-competition scenario.
explanation_options.b: Correct — since flooding the system with substrate reversed the toxic effect, compound A was a competitive, reversible inhibitor.
explanation_options.c: An irreversible inhibitor permanently disables the enzyme and can't be displaced by adding more substrate — but here, substrate reversed the effect.
explanation_options.d: Non-competitive inhibitors bind away from the active site and aren't overcome by adding more substrate — but here, substrate reversed the effect, pointing to competitive inhibition instead.

questions.question_text: Four plants are present in different environmental conditions. Plant A is present in warm climate with continuous rainfall, plant B is present in a cool forest, plant C is present in warm climate with little breeze while plant D is present in warm climate with high wind speed. Which one of the above plants will have highest rate of transpiration?
questions.explanation_short: Plant D (warm climate + high wind speed) will have the highest transpiration rate, since wind strongly increases water loss.
questions.explanation_long: Transpiration rate rises with heat, dryness, and especially wind (which continuously sweeps away the humid air layer at the leaf surface, steepening the diffusion gradient). Plant D, in a warm climate with high wind speed, combines both heat and maximal wind exposure, giving it the highest transpiration rate among the four.
questions.explanation_trick: Wind is one of the strongest environmental drivers of transpiration — always check for the plant with the highest wind exposure first when comparing conditions.

explanation_options.a: Plant B is in a cool forest, where lower temperature and less air movement reduce transpiration compared to warm, windy conditions.
explanation_options.b: Correct — high wind speed in a warm climate maximizes transpiration by continuously removing humid air from the leaf surface.
explanation_options.c: Plant C has only little breeze, far less effective at driving transpiration than Plant D's high wind speed.
explanation_options.d: Plant A has continuous rainfall (high humidity), which reduces the water-vapor concentration gradient and lowers transpiration compared to windy, drier conditions.

questions.question_text: Sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain of protein molecule corresponds to the sequence of nucleotides on mRNA for that protein. If reading frame of mRNA for a human protein is 993 nucleotide including a stop codon at the end, how many amino acids would be incorporated in the polypeptide chain?
questions.explanation_short: 993 nucleotides ÷ 3 per codon = 331 codons; minus 1 stop codon = 330 amino acids incorporated.
questions.explanation_long: Each amino acid is coded by a triplet (3 nucleotides), so 993 nucleotides represent 993/3 = 331 codons total. Since the last codon is a stop codon (coding for no amino acid), only 331 − 1 = 330 codons actually code for amino acids.
questions.explanation_trick: Always subtract one codon for the stop codon before converting nucleotide count to amino acid count — a very common trap in these calculations.

explanation_options.a: 331 is the total codon count before subtracting the non-coding stop codon.
explanation_options.b: 993 is the nucleotide count itself, not the amino acid count (which requires dividing by 3 and subtracting the stop codon).
explanation_options.c: 93 miscalculates the division of 993 by 3 (it should be 331, not 93).
explanation_options.d: Correct — 993/3 = 331 codons, minus the 1 stop codon = 330 amino acids incorporated.

questions.question_text: The major function of Basophils is to:
questions.option_b: Release heparin to prevent blood clotting
questions.explanation_short: Basophils release heparin (and histamine), helping prevent blood clotting and mediating inflammation/allergic responses.
questions.explanation_long: Basophils are white blood cells that release heparin (an anticoagulant) and histamine (an inflammatory mediator) as part of allergic and inflammatory responses — heparin specifically helps prevent excessive blood clotting.
questions.explanation_trick: Basophils and mast cells both release heparin and histamine — heparin's anticlotting role is the specific detail this question tests.

explanation_options.a: Phagocytosis of small particles is the job of neutrophils/macrophages, not the main function of basophils.
explanation_options.b: Correct — basophils release heparin, which helps prevent blood clotting.
explanation_options.c: Inactivating inflammation-producing substances describes eosinophils, not basophils.
explanation_options.d: Transporting oxygen is the job of red blood cells (via haemoglobin), not basophils.

questions.question_text: Large lymph vessels ultimately form larger lymph duct, which drains its lymph into:
questions.explanation_short: The thoracic (lymphatic) duct drains lymph into the subclavian vein, returning it to the bloodstream.
questions.explanation_long: Lymph collected throughout the body eventually drains into large lymphatic ducts (e.g. the thoracic duct), which empty into the subclavian veins near the neck/shoulder area, returning the fluid to the venous blood circulation.
questions.explanation_trick: Lymph always returns to the venous side of circulation — specifically the subclavian vein — never directly into an artery.

explanation_options.a: The carotid and aorta are arteries, and lymph doesn't drain into arteries.
explanation_options.b: The vena cava and aorta pairing is incorrect; the direct drainage point is specifically the subclavian vein, not the vena cava or the aorta (an artery).
explanation_options.c: Correct — large lymph ducts drain into the subclavian vein.
explanation_options.d: The subclavian artery is an artery, and lymph drains into a vein, not an artery.

questions.question_text: Blood group AB is an example of ___________.
questions.explanation_short: Blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are fully expressed together, is a classic example of co-dominance.
questions.explanation_long: In the ABO blood group system, the IA and IB alleles are co-dominant — when both are present (genotype IAIB), both A and B antigens are fully expressed simultaneously on red blood cells, producing blood type AB, rather than one allele masking the other.
questions.explanation_trick: Co-dominance = both alleles fully and simultaneously expressed (like AB blood type), different from incomplete dominance where a blended intermediate phenotype appears instead.

explanation_options.a: Complete dominance would mean one allele fully masks the other, which isn't what happens with A and B alleles together.
explanation_options.b: Recessive alleles are masked by a dominant one, but here A and B are both actively, simultaneously expressed — not masked.
explanation_options.c: Incomplete dominance produces a blended intermediate phenotype, whereas AB blood type shows both traits fully and separately, which is co-dominance.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the simultaneous full expression of both A and B antigens is a classic case of co-dominance.

questions.question_text: Passive processes for the movement of molecules across cell surface membrane are:
questions.explanation_short: Facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive transport processes, needing no cellular energy.
questions.explanation_long: Facilitated diffusion (movement of specific molecules through channel/carrier proteins) and osmosis (water movement across a membrane) both move substances down their concentration gradient without requiring ATP, making them passive transport processes.
questions.explanation_trick: Passive transport never needs ATP; anything involving vesicles (endo/exocytosis, phagocytosis, pinocytosis) is active and needs energy.

explanation_options.a: Correct — facilitated diffusion and osmosis are both passive processes, not requiring cellular energy.
explanation_options.b: Pinocytosis is a form of active endocytosis, requiring energy — not a passive process.
explanation_options.c: Exocytosis is an active, energy-requiring vesicular transport process, not passive.
explanation_options.d: Phagocytosis is an active, energy-requiring vesicular transport process, not passive.

questions.question_text: In glycine R is ___________.
questions.explanation_short: In glycine, the simplest amino acid, the R (side chain) group is just a hydrogen atom.
questions.explanation_long: Every amino acid has the general structure NH2-CH(R)-COOH, where R is the variable side chain. Glycine is unique among the 20 standard amino acids because its R group is simply a single hydrogen atom, making it the smallest and only achiral amino acid.
questions.explanation_trick: Glycine = 'no real side chain' — its R is just H, which is why it's the smallest, simplest amino acid.

explanation_options.a: A fatty acid chain would make for a bulky, hydrophobic R group, not glycine's minimal structure.
explanation_options.b: Ethane is a two-carbon hydrocarbon, far bulkier than glycine's actual single-hydrogen R group.
explanation_options.c: Correct — glycine's R group is a single hydrogen atom.
explanation_options.d: Methane is a full standalone molecule, not the tiny R group (just H) that glycine actually has.

questions.question_text: Glycolysis takes place in the ________ of cell.
questions.explanation_short: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm (cytosol) of the cell.
