questions.explanation_short: Hypophosphatemic rickets is the classic X-linked DOMINANT disorder, unlike hemophilia and color blindness which are X-linked recessive.
questions.explanation_long: Most well-known X-linked disorders (hemophilia, color blindness) are recessive. Hypophosphatemic rickets (vitamin D-resistant rickets) is a notable exception, following X-linked dominant inheritance — meaning even one copy of the mutant allele in females causes the disorder.
questions.explanation_trick: Hemophilia & color blindness = X-linked recessive; Hypophosphatemic rickets = the X-linked DOMINANT exception.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — haemophilia is X-linked recessive.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — color blindness is X-linked recessive.
explanation_options.c: Correct — hypophosphatemic rickets is X-linked dominant.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — hypertrichosis (in some forms) is Y-linked, not X-linked.

questions.question_text: Mode of inheritance in humans can be traced through:
questions.explanation_short: Pedigree analysis traces the mode of inheritance of traits through family history in humans.
questions.explanation_long: Since controlled experimental mating isn't ethical/possible in humans, geneticists use pedigree charts — diagrams tracking a trait across generations of a family — to determine whether a trait is dominant/recessive and autosomal/X-linked.
questions.explanation_trick: Humans can't be lab-bred — pedigree charts are the human equivalent of experimental crosses.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — experimental mating isn't ethically/practically done in humans to trace inheritance.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — chi-square is a statistical test for goodness-of-fit, not itself a way to trace inheritance patterns through generations.
explanation_options.c: Correct — pedigree analysis is used to trace human inheritance patterns.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — probability analysis calculates odds but isn't the direct method for tracing family inheritance history.

questions.question_text: One a. m .u stands for
questions.explanation_short: 1 a.m.u (atomic mass unit) is defined as exactly 1/12th of the mass of a Carbon-12 atom.
questions.explanation_long: The atomic mass unit (amu, now often 'u' or Dalton) is a standardized unit of mass defined as 1/12 the mass of one atom of Carbon-12 (the most common carbon isotope), which equals about 1.66×10⁻²⁴ g. This provides a consistent reference for measuring atomic and molecular masses.
questions.explanation_trick: amu = 1/12 of Carbon-12's mass — the universal atomic mass reference.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this describes an atom of C-12 itself, not the 1/12 fraction that defines the amu.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 1 amu = 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the amu is defined relative to carbon-12, not hydrogen.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this isn't a meaningful definition of amu.

questions.question_text: A compound of sodium oxide has 74.2 % sodium and 25.8% of Oxygen. The empirical formula of the compound is?
questions.explanation_short: With 74.2% Na and 25.8% O, mole ratio calculation gives Na2O as the empirical formula.
questions.explanation_long: Moles: Na = 74.2/23 ≈ 3.226; O = 25.8/16 ≈ 1.613. Dividing by the smaller value (1.613): Na ≈ 2.0, O ≈ 1.0. This gives a simplest whole-number ratio of Na:O = 2:1, so the empirical formula is Na2O (sodium oxide).
questions.explanation_trick: Divide grams by atomic mass, then divide by the smallest mole value to get the whole-number ratio.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — NaO would need a 1:1 mole ratio, not the calculated 2:1.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — NaO2 would need Na:O of 1:2, opposite of the calculated ratio.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the mole ratio calculation gives Na2O.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Na2O2 (sodium peroxide) isn't supported by this percentage composition.

questions.question_text: 30 grams of 2-propanol were mixed with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and boiled under reflux for 20 minutes. The organic product was then collected by distillation. The yield of product was 75.0%. What is the mass of product produced?
questions.explanation_short: 75% yield from 30g of 2-propanol via oxidation to acetone: theoretical yield ×0.75 ≈ 21.75 g.
questions.explanation_long: Moles of 2-propanol (MW=60) = 30/60 = 0.5 mol. Oxidation by K2Cr2O7 converts a secondary alcohol to a ketone (acetone, MW=58), 1:1 mole ratio, so theoretical yield = 0.5×58 = 29 g. At 75% yield: 29×0.75 = 21.75 g.
questions.explanation_trick: Theoretical yield (mol × product MW) × % yield = actual yield.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1.74g is far too low; doesn't match the mole calculation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 21.75 g matches 75% of the 29g theoretical yield.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 2.74g is off by roughly a factor of ten from the correct value.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 29g is the theoretical (100%) yield, not the actual 75% yield.

aliases: 30 grams of 2-propanol were mixed with excess acidified K2Cr2O7 and boiled under reflux for 20 minutes. The organic product was then collected by distillation. The yield of product was 75.0%. What is the mass of product produced?

questions.question_text: According to which scientist, the probability of finding an electron at a certain position is possible?
questions.explanation_short: Schrödinger's model describes electron position in terms of probability (electron cloud/orbital), not a fixed orbit.
questions.explanation_long: Erwin Schrödinger's wave equation treats electrons as probability distributions (orbitals) around the nucleus rather than fixed paths (as in Bohr's model). The square of the wave function gives the probability of finding an electron at a given point in space — the foundation of modern quantum mechanical atomic theory.
questions.explanation_trick: Schrödinger = probability clouds (orbitals); Bohr = fixed circular orbits.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Bohr's model used fixed circular orbits, not probability.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — de Broglie proposed wave-particle duality, a precursor concept, not the probability model itself.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Hund's rule concerns electron filling order in orbitals, not the probability concept.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Schrödinger's model describes electron position as a probability.

questions.question_text: Which gas in the discharge tube produces lightest canal ray particles?
questions.explanation_short: Helium produces the lightest canal ray (positive ion) particles among the given noble/light gases, being the lightest available gas here besides H2 — but since H2 is listed and lighter, H2 is actually correct: canal rays reflect the mass of the gas ionized, and H2 (as H2+) is lighter than He.
questions.explanation_long: Canal rays are positive ions formed from gas molecules in a discharge tube. Their mass corresponds to the gas used. Among Ar, He, H2, and Ne, hydrogen (H2, or H+ after ionization) has the smallest atomic/molecular mass, producing the lightest canal ray particles — even lighter than helium.
questions.explanation_trick: Lightest gas = lightest canal ray particle. Hydrogen (atomic mass ~1-2) beats Helium (~4).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Argon is a heavy noble gas, producing heavy canal ray particles.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Helium is light, but hydrogen is lighter still.
explanation_options.c: Correct — hydrogen gas produces the lightest canal ray particles (lowest mass).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Neon is heavier than both helium and hydrogen.

questions.question_text: Which element has the ground state electronic configuration of 1s², 2s², 2p⁶, 3s², 3p⁶?
questions.explanation_short: The configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (18 electrons) matches Argon (Ar), atomic number 18.
questions.explanation_long: Counting electrons: 2+2+6+2+6 = 18 electrons, corresponding to atomic number 18 — Argon, a noble gas with a completely filled valence shell (octet), making it chemically inert.
questions.explanation_trick: Count electrons in the configuration: 2+2+6+2+6=18 → Argon (atomic number 18).

explanation_options.a: Correct — this configuration (18 electrons) is Argon.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Chlorine (17 electrons) would end in 3p5, not 3p6.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Sodium (11 electrons) has a much shorter configuration (ends at 3s1).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Sulfur (16 electrons) would end in 3p4, not 3p6.

aliases: Which element has the ground state electronic configuration of 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p6?
Ar

questions.question_text: What is the proton (atomic number) of an element that has four unpaired electrons in its ground state?
questions.explanation_short: An element with 4 unpaired electrons in its ground state, atomic number 26, is Iron (Fe): [Ar] 3d6 4s2.
questions.explanation_long: Iron's electron configuration is [Ar]3d6 4s2. Applying Hund's rule, the 3d6 configuration has 4 unpaired electrons (one orbital doubly occupied, four singly occupied) — matching the description. Atomic number 26 = Iron.
questions.explanation_trick: Fe (26): 3d6 → four unpaired electrons by Hund's rule (one pair + four singles).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — atomic number 6 (Carbon) has only 2 unpaired electrons (2p2).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — atomic number 14 (Silicon) has only 2 unpaired electrons (3p2).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — atomic number 22 (Titanium) has only 2 unpaired electrons (3d2).
explanation_options.d: Correct — atomic number 26 (Iron) has 4 unpaired electrons in its 3d subshell.

questions.question_text: A gaseous mixture contains 9.6% NH₃, 22.6% N₂ and 67.8% H₂ gases. If the total pressure is 50 atm, then the partial pressure of H₂ is
questions.explanation_short: Partial pressure of H2 = mole fraction of H2 × total pressure = 67.8% × 50 atm, i.e., (67.8×50)/100.
questions.explanation_long: By Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures, each gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction (percentage/100) multiplied by the total pressure. For H2 at 67.8% in a mixture at 50 atm total: partial pressure = (67.8/100) × 50 = (67.8 × 50)/100 atm.
questions.explanation_trick: Partial pressure = (%composition/100) × total pressure — always percentage times total, divided by 100.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this formula divides total pressure incorrectly, not matching Dalton's Law setup.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this uses the wrong percentage value (should be 67.8%, not a generic 50×100/100).
explanation_options.c: Correct — (67.8 × 50)/100 correctly applies Dalton's Law for H2's partial pressure.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — addition isn't the correct operation for calculating partial pressure from mole fraction.

aliases: A gaseous mixture contains 9.6% NH3, 22.6% N2 and 67.8% H2 gases. If the total pressure is 50 atm, then the partial pressure of H2 is

questions.question_text: If we want to raise the temperature of one mole of an ideal gas by one kelvin, we have to provide how much amount of energy?
questions.explanation_short: To raise 1 mole of ideal gas by 1 K at constant volume requires (3/2)R ≈ 0.0821×... but per the ideal gas constant R=0.0821 dm³·atm/(mol·K), the energy per kelvin per mole in these units is 0.0821 dm3-atm.
questions.explanation_long: The gas constant R = 0.0821 dm³·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ (or 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹). Since the question asks for the amount of energy (in the dm³-atm unit system) to raise the temperature of 1 mole by 1 K, matching R's value directly in these units gives 0.0821 dm³-atm as the answer consistent with the option set provided.
questions.explanation_trick: R = 0.0821 dm3-atm/(mol·K) = 8.314 J/(mol·K) — two unit systems for the same constant.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 0.0821 joules uses the wrong unit system (R in joules is 8.314, not 0.0821).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 8.314 dm3-atm mismatches units; 8.314 is R's value in J/(mol·K), not dm3-atm.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 0.0821 kJ misapplies units; R in kJ would be a different tiny value (0.008314 kJ).
explanation_options.d: Correct — 0.0821 dm3-atm is R's value in this unit system, matching the energy needed per mole per kelvin.

questions.question_text: The process of heat flow between hotter and colder gases remains continued until all the molecules have equal
questions.explanation_short: Heat flow between gases continues until they reach equal average translational kinetic energy (i.e., the same temperature).
questions.explanation_long: Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of gas molecules. Heat naturally flows from hotter to colder gas until both reach thermal equilibrium — meaning their molecules share the same average translational kinetic energy (same temperature), as described by kinetic molecular theory.
questions.explanation_trick: Temperature = average translational KE. Thermal equilibrium = equal average translational KE.

explanation_options.a: Correct — heat flow stops when average translational kinetic energies (temperatures) equalize.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — rotational kinetic energy isn't the standard definition of temperature/thermal equilibrium in kinetic theory.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'translational potential energy' isn't a standard/meaningful term in this context.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — vibrational kinetic energy relates to molecular vibrations, not the temperature-defining translational motion.

questions.question_text: In liquid, with the change in dipole-dipole forces, there is a change in some physical properties. Select the property which is not affected by the strength of dipole-dipole forces?
questions.explanation_short: The number of moles present is not affected by the strength of dipole-dipole forces — it's simply a quantity, not a physical property influenced by intermolecular forces.
questions.explanation_long: Boiling point, heat of vaporization, and heat of sublimation all directly depend on how strong the intermolecular (dipole-dipole) forces are — stronger forces mean more energy is needed to separate molecules, raising these values. 'Moles' is just an amount of substance and isn't a physical property affected by intermolecular force strength.
questions.explanation_trick: Boiling point, vaporization/sublimation heat all scale with intermolecular force strength; 'moles' is just quantity, unaffected.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — boiling point IS affected by dipole-dipole force strength.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — heat of vaporization IS affected by these forces.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — heat of sublimation IS affected by these forces too.
explanation_options.d: Correct — moles (amount of substance) is not a property affected by dipole-dipole force strength.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factor does not affect the magnitude of vapor pressure?
questions.explanation_short: The size of individual molecules does not affect vapor pressure magnitude the way temperature, amount, or intermolecular forces do — actually 'amount of liquid' is the standard correct answer since vapor pressure is an intensive property independent of quantity.
questions.explanation_long: Vapor pressure is an intensive property — it depends on temperature and the strength of intermolecular forces (which relate to molecular structure), but NOT on how much liquid is present. Whether you have 10 mL or 1 L of the same liquid at the same temperature, the vapor pressure above it is identical.
questions.explanation_trick: Vapor pressure is intensive — independent of the AMOUNT of liquid present, just like density or boiling point.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the amount of liquid does not affect the magnitude of vapor pressure (intensive property).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — size/nature of molecule DOES affect vapor pressure via intermolecular force strength.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — temperature strongly and directly affects vapor pressure.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — intermolecular forces directly determine vapor pressure magnitude.

questions.question_text: A small building block which belongs to whole information about crystal structure is called?
questions.explanation_short: The unit cell is the smallest repeating building block that contains all structural information about a crystal lattice.
questions.explanation_long: A unit cell is the smallest 3D arrangement of atoms/ions/molecules that, when repeated in all directions, generates the entire crystal lattice. It fully represents the lattice's symmetry and structure in miniature.
questions.explanation_trick: Unit Cell = the crystal's 'LEGO brick' — smallest repeating unit building the whole structure.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'cell' alone is too generic/vague, not the specific crystallography term.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the unit cell is the small building block containing full crystal structure information.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — crystal lattice is the overall repeated arrangement, not the small building block itself.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'crystal unit' isn't the standard/precise crystallography term (unit cell is).

questions.question_text: Which type of solid is called as atomic solid?
questions.explanation_short: Metallic solids are called atomic solids since they're built from individual metal atoms held by metallic bonding.
questions.explanation_long: Atomic solids are those built up from individual atoms as the repeating structural units. Metallic solids fit this — array of metal atoms/cations in a 'sea of electrons.' Covalent solids (network atoms too, but usually classified separately), ionic solids (built from ions, not neutral atoms), and molecular solids (built from molecules) are distinguished as different solid types.
questions.explanation_trick: Metallic solids = atoms held by metallic bonds = classified as 'atomic solids' in this context.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — covalent (network) solids are typically classified separately from 'atomic solids' in this question's scheme.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — ionic solids are built from ions, not the term 'atomic solid'.
explanation_options.c: Correct — metallic solids are termed atomic solids.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — molecular solids are built from discrete molecules, not the 'atomic solid' category.

questions.question_text: The decrease in solubility of the salt in a solution that already contains an ion common to that salt is known as:
questions.explanation_short: The common ion effect describes decreased salt solubility when a solution already contains an ion common to that salt.
questions.explanation_long: By Le Chatelier's principle applied to solubility equilibria, adding an ion already part of a sparingly soluble salt's dissociation equilibrium shifts the equilibrium backward (toward the solid), decreasing that salt's solubility. This specific phenomenon is named the common ion effect.
questions.explanation_trick: Same ion already in solution 'crowds out' further dissolving — common ion effect.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Le Chatelier's principle is the general underlying rule, but the specific named phenomenon here is the common ion effect.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — solubility product (Ksp) is the equilibrium constant itself, not the name of this decreased-solubility phenomenon.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this decreased solubility due to a shared ion is the common ion effect.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Ksp is just the numeric equilibrium constant, not the name of the effect described.

questions.question_text: The precipitation occurs if the ionic concentration is:
questions.explanation_short: Precipitation occurs when the ionic concentration product exceeds the solubility product (Ksp), i.e., when it's more than Ksp.
questions.explanation_long: A precipitate forms only when the actual ion product (reaction quotient Q) in solution exceeds the solubility product constant Ksp for that compound — meaning the solution is supersaturated relative to equilibrium, and excess ions must precipitate out to restore equilibrium.
questions.explanation_trick: Q > Ksp → precipitate forms; Q < Ksp → more solid can dissolve; Q = Ksp → equilibrium (saturated, no change).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — if ionic concentration is less than Ksp, the solution is unsaturated; no precipitation occurs.
explanation_options.b: Correct — precipitation occurs when ionic concentration exceeds (is more than) Ksp.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — equal to Ksp means the solution is exactly saturated at equilibrium, not actively precipitating further.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — precipitation is concentration-dependent, not simply 'present in any amount'.

questions.question_text: One can estimate the direction in which equilibrium will shift with the help of:
questions.explanation_short: Le Chatelier's principle predicts the direction an equilibrium will shift in response to a change in conditions.
questions.explanation_long: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed (by changes in concentration, pressure, temperature), it shifts in the direction that counteracts (partially offsets) that disturbance, allowing prediction of shift direction.
questions.explanation_trick: Le Chatelier's principle = the 'equilibrium shift predictor' for any stress applied to the system.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Le Chatelier's principle predicts the direction of equilibrium shift.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the law of mass action describes the relationship between reactant/product concentrations and rate/equilibrium constant, not directly predicting shift direction under stress.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'Mess's law' isn't a real chemistry principle (likely a typo/distractor).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the law of heat of formation isn't a recognized principle for predicting equilibrium shift direction.

questions.question_text: What is the overall order of this rate equation? Rate = k[H₂][NO₂]²
questions.explanation_short: Overall reaction order = sum of exponents in the rate law = 1 (for H2) + 2 (for NO2) = 3rd order overall.
questions.explanation_long: For Rate = k[H2][NO2]^2, the order with respect to H2 is 1 and with respect to NO2 is 2. The overall order of reaction is the sum of these individual orders: 1 + 2 = 3 (third order overall).
questions.explanation_trick: Overall order = sum of all exponents in the rate law expression.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1 would only account for the H2 term alone, ignoring NO2's exponent.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 2 would only account for the NO2 term alone, ignoring H2's exponent.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 1+2 = 3, the overall reaction order.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 4 overstates the sum of the given exponents.

aliases: What is the overall order of this rate equation? Rate =k[H2][NO2]^2

questions.question_text: The catalysis in which the catalyst and the reactants are in the same phase is known?
questions.explanation_short: Homogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst and reactants exist in the same phase (e.g., all gases, or all in solution).
questions.explanation_long: In homogeneous catalysis, catalyst and reactants share the same physical phase (commonly all in the gas phase or all dissolved in the same liquid solution), allowing uniform mixing at the molecular level. Heterogeneous catalysis, by contrast, involves a catalyst in a different phase (typically a solid catalyzing gas/liquid reactants).
questions.explanation_trick: Homogeneous = 'same state/phase' for catalyst and reactants; Heterogeneous = different phases.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — heterogeneous catalysis specifically involves catalyst and reactants in DIFFERENT phases.
explanation_options.b: Correct — homogeneous catalysis has catalyst and reactants in the same phase.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'slow' isn't a phase-based classification of catalysis type.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'fast' isn't a phase-based classification of catalysis type.

questions.question_text: Born-Haber cycle is used to determine the Lattice energy of ionic compounds. It is the application of
questions.explanation_short: The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law, using a series of known enthalpy changes to indirectly calculate lattice energy.
questions.explanation_long: Since lattice energy can't be measured directly, the Born-Haber cycle sums up a sequence of measurable enthalpy changes (sublimation, ionization, dissociation, electron affinity, formation) via Hess's Law — which states that total enthalpy change is the same regardless of the pathway taken — to solve for the unknown lattice energy.
questions.explanation_trick: Born-Haber cycle = a practical application of Hess's Law to find lattice energy indirectly.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Henry's law relates gas solubility to pressure, unrelated to lattice energy cycles.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Le Chatelier's principle concerns equilibrium shifts, not this enthalpy-summing method.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the Born-Haber cycle is an application of Hess's Law.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the common ion effect concerns solubility equilibria, unrelated to lattice energy calculation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following term is state function?
questions.explanation_short: Enthalpy is a state function — its value depends only on the current state (initial/final), not the path taken to get there.
questions.explanation_long: A state function's value depends solely on the current state of the system, not on the process/path used to reach it. Enthalpy (H) is a classic state function, unlike freezing, decomposition, or sublimation, which are processes/path-dependent changes, not state functions themselves.
questions.explanation_trick: State functions = properties (like H, U, S); processes (freezing, decomposition, sublimation) are NOT state functions themselves.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — freezing is a process/phase change, not a state function itself.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — decomposition is a chemical process, not a state function.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — sublimation is a phase-change process, not a state function.
explanation_options.d: Correct — enthalpy is the state function among these options.

questions.question_text: An electrochemical cell is based upon which reaction?
questions.explanation_short: Electrochemical cells operate based on redox (oxidation-reduction) reactions, transferring electrons between electrodes.
questions.explanation_long: In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the anode (electron loss) and reduction at the cathode (electron gain), with electrons flowing through an external circuit — this electron transfer process is fundamentally a redox reaction, generating (or consuming, in electrolytic cells) electrical energy.
questions.explanation_trick: Electrochemistry = redox in action — electrons flow through wires because of oxidation/reduction.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — acid-base reactions involve proton transfer, not the electron transfer that powers electrochemical cells.
explanation_options.b: Correct — electrochemical cells are based on redox reactions.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — nuclear reactions involve changes in the atomic nucleus, unrelated to electrochemical cells.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — neutralization is a specific type of acid-base reaction, not the basis of electrochemical cells.

questions.question_text: In which of the following, oxygen shows fractional oxidation number?
questions.explanation_short: In KO2 (potassium superoxide), oxygen exists as the superoxide ion (O2⁻), giving it a fractional oxidation number of -1/2 per oxygen atom.
questions.explanation_long: In the superoxide ion O2⁻, the overall charge of -1 is shared between two oxygen atoms, giving each oxygen a fractional oxidation state of -1/2. This is unusual compared to typical oxygen oxidation states (-2 in most oxides, -1 in peroxides like Na2O2), making KO2 the example of fractional oxidation number.
questions.explanation_trick: Superoxide ion O2⁻ splits one negative charge over two oxygens → -1/2 each, the classic 'fractional oxidation state' example.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — in OF2, oxygen has an oxidation state of +2 (whole number, since F is more electronegative).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — in Na2O2 (peroxide), oxygen has oxidation state -1 (whole number).
explanation_options.c: Correct — in KO2 (superoxide), oxygen has a fractional oxidation number of -1/2.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — in Cl2O7, oxygen has oxidation state -2 (whole number).

aliases: In which of the following, oxygen shows fractional oxidation number?
OF2

questions.question_text: Which of the following element has smaller size?
questions.explanation_short: Among Na, K, Al, Li, Lithium (Li) has the smallest atomic size — it's the smallest atom listed due to fewer electron shells.
questions.explanation_long: Atomic size generally decreases across a period (due to increasing nuclear charge) and increases down a group (due to added electron shells). Among the options, Li (period 2) has fewer shells than Na and K (periods 3 and 4), and is smaller than Al despite Al being in the same period as Na — Li is the smallest overall due to being in the smallest period among these.
questions.explanation_trick: Li is period 2 — fewest electron shells among Na, K, Al, Li — so it's the smallest atom.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Na (period 3) is larger than Li (period 2).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — K (period 4) is the largest of the group, having the most electron shells.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Al, though smaller than Na within period 3, is still larger than Li.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Li has the smallest atomic size among Na, K, Al, Li.

questions.question_text: Among LiCl, BeCl2, NaCl, CsCl, the compounds with the greatest and the least ionic character respectively are:
questions.explanation_short: CsCl has the greatest ionic character (largest cation, most electropositive) and BeCl2 has the least (smallest, most polarizing cation, most covalent character).
questions.explanation_long: Ionic character increases with greater electronegativity difference and decreases when the cation is small/highly charged (causing polarization of the anion, per Fajans' rules). Cs (very large, low charge density) forms the most ionic bond (CsCl), while Be (very small, high charge density) polarizes Cl⁻ heavily, giving BeCl2 significant covalent character — the least ionic of the group.
questions.explanation_trick: Fajans' rule: small, highly-charged cations (like Be2+) = more covalent; large cations (like Cs+) = more ionic.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — while CsCl is indeed most ionic, CsCl is repeated as 'least' incorrectly in this option pairing.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — NaCl isn't the most ionic (CsCl is more ionic due to Cs+'s larger size); LiCl isn't the least (BeCl2 is less ionic).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — NaCl isn't the least ionic compound in this set; BeCl2 has more covalent character than NaCl.
explanation_options.d: Correct — CsCl has the greatest ionic character, BeCl2 has the least (most covalent) among these.

questions.question_text: Which statement describes the conversion of magnesium atoms to magnesium ions for ionic bond formation with chlorine?
questions.option_a: The change is reduction, because there has been a gain of electrons
questions.option_b: The change is oxidation, because there has been a loss of electrons
questions.option_c: The change is reduction, because there has been a loss of electrons
questions.option_d: The change is oxidation, because there has been a gain of electrons
questions.explanation_short: Mg atoms lose 2 electrons to form Mg2+ ions — this electron loss is oxidation.
questions.explanation_long: When magnesium reacts with chlorine to form the ionic compound MgCl2, each Mg atom loses two electrons (becoming Mg2+), which is by definition oxidation (loss of electrons — remember 'OIL RIG': Oxidation Is Loss). The chlorine atoms simultaneously gain those electrons (reduction) to become Cl⁻ ions.
questions.explanation_trick: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain — Mg loses electrons, so it's oxidized.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this incorrectly calls electron gain 'reduction' when describing Mg, which actually loses electrons (mismatched conclusion).
explanation_options.b: Correct — Mg's conversion to Mg2+ is oxidation, because it loses electrons.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — this incorrectly labels electron loss as reduction; electron loss is oxidation, not reduction.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this incorrectly claims Mg gains electrons; magnesium actually loses electrons to form Mg2+.

questions.question_text: AB4 Type with no Lone Pairs geometry enables to form which shape of molecule?
questions.explanation_short: An AB4 molecule with no lone pairs on the central atom adopts a regular tetrahedral geometry (like CH4).
questions.explanation_long: Following VSEPR theory, when a central atom (A) is bonded to 4 groups (B) with zero lone pairs, the electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible in three dimensions, forming a regular tetrahedron with 109.5° bond angles — the classic methane (CH4) geometry.
questions.explanation_trick: AB4 with no lone pairs = tetrahedral, like methane CH4 (109.5° angles).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — trigonal (planar) geometry describes AB3 with no lone pairs, not AB4.
explanation_options.b: Correct — AB4 with no lone pairs gives a regular tetrahedron shape.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — regular octahedron describes AB6 with no lone pairs, not AB4.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — regular pyramidal (trigonal pyramidal) describes AB3 WITH one lone pair, not AB4 with none.

questions.question_text: Why dimer of Aluminum chloride is formed
questions.option_b: Aluminum is having lone pair of electron
questions.option_c: Aluminum donates lone pair to form bridge
questions.option_d: Aluminum forms coordinate bonds with chlorine to complete its octet
questions.explanation_short: AlCl3 dimerizes to Al2Cl6 because Al forms coordinate (dative) bonds with chlorine to complete its incomplete octet.
questions.explanation_long: Aluminum in AlCl3 has only 6 electrons around it (an incomplete octet), making it electron-deficient. Two AlCl3 units combine, with chlorine atoms donating lone pairs to form coordinate covalent bridging bonds to the Al of the neighboring molecule, satisfying the octet and stabilizing the dimer Al2Cl6.
questions.explanation_trick: AlCl3 is electron-deficient (6 electrons) — it dimerizes via Cl lone-pair donation to complete Al's octet.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — aluminum is electron-DEFICIENT (6 electrons), not electron-rich.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — it's chlorine that donates the lone pair, not aluminum having one to give.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — it's chlorine (not aluminum) that donates its lone pair to form the bridging bond.
explanation_options.d: Correct — aluminum accepts coordinate bonds from chlorine's lone pairs to complete its octet, forming the dimer.

questions.question_text: Which group of the periodic table contain non-metals, metalloids and metals.
questions.explanation_short: Group IV A (the carbon family) uniquely contains non-metals (C), metalloids (Si, Ge), and metals (Sn, Pb).
questions.explanation_long: Group IVA spans the full range of element character: carbon (non-metal) at the top, silicon and germanium (metalloids) in the middle, and tin and lead (metals) at the bottom — making it the classic example of a group showing the non-metal-to-metal transition down a single group.
questions.explanation_trick: Group IVA = Carbon family: C (non-metal) → Si/Ge (metalloid) → Sn/Pb (metal), the trend within one group.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Group IB contains only transition metals (like Cu, Ag, Au).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Group VIIA (halogens) are all non-metals, no metals or metalloids.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Group IVA contains non-metals, metalloids, and metals.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Group VIA mostly contains non-metals (O, S, Se) with limited metalloid/metal character (Te, Po), not as clear a full spread as IVA.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sulfate compound is insoluble in water ?
questions.explanation_short: BaSO4 (barium sulfate) is insoluble in water, famously used as a contrast agent because it doesn't dissolve or get absorbed.
questions.explanation_long: Most sulfates are water-soluble, but Group 2 sulfates become progressively less soluble down the group. BaSO4 is essentially insoluble (very low Ksp), which is exactly why it's medically safe to use as an X-ray contrast agent — it passes through the digestive tract without dissolving into the bloodstream.
questions.explanation_trick: BaSO4 = the 'barium meal' X-ray contrast agent — insoluble by design, so it's safe to ingest.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — BeSO4 is actually soluble in water.
explanation_options.b: Correct — BaSO4 is insoluble in water.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — MgSO4 (Epsom salt) is well known to be soluble in water.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — CaSO4 is slightly soluble (more soluble than BaSO4).

questions.question_text: Which of the following complex show a tetrahedral geometry?
questions.explanation_short: [Cu(CN)4]2- shows a tetrahedral geometry, typical for Cu(I) complexes with 4 coordinated ligands.
questions.explanation_long: Copper(I) (d10 configuration) complexes with four ligands, like [Cu(CN)4]3- (or as given, a 4-coordinate copper cyanide complex), commonly adopt tetrahedral geometry, since a filled d10 shell has no strong preference for square planar arrangement (unlike d8 metals).
questions.explanation_trick: d10 metal ions (like Cu+) with 4-coordination typically go tetrahedral, not square planar.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — [Fe(CO)5] is trigonal bipyramidal (5-coordinate), not tetrahedral.
explanation_options.b: Correct — [Cu(CN)4]2- adopts a tetrahedral geometry.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — [Au(Cl)4]- (Au(III), d8) is square planar, not tetrahedral.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — [Pt(NH3)4]2+ (Pt(II), d8) is square planar, not tetrahedral.

questions.question_text: In which pair one has all Unpaired d orbitals while other have all paired d orbitals ?
questions.explanation_short: Cr has all unpaired d-electrons (d5, all 5 singly occupied), while Zn has all paired d-electrons (d10, fully filled).
questions.explanation_long: Chromium's unusual configuration is [Ar]3d5 4s1 — all five 3d electrons are unpaired (half-filled stability). Zinc's configuration is [Ar]3d10 4s2 — the d subshell is completely filled, so all 10 d-electrons are paired. This makes Cr and Zn a striking 'all unpaired vs all paired' contrast.
questions.explanation_trick: Cr = d5 (half-filled, all unpaired, extra stable); Zn = d10 (fully filled, all paired).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Cu (d10) and Zn (d10) both have all paired d-electrons, not a contrasting pair.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Cr (d5, unpaired) is correct for one, but Fe (d6) has 4 unpaired, not 'all paired'.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Cr has all unpaired d-electrons (d5), Zn has all paired (d10).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — Mn (d5, unpaired) and Co (d7, some paired/unpaired mix) don't form the clean 'all unpaired vs all paired' contrast that Cr/Zn does.

questions.question_text: In which of the following functional groups, the carbon atom is sp hybridized?
questions.explanation_short: The -C≡N (nitrile/cyanide) carbon is sp hybridized, due to the triple bond between carbon and nitrogen.
questions.explanation_long: A carbon involved in a triple bond (like in -C≡N, nitriles) undergoes sp hybridization — using one s and one p orbital, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals for the two pi bonds of the triple bond. -CHO, -COOH, and -COOR all contain a carbonyl (C=O) double bond, giving sp2 hybridization instead.
questions.explanation_trick: Triple bond → sp hybridization (nitriles, alkynes); double bond (C=O) → sp2 hybridization (aldehydes, acids, esters).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — -CHO (aldehyde) has a C=O double bond, giving sp2 hybridization, not sp.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — -COOH (carboxylic acid) has a C=O double bond, giving sp2 hybridization.
explanation_options.c: Correct — -CN (nitrile) has a C≡N triple bond, giving sp hybridization.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — -COOR (ester) has a C=O double bond, giving sp2 hybridization, not sp.

questions.question_text: The compounds containing R-SH functional group are known as:
questions.explanation_short: Compounds with the -SH (sulfhydryl) functional group are called thio-alcohols (thiols) — the sulfur analog of alcohols.
questions.explanation_long: Just as -OH defines alcohols, the -SH group defines thiols (thio-alcohols), where sulfur replaces oxygen. They're known for their strong, often unpleasant odor (e.g., in garlic, skunk spray) and are named with the suffix '-thiol'.
questions.explanation_trick: -OH = alcohol; -SH = thio-alcohol (thiol) — sulfur swaps in for oxygen.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — alcohols contain -OH, not -SH.
explanation_options.b: Correct — compounds with -SH are called thio-alcohols (thiols).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — thio-ethers have the structure R-S-R', not the -SH group.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — nitriles contain -C≡N, unrelated to the -SH group.

questions.question_text: What is the number of isomers of a hydrocarbon having a molecular formula, C₄H₈?
questions.explanation_short: C4H8 has 5 structural isomers: 1-butene, 2-butene, isobutylene (2-methylpropene), cyclobutane, and methylcyclopropane.
questions.explanation_long: For molecular formula C4H8, the structural isomers are: 1-butene, 2-butene (not counting cis/trans as separate structures), 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) — three alkenes — plus two cycloalkanes, cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane. That totals 5 distinct structural isomers.
questions.explanation_trick: C4H8 isomers: 3 alkenes (1-butene, 2-butene, isobutylene) + 2 cycloalkanes (cyclobutane, methylcyclopropane) = 5.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 2 isomers undercounts the possible C4H8 structures.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 3 isomers is still an undercount.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 4 undercounts by one compared to the correct total of 5.
explanation_options.d: Correct — C4H8 has 5 structural isomers.

aliases: What is the number of isomers of a hydrocarbon having a molecular formula, C4H8?

questions.question_text: Alkylbenzene is formed when benzene is treated with an alkyl halide in the presence of anhydrous aluminum chloride. Identify the type of reaction.
questions.explanation_short: Attaching an alkyl group onto benzene using an alkyl halide + AlCl3 is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction.
questions.explanation_long: Friedel-Crafts alkylation uses an alkyl halide and a Lewis acid catalyst (like anhydrous AlCl3) to generate a carbocation that attacks the benzene ring via electrophilic aromatic substitution, installing an alkyl group and forming alkylbenzene.
questions.explanation_trick: Alkyl halide + AlCl3 + benzene = Friedel-Crafts ALKYLation (adds an alkyl group).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — halogenation would substitute a halogen directly onto benzene, not add an alkyl group.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Friedel-Crafts ACYLation uses an acyl halide (RCOCl), producing a ketone, not an alkylbenzene.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — sulphonation adds a -SO3H group using fuming sulfuric acid, not an alkyl group.

questions.question_text: Three alternate single and double bonds in benzene are called?
questions.explanation_short: The three alternating single and double bonds in benzene's ring are called conjugate (conjugated) bonds.
questions.explanation_long: Benzene's ring structure has alternating single and double C-C bonds, allowing continuous overlap of p-orbitals around the ring (delocalized pi electron system) — this alternating single-double bond pattern is termed a conjugated system, giving benzene its aromatic stability.
questions.explanation_trick: Alternating single-double bonds = conjugation, the source of benzene's extra stability (resonance/delocalization).

explanation_options.a: Correct — benzene's alternating bonds are termed conjugate (conjugated) bonds.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — coordinate covalent bonds involve one atom donating both electrons, unrelated to benzene's alternating bond pattern.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'fixed bonds' isn't the standard term (in reality, benzene's bonds are actually equal-length/delocalized, not fixed single/double).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — ionic bonds involve electron transfer between atoms, not benzene's covalent ring bonding.

questions.question_text: Which of the following compound is more acidic?
questions.explanation_short: Among alkane, alkene, alkyne, and cycloalkane, the alkyne (with sp carbon, terminal C-H) is the most acidic due to greater s-character.
questions.explanation_long: Terminal alkynes (R-C≡C-H) are more acidic than alkenes or alkanes because their sp-hybridized carbon has 50% s-character, pulling electron density closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the resulting carbanion better than sp2 (alkene, 33% s-character) or sp3 (alkane, 25% s-character) carbons.
questions.explanation_trick: More s-character = more acidic C-H: sp (alkyne, most acidic) > sp2 (alkene) > sp3 (alkane, least acidic).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — alkanes (sp3, 25% s-character) are the LEAST acidic hydrocarbons.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — alkenes (sp2) are more acidic than alkanes but less than alkynes.
explanation_options.c: Correct — alkynes (sp, 50% s-character) are the most acidic hydrocarbon type.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — cycloalkanes behave similarly to alkanes (sp3), not particularly acidic.

questions.question_text: Consider the chlorination of methane, the attack of chlorine free radical on methane form methyl free radical occurs in ?
questions.explanation_short: The methyl free radical forms during the propagation step of methane's free-radical chlorination mechanism.
questions.explanation_long: Radical chlorination has three stages: initiation (Cl2 splits into 2 Cl• radicals via light/heat), propagation (Cl• abstracts H from CH4 forming CH3• and HCl, then CH3• reacts with Cl2 to form CH3Cl and regenerate Cl•), and termination (radicals combine to end the chain). The methyl radical specifically forms in the first propagation step.
questions.explanation_trick: Initiation makes the first radical (Cl•); Propagation is where that radical attacks the substrate (forming CH3•).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — initiation only splits Cl2 into Cl radicals; it doesn't yet produce the methyl radical.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the methyl free radical forms during the propagation step.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — termination combines existing radicals to end the reaction, not form new methyl radicals.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'last step' isn't a standard named step in the radical mechanism (termination is the correct term, and methyl radical doesn't form there).

questions.question_text: The ratio of sigma to pi electrons in benzene is?
questions.explanation_short: Benzene has 24 sigma electrons (12 sigma bonds: 6 C-C + 6 C-H) and 6 pi electrons (3 delocalized C=C pi bonds), giving a sigma:pi electron ratio of 4:1.
questions.explanation_long: Benzene (C6H6) has 12 sigma bonds total — 6 C-C ring sigma bonds and 6 C-H sigma bonds — holding 24 sigma electrons. Its delocalized pi system comes from 3 pi bonds (6 pi electrons) spread around the ring. Comparing electron counts: 24 sigma electrons to 6 pi electrons simplifies to a 4:1 ratio.
questions.explanation_trick: Benzene: 12 sigma bonds (24 electrons) vs 3 pi bonds (6 electrons) → 24:6 = 4:1.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1:3 inverts and misstates the actual ratio.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 3:1 is close in form but not the correct calculated ratio.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 24 sigma electrons to 6 pi electrons simplifies to 4:1.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 1:4 inverts the correct ratio.

questions.question_text: When halogen is removed from an alkyl halide a carbocation is formed, identify the most reactive carbocation
questions.explanation_short: The tertiary carbocation is the most stable/reactive due to maximum alkyl group hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation.
questions.explanation_long: Carbocation stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, because more alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon donate electron density (through hyperconjugation and the inductive effect), stabilizing the positive charge. More stable carbocations form more readily and react faster, making tertiary the most 'reactive' in this sense.
questions.explanation_trick: Carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl — more alkyl groups = more stabilization = easier to form.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — primary carbocations are among the least stable/reactive, not the most.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — secondary carbocations are more stable than primary but less than tertiary.
explanation_options.c: Correct — tertiary carbocations are the most stable and reactive.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — methyl carbocations are the LEAST stable of all, with no alkyl stabilization.

questions.question_text: Freon is commonly known as ?
questions.explanation_short: Freon is the common trade name for chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), widely used as refrigerants.
questions.explanation_long: Freon is DuPont's trademark name for a family of CFC (and related) compounds historically used as refrigerants in air conditioners and refrigerators, and as aerosol propellants — now phased out due to their role in ozone layer depletion.
questions.explanation_trick: Freon = CFC = classic refrigerant gas (also infamous for ozone depletion).

explanation_options.a: Correct — Freon is commonly known as a refrigerant.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Freon isn't typically used/known as a general solvent.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Freon is not an insecticide.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — while some halon fire extinguishers are related compounds, 'Freon' itself is specifically known as a refrigerant, not a fire extinguisher.

questions.question_text: Neopentylchloride belongs to which class of alkyl halides?
questions.explanation_short: Neopentyl chloride is a primary alkyl halide — the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon (despite being near a bulky tertiary carbon).
questions.explanation_long: Neopentyl chloride, (CH3)3C-CH2-Cl, has its chlorine on a CH2 carbon that is attached to only ONE other carbon (the bulky tertiary carbon next to it doesn't change this classification) — the carbon bearing Cl is bonded to just 1 other carbon, making it primary by definition, despite its high steric hindrance from the adjacent tert-butyl group.
questions.explanation_trick: Classification (1°/2°/3°) depends on carbons attached to the C-Cl carbon itself, not neighboring bulkiness — neopentyl chloride's C-Cl carbon touches only 1 other carbon = primary.

explanation_options.a: Correct — neopentyl chloride is classified as a primary alkyl halide.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — secondary would require the C-Cl carbon to be attached to 2 other carbons.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — tertiary would require the C-Cl carbon attached to 3 other carbons (that's the adjacent carbon, not the C-Cl carbon itself).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'quaternary alkyl halide' isn't a standard classification (quaternary carbons can't bear a leaving group and 4 substituents simultaneously in this sense).

questions.question_text: What is the common name of 1,2,3-propanetriol?
questions.explanation_short: 1,2,3-propanetriol is the IUPAC name for glycerol (glycerin), a triol with three -OH groups.
questions.explanation_long: Glycerol (common name) / 1,2,3-propanetriol (IUPAC name) is a three-carbon molecule with hydroxyl groups on each carbon, widely used in cosmetics, food, and as a byproduct of soap-making (saponification) and biodiesel production.
questions.explanation_trick: 1,2,3-propanetriol = glycerol — three carbons, three -OH groups (tri-ol).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — butyl alcohol is a single -OH, 4-carbon alcohol, not a triol.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — glycol usually refers to ethylene glycol, a diol (2 -OH groups), not a triol.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 1,2,3-propanetriol's common name is glycerol.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — propyl alcohol is a single -OH, 3-carbon alcohol, not a triol.

questions.question_text: Benzene is formed when Na reacts with which of the following?
questions.explanation_short: The official key marks phenol here, though note: Na metal reacting with phenol actually gives sodium phenoxide + H2 gas, not benzene itself — the classic reaction that truly yields benzene is zinc-dust distillation of phenol (C6H5OH + Zn → C6H6 + ZnO).
questions.explanation_long: As literally worded, none of the given options cleanly produces benzene by reacting with sodium metal — Na + phenol (like Na + any alcohol) releases H2 gas and forms sodium phenoxide, not benzene. The well-known reaction that actually converts phenol to benzene is distillation with zinc dust, not a reaction with sodium. Among the four options, phenol is the one most closely associated with a real benzene-forming reaction (via the zinc-dust route), which is likely why the key marks it — but the question's exact phrasing ('Na reacts with...') doesn't precisely match that real reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Real benzene-from-phenol reaction: phenol + zinc dust (distillation) → benzene. Na + phenol just gives sodium phenoxide + H2, not benzene.

explanation_options.a: Wrong (per key) — 'Alcohol' is too generic and doesn't match the key's specific answer.
explanation_options.b: Wrong (per key) — butyl alcohol reacting with Na would give sodium butoxide + H2, not benzene.
explanation_options.c: Wrong (per key) — propanol reacting with Na would give sodium propoxide + H2, not benzene.
explanation_options.d: Marked correct by the official key — phenol is the compound most associated with a real benzene-forming reaction, though that reaction actually uses zinc dust distillation rather than sodium metal as this question states.

questions.question_text: When Phenol reacts with formaldehyde, which of the following product is produced?
questions.explanation_short: Phenol + formaldehyde (under condensation polymerization conditions) forms an adduct as an intermediate, eventually leading to Bakelite-type resins.
questions.explanation_long: In the industrially important phenol-formaldehyde reaction (used to make Bakelite), phenol reacts with formaldehyde to first form an addition product (adduct/methylol phenol), which then undergoes further condensation to form cross-linked polymer resins.
questions.explanation_trick: Phenol + formaldehyde → adduct intermediate → eventually Bakelite (an early industrial plastic).

explanation_options.a: Correct — phenol and formaldehyde initially form an adduct.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — hydronium ion (H3O+) isn't a product of this organic reaction.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — oxonium ion isn't the standard product described for this reaction.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — phenoxide ion would form under basic/ionization conditions, not as the direct reaction product with formaldehyde here.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct name of CH3CH2CH2COCH2CHO?
questions.explanation_short: CH3CH2CH2COCH2CHO has a ketone at C3 (oxo) and an aldehyde at C1, named 3-oxohexanal.
questions.explanation_long: Numbering from the aldehyde carbon (C1) as the principal characteristic group: C1=CHO, C2=CH2, C3=C=O (ketone, so 'oxo' substituent), C4-C6=CH2CH2CH3. This gives 3-oxohexanal — 'oxo' prefix denotes the ketone since the aldehyde takes priority as the suffix (-al).
questions.explanation_trick: When both aldehyde and ketone are present, aldehyde is the suffix (-al); ketone becomes the 'oxo-' prefix.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 3-oxohexanal correctly names this aldehyde-ketone compound.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'hexanal' with '3-one' misapplies naming; the ketone must be named as 'oxo-' prefix when an aldehyde is present, not as a separate '-one' suffix.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'hexanol' implies an alcohol (-ol), not the aldehyde (-al) that's actually present.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — '3-keto hexanol' incorrectly uses 'hexanol' (alcohol) instead of 'hexanal' (aldehyde), and 'keto' isn't standard IUPAC (oxo- is).

questions.question_text: Which is the most suitable reagent for the conversion of R-CH₂OH → RCHO?
questions.explanation_short: CrO3 (chromium trioxide, in the Collins/PCC-type oxidation) is a mild oxidizer that stops primary alcohol oxidation at the aldehyde stage (RCH2OH → RCHO).
questions.explanation_long: Strong oxidizers like K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 push oxidation all the way to a carboxylic acid, but mild, controlled reagents based on CrO3 (like PCC, pyridinium chlorochromate, a CrO3-derived reagent) stop the oxidation cleanly at the aldehyde stage, making CrO3-based reagents the most suitable choice for RCH2OH → RCHO.
questions.explanation_trick: Strong oxidant (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 conc.) → carboxylic acid; Mild CrO3-based reagent → stops at aldehyde.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — KMnO4/NaOH is a strong oxidizer that typically over-oxidizes primary alcohols to carboxylic acids.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — concentrated K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is a strong oxidizer, driving oxidation past the aldehyde to the acid.
explanation_options.c: Correct — CrO3-based mild oxidation is most suitable for stopping at the aldehyde stage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'Cr2O4/H2SO4 (Conc.)' isn't a standard, correctly-formulated oxidizing reagent (likely a distractor formula).

aliases: Which is the most suitable reagent for the conversion of R-CH2OH -> RCHO?
KMnO4/NaOH

questions.question_text: Which of the following is also called silver mirror test?
questions.explanation_short: Tollen's reagent test is also called the silver mirror test, since it deposits a shiny silver layer when it detects an aldehyde.
questions.explanation_long: Tollen's reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) oxidizes aldehydes while itself being reduced — silver ions (Ag+) are reduced to metallic silver (Ag), which deposits as a shiny mirror-like coating on the test tube's inner surface, giving this test its 'silver mirror test' nickname.
questions.explanation_trick: Tollen's reagent = silver ions → gets reduced to shiny silver metal 'mirror' on a positive aldehyde test.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Benedict's test uses copper ions, giving a brick-red precipitate, not a silver mirror.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Fehling's test also uses copper ions with a similar brick-red precipitate result, not silver.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the iodoform test detects methyl ketones/certain alcohols via a yellow precipitate, unrelated to silver.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Tollen's reagent test is also called the silver mirror test.

questions.question_text: Which among the following have least pH?
questions.explanation_short: CH3CHCl2COOH has the lowest pH (most acidic) since two electronegative chlorine atoms on the same carbon strongly withdraw electron density, greatly stabilizing the conjugate base.
questions.explanation_long: The inductive effect of electronegative halogens increases acid strength, and this effect is strongest when halogens are close to the carboxyl group and more numerous. CH3CHCl2COOH has two chlorines on the alpha carbon (right next to -COOH), giving the strongest combined inductive electron-withdrawal among the options, making it the most acidic (lowest pH).
questions.explanation_trick: More halogens + closer to -COOH = stronger inductive effect = lower pH (more acidic).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — CH3CH2COOH (propanoic acid) has no halogen substitution, making it the least acidic (weakest, highest pH) of the group.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — CH2ClCH2COOH has only one Cl, farther from -COOH (beta position), giving a weaker inductive effect than the dichloro compound.
explanation_options.c: Correct — CH3CHCl2COOH (two Cl on the alpha carbon) has the strongest inductive effect, giving the lowest (most acidic) pH.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — CH3CH2CH2COOH (butanoic acid) has no halogens, making it one of the least acidic options.

questions.question_text: If carboxylic acid and ketone groups C=O are present in a chain then final name will be given as
questions.explanation_short: When both a carboxylic acid and a ketone (C=O) group are present in one chain, the name uses 'oxo' for the ketone and '-oic acid' as the suffix.
questions.explanation_long: IUPAC nomenclature prioritizes the carboxylic acid as the principal characteristic group (suffix '-oic acid'), while any ketone present elsewhere in the chain is named using the prefix 'oxo-'. So a compound with both groups is named as an '...oxo...oic acid'.
questions.explanation_trick: Carboxylic acid always outranks ketone in naming priority — acid = suffix ('-oic acid'), ketone = prefix ('oxo-').

explanation_options.a: Correct — such compounds are named using 'oxo' (for ketone) and 'oic acid' (for the acid) together.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'one, oic acid' misapplies '-one' (the ketone suffix used only when no higher-priority group like acid is present).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — since only the 'oxo, oic acid' naming convention applies here, 'both 1 and 2' incorrectly includes the wrong option too.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — since option (a) does correctly describe the naming, 'none of these' is incorrect.

questions.question_text: When carboxylic acids and dicarboxylic acids have similar molecular weights, how do their melting points compare?
questions.option_a: Carboxylic acids have greater melting points
questions.option_b: Dicarboxylic acids have greater melting points
questions.option_c: Both acids have similar melting points
questions.explanation_short: Dicarboxylic acids have greater melting points than monocarboxylic acids of similar molecular weight, due to stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding (two -COOH groups per molecule).
questions.explanation_long: With two carboxylic acid groups instead of one, dicarboxylic acids can form more extensive hydrogen bonding networks between molecules, requiring more energy (higher temperature) to break these interactions and melt — giving them notably higher melting points than similarly-sized monocarboxylic acids.
questions.explanation_trick: Two -COOH groups = double the hydrogen bonding sites = higher melting point than a single-acid compound of similar size.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this reverses the actual trend; carboxylic (mono) acids have LOWER melting points than dicarboxylic acids of similar weight.
explanation_options.b: Correct — dicarboxylic acids have greater melting points due to more extensive hydrogen bonding.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — melting points are NOT similar; the extra -COOH group in dicarboxylic acids meaningfully raises the melting point.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — there IS a consistent trend (dicarboxylic > monocarboxylic in melting point for similar MW), contrary to this option's claim.

questions.question_text: When food reaches stomach, the action of which of the following come to an end due to acidic PH?
questions.explanation_short: Salivary amylase's action ends when food reaches the acidic stomach environment, since amylase is denatured/inactivated at low pH.
questions.explanation_long: Amylase (from saliva) works optimally at near-neutral pH in the mouth, beginning starch digestion. Once food (bolus) enters the strongly acidic stomach (pH ~1.5-3.5), amylase is denatured and its activity stops — digestion of starch pauses until the food reaches the more neutral small intestine, where pancreatic amylase resumes it.
questions.explanation_trick: Salivary amylase works in the mouth (neutral pH) — stomach acid switches it off until intestinal pH returns.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — lipase (fat-digesting) is not primarily active before the stomach in a way that's 'ended' specifically by stomach acid in this classic context; the key targets amylase.
explanation_options.b: Correct — amylase's (starch-digesting) action ends when food reaches the acidic stomach.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — maltase acts later, in the small intestine, not relevantly 'ended' by stomach acid in this sequence.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'hydrolases' is too broad a category (amylase itself is a hydrolase), not the specific intended answer.

questions.question_text: Which of the following proteins acts as carrier of copper in blood plasma?
questions.explanation_short: Ceruloplasmin is the copper-carrying (and copper-oxidizing) protein in blood plasma.
questions.explanation_long: Ceruloplasmin is a plasma glycoprotein that binds and transports the majority of copper in the blood, and also has ferroxidase activity (oxidizing Fe2+ to Fe3+) to assist iron transport. It's a key marker in diagnosing Wilson's disease (copper metabolism disorder).
questions.explanation_trick: Ceruloplasmin = the body's copper-carrier protein in blood (think 'cerulo-' relating to its blue color from bound copper).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — hemoglobin carries oxygen (via iron), not copper.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'glycoprotein' is too generic; the specific copper-carrying glycoprotein is named ceruloplasmin.
explanation_options.c: Correct — ceruloplasmin is the copper-carrier protein in blood plasma.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — histone is a DNA-packaging protein found in the nucleus, unrelated to blood copper transport.

questions.question_text: What is the shape of velocity-time graph for constant acceleration?
questions.explanation_short: Constant acceleration produces a straight-line velocity-time graph, since velocity changes at a steady rate.
questions.explanation_long: For constant acceleration, v = u + at, a linear equation in t. Plotting v against t therefore gives a straight line, with slope equal to the acceleration. A curving graph would indicate changing (non-constant) acceleration.
questions.explanation_trick: v = u + at is linear in t → straight-line v-t graph for constant a.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a parabola describes displacement-time (not velocity-time) under constant acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Correct — constant acceleration gives a straight-line v-t graph.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — an incline curve would suggest changing acceleration, not constant.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a decline curve also implies non-constant (changing) acceleration.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct definition of variable velocity?
questions.option_a: Unequal distances are covered in equal intervals of time
questions.option_b: Equal displacements are made in unequal intervals of time
questions.option_c: Unequal displacements are made in equal intervals of time
questions.option_d: Equal displacements are made in equal intervals of time
questions.explanation_short: Variable velocity means unequal displacements occur in equal time intervals — the object speeds up or slows down.
questions.explanation_long: If a body covers unequal displacements in successive equal time intervals, its velocity is changing (variable). Constant/uniform velocity, by contrast, means equal displacements occur in equal time intervals.
questions.explanation_trick: Equal displacement/equal time = constant velocity; Unequal displacement/equal time = variable velocity.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'unequal distances in equal time' is close, but the precise definition uses displacement, and this option's structure doesn't match the standard phrasing used for variable velocity in the key as well as option c.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'equal displacement in unequal time' isn't the standard formulation of variable velocity.
explanation_options.c: Correct — unequal displacements in equal time intervals defines variable velocity.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'equal displacements in equal time intervals' defines constant (uniform) velocity, not variable.

questions.question_text: A stone thrown horizontally from the top of a tall building follows a path that is:
questions.option_b: Made of two straight line segments
questions.explanation_short: A horizontally thrown stone follows a parabolic path due to combined uniform horizontal motion and accelerating vertical fall.
questions.explanation_long: Projectile motion combines constant horizontal velocity with uniformly accelerated vertical motion (due to gravity). This combination of a linear horizontal component and a quadratic vertical component (y ∝ x²) traces out a parabolic trajectory — one of the most classic results in mechanics.
questions.explanation_trick: Projectile motion = horizontal (constant v) + vertical (constant a) = parabolic path.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a circular path would require centripetal force directed toward a fixed center, not gravity acting purely downward.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the path is a smooth curve, not two straight segments.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — hyperbolic paths arise in different force scenarios (like orbital mechanics under certain conditions), not simple projectile motion.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the stone follows a parabolic path.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is incorrect?
questions.option_a: Reaction force on a body is always balanced by the action force
questions.option_b: Reaction and action forces are always equal
questions.option_c: Action and reaction forces never act on the same body
questions.option_d: Newton's Third Law is always valid in all situations
questions.explanation_short: It is incorrect to say reaction force is 'balanced' by the action force on the SAME body — action and reaction act on different bodies and never balance each other out.
questions.explanation_long: Newton's Third Law states action-reaction pairs are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, but act on DIFFERENT objects — so they never cancel or 'balance' each other (since forces only balance if acting on the same object). Saying the reaction force is 'balanced by' the action force implies they act together on one body, which is the incorrect statement being tested.
questions.explanation_trick: Action-reaction pairs act on DIFFERENT bodies — they never balance each other (since balancing requires same-body, opposite forces).

explanation_options.a: Correct (as the INCORRECT statement) — action and reaction don't 'balance' each other since they act on different bodies.
explanation_options.b: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — action and reaction forces are indeed always equal in magnitude.
explanation_options.c: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — action and reaction forces do act on different bodies, never the same one.
explanation_options.d: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — Newton's Third Law is universally valid.

questions.question_text: A fireman wants to slide down a rope. The breaking load of the rope is 3/4 th of the weight of the man. With what acceleration should the fire man slide down? ( Acceleration due to gravity is 'g')
questions.explanation_short: With breaking load 3/4 of weight, the rope can only support 3/4 mg, so the fireman must accelerate downward at g/4 to reduce the effective tension to that limit.
questions.explanation_long: For the fireman not to break the rope, tension T ≤ (3/4)mg. Using Newton's second law for the fireman sliding down: mg - T = ma → a = g - T/m. Setting T = (3/4)mg (max safe tension): a = g - (3/4)g = g/4. So the fireman must accelerate downward at least g/4 to keep tension at or below the rope's breaking load.
questions.explanation_trick: mg - T = ma; with T=(3/4)mg, solve: a = g - (3/4)g = g/4.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — sliding at a=g means free-fall, requiring T=0, more caution than actually needed (and doesn't match the calculated minimum).
explanation_options.b: Correct — a = g/4 is the minimum acceleration keeping tension within the rope's breaking load.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a=3g/4 would mean tension T=mg/4, well below the breaking load's needed value — this isn't the calculated answer.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a=0 (not sliding) would require T=mg, exceeding the rope's 3/4 mg breaking load, snapping it.

questions.question_text: When a heavy coin falls a short distance towards the ground it does not reach terminal velocity. Why is this so?
questions.option_a: The coin has not hit the ground
questions.option_b: The weight of coin is equal to air resistance
questions.option_c: The weight of coin increases as air resistance increases
questions.option_d: The weight of coin is more than air resistance
questions.explanation_short: A coin falling only a short distance hasn't yet built up enough speed for air resistance to equal its weight, so it hasn't reached terminal velocity.
questions.explanation_long: Terminal velocity occurs when air resistance (drag, which increases with speed) grows to equal the falling object's weight, resulting in zero net force. Over a short fall, the coin hasn't accelerated long enough to reach the speed where drag force balances gravity — so its weight still exceeds the air resistance acting on it.
questions.explanation_trick: Terminal velocity reached only when air resistance = weight; short falls haven't built up enough speed/drag yet.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the coin has been falling and moving; not having hit the ground yet isn't why it lacks terminal velocity.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — if weight equalled air resistance, it WOULD be at terminal velocity, contradicting the premise.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — air resistance hasn't yet increased enough over the short distance/time; it's the weight that still exceeds resistance, not increasing weight itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — over a short fall, the coin's weight still exceeds the (still-building) air resistance, so it hasn't reached terminal velocity.

questions.question_text: The consumption of energy by a 60 W bulb in 2 s is:
questions.explanation_short: Energy = Power × time = 60 W × 2 s = 120 J.
questions.explanation_long: Using the basic relation E = Pt: a 60 W bulb consumes energy at a rate of 60 joules per second. Over 2 seconds, total energy consumed = 60 × 2 = 120 J.
questions.explanation_trick: Energy (J) = Power (W) × time (s) — simple direct multiplication.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 60 W × 2 s = 120 J.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 60 J would be the energy consumed in just 1 second, not 2.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 30 J doesn't match the direct P×t calculation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0.02 J is far too small; likely from an incorrect unit manipulation.

questions.question_text: A long spring, when stretched by a distance x, has potential energy V. On increasing the stretching to nx, the potential energy of the spring will be:
questions.explanation_short: Spring PE scales with the square of extension (V ∝ x²), so stretching to nx gives potential energy n²V.
questions.explanation_long: Elastic potential energy stored in a spring is given by PE = (1/2)kx², which is proportional to the square of the extension. If extension increases from x to nx, the new PE = (1/2)k(nx)² = n² × (1/2)kx² = n²V.
questions.explanation_trick: PE ∝ x² — doubling extension (n=2) quadruples PE (n²=4), not just doubles it.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — nV assumes a linear relationship, but PE actually scales with the SQUARE of extension.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — V/n would represent decreasing PE, opposite of what happens when extension increases.
explanation_options.c: Correct — potential energy scales as n²V when extension is multiplied by n.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — V/n² would represent PE decreasing with the square, the opposite of the actual relationship.

questions.question_text: Ignoring details associated with friction, extra forces exerted by arm and leg muscles, and other factors, we can consider a pole vault as the conversion of an athlete's running kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy. If an athlete is to lift his body 5 m during a vault, what speed must he have when he plants his pole?
questions.explanation_short: Using energy conservation (KE→PE), lifting 5 m requires v = √(2gh) = √(2×10×5) = 10 m/s.
questions.explanation_long: Setting kinetic energy equal to gravitational potential energy gained: (1/2)mv² = mgh → v = √(2gh). With h=5m and g≈10 m/s²: v = √(2×10×5) = √100 = 10 m/s.
questions.explanation_trick: KE = PE at the top of the vault: v = √(2gh) — a standard energy conservation formula.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 5 m/s would only correspond to a much smaller height, not 5 m.
explanation_options.b: Correct — v = √(2×10×5) = 10 m/s is needed to lift the body 5 m.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 15 m/s would correspond to a much greater height than 5 m.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 20 m/s would give a height far exceeding 5 m (h=v²/2g=20m).

questions.question_text: A particle of mass m at rest is acted upon by a force P for time t. Its kinetic energy after time t is:
questions.explanation_short: Impulse Pt = mv gives v = Pt/m; KE = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)m(Pt/m)² = (P²t²)/(2m).
questions.explanation_long: Using impulse-momentum theorem: Force × time = change in momentum, so Pt = mv (starting from rest), giving v = Pt/m. Substituting into KE = (1/2)mv²: KE = (1/2)m(Pt/m)² = (P²t²)/(2m).
questions.explanation_trick: Impulse Pt = mv → v = Pt/m; then plug into KE = (1/2)mv² to get (P²t²)/(2m).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — (P²t²)/m is double the correct value, missing the 1/2 factor from the KE formula.
explanation_options.b: Correct — (P²t²)/(2m) correctly follows from combining impulse and kinetic energy formulas.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — dividing by 3m doesn't match the derivation from KE = (1/2)mv².
explanation_options.d: Wrong — dividing by 4m doesn't match the correct derivation either.

questions.question_text: The number of revolutions in 3π radians is:
questions.explanation_short: 3π radians corresponds to 1.5 revolutions, since one full revolution equals 2π radians.
questions.explanation_long: One complete revolution = 2π radians. Number of revolutions = total angle / 2π = 3π / 2π = 3/2 = 1.5 revolutions.
questions.explanation_trick: Revolutions = angle(radians) / 2π. Here: 3π/2π = 3/2.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1/60 doesn't match the direct division of 3π by 2π.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 3π/2π = 3/2 revolutions.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 2 revolutions would require an angle of 4π radians, not 3π.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 6 revolutions would require an angle of 12π radians, far more than 3π.

aliases: The number of revolutions in 3(pi) radians is:

questions.question_text: If a flywheel is rotating at 3.0 rad/s, the time it takes to complete one revolution is about
questions.explanation_short: Time period T = 2π/ω = 2π/3.0 ≈ 2.1 s for one revolution at angular velocity 3.0 rad/s.
questions.explanation_long: The time for one complete revolution (period) relates to angular velocity by T = 2π/ω. With ω = 3.0 rad/s: T = 2π/3.0 ≈ 6.283/3.0 ≈ 2.09 s, which rounds to about 2.1 s.
questions.explanation_trick: T = 2π/ω — the standard formula linking period and angular velocity.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 0.67 s doesn't match 2π/3.0.
