explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1.0 s underestimates the correct period.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 1.3 s is still less than the correct value.
explanation_options.d: Correct — T = 2π/3.0 ≈ 2.1 s.

questions.question_text: A fighter plane is moving in a vertical circle of radius r. Its minimum velocity at the highest point of the circle will be ?
questions.explanation_short: At the highest point of vertical circular motion, minimum velocity occurs when gravity alone provides the centripetal force: v_min = √(gr).
questions.explanation_long: At the top of a vertical circle, for the object to just maintain contact (minimum speed condition), gravity alone supplies the necessary centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, giving v² = gr, so v_min = √(gr). Below this speed, the object would fall away from the circular path.
questions.explanation_trick: At the top of a vertical loop: mg = mv²/r → v_min = √(gr) (classic 'minimum speed at the top' formula).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — √(3gr) is not the standard minimum-speed formula for the top of a vertical circle.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — √(2gr) is a value associated with different problems (like just completing a loop from the bottom), not this direct minimum condition.
explanation_options.c: Correct — v_min = √(gr) at the highest point of a vertical circle.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — √(gr/2) underestimates the required minimum speed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following increase by increasing amplitude?
questions.explanation_short: Loudness of a wave increases with increasing amplitude, since loudness relates to sound intensity, which depends on amplitude squared.
questions.explanation_long: Amplitude determines the energy (and hence intensity/loudness) carried by a wave — larger amplitude means louder sound. Wavelength and frequency are independent properties determined by the source and medium, not directly caused by amplitude changes.
questions.explanation_trick: Bigger amplitude = more energy = louder sound. Amplitude and loudness go hand in hand.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — wavelength is determined by frequency and wave speed, not by amplitude.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — frequency (pitch) is independent of amplitude; it doesn't increase with amplitude.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'zero' isn't a meaningful quantity that increases with amplitude.
explanation_options.d: Correct — loudness increases as amplitude increases.

questions.question_text: An airplane travels at a speed of 0.5v where v is the speed of sound. The airplane approaches a stationary observer. The frequency of sound emitted by the aircraft is 200 Hz. Which frequency does the observer hear?
questions.explanation_short: Using the Doppler formula for an approaching source: f' = f/(1-v_s/v) = 200/(1-0.5) = 400 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: For a source approaching a stationary observer, apparent frequency f' = f × v/(v - v_s), where v_s = 0.5v (source speed). Substituting: f' = f × v/(v - 0.5v) = f × v/(0.5v) = 2f = 2×200 = 400 Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: Approaching source: f' = f × v/(v-v_s). With v_s=0.5v: f' = 2f — frequency doubles.

explanation_options.a: Correct — f' = 200 × v/(0.5v) = 400 Hz.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 100 Hz would result from a receding source at this speed, not approaching.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 120 Hz doesn't match the Doppler formula for this scenario.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 180 Hz doesn't match the calculated doubled frequency.

questions.question_text: If the wavelength of light coming from a galaxy shifts towards the red end of spectrum, then galaxy is:
questions.explanation_short: A redshift (wavelength shifting toward the red/longer-wavelength end) indicates the light source (galaxy) is receding (moving away) from Earth.
questions.explanation_long: By the Doppler effect applied to light, when a source moves away from an observer, its emitted wavelengths stretch (redshift). Edwin Hubble used this observation across galaxies to establish that the universe is expanding — nearly all distant galaxies show redshift, meaning they are receding from us.
questions.explanation_trick: Red shift = moving away (receding); Blue shift = moving toward (approaching) — 'red' rhymes with 'retreat/recede'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — approaching sources cause a blueshift (shorter wavelength), not redshift.
explanation_options.b: Correct — redshift indicates the galaxy is receding from Earth.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a stationary source would show no wavelength shift at all.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — since a shift IS observed (redshift), the source can't be simply 'approaching or stationary' — it's specifically receding.

questions.question_text: The shortest distance between any two points in phase on a wave is called:
questions.explanation_short: Wavelength is defined as the shortest distance between any two points on a wave that are in phase.
questions.explanation_long: Two points are 'in phase' when they have the same displacement and are moving in the same direction at the same time. The shortest such distance along a wave — from one crest to the next crest, or trough to trough — defines the wavelength.
questions.explanation_trick: Wavelength = distance between two consecutive in-phase points (e.g., crest to crest).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — displacement is the distance of a point from its equilibrium position at an instant, unrelated to this definition.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium, not a distance between in-phase points.
explanation_options.c: Correct — wavelength is defined as this shortest in-phase distance.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — frequency is the number of oscillations per unit time, not a spatial distance.

questions.question_text: When will the oscillations stop in the absence of resistive forces?
questions.explanation_short: Without resistive (damping) forces, oscillations continue indefinitely — they never stop (simple harmonic motion persists forever).
questions.explanation_long: In an idealized system with no friction, air resistance, or other damping forces, energy is conserved and oscillations continue with constant amplitude forever, since there's nothing to dissipate the system's mechanical energy. Real oscillators always eventually stop due to damping (resistive forces).
questions.explanation_trick: No damping = no energy loss = oscillations never stop (idealized SHM).

explanation_options.a: Correct — without resistive forces, oscillations never stop.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'after 10 minutes' implies eventual damping, contradicting the absence of resistive forces.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'in 10 minutes' also implies energy loss over time, which shouldn't happen without resistive forces.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'immediately' contradicts the very nature of oscillation without any opposing force.

questions.question_text: The mechanical waves are not generated by:
questions.explanation_short: Mechanical waves require a physical medium to propagate — but electric and magnetic fields (electromagnetic waves) don't need a medium, making them NOT a source of mechanical waves.
questions.explanation_long: Mechanical waves need a material medium (like ropes, springs, or water) to transfer energy through particle vibrations. Electromagnetic waves, generated by oscillating electric and magnetic fields, can travel through a vacuum and are fundamentally different — not generated the way mechanical waves are (via physical medium disturbance).
questions.explanation_trick: Mechanical waves need matter (ropes, springs, water); EM waves (from E & M fields) don't — they're a different category.

explanation_options.a: Correct — electric and magnetic fields generate electromagnetic waves, NOT mechanical waves.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — coils of springs DO generate mechanical waves (e.g., a slinky).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — ropes DO generate mechanical waves when disturbed.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — water DOES support/generate mechanical waves (like ripples).

questions.question_text: Reducing mass M of a suspending body to one fourth will change the frequency of oscillation to:
questions.explanation_short: Frequency of oscillation for a mass on a spring is f ∝ 1/√M, so reducing mass to 1/4 makes frequency double.
questions.explanation_long: For a mass-spring system, f = (1/2π)√(k/M), so f is inversely proportional to the square root of mass. If M becomes M/4, new frequency = (1/2π)√(k/(M/4)) = (1/2π)√(4k/M) = 2×(1/2π)√(k/M) = 2f — the frequency doubles.
questions.explanation_trick: f ∝ 1/√M — reducing mass to 1/4 means √(1/4)=1/2, so frequency increases by factor 1/(1/2)=2 (doubles).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'one fourth' would be the change if frequency were directly proportional to mass, but it's inversely proportional to the square root.
explanation_options.b: Correct — reducing mass to 1/4 doubles the oscillation frequency.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'quadruple' overstates the change; the actual factor is 2 (double), not 4.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'half' would occur if mass were quadrupled, not reduced to a quarter.

questions.question_text: A distant star is receding from the Earth with a speed of 1.40 × 10⁷ m/s. It emits light of frequency 4.57 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. The Doppler effect formula can be used with light waves. What will be the frequency of this light when detected on Earth?
questions.explanation_short: Using the Doppler redshift formula for light, f' = f(1 - v/c) = 4.57×10^14 × (1 - 1.4×10^7/3.0×10^8) ≈ 4.37×10^14 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: For a receding light source (v much less than c), the observed frequency is approximately f' = f(1 - v/c). Plugging in: v/c = 1.40×10^7/3.0×10^8 ≈ 0.0467. f' = 4.57×10^14 × (1 - 0.0467) = 4.57×10^14 × 0.9533 ≈ 4.36×10^14 Hz, matching option b (4.37×10^14 Hz).
questions.explanation_trick: Receding source: f' = f(1 - v/c) — frequency decreases (redshifts) as the star moves away.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 2.04×10^13 Hz is far too small a reduction for the given speed ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — f' ≈ 4.37×10^14 Hz, matching the Doppler redshift calculation.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 4.57×10^14 Hz is the original (unshifted) frequency, not accounting for the recession.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 4.79×10^14 Hz would represent a blueshift (frequency increase), but the star is receding, so frequency should decrease.

aliases: A distant star is receding from the Earth with a speed of 1.40 x 10^7 m/s. It emits light of frequency 4.57 x 10^14 Hz. The speed of light is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. The Doppler effect formula can be used with light waves. What will be the frequency of this light when detected on Earth?

questions.question_text: Thermodynamics is that branch of Physics in which we study
questions.option_a: relations between heat and mechanical energies
questions.option_b: relations between heat and ionization energies
questions.option_c: relations between chemical and mechanical energies
questions.option_d: relations between kinetic and potential energies
questions.explanation_short: Thermodynamics studies the relationship between heat and mechanical energy (work).
questions.explanation_long: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics concerned with heat, work, temperature, and energy transformations — specifically how heat energy converts to/from mechanical work, governed by its four laws.
questions.explanation_trick: Thermo (heat) + dynamics (motion/work) = the study of heat-to-mechanical-energy relationships.

explanation_options.a: Correct — thermodynamics studies relations between heat and mechanical energy.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — heat and ionization energy relations belong to atomic/chemical physics, not core thermodynamics.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — chemical and mechanical energy relations aren't the defining focus of thermodynamics.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — kinetic and potential energy relations are general mechanics topics, not specifically thermodynamics' definition.

questions.question_text: When a gas is compressed isothermally, the product of its pressure and volume during the process is:
questions.explanation_short: Isothermal compression keeps temperature constant, so by Boyle's Law, the product PV remains constant throughout the process.
questions.explanation_long: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process (constant T), Boyle's Law states PV = constant (since PV = nRT, and T doesn't change, nRT stays fixed). So even as pressure increases and volume decreases during compression, their product remains unchanged.
questions.explanation_trick: Isothermal = constant T → PV = nRT = constant (Boyle's Law in action).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — PV is NOT changing during an isothermal process; it stays constant.
explanation_options.b: Correct — PV remains constant during isothermal compression (Boyle's Law).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — PV isn't zero; it retains a constant non-zero value throughout.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — PV isn't related to entropy in this simple isothermal gas law context.

questions.question_text: Temperature of given mass of a gas is changed from 150 C to 300 C during an isobaric process, volume of the gas will become:
questions.explanation_short: By Charles's Law (isobaric process), volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature; going from 150°C to 300°C, volume increases by a factor less than double (since absolute temperatures aren't simply doubled).
questions.explanation_long: Convert to Kelvin: 150°C = 423 K, 300°C = 573 K. Since V1/T1 = V2/T2 (constant pressure), V2 = V1×(573/423) ≈ 1.35×V1 — an increase, but LESS than double (since doubling in Celsius isn't doubling in Kelvin).
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert to Kelvin for gas law ratios — doubling Celsius temperature is NOT doubling Kelvin temperature.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — volume increases (temperature rises), it doesn't become half.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'double' would require the Kelvin temperature to double (150°C→300°C isn't a doubling in Kelvin: 423K→573K, only ~1.35x).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the temperature does change, so volume must also change (not remain the same).
explanation_options.d: Correct — volume increases, but by less than double, since the Kelvin temperature ratio (573/423) is only about 1.35, not 2.

questions.question_text: A capacitor is charged with a battery and energy stored is U. After disconnecting battery another capacitor of same capacity is connected in parallel to the first capacitor. Then energy stored in each capacitor is
questions.explanation_short: When an identical uncharged capacitor is connected in parallel to a charged one (battery disconnected), the total charge splits equally, and energy stored in each becomes U/4.
questions.explanation_long: Charge conservation: total charge Q stays the same, now split equally between two identical capacitors (Q/2 each). Since energy = Q²/(2C), each capacitor's new energy = (Q/2)²/(2C) = (1/4)×[Q²/(2C)] = U/4. So each capacitor now stores U/4 (total stored energy drops to U/2 overall, since some energy is 'lost' redistributing charge).
questions.explanation_trick: Splitting charge equally between two identical capacitors: each has half the charge → energy (∝Q²) drops to 1/4 per capacitor.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — U/2 would be the case if energy (not charge) simply split, but energy actually scales with charge squared.
explanation_options.b: Correct — each capacitor ends up storing U/4 of energy.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 4U would mean energy increased dramatically, which contradicts charge redistribution losing net energy.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 2U also incorrectly suggests increased energy, not the actual decrease from redistribution.

questions.question_text: What is the potential difference between two points in an electric field if it takes 600 J of energy to move a charge of 2 C between these two points?
questions.explanation_short: Potential difference V = Work/Charge = 600 J / 2 C = 300 J... units should be Volts, but numerically V = 300 (V).
questions.explanation_long: By definition, potential difference V = W/Q, where W is work done (energy) and Q is charge moved. Here: V = 600 J / 2 C = 300 V (the unit is technically volts, though the option lists it as 'J' — matching the numeric value 300).
questions.explanation_trick: V = W/Q — divide energy by charge to get potential difference.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1200 would result from multiplying instead of dividing (600×2), not the correct operation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 800 doesn't match the direct division of 600/2.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 600/2 = 300, matching this option's value.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0 would only be correct if no energy were needed to move the charge, contradicting the given 600 J.

questions.question_text: Gauss law cannot be used to find which of the following quantity?
questions.explanation_short: Gauss's Law directly relates electric flux to enclosed charge — it cannot be used to find permittivity, which is a fixed material property, not a field/flux/charge quantity solved via Gauss's law.
questions.explanation_long: Gauss's Law (∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε₀) is used to calculate electric field intensity, electric flux density, and enclosed charge for symmetric charge distributions. Permittivity (ε₀ or ε) is a constant property of the medium that appears IN the equation, not something typically 'found' by applying Gauss's Law to a scenario.
questions.explanation_trick: Gauss's Law finds E, flux, or Q — but permittivity is a built-in constant of the formula itself, not a solved-for output.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — electric field intensity CAN be found using Gauss's Law for symmetric charge distributions.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — electric flux density CAN be directly calculated via Gauss's Law.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — enclosed charge CAN be found using Gauss's Law if the field is known.
explanation_options.d: Correct — permittivity is not something found via Gauss's Law; it's a constant already built into the equation.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is true?
questions.option_a: electrostatic force obeys inverse square law while gravitational force does not
questions.option_b: both gravitational force and electrostatic force are repulsive in nature
questions.option_c: gravitational force is much weaker than electrostatic force
questions.option_d: Both electrostatic force and gravitational force don't obey inverse square law
questions.explanation_short: Gravitational force is much weaker than electrostatic force — comparing the two forces between fundamental particles shows gravity is many orders of magnitude smaller.
questions.explanation_long: Both electrostatic and gravitational forces obey inverse-square laws (F ∝ 1/r²), so that's not a valid distinction between them. What IS true: gravitational force between charged particles (like two electrons) is vastly weaker (by a factor of about 10^42) than the electrostatic force between them — making gravitational force much weaker than electrostatic force in comparable situations.
questions.explanation_trick: Both gravity and Coulomb's law are inverse-square, but gravity is enormously weaker in magnitude — ~10^42 times weaker between electrons.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — BOTH forces obey the inverse square law; this option incorrectly claims otherwise for gravity.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — gravitational force is always attractive, never repulsive, contradicting this statement.
explanation_options.c: Correct — gravitational force is much weaker than electrostatic force.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — both forces DO obey the inverse square law; this statement is false.

questions.question_text: The Coulomb's constant k depends upon:
questions.option_d: nature of medium and system of units
questions.explanation_short: Coulomb's constant k depends on both the nature of the medium (permittivity) and the system of units used.
questions.explanation_long: Coulomb's constant k = 1/(4πε), where ε is the permittivity of the medium — so k varies with the medium. Additionally, its numerical value depends on which unit system (SI vs CGS, etc.) is used for charge, distance, and force. Both factors combine to determine k's value.
questions.explanation_trick: k = 1/(4πε) — depends on ε (medium) AND the chosen unit system together.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'nature of medium' alone is incomplete; the unit system also affects k's numerical value.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'system of units' alone is incomplete; the medium's permittivity also affects k.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the type of charge (positive/negative) doesn't affect the value of Coulomb's constant.
explanation_options.d: Correct — k depends on both nature of medium and system of units together.

questions.question_text: A charged particle is moving in a uniform electric field. For the motion of the particle due to the field, which quantity has a constant non-zero value?
questions.explanation_short: In a uniform electric field, a charged particle experiences constant acceleration (non-zero, constant magnitude and direction) throughout its motion.
questions.explanation_long: A uniform E field exerts a constant force (F=qE) on a charged particle, giving constant acceleration a=qE/m. Velocity and displacement continuously change (not constant), and rate of change of acceleration is zero (since acceleration itself is constant), so acceleration is the only quantity here that stays constant and non-zero.
questions.explanation_trick: Uniform field → constant force → constant acceleration (velocity keeps changing, but acceleration doesn't).

explanation_options.a: Correct — acceleration remains constant and non-zero in a uniform electric field.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — displacement continuously changes as the particle moves, it's not constant.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — since acceleration is constant, its rate of change is zero, not a 'constant non-zero value'.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — velocity continuously changes (accelerating), so it isn't constant.

questions.question_text: A capacitor of capacitance 'C' has a charge 'Q' and stored energy is 'w'. If the charge is increases to '2Q'. The stored energy will be:
questions.explanation_short: Capacitor energy formula: W = Q²/(2C), so if charge doubles to 2Q, energy becomes (2Q)²/(2C) = 4×[Q²/(2C)] = 4W.
questions.explanation_long: Energy stored in a capacitor: W = Q²/(2C). Doubling the charge to 2Q gives new energy = (2Q)²/(2C) = 4Q²/(2C) = 4W — energy scales with the SQUARE of charge, not linearly.
questions.explanation_trick: W ∝ Q² — doubling charge quadruples stored energy (not just doubles it).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 2W assumes a linear relationship between charge and energy, but energy actually scales as Q².
explanation_options.b: Correct — doubling charge quadruples energy: (2Q)²/(2C) = 4W.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — W/4 would represent energy decreasing, opposite of what happens when charge increases.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — W/2 also incorrectly shows decreasing energy.

questions.question_text: How much potential drop exist across closed switch?
questions.explanation_short: An ideal closed switch has zero resistance, so there's no potential drop across it (V=IR=I×0=0).
questions.explanation_long: A closed (ON) switch, ideally, offers negligible/zero resistance to current flow. By Ohm's law, V=IR, with R≈0, the potential drop across the closed switch is essentially 0 V — all the circuit's voltage drop occurs across the other resistive components, not the switch itself.
questions.explanation_trick: Closed switch = ideal wire (R=0) → V=IR=0. Open switch = infinite resistance → all voltage drops across it instead.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a closed switch has (ideally) zero potential drop across it.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1V would imply some resistance in the switch, contrary to the ideal closed-switch assumption.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 2V also implies non-zero resistance, not matching an ideal closed switch.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 3V is even further from the expected zero-resistance behavior.

questions.question_text: A 3 V battery is connected in series with ammeter and 2 ohm resistance after short circuiting. What will be the reading of ammeter?
questions.explanation_short: During a short circuit (bypassing the 3V battery's other components), the ammeter reads I=V/R=3V/2Ω=1.5 A.
questions.explanation_long: With the battery (3V) connected in series with just an ammeter and a 2Ω resistor (short-circuiting any other higher-resistance path), applying Ohm's Law: I = V/R = 3/2 = 1.5 A.
questions.explanation_trick: Simple series circuit: I = V/R = 3V/2Ω = 1.5A.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 1A would require a resistance of 3Ω, not the given 2Ω.
explanation_options.b: Correct — I = 3V/2Ω = 1.5 A.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 5A would require a much lower resistance (0.6Ω), not 2Ω.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 6A would require an even lower resistance (0.5Ω).

questions.question_text: The resistance of a conductor does not depend on which of the following?
questions.explanation_short: A conductor's resistance depends on its length, area, and resistivity — but NOT on its mass directly.
questions.explanation_long: Resistance is given by R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity (material property), L is length, and A is cross-sectional area. Mass doesn't appear in this formula — two conductors of the same material, length, and cross-section have the same resistance regardless of any mass difference (e.g., due to density variations within tolerance), so resistance doesn't directly depend on mass.
questions.explanation_trick: R = ρL/A — only resistivity, length, and area matter; mass isn't in the formula.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — area DOES affect resistance (inversely, per the formula).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — resistivity DOES directly determine resistance.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — length DOES directly affect resistance (directly proportional).
explanation_options.d: Correct — mass does NOT appear in the resistance formula R=ρL/A.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statement is NOT CORRECT about Kirchhoff's rule?
questions.option_a: Kirchhoff's current rule based upon the law of conservation of charge
questions.option_b: Wheatstone bridge is an application of Kirchhoff's rule
questions.option_c: Kirchhoff's rules are more suitable in AC circuits
questions.option_d: Kirchhoff's voltage rule based upon the law of conservation of energy
questions.explanation_short: Kirchhoff's rules apply to both AC and DC circuits generally, but they're especially foundational for DC analysis — the claim that they're 'more suitable' specifically for AC circuits is the incorrect statement.
questions.explanation_long: Kirchhoff's current rule (conservation of charge) and voltage rule (conservation of energy) are general circuit laws applicable to both DC and AC circuits (with AC requiring phasor/complex treatment for reactive elements) — Wheatstone bridge is indeed a classic DC application. There's no basis for claiming Kirchhoff's rules are specifically 'more suitable' for AC circuits over DC; if anything, they're most straightforwardly taught and applied in DC contexts.
questions.explanation_trick: Kirchhoff's rules work for both AC & DC — no special preference for AC; that's the false statement here.

explanation_options.a: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — Kirchhoff's current rule is indeed based on conservation of charge.
explanation_options.b: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — Wheatstone bridge is a genuine application of Kirchhoff's rules.
explanation_options.c: Correct (as the NOT CORRECT statement) — Kirchhoff's rules aren't specifically 'more suitable' for AC circuits; this claim is false.
explanation_options.d: Wrong (this is actually TRUE) — Kirchhoff's voltage rule is indeed based on conservation of energy.

questions.question_text: What do the substances whose resistance decreases with increase in temperature have?
questions.explanation_short: Substances whose resistance decreases as temperature increases have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance (typical of semiconductors).
questions.explanation_long: Most metals have a positive temperature coefficient (resistance increases with temperature), but semiconductors and some other materials show the opposite behavior — as temperature rises, more charge carriers become available, decreasing resistance. This inverse relationship defines a negative temperature coefficient.
questions.explanation_trick: Metals: resistance up with heat (positive coefficient). Semiconductors: resistance down with heat (negative coefficient).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'high temperature coefficient' doesn't specify the sign/direction of the resistance-temperature relationship.
explanation_options.b: Correct — a negative temperature coefficient describes decreasing resistance with increasing temperature.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a positive temperature coefficient describes resistance INCREASING with temperature (the opposite of what's described).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — a zero temperature coefficient would mean resistance doesn't change with temperature at all.

questions.question_text: A low voltage supply with an e.m.f. of 20 V and an internal resistance of 1.5 ohms is used to supply power to a heater of resistance 6.5 ohms in a fish tank. What is the power supplied to the water in the fish tank?
questions.explanation_short: Power delivered to the external heater = I²R_heater, where I = EMF/(R_internal+R_heater) = 20/(1.5+6.5) = 2.5A; P = 2.5² × 6.5 ≈ 40.6 W ≈ 41 W.
questions.explanation_long: Total circuit resistance = internal (1.5Ω) + heater (6.5Ω) = 8Ω. Current I = EMF/R_total = 20/8 = 2.5 A. Power delivered to the heater (external resistance) = I²×R_heater = 2.5² × 6.5 = 6.25 × 6.5 = 40.625 W ≈ 41 W.
questions.explanation_trick: Find current using total resistance (internal + external), then apply P=I²R to just the external (heater) resistance.

explanation_options.a: Correct — P = I²×R_heater = 2.5² × 6.5 ≈ 41 W.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 50W would result from a different (incorrect) resistance combination.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 53W doesn't match the correct current/resistance calculation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 62W overstates the actual power delivered to the heater.

questions.question_text: Electric forces change the magnitude and direction of velocity while magnetic forces change_________ of velocity
questions.explanation_short: Magnetic forces change only the direction of velocity (never the speed/magnitude), unlike electric forces which change both magnitude and direction.
questions.explanation_long: The magnetic force on a moving charge (F=qv×B) is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does no work and cannot change the speed (magnitude) of the particle — it can only curve the path, changing direction. Electric forces, by contrast, act along the field direction and can both speed up/slow down (change magnitude) and redirect (change direction) a charge.
questions.explanation_trick: Magnetic force ⊥ velocity always → does no work → changes direction only, never speed/magnitude.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — magnetic force doesn't change magnitude/speed at all, so 'only magnitude' is incorrect.
explanation_options.b: Correct — magnetic forces change only the direction of velocity.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — magnetic forces can't change magnitude (since F⊥v does no work); this option wrongly includes magnitude.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — magnetic forces DO change direction (they just don't change magnitude), so 'neither' is incorrect.

questions.question_text: Which surface has greater magnetic flux in same magnetic field, each has an area 1 m².
questions.explanation_short: Magnetic flux depends only on area and field orientation, not on the shape of the surface — so all shapes with the same area (1 m²) in the same field have equal flux.
questions.explanation_long: Magnetic flux Φ = B·A·cos(θ), which depends on the magnitude of the perpendicular area and the field strength/orientation — not on the specific geometric shape of that area. Since all given surfaces (circular, rectangular, square) have the same area (1 m²) in the same magnetic field, their flux is identical regardless of shape.
questions.explanation_trick: Flux Φ = B·A·cosθ — only area and orientation matter, shape (circle vs square vs rectangle) is irrelevant.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a circular surface doesn't have inherently greater flux just because of its shape.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a rectangular surface doesn't have inherently greater flux due to shape alone.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — a square surface doesn't have inherently greater flux due to shape alone.
explanation_options.d: Correct — flux is independent of shape; only area and field orientation matter.

aliases: Which surface has greater magnetic flux in same magnetic field, each has an area 1 m^2.
Circular

questions.question_text: The source of magnetic field is:
questions.explanation_short: The source of magnetic fields is moving electric charge — most fundamentally represented by a current loop.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike electric fields (sourced by static charges), magnetic fields are generated by moving charges (currents). A current loop is the classic elementary source/model of a magnetic field (acting like a magnetic dipole), unlike isolated magnetic poles (which don't exist in nature) or static charges (which produce only electric, not magnetic, fields).
questions.explanation_trick: Moving charge = magnetic field source. Current loop = the fundamental magnetic dipole model.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) don't exist in nature/aren't the standard source described.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — static electric charge produces only an electric field, not a magnetic one.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — nonmagnetic substances don't inherently generate magnetic fields.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a current loop (moving charge) is the fundamental source of magnetic fields.

questions.question_text: One meter long copper rod is moving with speed 20 m/sec in the magnetic field of strength 0.6 tesla. What is the value of induced emf ?
questions.explanation_short: Motional EMF = BLv = 0.6 × 1 × 20 = 12 V.
questions.explanation_long: For a straight conductor of length L moving with velocity v perpendicular to a magnetic field B, the induced (motional) EMF = BLv. Substituting: EMF = 0.6 T × 1 m × 20 m/s = 12 V.
questions.explanation_trick: Motional EMF formula: ε = BLv — multiply field, length, and velocity directly.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 10V doesn't match the direct multiplication of B×L×v.
explanation_options.b: Correct — EMF = 0.6 × 1 × 20 = 12 V.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 14V doesn't match the calculation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 16V overstates the correct calculated value.

questions.question_text: The unit of change in flux / change in time can be written as ?
questions.explanation_short: The unit of Δφ/Δt (rate of change of magnetic flux, i.e., EMF) is the volt, which in base SI units is Nm·A⁻¹·s⁻¹.
questions.explanation_long: By Faraday's law, EMF = -Δφ/Δt, so the unit of Δφ/Δt is the volt (V). Expressing volts in base SI units: V = J/C = (N·m)/(A·s) = N·m·A⁻¹·s⁻¹, matching option c.
questions.explanation_trick: Volt = Joule/Coulomb = (N·m)/(A·s) = N·m·A⁻¹·s⁻¹ — the base-unit breakdown of EMF/flux-rate.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the exponent on A should be -1, not -2, for the volt's base-unit expression.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is missing the negative exponent notation on A, not matching standard base-unit form (and represents a different combination).
explanation_options.c: Correct — NmA⁻¹s⁻¹ correctly expresses the volt (unit of Δφ/Δt) in base SI units.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — this has an incorrect sign on the time exponent, not matching the volt's proper base-unit form.

aliases: The unit of change in flux / change in time can be written as ?
NmA-2s-1

questions.question_text: Working principal of magnetic levitation train is according to ?
questions.explanation_short: Maglev (magnetic levitation) trains work based on Lenz's law — induced currents oppose the change in flux, creating repulsive/lifting forces.
questions.explanation_long: Maglev trains use electromagnetic induction: as the train moves, changing magnetic flux induces eddy currents in conducting tracks, and by Lenz's law, these induced currents create magnetic fields that oppose the motion/flux change — generating a repulsive force that lifts (levitates) and propels the train without physical contact.
questions.explanation_trick: Lenz's law = 'opposition creates levitation' — induced currents fight the change, generating lift for maglev trains.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Faraday's law describes that an EMF is induced by changing flux, but Lenz's law specifically explains the DIRECTION (opposing/repulsive nature) that enables levitation.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — Max Planck's law relates to blackbody radiation/quantum theory, unrelated to magnetic levitation.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance, not the levitation mechanism.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Lenz's law (opposing induced currents) explains the working principle of magnetic levitation trains.

questions.question_text: A copper hoop is held in a vertical east-west plane in a uniform magnetic field whose field lines run along the north-south direction. The largest induced emf is produced when the hoop is ?
questions.option_c: Moved rapidly, without rotation, toward the east
questions.option_d: Moved rapidly, without rotation, toward the south
questions.explanation_short: Largest induced EMF in a rotating hoop occurs when it's rotated about an axis perpendicular to the field — here, rotating about the east-west axis (perpendicular to the north-south field) maximizes the rate of flux change.
questions.explanation_long: EMF induction depends on the rate of change of flux through the loop. Rotating the hoop about an axis that is perpendicular to the magnetic field direction causes the flux through the hoop to vary maximally (from max to zero) as it spins, producing the largest induced EMF. Since the field runs north-south, rotating about the perpendicular east-west axis produces this maximum flux change.
questions.explanation_trick: Maximum EMF occurs when rotation axis is perpendicular to the field direction, causing the fastest flux variation.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — rotating about the north-south axis (parallel to field) keeps flux through the hoop constant, giving zero induced EMF, not the largest.
explanation_options.b: Correct — rotating about the east-west axis (perpendicular to the north-south field) maximizes the induced EMF.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — moving without rotation, even rapidly, doesn't necessarily maximize the RATE of flux change the way proper rotation does in this comparison.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — similarly, translational motion without rotation isn't the scenario that produces maximum induced EMF here.

questions.question_text: In transformer, there is no _______ connection between the two coils but they are ______ linked ?
questions.explanation_short: Transformer coils have no electrical (direct wire) connection between primary and secondary, but they are magnetically linked via a shared iron core.
questions.explanation_long: A transformer works purely through electromagnetic induction — the primary coil creates a changing magnetic flux in a shared iron core, which induces an EMF in the secondary coil. There's no direct electrical contact between the two coils; they're coupled only magnetically.
questions.explanation_trick: Transformers: NO electrical connection between coils, only magnetic coupling via the shared core.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this reverses the correct pairing; there's no magnetic-only connection missing, but it IS electrical connection that's absent, and coils ARE magnetically (not electrically) linked.
explanation_options.b: Correct — no electrical connection exists between the coils, but they are magnetically linked.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'magnetic, magnetically' repeats the same word for both blanks incorrectly; the first blank should be 'electrical' (absent), not 'magnetic'.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — transformer coils aren't optically linked; they're magnetically linked.

questions.question_text: When the temperature of semiconductor suddenly drops to zero kelvin, then a semiconductor acts as:
questions.explanation_short: At absolute zero, a semiconductor has no thermally excited charge carriers, so it behaves as a perfect insulator.
questions.explanation_long: Semiconductor conductivity relies on thermal energy exciting electrons across the band gap into the conduction band. At 0 K, there's no thermal energy available, so no electrons can be excited — the valence band stays completely full and the conduction band completely empty, making the material behave as an insulator.
questions.explanation_trick: No heat = no excited electrons in a semiconductor = behaves like an insulator at 0 K.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — a conductor still conducts even without heat (it doesn't require thermal excitation across a gap).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — a 'semiconductor' still implies some conduction; at 0K it fully stops conducting, matching insulator behavior instead.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — superconductivity requires a specific material/critical temperature phenomenon, not just any semiconductor cooling to 0K.
explanation_options.d: Correct — at 0 K, a semiconductor behaves as an insulator (no charge carriers available).

questions.question_text: If electron, proton, neutron, and alpha particle have same velocity, which of them has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation_short: De Broglie wavelength λ=h/(mv) is inversely proportional to mass, so at equal velocity, the heaviest particle (the alpha particle) has the shortest wavelength.
questions.explanation_long: De Broglie wavelength: λ = h/(mv). At the same velocity v, wavelength is inversely proportional to mass (λ ∝ 1/m). Among electron, proton, neutron, and alpha particle, the alpha particle has by far the largest mass (about 4 atomic mass units, ~7000× an electron's mass), so it has the smallest (shortest) wavelength.
questions.explanation_trick: λ = h/(mv) — at equal velocity, the HEAVIEST particle has the SHORTEST wavelength (inverse relationship with mass).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the electron, being the lightest particle, has the LONGEST wavelength at equal velocity, not the shortest.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the proton is much lighter than the alpha particle, so it has a longer wavelength than the alpha's.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the neutron has similar mass to the proton, still much lighter than the alpha particle, giving it a longer wavelength.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the alpha particle, being the heaviest, has the shortest de Broglie wavelength at equal velocity.

questions.question_text: The process of ejection of loosely bound electrons from a certain photo sensitive surface by absorption of photon is called:
questions.explanation_short: The photoelectric effect is the ejection of loosely bound electrons from a photosensitive surface upon absorbing photons.
questions.explanation_long: When photons of sufficient energy (above the material's work function) strike a metal surface, they can eject electrons directly — this phenomenon, explained by Einstein using the photon concept, is called the photoelectric effect, and was key evidence for the particle nature of light.
questions.explanation_trick: Photoelectric effect = photon in, electron out — Einstein's Nobel-winning explanation.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Compton effect involves photon-electron scattering with a wavelength shift, not simple ejection via absorption.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the photoelectric effect describes electron ejection via photon absorption.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — pair production is the conversion of a high-energy photon into a particle-antiparticle pair (electron-positron), a different phenomenon.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — black body radiation describes the emission spectrum of a heated object, unrelated to this ejection process.

questions.question_text: In a photoelectric effect experiment, the stopping potential is:
questions.option_a: The kinetic energy of the most energetic electron ejected
questions.option_b: The potential energy of the most energetic electron ejected
questions.option_d: The electric potential that causes the electron current to vanish
questions.explanation_short: Stopping potential is the electric potential needed to just stop (halt) the flow of photoelectrons — i.e., the potential that causes even the most energetic ejected electrons to be stopped.
questions.explanation_long: The stopping potential (V0) in a photoelectric experiment is the reverse voltage applied that's just enough to stop the most energetic photoelectrons from reaching the collector, reducing the photocurrent to zero. It directly relates to the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons via eV0 = KE_max, but stopping potential itself IS defined as this halting electric potential.
questions.explanation_trick: Stopping potential = the voltage that just cancels out (stops) even the fastest photoelectrons, making current vanish.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this describes the maximum kinetic energy itself (related via eV0=KE), not the stopping potential definition directly.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'potential energy of the electron' isn't the standard defining phrase for stopping potential.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — photon energy is a separate related quantity (hf), not the definition of stopping potential itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — stopping potential is defined as the potential that causes the photoelectron current to vanish.

questions.question_text: The line spectrum of hydrogen atom contains the spectral lines in the region of:
questions.explanation_short: Hydrogen's line spectrum spans multiple regions: Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), and Paschen/Brackett/Pfund series (infrared) — so 'all of these' is correct.
questions.explanation_long: The hydrogen emission spectrum consists of several series named after their discoverers, each corresponding to electron transitions ending at different energy levels: Lyman (to n=1, ultraviolet), Balmer (to n=2, visible), and Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (to n=3,4,5, infrared) — together spanning ultraviolet, visible, and infrared regions.
questions.explanation_trick: Hydrogen spectrum: Lyman=UV, Balmer=visible, Paschen(+)=IR — spans all three regions listed.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — ultraviolet alone (Lyman series) is only part of the full hydrogen spectrum.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — infrared alone (Paschen etc.) is only part of the spectrum.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — visible alone (Balmer series) is only part of the spectrum.
explanation_options.d: Correct — hydrogen's spectral lines span all three regions: UV, visible, and infrared.

questions.question_text: The speed of electron in the first Bohr orbit is:
questions.explanation_short: Bohr's first orbit electron speed is v1 = 2.19×10^6 m/s, a standard quoted physical constant value.
questions.explanation_long: Using Bohr's model, the velocity of an electron in the first (ground state, n=1) orbit of hydrogen is calculated to be approximately 2.19×10^6 m/s — a commonly memorized/quoted value in atomic physics (about 1/137th the speed of light, related to the fine-structure constant).
questions.explanation_trick: Bohr's first-orbit electron speed = 2.19×10^6 m/s — a standard textbook constant to memorize.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the first Bohr orbit electron speed is 2.19×10^6 m/s.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 2.19×10^-6 m/s is far too slow, off by many orders of magnitude.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 2.19×10^4 m/s underestimates the actual value by two orders of magnitude.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 2.19×10^-4 m/s is drastically too slow, not matching the known value.

aliases: The speed of electron in the first Bohr orbit is:

questions.question_text: A low energy neutron has RBE factor of 10. How much energy is absorbed by a man of mass 80 Kg if the value of equivalent dose is 400 rem?
questions.explanation_short: Absorbed (physical) dose = equivalent dose / RBE = 400 rem / 10 = 40 rem, then converting to joules using standard rad-to-Gy-to-J/kg relations and the given mass gives 32 J.
questions.explanation_long: Equivalent dose (rem) = Absorbed dose (rad) × RBE. So Absorbed dose = 400/10 = 40 rad = 0.4 Gy = 0.4 J/kg. Energy absorbed = Absorbed dose (J/kg) × mass (kg) = 0.4 × 80 = 32 J.
questions.explanation_trick: Equivalent dose = Absorbed dose × RBE → find absorbed dose, convert to Gy (J/kg), multiply by body mass.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 16J underestimates the calculated energy by half.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 0.4 Gy × 80 kg = 32 J.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 48J overstates the correct calculated energy.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 64J is double the correct calculated value.

questions.question_text: It has been observed that Thorium (Z=90, mass 234) is transformed into Protactinium (Z=91, mass 234) after the emission of ..................... particle:
questions.explanation_short: Thorium-234 transforms into Protactinium-234 by beta decay, since the atomic number increases by 1 while mass number stays the same.
questions.explanation_long: In beta decay, a neutron converts to a proton (emitting a beta particle/electron), increasing the atomic number by 1 while mass number stays constant. Th-234 (Z=90) becoming Pa-234 (Z=91) — same mass number, atomic number up by 1 — is the signature of beta decay, not alpha (which decreases mass by 4, Z by 2) or gamma (no change in Z or mass).
questions.explanation_trick: Beta decay: Z increases by 1, mass number unchanged — matches Th(90)→Pa(91), same mass 234.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — alpha decay would decrease both atomic number (by 2) and mass number (by 4), not matching this transformation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — beta decay explains the Z+1, same-mass-number transformation from Th-234 to Pa-234.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — gamma emission doesn't change atomic number or mass number at all.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — since beta decay alone explains this specific transformation, 'alpha, beta, gamma' together is an overly broad/incorrect answer.

questions.question_text: The half-life of Strontium (Sr) is 8.70 hours. Its decay constant is:
questions.explanation_short: Decay constant λ = 0.693/half-life = 0.693/8.70 hours ≈ 0.0796/hour, which converts to about 0.000022 per second.
questions.explanation_long: λ = ln(2)/t½ = 0.693/8.70 hours ≈ 0.0796 per hour. Converting to per second: 0.0796/3600 ≈ 0.0000221 per second ≈ 0.000022 /s.
questions.explanation_trick: λ = 0.693/half-life, then convert hours to seconds (÷3600) for the per-second decay constant.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — this option lacks the correct unit (should be /s, a rate, not a plain 's' value).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 45000 /s is drastically too large; doesn't match the calculated small decay rate.
explanation_options.c: Correct — λ ≈ 0.000022 /s matches the calculation.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 0.000032 /s is close in magnitude but doesn't match the precise calculation from 8.70 hours.

questions.question_text: Synonym of the word "Capricious" is:
questions.explanation_short: 'Capricious' means unpredictable/impulsive in mood or behavior — its closest synonym is 'fickle'.
questions.explanation_long: 'Capricious' describes someone or something given to sudden, unpredictable changes in mood or behavior (e.g., 'capricious weather'). 'Fickle' carries the same sense of changeable, inconsistent behavior, making it the correct synonym — while 'predictable', 'uniform', and 'invariable' are near-opposites (describing consistency, the opposite of capriciousness).
questions.explanation_trick: Capricious = fickle = changeable on a whim. Both start with a sense of unpredictability.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'fickle' means changeable/unpredictable, matching 'capricious'.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'predictable' is essentially an antonym of capricious.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'uniform' implies consistency, the opposite of capricious.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'invariable' also implies unchanging, opposite of capricious.

questions.question_text: Diseases like diabetes are supposed to be taken seriously or they can be ............. Which of the following words will fill in the blank most appropriately?
questions.explanation_short: Diseases like diabetes, if not taken seriously, can become 'fatal' (life-threatening) — the word that fits the warning tone of the sentence.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence warns about the consequence of not taking diabetes seriously. 'Fatal' (deadly, can cause death) fits this cautionary context perfectly, while 'cursing', 'healthy', and 'impersonating' don't logically complete a warning about disease severity.
questions.explanation_trick: A serious disease taken lightly can become 'fatal' — the logical, warning-toned word choice.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'cursing' doesn't fit the medical/warning context at all.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'healthy' contradicts the negative warning tone of the sentence (diseases becoming 'healthy' makes no sense).
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'fatal' fits the warning that untreated diabetes can become deadly.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'impersonating' is unrelated to disease severity.

questions.question_text: Choose the most appropriate antonym for "abandonment":
questions.explanation_short: 'Abandonment' (giving up/leaving) is most directly opposed by 'extension' (continuing/prolonging) among the choices given.
questions.explanation_long: Abandonment means giving something up entirely or deserting it. Among the options, 'extension' (to continue or prolong) is the best available opposite, representing continuation rather than cessation — while cessation, stoppage, and halt are all near-synonyms of abandonment (all mean stopping), not antonyms.
questions.explanation_trick: Cessation/stoppage/halt all mean 'stopping' (synonyms of abandonment); 'extension' means continuing — the true opposite.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'cessation' means stopping, a synonym of abandonment, not its antonym.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'stoppage' is also a synonym (stopping), not an antonym.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'halt' is likewise a synonym (stopping), not an antonym.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'extension' (continuing) is the best antonym for abandonment among the options.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank with the correct word. The shepherd ploughed this mountain with cattle the first time it ....... ever ploughed.
questions.explanation_short: 'Had been' correctly expresses the past perfect passive — the mountain 'had never been ploughed' before this first time.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence describes an action (ploughing) that had not occurred before a specific past point in time — this requires the past perfect passive construction 'had been' (auxiliary 'had' + been + past participle), correctly framing 'never ploughed before this occasion' relative to the past narrative.
questions.explanation_trick: Describing something that 'had (never) happened before' a past event needs past perfect: 'had been'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'was' alone doesn't correctly form the needed past perfect passive construction.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'was been' is grammatically incorrect (double past-tense auxiliary error).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'had' alone (without 'been') doesn't complete the passive construction correctly here.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'had been' completes the past perfect passive: 'it had (never) been ploughed'.

questions.question_text: To give one some idea of Rabies' horrors, one ......... only read such descriptions as the following: spasms, restlessness, shudders at the least breath of air, an ardent thirst, convulsive movements, and fits of furious age.
questions.explanation_short: 'Needs' (present tense, third person singular subject 'one') correctly completes the sentence describing a general, ongoing truth.
questions.explanation_long: The subject 'one' takes a third-person singular present-tense verb: 'one needs'. The sentence describes a general/timeless truth (how horrifying such descriptions are), which calls for simple present tense, making 'needs' the grammatically correct choice.
questions.explanation_trick: 'One' (3rd person singular) + present tense general truth → 'needs' (not 'need', 'needed', or 'has needed').

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'needs' matches the singular subject 'one' in the present tense.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'need' lacks the necessary '-s' for third-person singular agreement with 'one'.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'needed' (past tense) doesn't match the general-truth present tense context.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'has needed' (present perfect) doesn't fit the simple, timeless statement being made.

questions.question_text: By 2030, people ................... been reading the works of Charles Dickens for more than 190 years.
questions.explanation_short: 'Will have' correctly forms the future perfect tense needed for an action ('reading') that will have continued up to a future point (2030).
questions.explanation_long: The sentence describes an action continuing up to a specified future time ('By 2030... for more than 190 years'), which requires the future perfect (continuous) tense: 'will have been reading'. Among the choices, 'will have' is the correct auxiliary combination for this future perfect construction.
questions.explanation_trick: 'By [future date]... for [duration]' signals future perfect tense: 'will have + been + verb-ing'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'had' (past perfect) doesn't fit a sentence describing a future point in time (2030).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'will' alone lacks the 'have' needed to form future perfect tense.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'have' alone (without 'will') doesn't project the action into the future as the sentence requires.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'will have' correctly forms the future perfect tense needed here.

questions.question_text: Choose the most suitable/appropriate sentence out of the following:
questions.option_a: Penny did not let me to get my book.
questions.option_b: Penny was not leaving me to get my book.
questions.option_c: Penny did not let me get my book.
questions.option_d: Penny had not left me get my book.
questions.explanation_short: 'Penny did not let me get my book' is grammatically correct — 'let' takes a bare infinitive (no 'to'), unlike verbs such as 'allow'.
questions.explanation_long: The causative verb 'let' is followed by a bare infinitive (object + base verb, no 'to'): 'let me get', not 'let me to get'. This makes 'Penny did not let me get my book' the only grammatically correct sentence among the options, which otherwise misuse 'let'/'leave'/tense forms.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Let' + object + bare infinitive (no 'to') — 'let me GO', not 'let me TO go'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'let me TO get' incorrectly adds 'to' after the causative verb 'let'.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'was not leaving me to get' awkwardly and incorrectly uses 'leaving' instead of the intended causative structure.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'did not let me get my book' correctly uses the bare infinitive after 'let'.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'had not left me get' incorrectly mixes 'left' (past of leave) with a bare infinitive construction that doesn't fit.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is correct?
questions.option_a: We visited, Istanbul, Turkey, and Kowloon, Hong Kong last summer.
questions.option_b: We visited: Istanbul, Turkey, and Kowloon, Hong Kong last summer.
questions.option_c: We visited Istanbul, Turkey, Kowloon, Hong Kong last summer.
questions.option_d: We visited Istanbul, Turkey, and Kowloon, Hong Kong last summer.
questions.explanation_short: 'We visited Istanbul, Turkey, and Kowloon, Hong Kong last summer' correctly uses commas to separate city-country pairs without extra/incorrect punctuation.
questions.explanation_long: When listing city, country pairs (Istanbul, Turkey and Kowloon, Hong Kong), commas separate the city from its country and separate each pair from the next, with no comma needed right after the verb 'visited' or a colon inserted mid-sentence — matching option d's clean punctuation.
questions.explanation_trick: City-country pairs: 'City, Country, and City, Country' — commas group the pairs correctly without extra punctuation.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the comma right after 'visited' incorrectly separates the verb from its object.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — inserting a colon after 'visited' is grammatically unjustified here (no list introduction context requiring a colon).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — missing the comma before 'Kowloon' breaks the city-country pairing pattern (should be 'Turkey, and Kowloon').
explanation_options.d: Correct — commas properly separate the city-country pairs without extraneous punctuation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is correct?
questions.option_a: How could Sarah perswad her mum to stay out later?
questions.option_b: How could Sarah persuade her mum to stay out later?
questions.option_c: How could Sarah persuad her mum to stay out later?
questions.option_d: How could Sarah parsuade her mum to stay out later?
questions.explanation_short: 'How could Sarah persuade her mum to stay out later?' is correct — 'persuade' is the properly spelled word.
questions.explanation_long: The other options ('perswad', 'persuad', 'parsuade') are misspellings of 'persuade' (to convince someone to do something). Only option b spells the word correctly, making the sentence grammatically and orthographically correct.
questions.explanation_trick: Persuade = per-SUADE (correct spelling) — watch for common misspellings like perswad/persuad/parsuade.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'perswad' is a misspelling of 'persuade'.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'persuade' is spelled correctly here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'persuad' is missing the final 'e', a misspelling.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'parsuade' has an incorrect 'a' instead of 'e' in the first syllable, a misspelling.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence with the correct use of article.
questions.option_a: Natasha can play a piano and a violin.
questions.option_b: Natasha can play the piano and the violin.
questions.option_c: Natasha can play the piano and a violin.
questions.option_d: Natasha can play piano and violin.
questions.explanation_short: 'Natasha can play the piano and the violin' correctly uses 'the' before specific musical instruments, per standard English convention.
questions.explanation_long: English convention uses the definite article 'the' before names of musical instruments when speaking generally about someone's ability to play them (e.g., 'play the piano', 'play the guitar') — so 'the piano and the violin' is correct, unlike using 'a' (which implies one unspecified instance) or omitting the article entirely.
questions.explanation_trick: Playing musical instruments in English: always 'the' + instrument (e.g., 'play THE piano'), a fixed idiomatic rule.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'a piano and a violin' incorrectly uses indefinite articles instead of 'the' for musical instruments.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'the piano and the violin' correctly uses definite articles for musical instruments.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — mixing 'the piano' (correct) with 'a violin' (incorrect) is inconsistent article usage.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — omitting articles entirely ('piano and violin') doesn't follow the standard convention requiring 'the'.

questions.question_text: Distribute the handouts _________ the candidates. The correct preposition to be filled in is:
questions.explanation_short: 'Distribute the handouts among the candidates' — 'among' is the correct preposition for distribution across more than two people.
questions.explanation_long: 'Among' is used when referring to distribution or relationships involving three or more people/things, while 'between' is reserved for exactly two. Since 'the candidates' implies more than two people, 'among' is the grammatically correct preposition for distributing the handouts.
questions.explanation_trick: Between = 2 things/people; Among = 3 or more — 'candidates' (plural, likely more than 2) needs 'among'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'into' implies movement inside something, not distribution to people.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'among' is the correct preposition for distributing to multiple (3+) candidates.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'in' doesn't convey the distributive sense needed here.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'on' doesn't fit the meaning of distributing handouts to people.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence:
questions.explanation_short: 'These scissors are very sharp' is correct — 'scissors' is a plural-only noun (a 'pair of scissors') that always takes a plural verb.
questions.explanation_long: 'Scissors' belongs to a category of nouns (like 'trousers', 'glasses') that are grammatically always plural, even referring to a single item — so it must be paired with 'these/those' and a plural verb ('are'), never 'this/that' or singular 'is'.
questions.explanation_trick: Scissors, trousers, glasses = always plural nouns — 'these scissors ARE', never 'this scissor IS'.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'these scissors are very sharp' correctly treats scissors as plural.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'this scissors is' incorrectly mixes singular 'this/is' with the inherently plural noun 'scissors'.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'this scissor' incorrectly treats scissors as a singular countable noun ('scissor' isn't standard usage).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'these scissor' incorrectly drops the 's', misusing the noun's fixed plural form.

questions.question_text: Identify the sentence, out of the following, that is error free:
questions.option_a: I do not enjoy being laughed at by other people
questions.option_b: I did not enjoy laughing by other people
questions.option_c: I am not enjoying laughing by other people
questions.option_d: I do not enjoying being laughed at by other people
questions.explanation_short: 'I do not enjoy being laughed at by other people' is the only grammatically error-free sentence — correct gerund and passive-voice construction.
questions.explanation_long: This sentence correctly uses the gerund 'being laughed at' (passive gerund form) after 'enjoy', with correct tense and preposition ('at by other people'). The other options have tense mismatches, incorrect verb forms ('laughing by' instead of 'being laughed at'), or double gerund errors.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Enjoy' + gerund; passive gerund 'being laughed at' (not just 'laughing by') is the correct construction for being on the receiving end.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this sentence is grammatically error-free.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'laughing by other people' incorrectly uses active gerund instead of the needed passive form 'being laughed at'.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'enjoying laughing by' is also an incorrect active construction, not matching the passive sense intended.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'enjoying' + 'being laughed' creates a double gerund/tense error ('do not enjoying' is ungrammatical — should be 'do not enjoy').

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.
questions.option_a: We agreed that the play was rather boring so we felt bored
questions.option_b: We agreed that the play was rather bored so we felt boring
questions.option_c: We agreed that the play was rather boring so we felt bore
questions.option_d: We agreed that the play was rather bores so we felt bored
questions.explanation_short: 'We agreed that the play was rather boring so we felt bored' correctly uses 'boring' (describing the play) and 'bored' (describing how we felt).
questions.explanation_long: '-ing' adjectives (boring) describe the thing causing a feeling, while '-ed' adjectives (bored) describe the person experiencing that feeling. The play is boring (it causes boredom); we felt bored (we experienced it) — matching this pattern correctly, unlike the other options which swap or misuse these forms.
questions.explanation_trick: -ing = causes the feeling (the play is boring); -ed = experiences the feeling (we felt bored). Don't swap them.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'boring' (play) and 'bored' (us) are used in their proper causative/experiential roles.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this sentence swaps the forms: calls the play 'bored' and how we felt 'boring', which is backwards.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'felt bore' is not a correct adjective form (should be 'bored').
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'rather bores' misuses the verb form, and 'bores' isn't a correct adjective here.

questions.question_text: I decided to sell the piece of land when I was offered more _____ price. The most appropriate word to be filled in here is:
questions.explanation_short: 'Realistic' is the most appropriate word — offered a more realistic (achievable/sensible) price for the land.
questions.explanation_long: In context, the seller decided to sell when offered a better price — 'realistic' fits naturally, meaning a sensible, achievable market-value price, unlike 'true' (odd fit for 'price'), 'exact' (implies precision, not persuasiveness), or 'perfect' (too absolute/unlikely for a real negotiation context).
questions.explanation_trick: Land deals close on a 'realistic' (fair, sensible) price — the natural word for real-world negotiation context.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'true price' isn't idiomatic phrasing in this negotiation context.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'realistic price' naturally fits the context of a sensible offer that prompted the sale.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'exact price' emphasizes precision, not the persuasive/sensible quality implied by the context.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'perfect price' is an unnatural, overly absolute phrase for a real-world negotiation.

questions.question_text: 'To cut off the head'. Idiom means:
questions.explanation_short: 'To cut off the head' as an idiom means to 'decapitate' — literally removing the head.
questions.explanation_long: 'Decapitate' directly means to cut off someone's head — matching the idiom's literal definition precisely. 'Defrock' (strip clergy of office), 'impaled' (pierced through), and 'urbanite' (city dweller) are unrelated terms.
questions.explanation_trick: Decapitate = de- (remove) + capit- (head, Latin) — literally 'to cut off the head'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'defrock' means removing someone from a religious/clerical position, unrelated to beheading.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'decapitate' precisely means to cut off the head.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'impaled' means pierced through with a sharp object, not specifically beheading.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'urbanite' means a city dweller, completely unrelated to this idiom.

questions.question_text: Wasim was so good at Mathematics that people considered him to be a ______. Fill in the blank with the correct response.
questions.explanation_short: 'Prodigy' describes someone exceptionally talented at a young age — fitting Wasim's extraordinary math ability.
questions.explanation_long: A 'prodigy' is a person, especially a young one, with exceptional talent or ability in a particular field. Wasim being 'so good at Mathematics' that people considered him exceptional matches this word precisely, while 'prodigal' (wastefully extravagant), 'primeval' (ancient/primitive), and 'profligate' (recklessly extravagant) don't fit the context of skill/talent.
questions.explanation_trick: Prodigy = a gifted young talent (math prodigy, chess prodigy) — don't confuse with the similar-sounding 'prodigal' (wasteful).

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'prodigy' fits describing someone remarkably talented at math.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'prodigal' means wastefully extravagant, unrelated to mathematical talent.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'primeval' means ancient or primitive, unrelated to talent.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'profligate' means recklessly wasteful, unrelated to skill or talent.

questions.question_text: The newly elected president and CEO for the newly established branch of our company _____ arrived recently. Fill in the blank with appropriate choice.
questions.explanation_short: 'Has' correctly agrees with the singular compound subject ('the newly elected president and CEO', referring to one person holding both titles).
questions.explanation_long: Although 'president and CEO' looks like two things joined by 'and', it refers to a single person holding both titles (a common construction in business contexts), so it takes a singular verb: 'has arrived', not the plural 'have arrived'.
questions.explanation_trick: 'President and CEO' (one person, two titles) = singular subject → singular verb 'has', not 'have'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'have' would be correct only if the subject were plural (multiple people), not one person with two titles.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 'having' is a gerund/participle form, not a finite verb that completes the sentence correctly here.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 'have been' (plural present perfect continuous) doesn't match the singular subject.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 'has' correctly agrees with the singular 'president and CEO' subject.

questions.question_text:
Read the passage and the following statements below. Then choose the correct option, basing your answer only on the information provided.

Queen Elizabeth II's Platinum Jubilee, celebrating her 70 years on the British throne, was above all a tribute to one of history's great acts of constancy. Her reign spanned virtually the entire post-World War II era, making her witness to cultural upheavals from the Beatles to Brexit.

STATEMENTS:
I. There has been another queen of the British throne named Elizabeth before her.
II. Brexit is a normal occurrence.
III. Elizabeth was Queen of the British during World War II.
questions.option_a: I, II and III all are correct
questions.option_d: Only I and III are correct
questions.explanation_short: Only statement I is directly supported: the passage calls her 'Elizabeth II', which by itself implies an earlier 'Elizabeth I' held the British throne before her.
questions.explanation_long: This is a careful-reading exercise — you must judge each statement using ONLY what the passage states, not outside knowledge. The passage names her 'Elizabeth II', and numbering a monarch 'II' inherently implies a prior monarch of the same name ('Elizabeth I') existed — so statement I is directly supported by the text itself. Statement II ('Brexit is a normal occurrence') is never claimed by the passage — it only says her reign witnessed Brexit as an upheaval, not that Brexit is normal. Statement III ('she was Queen during WWII') isn't supported either — the passage says her reign spanned the era AFTER WWII ('post-World War II era'), not that she reigned during the war itself.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Elizabeth II' is the giveaway — a 'II' in a name always implies a first ('Elizabeth I') came before, straight from the text.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — statement II is never asserted by the passage, and statement III is contradicted (her reign is described as post-WWII, not during it).
explanation_options.b: Wrong — statement III isn't supported; the passage places her reign after WWII, not during it.
explanation_options.c: Correct — only statement I is directly supported, via the implication of 'Elizabeth II'.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — statement III isn't supported by the passage's wording about the post-WWII era.

questions.question_text: Observe the pattern and select the next term in the sequence: CAB, FAE, IAH, ____
questions.explanation_short: Pattern CAB, FAE, IAH: each term's first letter jumps 3 ahead (C→F→I), so the next jumps to L, giving LAK.
questions.explanation_long: Looking at first letters: C(3), F(6), I(9) — each jumps forward by 3 letters. Following this pattern, the next first letter is L(12). Applying the same internal pattern seen in the terms (middle letter stays 'A', last letter jumps similarly: B→E→H, each +3, so next is K), the next term is LAK.
questions.explanation_trick: Track each letter position separately: 1st letters jump +3 (C,F,I,L); last letters also jump +3 (B,E,H,K); middle stays 'A'.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — JHK doesn't follow the consistent +3 pattern seen in first and last letters.
explanation_options.b: Correct — LAK follows the pattern: L (first letter +3), A (unchanged middle), K (last letter +3).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — JGK breaks the established +3 letter-jump pattern.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — IGJ repeats letters already used and doesn't continue the forward-jumping pattern.

questions.question_text:
Read the following and choose the correct answer.

Drake was wearing a blue shirt with black jean and brown shoes. John was wearing a red shirt with black jeans and black shoes. Ahmed was wearing blue shirt with blue jeans and brown shoes. Nahaz claims he saw someone wearing black jeans, a blue or red shirt, and shoes that were not black. Whom did he see?
questions.explanation_short: Matching all three clues (black jeans + blue-or-red shirt + non-black shoes) uniquely identifies Drake, who wore a blue shirt, and (per the puzzle's intended data) black jeans with brown (non-black) shoes.
questions.explanation_long: Checking each person against Nahaz's three criteria — black jeans, a blue or red shirt, and non-black shoes: Drake wore a blue shirt with (per the question's stated clue) black jeans and brown shoes, satisfying all three conditions (blue shirt ✓, non-black brown shoes ✓, black jeans ✓) uniquely among the three named people.
questions.explanation_trick: Check each of the 3 clues against each person one by one — Drake is the only one matching all three simultaneously.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — Ahmed wore blue jeans (not black) and brown shoes, failing the 'black jeans' criterion.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — John wore black shoes, failing the 'shoes that were not black' criterion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Drake matches all three criteria: black jeans, blue shirt, and non-black (brown) shoes.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — since Drake uniquely satisfies all clues, the answer can be determined; 'cannot elicit' is incorrect.

questions.question_text:
Some bags are pouches. All pouches are cases. No cases are purses. Which of the following conclusions are NECESSARILY TRUE?

CONCLUSIONS:
I. Some pouches are purses
II. Some bags are cases
